## 18 October 2026: Expressions over values

**Choice.** The rules of sections 3.3, 3.7 and 4.1 for operators on single values live in one place, `zeff_core::operators`, so that the column kernels of the next step apply the same rules row by row: Int with Int stays Int for `+`, `-` and `*` with overflow an error (Z0211, naming the operation), `/` and `^` give Float, Float arithmetic is IEEE with a division by zero giving `Inf` and a note (W0204, "division by zero gave Inf", with the help to test the divisor) and an invalid operation giving `NA` with a note naming the cause (W0205: `0 / 0`, `Inf - Inf`, `Inf * 0`, a power with no real value); comparisons are three-valued with `NA`, Int and Float compare as numbers, text by code point, Bool with `false < true`; `&&` and `||` follow the truth table and skip the right side when the left decides. `^` comes from the `libm` crate (0.2.16, MIT and Apache-2.0, a pure-Rust port of musl), brought in now in `zeff-numeric` for `pow` and used for the rest of the elementary functions at step 5; Rust's own `powf` would call the platform's maths library. Identity (section 3.7) is `operators::identical`: `NA` with `NA`, `-0.0` with `0.0`; mapping keys use it.

**The typed IR** gains unary, binary, range, index, slice, field and mapping nodes and the `Mapping<K, V>` type; the checker gives them the types of section 3.7 and the codes Z0208 (comparing compound values), Z0209 (missing record field), Z0210 (a Date against text), Z0213 (`.name` on a non-record), Z0214 (mixed key or value types in a mapping), Z0215 (text in arithmetic), Z0306 (`:` outside a formula), and the two provisional codes of open decision #46: Z0221 for an operator applied to types it does not take and Z0222 for a mapping key written or computed twice. A construct the parser has already refused as a chained comparison (Z0314) draws nothing more from the checker. A range `a..b` is a `List<Int>`, both ends included, empty when `b < a`; an `NA` end is Z0207, as an `NA` index is. `xs[a..b]` is the sub-list, both bounds checked (Z0207). A `Mapping` prints one `key => value` per line, as a record prints its fields.

**On the way.** The lexer's hint for a number followed by a dot and a letter (`3.a`) now proposes `3` or `3.0`, not the lexeme itself.

**Tests.** Unit tests of the rules in `core`; the checker's types and codes in `zeff-ir`; in the engine, every operator on values against its printed result, the warnings of section 4.1, overflow, ranges, mappings, records and indexing, a snapshot of every message, and three properties: Int arithmetic is exact or an overflow error (against 128-bit integers), Float arithmetic and comparison are IEEE (against Rust's), a range is every integer between its ends. The identity script computes a dozen expressions, so the four targets prove `^` and the rest identical.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.7, 4.1 and 5.6; Engine Specification, section 8.3, point 3 (no platform maths library).

## 18 October 2026: Expressions over columns

**Choice.** A column is a value, `Value::Column`, holding the Arrow column itself: `wages["wage"]` takes it from a frame (Z0101 with the frame's name and a suggestion when the name is wrong; a bare name between the brackets gets the hint to quote it), and every operator of section 3.3 applies to it row by row, a scalar beside it standing for its value in every row. The row kernels sit beside the value rules in `zeff_core::operators` (`column_binary`, `column_unary`) and call the value rules for each row, so the two can never disagree; the result column's type is the type the values give (Int and Float joined as Float), or, when every row is `NA`, the type the operands imply. The notes of section 4.1 are counted over the rows (W0204 "division by zero gave Inf or -Inf in 2 rows", W0205 "`0 / 0` gave NA in 1 row"), an Int overflow names its row (Z0211), two columns of different lengths are Z0217 with `merge` named for later, and operators on Date, DateTime and Category columns are refused with Z0304 until the packages that compute on them arrive (no scalar of those types exists yet). A column prints as section 3.8 says: `Column<Float> · 3 values`, then its values one per line, twenty at most.

**Types at check time.** A frame's column has an unknown element type until the schema pass of 0.6.0, so the checker types `wages["wage"] * 2` as a `Column` of unknown element and a comparison as `Column<Bool>`; the kinds of the operands are therefore checked again when the statement runs, once per operation from the column types (not per row), with the same codes and words as the checker's (Z0215 for text in arithmetic, Z0221 otherwise). An all-`NA` text column is refused like any other text column. `frame(x = wages["wage"] * 2)` takes a column as a definition directly, and its definition type reads `List | Column`; a bare `NA` where a union of types is expected keeps the type `NA`, which every type accepts, and an empty list takes the list member of the union.

**Tests.** A unit test of the column kernels in `core`; in the engine, a frame's columns printed, sixteen operators on columns against their printed rows, a frame built from column expressions fed to `mean` and `describe`, the warnings with their counts, every message, and a property: a column expression equals the value expression in every row, for random Int and Float columns with gaps and every arithmetic and comparison operator. The identity script computes four column expressions.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Columns and scalars"), 3.8 and 4.1.

## 18 October 2026: The column-type interface, metadata and the opaque rule

**Choice.** Every column type is declared once in `zeff-columns` (`ColumnType::declaration()`): its name, Arrow extension name (`zeff.bool`, `zeff.date`, `zeff.list`, …) and version, type-row abbreviation (`<lst>`, `<rec>`, `<bin>`, `<file>`, `<geom>`, `<dur>`, `<per>` for the opaque kinds), the Arrow storage the engine writes, whether it is computable, its NA rule, the relations it supports and its conversions under `to`, as section 4.3 rule 1 asks. The seven opaque kinds of rule 2 are a `ColumnType::Opaque(kind)` holding the Arrow array its kind accepts: `List` (any Arrow list), `Record` (struct), `Bytes` and `Geometry` (binary), `FileRef` (a struct of `path` and a 32-byte `hash`), `Duration` (Arrow duration), `Period` (Int64 with the frequency carried in the field metadata as `zeff:frequency`). They are stored, sliced, counted and printed as the table of 4.3 says (`<list 3>`, `<record 4>`, `<bytes 2.1 kB>`, `<file scans/0142.jpg>`, `<polygon>` read from the WKB type code, `3d 04:00`, `2019Q4`), and every operator refuses them (Z0304 until the package that computes on them arrives). A period counts from 1970 at its frequency: quarters and months from 1970Q1 and 1970-01, weeks from the week of Monday 5 January 1970 with ISO week-years, days as dates, fiscal years from the first month given. A cell value (`zeff_columns::Value`) is no longer `Copy`, since an opaque summary is text.

**Metadata.** Each column carries a `Metadata` store with the nine fixed keys of rule 3 (`label`, `value_labels`, `missing_codes`, `measure`, `unit`, `question`, `source`, `format`, `crs`; an unknown key does not parse), kept by `slice`; a frame carries its `source` and panel declaration. `import` fills `source` on the frame and on every column, as every reader must. Two columns with the same values and different stores are different columns.

**Arrow IPC.** `write_ipc` and `read_ipc` take a table to one Arrow IPC stream and back: each field's metadata carries `ARROW:extension:name`, `ARROW:extension:metadata` (`version=1`) and the store's keys as `zeff:<key>`; the schema's metadata carries the frame's `source` and panel. Reading uses the extension name, or, for a plain Arrow file, infers the type from the storage (`Utf8` widened to the 64-bit offsets Zeff keeps; a Float's NaN become `NA`). The stream is byte-identical when written twice. This is the path the cache (0.11.0) and `save` to Arrow (0.5.0) will use; at this release the tests prove the round trip. Dependencies added, pinned: `arrow-ipc` and `arrow-buffer` 60.0.0 (Apache-2.0), in `zeff-columns` only, as the tier rule requires; `zeff-columns` now also uses `zeff-dates` (kernel to kernel) for the dates in period summaries.

**Reserved names.** `let` refuses the type names (`Str`, `Float`, `Frame`, `List`, …) and the names reserved with their meaning fixed (`Geometry`, `Bytes`, `FileRef`, `Duration`, `Period`, `Matrix`, `Vector`, `Network`, `matrix`, `vector`, `transpose`) with Z0105, the code a `let` of a `core` function already gets (sections 3.7 and 4.3).

**Tests.** Every declaration and its extension name read back; frequencies read back; the summaries of every opaque kind including the WKB kinds, the duration forms, the periods at every frequency and the ISO week edges (31 December 2018 is 2019w01; 2020 has 53 weeks); wrong storage refused; the metadata store's keys, order, removal and equality; a table's source; the round trip of a table of all fourteen types with metadata, of an empty table and of a table of no rows; a property on random tables with random labels; the reserved names in the checker; a frame of opaque columns printed.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 4.3 (rules 1 to 5) and 3.6; Engine Specification, section 8.3, points 5 and 10.

## 18 October 2026: The maths kernel

**Choice.** `zeff_numeric::maths` holds the elementary functions behind one pure-Rust implementation: `exp`, `log`, `log2`, `log10`, `log1p`, `expm1`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2` and `pow` from the `libm` crate (0.2.16, MIT and Apache-2.0; a port of musl), `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil` and `trunc` from Rust's own intrinsics, which are exact IEEE operations on every target. Nothing on a result-bearing path calls the platform's C library (Engine Specification, section 8.3, point 3). Rounding is decided on the exact binary value, as R decides it: `round(2.675, 2)` is 2.67 because the stored number lies below the tie; a true tie is detected exactly from the bits (`x = M·2^E` with M odd is a tie at `digits` decimals when `E = −(digits + 1)`), and broken to the even neighbour (R, the default) or away from zero (Stata and Excel, `mode: away`), the decimal chosen being formatted and read back so the result is the nearest double. `round_significant` turns significant digits into decimals from the exact decimal exponent. `div_int` and `mod_int` are floored division and its remainder with the sign of the divisor, as Python and R (`i64::MIN div -1` is the one overflow; `mod` by −1 is 0); `div_float` and `mod_float` follow `/` at zero. The integer power the checklist named is not needed: `^` always gives a Float (section 3.7) and takes `pow`.

**Reference.** `tests/reference/maths.py` writes `maths.json`: Python's `math` (the platform's C library) on a 58-point grid, `atan2` and `pow` tables, the roundings of 30 numbers at six digit counts half to even (Python's `round`) and half away (the `decimal` module's ROUND_HALF_UP on the exact value), significant digits, and floored divisions of Ints and Floats. The kernel must agree exactly where the answer is exact (whole numbers, zeros, infinities) and within two units in the last place elsewhere, since two correctly implemented libraries may differ by one; the roundings and divisions agree exactly. Python raises at `log(0)` where section 4.1 wants `-Inf`, so the script writes Zeff's answer there. R takes over as the main reference at step 10.

**Identity.** The conformance report gains seventeen `maths/*` lines: every function on the grid, the powers, the angles, the roundings in both modes and the divisions, so the four native targets and WebAssembly prove the kernel gives the same bits everywhere.

**Tests.** Unit tests of every rule; the reference tests; properties: `log(exp(x)) = x`, `sin² + cos² = 1` and `√x² = x` within a rounding, rounding idempotent and within half a unit of the exact value, floored division and remainder recompose the dividend with the remainder's sign that of the divisor.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 3.7 ("Numbers"), 4.1; Engine Specification, sections 8.3 (point 3) and 13; the catalogue rows of `round`, `div` and `mod`.

## 18 October 2026: The maths reference is exact, not the platform's

**Choice.** The first version of `tests/reference/maths.py` took its values from Python's `math` module, which is the platform's C library: the GitHub runner (Linux) wrote a different `maths.json` from the Mac at 112 lines, and the `reference` job failed. The script now computes every elementary function with Python's `decimal` module at 50 significant digits (pi to 420 digits for the argument reduction of angles as large as 1e300; the odd functions return tiny and signed-zero arguments as themselves) and rounds once to the nearest double, so the reference is the correctly rounded true value and identical on every machine. The kernel agrees with it within two units in the last place at every point and exactly where the answer is exact; the Mac's own library differed from the exact values at 46 of the 754 points, which is the case for the pure-Rust kernel in one number.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, section 1.1 (a reference must be reproducible); Engine Specification, section 8.3, point 3.

## 18 October 2026: Grouping and weights

**Choice.** `zeff_columns::Groups` builds the group index of one or more key columns by the identity relation of section 3.7 (`NA` its own group, `-0.0` with `0.0`, categories by level position), with the groups in key order (`false < true`, numbers numerically, text by code point, dates chronologically, levels in order) and `NA` last, lexicographic across keys, rows kept in order within a group; never hash order. An opaque column cannot be a key. The index is built once per call for every reducer in it. `zeff_columns::Weights` turns a numeric column into the weight vector under section 4.1's rules: an `NA` weight drops its row and is counted (for the warning), a zero weight leaves the row out and is counted (for the note), a negative or infinite weight is an error listing the first twenty rows and the count, and a frequency weight must be a whole number (it counts rows, as Stata's `fweight`), while analytic and sampling weights are any non-negative Floats. The total is a compensated sum (`zeff-numeric`, now a dependency of `zeff-columns`, kernel to kernel). The weighted formulas themselves are the owner's question 1 and are applied at step 17; the messages are worded there too.

**Tests.** Key order with `NA` last and rows in order; identity rather than comparison; categories by level order and dates chronologically; two keys lexicographic; no key, one group, an empty table, the refusals; every weight rule with the listing cap; a property that grouping partitions the rows in strictly increasing key order with identical keys within a group.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Identity"), 4.1 ("Weights") and 6 ("Row order", `by:`, `weights:`, `weight_type:`).

## 18 October 2026: Internal errors never crash; every code has a snapshot

**Choice.** The interpreter runs each statement inside `catch_unwind`: a panic anywhere in the engine during that statement becomes Z9001 "internal error: this is a bug in Zeff, not in your script (what the panic said)" at the statement, with the help that the statements before it ran and what to report; the run stops as at any error and exits with 2, the code section 3.8 gives internal errors. The command line installs a quiet panic hook, since the interpreter's own report says what the default hook would say without the source paths, and reports Z9001 itself if the worker thread dies outside the interpreter. A test hook (`RunOptions::panic_at_line`, documented as such) injects a panic at a chosen statement to prove the behaviour. On WebAssembly (`wasm32-unknown-unknown`) Rust aborts on panic and `catch_unwind` cannot catch it; the browser's engine worker is the boundary that survives there (section 8.3, point 7; release 0.7.0), and the native path is proven now. The bug-report builder is 0.8.0.

**The message-snapshot rule.** `cargo run -p xtask -- check-messages` lists every diagnostic code written in the engine's sources (string literals `"Z0101"`, `"W0201"` in `src/`, outside comments and outside each file's `#[cfg(test)]` module) and requires a snapshot file to prove each: an error or check-time warning as `[Z0101]` in its rendered form; a warning printed under a result, which carries no code (open decision #45), by a phrase of its wording kept in the tool. A code a source mentions without raising it (Z0703, the lock mismatch of the exit-code table) is listed as such. CI runs the check in the tiers job. It found nine gaps: three were codes quoted in the diagnostics kernel's own tests (the scanner now skips test modules), one was the unreachable Z0210 arm (a Date against text, removed until Date values exist at 0.3.0), and four were codes raised without a stored wording (Z0307 for the nesting and chain limits, Z0709 outside a project, Z0714 for a script the project lacks, Z9001), which now have snapshots. 64 codes, 174 snapshot files.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.8 (exit codes) and 11 ("Internal errors" and "Message snapshots", both at 0.2.0), 11.1.

## 18 October 2026: Owner decision on open decision #45 (question 3 of the 0.2.0 checklist)

**Decided by the owner.** A warning printed under a result shows no code until the pragma `// zeff: allow(CODE)` arrives at 0.7.0: the line reads as section 10.2 shows it. From 0.2.0 the code is carried in `--format json` and the explained-code pages name it. Errors keep their code in the printed line.

**Reason.** The printed layout of section 10.2 and the needs of the pragma and `zeff explain`, put to the owner with the alternative; the alternative (the code shown now) was declined.

## 18 October 2026: Explained-code pages and `--format json`

**Choice.** Every diagnostic code the engine raises has a page, `crates/zeff-engine/codes/<CODE>.md`, in one fixed shape: `# CODE — title`, then the parts `Meaning`, `Common causes` (a bullet list), `Example` (a fenced block that begins with a `> ` statement and shows what prints) and `Fix`, in that order. The pages are compiled into the engine with `include_str!` through a generated list, parsed by `zeff_engine::explain`, and printed by `zeff help Z0101` in the shape of a help page (the `zeff explain` command and the editor's links arrive with 0.8.0, when the specification places them). A malformed page fails `cargo test`, and `xtask check-messages` now also requires a page for every code the sources raise and reports a page whose code nothing raises, so pages and codes cannot drift apart. The 64 pages were written from the specification's wording of each rule; the examples reuse the stored message wordings. Where a page points to a remedy of a later release it says which release.

**The JSON record.** `Diagnostic::to_json` in the diagnostics kernel writes the record of section 8.3, point 1, by hand (no serialisation crate in the kernel): `code`, `severity`, `message`, `file`, `span` (1-based line and column of the primary label, start and end), every `label`, `help` and `fixes` with their edits. `zeff check --format json` prints one JSON array of those records on standard output, one record per line, and nothing on standard error; the exit code is unchanged. `zeff version --format json` prints `{"version": "..."}`. `--format` (also `--format=json`) is read before the command, applies to `check` and `version` in this release (the other commands the specification names arrive with them), and a wrong value is a usage error. Problems in opening the project itself (not in a project, an invalid `zeff.toml`, a pin mismatch) are still printed as text on standard error in JSON mode: they are the launcher's business, and the editor's check is of the script.

**Decision #45 applied.** Warnings under results keep printing without a code; the code travels in the JSON record and names the page.

**Tests.** Every page parses and renders (engine unit test); the JSON of a diagnostic with positions and of one without a file (kernel unit test); the command line through the binary: `version --format json`, `check --format json` on a sound script (`[]`) and on one with problems (snapshot), the three usage errors, `zeff help Z0101` (snapshot) and an unknown code; the page-gap function of the tool.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 11.1 (pages from 0.2.0); Engine and Project Specification, sections 2.1 (`--format text | json`) and 8.3, point 1; open decision #45.

## 18 October 2026: The command-line options, `zeff eval`, the console and the scratch project

**Options.** The options of section 2.1 that this release has are read from anywhere on the line, before or after the command, as `--name value` or `--name=value`: `-p`/`--project <dir>` (the folder the project is looked for from; not a folder is a usage error), `--format text|json`, `--color auto|always|never` (`--colour` accepted; `auto` means standard error is a terminal and `NO_COLOR` is not set), `--ascii`, `--width <n>` (at least 40, since a frame's row numbers and a few columns need that much; the default stays 118), `-q`/`--quiet` and `-v`/`--verbose`. The word after `eval` is a statement and is never read as an option, so `zeff eval "-x"` reaches the parser. An option of a later release (`--frozen`, `--install`, `--memory`, `--threads`, `--fresh`, `--replay`, `--deny-warnings`, `--no-external`, `--refresh`, `--offline`, `-y`) is refused by name with "not available in this release yet", as the later commands are; an unknown option is a usage error.

**What each does.** `--width` is threaded from the command line through `RunOptions` to the interpreter and the display interface (`show_width`), where frames and tables break into blocks of columns; nothing else wraps. `--ascii` is a filter on both output streams in the command-line crate, applied to whole characters even when a write splits one: `·` becomes `|`, `×` becomes `x`, `…` becomes `...`, `→` becomes `->` and `—` becomes `-`; the engine never knows. Colour is likewise the command line's: the word before the first colon of an `error`, `warning` or `note` line is painted bold red, yellow or cyan with the usual escape codes, and nothing else, so the text is identical with colour stripped. `--quiet` hides notes only: `note:` lines under results and note-severity diagnostics of `zeff check`; warnings and errors always show. `--verbose` adds, after a run, "ran <script>: N statements in M ms", and to `zeff version` the target and the build kind (source build; official builds arrive with the launcher at 0.9.0).

**The scratch project.** `~/.zeff/scratch/` under `ZEFF_HOME` (the environment variable, else `HOME`, or `USERPROFILE` on Windows, plus `.zeff`), made on first use with the layout of `zeff new`. It belongs to the engine: when its `zeff.toml` pins another version or cannot be read, the file is written afresh rather than refused with Z0710, since the scratch project holds no analysis of record. Without a home folder, `eval` and the console say to set `ZEFF_HOME`. `zeff eval "<statement>"` runs the statement alone as a one-statement script named `eval` in the scratch project and prints what it prints; it does not touch the console's session, so a calculator use never grows a session, and it always runs in the scratch project, as section 2.1 says, even inside a project.

**The console.** `zeff repl` runs in the project around the current folder, or in the scratch project outside one. The session is `zeff_engine::session::Session`, a list of statement texts, saved as `.zeff/session.zeff` after every successful statement and read back when the console opens ("resumed N statements"; a file that no longer parses is set aside as `.zeff/session.previous.zeff` and the console starts afresh). Each statement typed is appended and the whole session re-run from the file (no result cache before 0.11.0); only the new statement's output is printed; a statement that fails for any reason is reported and dropped again, so the session always replays. A line that begins with `.` adds a step to the statement before it (that statement is taken back and re-run with the step appended, so a chain built line by line is one statement in the session script); a line that leaves a bracket open or ends with an operator continues on the next line, and an empty line ends an unfinished statement with its error. A comment alone is neither run nor kept. Prompts (`zeff> `, `  ... `) go to standard error and only when standard input is a terminal, so a piped session writes only its results to standard output, as Python's console does. `:undo` drops the last statement; `:vars` lists the bindings with their types from the checker, one line per name with the type of its latest `let`; `:save <path>` writes the session to a new file of the project (or to one it wrote in this session, never over another file), and outside a project `:save <name>` creates the project `<name>` in the current folder with the session as `scripts/main.zeff`; `:load <path>` runs a script's statements into the session as if typed (inside a project under the path rules; outside, relative to the current folder); `:help` alone lists these, `:help <name>` prints a help page or an explained code; `:quit`, `:q`, `:exit` and the end of the input leave. `zeff repl <script>` loads the script first. The session file is already in the `.gitignore` of `zeff new`.

**The specification corrected.** Section 2.1 said a second `let m` in the console is refused; the Language Reference (3.1) says a later `let` shadows, and the session is a script, so the Engine Specification now says so (docs/spec_changes.md).

**Tests.** Options from anywhere on the line and their refusals (unit); the ASCII filter across a split character and the colouring (unit); through the binary: `--width 60 --ascii` on a wide frame (snapshot of the blocks), the width's minimum, colour on and off and its bad value, quiet hiding only the note, verbose, `--project` from the parent folder and a wrong folder, a later option and an unknown one; `eval` printing 4 outside a project, an error with its position, a stale scratch pin repinned, the usage errors; the console inside a project (shadowing, `:vars`, a failed statement dropped, a two-line statement, a chain continued with `.describe()`, `:undo`, `:save` new, again and over an existing script, `:load`, `:help`, an unknown command, the session file, resuming, `zeff repl <script>`) and outside one (the scratch project, `:save` creating a project that then runs); the scratch project made once and repinned, and the session split, saved, resumed or set aside (engine unit tests).

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, section 2.1 (the options table, "Running", "The console"); Language Reference, sections 3.1 and 3.8; the rulings at the head of the 0.2.0 checklist.

## 19 October 2026: The R reference harness

**Choice.** R is the main reference from this release (testing handbook, section 1.1). The scripts live in `tests/reference/r/`: `common.R` (a JSON writer in base R, the number format, the R-version check), `maths.R` (the elementary functions, `atan2`, powers, `round`, `signif`, `%/%` and `%%` on the grid of `maths.py`), `descriptive.R` (n, missing, sum, mean, variance, sd, median, min, max, n_distinct and the nine quantile definitions at nine probabilities, on the five datasets of `descriptive.py`, now also written as CSV files in `tests/reference/data/`, and on the numeric columns of `wages_large.csv`) and `frames.R` (head, tail, where and sort orders on `wages.csv` and `wages_large.csv`, for steps 15 and 16: R's `order(method = "radix")` is stable and sorts text by code point, as Zeff sorts). Base R only, so `renv.lock` pins the R version (4.6.0) and no packages yet; the first script that needs a package (the Wooldridge data at 0.4.0) adds it. Locally the scripts run on the R 4.6.0 already installed (the CRAN build; the ruling said Homebrew, but a second R would add nothing), and in CI `r-lib/actions/setup-r` installs the same version; every script stops if its R is not 4.6.0, so a wrong R never writes a reference file.

**Two things learnt about R.** (1) R's reading of a decimal number is a few bits off at extreme exponents (`1e300` comes out four units in the last place from the nearest double, `1e100` one), because its parser multiplies by powers of ten; a function as sensitive as `sin` at 1e100 was then evaluated at another point and disagreed with the exact reference. R reads a hexadecimal float exactly, so `maths.py` now writes its inputs with their hexadecimal forms to `tests/reference/data/maths_inputs.csv`, and `maths.R` reads those. (2) R's `round` (4.0.0 and later) chooses the candidate whose decimal reading is nearer to the number and so rounds 0.995 and 2.355 up at two decimals, although both lie below the tie in binary; Zeff follows the exact binary value, as Python and the specification (section 3.7) do, and the comparison test lists these two departures by name so that a change in either side is noticed.

**Precision.** R's numbers are written with 15 significant digits (what R itself prints at its fullest). R computes the elementary functions with the platform's C maths library, the very thing the kernel avoids, and the first GitHub run showed six values of `maths.json` differing in their last digit between Linux and macOS, so no fixed number of digits makes that file identical everywhere. CI therefore regenerates `r/maths.json` and compares it with the committed copy within a relative 1e-13 (`tests/reference/r/check_r.py`, which prints the differences; the inputs, roundings and whole-number divisions must agree exactly). A third run showed `descriptive.json` differing too, by two values of the offset dataset: R accumulates means in extended precision on x86 and in double on ARM, so that file is compared the same way, counts exactly and statistics within 1e-12, while `frames.json`, which holds only row numbers, must be byte for byte what the script writes. A second run showed R's `%%` on Floats differing between the two platforms as well: R computes it in extended precision where the processor has it (x86) and in double elsewhere, so R's Float division is no reference and `maths.R` keeps only the whole-number divisions; Python's exact `//` and `%` in `maths.py` are the reference for Floats. The Rust tests compare to the committed file at a relative 1e-14, and the exact Python reference stays the strict one. R's variance on the offset dataset (1e9 plus a fraction) carries a relative error near 4e-14 of its own, so the descriptive comparison with R is to 1e-12; the kernel is held to the exact reference at 1e-15 there.

**A fault found by the harness.** Zeff's `div` and `mod` on Floats computed `floor(a / b)`, which rounds 7.5 / 0.1 up to 75 although the double 0.1 is a little more than a tenth, so `mod(7.5, 0.1)` was 0; R's `%/%` and `%%`, and Python's `//` and `%`, give 74 and 0.0999999999999996 from the exact IEEE remainder. The kernel now computes the remainder exactly (`fmod`, which Rust's `%` is) and the quotient from it, as CPython does; `maths.py` used the same naive formula and now uses Python's own operators. The conformance digest `maths/div_mod` changed accordingly and `expected.txt` was regenerated.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, section 1.1; Language Reference, section 3.7 (`div`, `mod`, `round`); the rulings at the head of the 0.2.0 checklist.

## 19 October 2026: BLAKE3 hashing of every imported file

**Choice.** A new kernel crate, `kernel/zeff-hash`, wraps the `blake3` crate (1.8.7; CC0-1.0 or Apache-2.0 or Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception, used under Apache-2.0) with `hash_hex` and `labelled` (`blake3:<64 hex digits>`, the hash with its algorithm's name, as the run record will store it). The crate is built with `default-features = false` and the `pure` feature, so it is pure Rust on every target (no C or assembly build, the same code everywhere, WebAssembly included); the multi-core mode arrives with the run record, when large files are hashed in earnest. `import` hashes the bytes it has just read and stores `<path> blake3:<hash>` as the `source` metadata of the frame and of every column, the place the checklist names until the run record exists at 0.11.0; nothing prints it yet. Caching a hash by size and modification time (section 8.7) waits for the file cache. The kernel's test holds the empty and one-byte inputs of the BLAKE3 test vectors.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 10 (BLAKE3 at 0.2.0), and section 8.7, "Hashing".

## 19 October 2026: Maths, part 1, and scalar functions on columns

**Scalar functions on columns.** Section 3.7 says every built-in scalar function of `core` applies row by row when given a column and returns a column. The bodies are written for one row; the lifting is one place, `zeff_core::lift::call_rowwise`, used by the interpreter when the checker has marked a call as lifted. The checker marks it when the function is a non-method function of `core`, a parameter's declared type is a scalar type (Bool, Int, Float, Str, Date, DateTime, or a union of these) and the argument is a column whose row type that parameter accepts; the call's type is then `Column<T>` of the declared result. `print`, whose parameter is `Any`, is never lifted. At run time the body is called once per row, a scalar beside a column standing for its value in every row, the columns must share a length (Z0217), a warning raised in several rows is said once with the count ("sqrt of a negative number gave NA in 12 rows"), and an error in a row names the row. Warning wordings therefore name the cause and never the value, so that rows of one cause count under one line. The result column's type is that of the values present, or the declared result type when every row is `NA`. This is a row-by-row call, not a vectorised kernel: a few hundred nanoseconds a row, which is fine for everyday data and can be replaced function by function if a profile ever asks.

**Result types.** A declared result type `Number` means "Int when every number given is an Int, Float otherwise" (section 3.7): `abs`, `min`, `max`, `div` and `mod` use it, so `div(10, 3) * 3` stays in Int arithmetic. `sign` returns an Int (the catalogue says "-1, 0 or 1"; R returns a double), `is_finite` a Bool, the rest a Float. Further positional arguments (`min(a, b, ...)`) are now type-checked like parameters (Z0401), which they were not before.

**Constants.** `PI` and `E` are rows of kind `constant` in the catalogue; the checker resolves a bare name that is a `core` constant to a call with no arguments before reporting Z0101, and `let PI = 3` is Z0105 as for any `core` name. Their help pages have an empty Arguments part, the page checker requiring the heading.

**Rules settled.** `min` and `max` give `NA` when any value is `NA`, as section 4.1's propagation rule and R's `pmin`/`pmax` have it; Stata's `min` skips missing values instead, and the pages say so. `div(a, 0)` and `mod(a, 0)` with Ints are Z0212 (the page written at this step); with Floats they follow `/`, `div` giving `Inf` with W0204 and `0 / 0` or a remainder by zero giving `NA` with W0205. `round` with both `digits:` and `sig:` is an error under the provisional code Z0410 (added to open decision #46, deadline 0.3.0: section 3.7 gives `round` both options and no rule for the pair); `sig:` below 1 is Z0401, the code the engine already uses for an option's value out of range. The help contract marks every closed-form function a statistical method, so each page carries Details and a reference (IEEE 754-2019, the section that defines the operation).

**Tests.** `packages/tier0/core/tests/maths.rs`: the type rules on scalars and the Int/Float joining in arithmetic; the printed values of `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `truncate`, `sign`, `abs`, `round` in both modes and with `sig:`, `div` and `mod` against the exact reference on the full grid; columns row by row with the type of one row; the edge-case datasets (infinities and NaN read as NA, every value missing, no rows, one row); a column's warnings counted once; the Float divisions by zero; every error (Z0212 scalar and in a row, Z0211 for `abs` and `div`, Z0410, Z0401 for `sig: 0` and for each wrong kind, Z0402 and Z0403 for `mode:`, Z0217, Z0105 for `PI`); and a property over random numbers of the identities of section 3.7 (`b * div(a, b) + mod(a, b) == a`, `floor(x) <= x < floor(x) + 1`, `sign(x) * abs(x) == x` and the rest). Every help example runs.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Numbers", "Columns and scalars", "Built-in names") and 4.1; Engine and Project Specification, section 9.1; the catalogue rows 1 to 35.

## 19 October 2026: Owner decisions on questions 1 and 2 of the 0.2.0 checklist

**Decided by the owner, both as recommended.**

**Weighted statistics (question 1, applied at step 17).** Frequency weights replicate rows: the observation count N is the sum of the weights and the variance divisor is that sum less one. Analytic and sampling weights give the weighted mean Σwx / Σw and, as Stata's `summarize [aweight]` does, a variance with the weights scaled to sum to n and the divisor n − 1. `sum` with sampling weights is the weighted total Σwx. `median` and `quantile` use the cumulative weight. `n` is the row count under analytic and sampling weights and the weight sum under frequency weights. The rules of section 4.1 on the weights themselves (an `NA` weight drops its row with a warning, a zero weight leaves it out with a note, a negative weight is an error) were built at step 6.

**The synthetic `wages` dataset (question 2, applied at step 18).** The generating model (variables, distributions, coefficients with a return to education of 0.074, the panel of workers over years, the missing-value pattern) is drafted for the owner's approval before step 18 begins. Until `draw` exists at 0.3.0 the file is generated by a committed Python script with a fixed seed; at 0.3.0 a Zeff script regenerates it, under a new name if any value changes, since a dataset never changes within an engine version (section 8.5).

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 4.1 ("Weights") and 6; Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.5 and 10.2; put to the owner at the start of the release with the recommendation.

## 19 October 2026: Maths, part 2

**Choice.** `exp`, `log` (with `base:`), `log2`, `log10`, `log1p`, `expm1`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan` and `atan2` are bodies of one value over the maths kernel of step 5, lifted to columns by the machinery of step 11; every one returns a Float and gives `NA` for `NA`. The warnings of section 4.1: the logarithm of zero gives an infinity with W0204 ("log of zero gave -Inf", the help naming `log1p` and a `where` filter; a base below 1 makes it `Inf`), the logarithm of a negative number `NA` with W0205, and so for `log2`, `log10` and `log1p` (at -1 and below it); a base that is not positive or is 1 gives `NA` with W0205 rather than R's `NaN` or infinity; `sin`, `cos` and `tan` of an infinite angle, and `asin` and `acos` outside [-1, 1], give `NA` with W0205. Every wording names the cause and not the value, so that a column's rows count under one line. `exp` overflows to `Inf` and underflows to zero silently, as R does and as section 4.1 lists no warning for it. `atan2` takes `y` first, as R, C and Python do, and is defined everywhere, `atan2(0, 0)` being 0. The message check learnt the new W0204 phrases ("of zero gave", "log1p of -1 gave").

**Tests.** `packages/tier0/core/tests/maths2.rs`: every function on the whole grid against the exact reference and, numerically at six digits, against R's values; `log` with bases 2 and 10 against `log2` and `log10`; every edge of section 4.1 on scalars (one snapshot of the fifteen warnings); columns row by row with their warnings counted (snapshot), the infinities, the empty and the all-missing datasets; the wrong kinds of argument (snapshot); and a property of the identities (`sin² + cos² = 1`, `tan = sin / cos`, `exp(log(x)) = x`, `log(x, base: 2) = log2(x)`, `expm1(log1p(x)) = x`, `atan2(x, 1) = atan(x)`, the inverses on their principal ranges), the inverse cosine tested away from zero, where it is ill-conditioned. Every help example runs; 28 of the 68 functions of `core` ship.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7, 4.1 and 5.6; the catalogue rows 4 to 9 and 19 to 25.

## 19 October 2026: `is_missing`, `coalesce`, `warn` and `error`

**Choice.** Two new modules of `core`, one per family of the catalogue: `missing.rs` (`is_missing`, `coalesce`) and `program.rs` (`warn`, `error`; `print` stays in `lib.rs`). Both missing-value functions take the union of the computable scalar types, `Bool | Int | Float | Str`, so that they lift to a column of any of them; a union now reads in a message as "a Bool, Int, Float or Str". `is_missing` is true for `NA` alone, false for `Inf`, zero and the empty text, and never `NA` itself. `coalesce` returns the first argument that is not `NA`; its result type is the join of its arguments (section 3.7, "Joining types"), which the checker now computes for a declared result type `Join` and refuses with Z0214 naming both types when they do not join; because a column indexed from a frame has an unknown type before the run, the body checks the joining rule again at run time (numbers join, Bool and Str only with themselves) and raises the same Z0214 naming the row. An Int chosen beside a Float becomes a Float, and a lifted result column whose inputs include a Float is a Float column even where every Float cell was `NA` in the rows that gave a value, so that the column's type is the one the checker joined. A result column that no row fills takes its type from the declared result type, or from the kinds of its inputs for `Number` and `Join`.

**`warn` and `error`.** `warn(message)` raises a warning without a code, printed `warning: <message> (line N)` and carried to the JSON record with an empty code: the script's own warning has no catalogue code and the specification gives it none; the diagnostics kernel gained `plain_warning` beside `plain_note`, and its debug assertion now admits an empty code for any severity but error. `error(message)` stops the script with Z0001 (its explained page written at this step), the call marked "the script stops here", exit code 1; its page carries the rendered error as its last example, which the example runner compares like any output. Both return `Nothing`, so binding or passing their result is Z0206 as for `print`. A message that is `NA` prints as the word.

**Tests.** `packages/tier0/core/tests/missing.rs`: both functions on scalars and on columns of each type, the all-missing and the empty datasets, the types that do not join (check time and run time, snapshot), `warn` carrying on and `error` stopping with the statements after it unrun (snapshots), their misuse, and a property that `coalesce` of random optional Ints is the first present one. 32 of the 68 functions of `core` ship.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Joining types", `Nothing`), 4.1, 5.4 and 5.6 (Z0001); the catalogue rows 55, 57, 60 and 61.

## 19 October 2026: The remaining options of `import` for delimited text

**Choice.** `quote:`, `decimal:`, `thousands:` and `encoding:` complete the options of section 6.1 for delimited text. `quote:` is one ASCII character (`"` by default) and `quote: ""` turns quoting off, so that a quotation mark is an ordinary character; the record splitter and the delimiter detection take the quote character as a parameter. `decimal:` and `thousands:` are one character each, held in a `NumberFormat` that every number parser of the reader takes (type guessing, the cells, the `na_values:` codes), so that the whole file is read under one rule: a value is a number when, after the grouping separators are removed, it is a number written with `.`; a grouping separator must stand between groups of exactly three digits after a first group of one to three, and only before the decimal mark, so `1,23` and `12,3456` are text under `thousands: ","` rather than numbers read wrongly; with a decimal comma a `.` makes the value text; the words `Inf` and `NaN` are numbers in every format. With `decimal: ","` the usual delimiter is `;` (a tab is still detected; `delim:` still wins), since the comma cannot be both; `delim:` equal to `decimal:`, or `thousands:` equal to `decimal:`, is a usage error (Z0401), as is a value of more than one character or an unknown encoding name. `encoding:` takes any label of the WHATWG encoding list through the `encoding_rs` crate (0.8.42; Apache-2.0 or MIT, with BSD-3-Clause for its mapping tables, the data package's dependency), decodes the whole file to UTF-8 before the splitter sees it, and names the row of the first undecodable byte sequence (Z0608, a new `Undecodable` error beside `NotUtf8`; UTF-16 lines cannot be told apart, so no row is named there). The single-byte encodings of the list give every byte a character, so the error arises in the multi-byte ones. The Z0608 help for a file that is not UTF-8 now names `encoding:`.

**The catalogue corrected.** Row 97's usage lacked `quote: Str`, which section 6.1 names; added after `delim: Str` and logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`.

**Tests.** Five reference files added to `csv_cases.py` and its JSON (another quote character, no quoting, Windows-1252, a decimal comma, grouped digits), the split compared with Python's `csv` module under the same quote character and encoding; the reader's rules for each option, including the German and French ways of writing numbers and UTF-16 with a byte-order mark; the undecodable byte named by row (snapshot); through `import`, a German-style file read with all three options and refused without them; every option value that is checked (snapshot). The fixture project of the help examples gained `wages_de.csv`, a Windows-1252 file with a decimal comma and grouped digits, which the page of `import` reads in its new example.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.8 ("CSV reading", "Encoding"), 4.1 and 6.1; the catalogue row 97.

## 19 October 2026: Frame verbs, part 1, and names inside a frame method

**Names inside a frame method.** `where(hours > 36)` needs a bare name in a frame method's argument to mean a column of the receiver, which the specification orders before a script binding (section 3.7, "Name lookup") and which the engine did not have. The checker now marks a call as a frame method when its receiver parameter is a `Frame`, and checks every argument whose parameter type takes a column (`Column<Bool>`, `Column`, a union with one; `Var`, `Vars`, words and plain scalars keep their own rules) with the receiver's columns in scope: a bare name there lowers to a new IR node, a frame name holding the name and the binding of that name if one is in scope. Since the frame's columns are not known before the run (the schema cache is 0.3.0), the node is resolved by the interpreter, which keeps a stack of the frames whose methods are being called: the receiver is evaluated first, as section 3.7's argument order already had it, and pushed while the other arguments are evaluated. The column wins; the binding is used when the frame has no such column; both at once is the column with a warning, the provisional W0102, added to open decision #46 (the specification asks for the warning and gives it no code); neither is Z0101 with the frame's variables suggested. A frame name with a binding in scope is typed as unknown, so that `where(hours > w.mean(hours))` can still call a method on the binding; without one it is a column of unknown type. The interpreter also records which columns a call's arguments named, in the order first used, and hands them to the body (`columns_used` on the call context, beside the script's text so that a body may quote an argument as written), which is how `where`'s note names the variable whose `NA` dropped rows: the first used column that has any `NA`, as `wages.where(is_missing(exper))` in the specification's own example. A `Column<Bool>` parameter given a single Bool or `NA` is refused by the checker as Z0203, in the words section 5.6 uses, rather than as a generic Z0401.

**Variable ranges.** `x1..x9` where variables are expected (a parameter of type `Vars`, alone or inside a list) is kept as one entry `x1..x9` of the variable list and expanded against the frame by the data package's `resolve_vars`, which also drops a repeated name and refuses a range that runs backwards (Z0401, listing the frame's variables in order); the shared helper is there for every verb and reducer that takes variables.

**The verbs.** `head` and `tail` slice (a count below zero or `NA` is Z0401); `where` takes a Bool column of the frame's length (another type is Z0203, another length Z0217), keeps the true rows, counts the `NA` rows into the note with the statement that lists them, and says when nothing is kept; `select`, `drop` and `rename` share the parent's columns, keeping every column's metadata and the frame's, and `rename` refuses a name another variable has (Z0401). A derived frame has no name until a `let` gives it one, so it prints as `frame · …` and its messages say "the frame". In the column kernel, `Column::take` gathers rows through `arrow-select` (60.0.0, Apache-2.0, the arrow family already recorded), which handles every storage, the opaque kinds included, and `Table` gained `tail`, `take_rows`, `select`, `without` and `rename`. The selection vector of section 6 (sharing the parent's buffers until a later step reads a column) is not built yet: `where` gathers at once, which is correct and simple; the lazy form arrives with the result cache.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/data/tests/verbs.rs`: `head`, `tail`, `where` and the counts against R's `frames.json` on the large wages file (the first ten ids of each selection and the rows dropped for `NA`); the counts of `head` and `tail` from zero to everything and their refusals (snapshot); `where` keeping, dropping with the note, naming a binding, a method on a binding, a nested function in the condition, and carrying infinities and `NA` through (snapshot); every refusal of a condition (snapshot); the variable-and-binding warning (snapshot); `select`, `drop` and `rename` with names, lists and ranges, and their errors (snapshot); the empty, all-missing and one-row datasets (snapshot); a property that `where(c)`, `where(!c)` and the `NA` rows partition the frame. Every help example runs, `where`'s with the note the specification shows. The specification's own `where` example on `zeff:wages.csv` waits for the dataset of step 18.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Name lookup", "Variable ranges", "Arguments"), 4.1, 4.3, 5.6 (Z0203) and 6; the catalogue rows 103 to 108; `docs/spec/zeff_help_examples.md`, the page of `where`.

## 19 October 2026: Frame verbs, part 2: `add`, `update` and `sort`

**Definitions that see earlier ones.** Section 3.7 says the definitions of `add` and `update` are evaluated left to right and a later one may use an earlier one. The interpreter's receiver entry now holds two frames: the frame as given, which the call's options see, and the frame extended with every definition evaluated so far, which the definitions after it see; a flag says which is being evaluated. The first attempt extended one frame for everything, and `update(hours = 38, where: is_missing(hours))` then saw no missing hours in its condition; the help example caught it. A scalar definition (`year = 2026`) is broadcast to a column of the frame's length for this purpose and for the result (`zeff_core::lift::broadcast`, shared with the verbs).

**`add`.** Each definition becomes a column of the frame's length: a column of that length (another length is Z0217), or a scalar in every row; `NA` alone has no type (Z0219, with the hint to build it from a variable); a list or a record is refused (Z0401). A name the frame has is replaced, with the note the specification asks for, the new column carrying no metadata; the other columns are shared with the parent. `by:` and reducers inside a definition arrive with step 17, so `by:` is not registered yet (the catalogue's usage lists it; the registry allows a parameter to come later).

**`update`.** Only variables the frame has (Z0101, with the hint that `add` creates one); the variable keeps its type, its metadata and its position, so the new values must be of its type, an Int being allowed into a Float variable (Z0401 otherwise, pointing to `add`); a Date, DateTime or Category variable waits for its package (Z0304). `where:` is a Bool column of the frame's length (Z0203 for a single Bool, `NA` or another type, the checker's rule for `Column<Bool>` parameters covering the single value; Z0217 for another length); rows where it is `NA` are left unchanged and counted in a note, the counterpart of `where`'s rule in section 4.1, which the specification does not state for `update` but which keeps `NA` from passing silently.

**`sort`.** `zeff_columns::sort_rows` orders rows by one or more key columns under the identity order of section 3.7 (the grouping kernel's `Key`: `false < true`, numbers numerically, text by code point, dates chronologically, categories by level position), stable, with `NA` last whether ascending or descending; `desc: true` reverses every key, as the catalogue gives one flag. An opaque key is Z0401. The result gathers the rows at once (`Table::take_rows`), as `where` does.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/data/tests/verbs2.rs`: `sort` against R's `order(method = "radix")` on the large file for every key, both directions and two keys (first and last ten ids); `add` with definitions in a chain, a replacement, scalars and a binding, and its refusals (snapshots); `update` with and without `where:`, the type rules, a Str variable, a chain, and its refusals (snapshots); `sort`'s stability, `NA` last, code-point order of text and Bool order on a small file, its refusals, and the empty frame; a property that `sort` is the stable permutation with `NA` last in either direction. Every help example runs.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Definitions in one call", "Identity"), 3.8 ("Comparison and order"), 4.1 and 6 ("Row order"); the catalogue rows 109 to 111.

## 19 October 2026: The reducers, `by:` and `weights:`

**One engine for every statistic.** `reducers.rs` now computes every descriptive statistic (`mean`, `sd`, `variance`, `median`, `quantile`, `min`, `max`, `sum`, and the columns of `summary`) through one path: the frame and the variable, the weights of `weights:` with `weight_type:` (the kernel's `Weights` of step 6, with its rules of section 4.1: an `NA` weight drops its row with a warning, a zero weight leaves it out with a note, a negative, infinite or, under frequency weights, fractional weight is an error listing the rows), the groups of `by:` (the kernel's `Groups`, in key order with `NA` last), and a `Sample` per group holding the values that count, their weights and the number of `NA` values skipped. Without `by:` the result is a value; with it a table titled `mean · wage by region`, the keys in the first columns and the statistic to three decimals (section 3.8's rule for tables), in the layout section 10.2 shows for `summary`. The warnings are counted across groups and said once. `summary` and `describe` take `by:` the same way, `describe` with one block of rows per group.

**The weighted formulas (the owner's decision of question 1).** In the numeric kernel (`zeff_numeric::order`): `weighted_mean` is Σwx / Σw for every weight type; `weighted_variance` under frequency weights replicates rows (divisor Σw − 1) and under analytic and sampling weights scales the weights to sum to n with divisor n − 1, as Stata's `summarize [aweight]`; `weighted_sum` is Σwx under frequency and sampling weights and n · Σwx / Σw under analytic weights; `weighted_quantile` and the weighted median take the smallest value whose cumulative weight reaches p of the total, the type-1 quantile of the replicated sample under frequency weights; `n` in `summary` is the weight sum under frequency weights and the row count otherwise; `min` and `max` ignore the weights beyond leaving out the rows that do not count. The R script `descriptive.R` now writes these statistics on the large wages file with `educ` as the weights (base R: `weighted.mean` and the formulas written out), and the kernel is held to them within 1e-12; without weights, `sd` and `variance` keep the kernel's scaled two-pass algorithms, since a square root of a weighted variance would underflow for values near 1e-300 (the test on the magnitudes dataset caught the first version).

**The nine quantile definitions.** `zeff_numeric::order::quantile` is R's `quantile.default` written out, its fuzz against rounding in the index included, so the nine types agree with R to the bit on every dataset of the reference at nine probabilities; the small-sample unit test records that types 3 and 4 differ from the others at the median of 1, 2, 3, 4, 10 (2 and 2.5 where the rest give 3). `type:` outside 1 to 9, and `p:` outside [0, 1] or not a number, are Z0401 (the code Z0413 of section 4 is for the probabilities given to distributions, which arrive at 0.3.0); `p:` missing is Z0406.

**Reducers inside `add` and `update`.** Section 6 makes every statistic a reducer inside a definition: `add(dev = lwage - mean(lwage), by: firm)`. Three pieces: (1) a bare call to a frame method inside a frame method's definition is an *implicit-receiver* call, which the interpreter gives the enclosing frame as its receiver (the group under `by:`); when a name has a row-wise home in `core` and a reducer home in `data` (`min`, `max`), the reducer is chosen inside a definition when the arguments fit it (one variable, where the row-wise function needs two values), section 8.1's rule 6 read at the call; (2) under `by:`, a definition is evaluated once per group on the group's rows (the receiver's view) and the results are put back in row order, a scalar filling the group's rows, a column of the group's length placed row by row, another length Z0217, kinds that do not join across groups Z0214; so `n()` and `n_distinct(x)` count within the group with no special case; (3) the options of a frame method that takes definitions are evaluated before its definitions whatever the written order, since `by:` shapes them, a reading of section 3.7's "positional then named" that puts the named options first. The messages of a definition evaluated per group are said once per distinct wording. `n()` outside a frame method is Z0401 pointing to `n_rows`; `n_distinct` counts by identity, `NA` one value, as the catalogue says. The call context carries the enclosing frame as the call sees it, for `n()`.

**Tests.** `reducers2.rs`: every statistic and all nine quantile types on the large file against R; the weighted statistics against R under the three weight types; the four exact Python datasets; `by:` tables in key order with `NA` last (snapshot); reducers inside `add` and `update` per group; Int staying Int (`sum`, `min`, `max`) with the overflow error, Bool counting true, the all-missing and empty frames (snapshot); the weights rules and their errors (snapshots); the refusals of `quantile` and `n()` (snapshot); `describe(by:)`; a property that the group means put back on every row average to the grand mean and the group deviations sum to zero. Every help example runs. The catalogue rows 142, 143, 146 to 150 and 434 are marked implemented.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7, 4.1 ("Statistics", "Weights"), 6 ("Statistics as methods and reducers", `by:`, `weights:`, `weight_type:`) and 10.2; the owner's decision on question 1; the catalogue rows of the reducers.

## 19 October 2026: The `datasets` package

**What ships.** Two datasets, embedded in the engine with `include_bytes` so the browser needs no fetch: `sleep`, Student's 1908 data (public domain; twenty observations, the two drugs as a Category with their names), and `wages`, the synthetic panel of question 2 (CC0-1.0; 18,412 rows on 3,911 workers over 2010 to 2021). Each ships twice: as CSV (the raw file, under one megabyte each, 807 kB for `wages`), served by the `zeff:` root to `import`, and as Arrow IPC with the labels, units, value labels, categories and the panel declaration, read by `dataset(name)`. The Parquet reader and writer belong to 0.11.0 (Engine 8.7), so Parquet is not pulled forward: the typed copy is Arrow IPC, which `zeff-columns` already reads and writes, and `zeff:wages.parquet` arrives with Parquet. The embedded bytes total about 2.2 MB for `wages`; the size is recorded in the `datasets()` table and the bundle-size measurement of every build shows the cost.

**Ten raw variables, a younger sample.** Section 10.2 illustrates thirteen variables; the shipped file carries the ten raw ones (`worker`, `year`, `wage`, `educ`, `exper`, `age`, `hours`, `union`, `female`, `industry`) and leaves `lwage`, `exper2` and the like to `add`, which keeps the CSV under the megabyte and gives the help pages their natural examples. Workers are 18 to 40 in 2010 for the same reason. The generating model, its parameters and its seed (20261019) are on the `wages` help page under Generation, as section 9.1 asks.

**Generators and checksums.** `packages/tier1/datasets/generate/*.py` are plain Python using only the standard library, `decimal` for the exponential so the file is the same on every platform; `cargo xtask build-datasets` declares each dataset's metadata (labels, units, value labels as JSON, Category levels, the panel) and writes the Arrow files and `data/CHECKSUMS` (BLAKE3, labelled). CI regenerates both and fails on any difference, so the shipped bytes are those the scripts produce. The dataset test checks the embedded bytes against the checksums and the files on disk.

**Dataset help pages in the registry.** The registry gains a second kind of page: a dataset page with Summary, Description, Format (a table of variable, type, label, unit and value labels, checked against the Arrow metadata so the page cannot drift from the file), Source or Generation, Licence, References and Examples, parsed and checked at `cargo test` like a function page and served by `zeff help wages`. The `dataset` and `datasets` functions have ordinary pages in the same package.

**Labelled values print their labels.** A column with value labels (`female`, `union`) prints the label in frames, tables and the `describe` example column, left-aligned like text, while the stored Int is what computes; `describe` marks the type `Int (lab)`. The specification shows labelled printing in section 10.2 and this is the first release with labelled data; the printed Int stays available through `print` of the bare column.

**The `datasets()` table.** Title `datasets · N shipped with this release`, columns name, rows × columns, kind (public or synthetic), licence, source and size; it wraps into two blocks at the default width like any table.

**Existing examples kept on `data/wages.csv`.** The step allowed moving earlier pages' examples to the `zeff:` datasets where that reads better. The example runner's `data/wages.csv` is the thirteen-variable file section 10.2 illustrates, and the 53 examples that use it read as the specification writes them, so they stay; the new pages use the shipped datasets.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/datasets/tests/datasets.rs`: checksums and embedded bytes against the files on disk; the shape, labels, categories, missing counts and panel of `wages`; loading through the engine and through `zeff:wages.csv` with the same mean; the documented moments of the generating model (mean log wage 3.19, spread 0.49, 3,911 workers, twelve years, 47 per cent women); the refusals Z0101 and Z0715 with their suggestions as snapshots. The example runner runs the four new pages.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, sections 2 (data roots), 8.5, 8.7 and 9.1; the owner's approval of the dataset draft; the catalogue rows 458 and 459.

## 19 October 2026: The 0.2.0 sample project and the script tests

**Choice.** The second sample project lives in `samples/data_cleaning/`: `zeff.toml` (pinned to `0.2.0-dev` like the first), `data/staff_de.csv` (360 staff records as a German spreadsheet exports them: `;` between fields, a decimal comma, a point between groups of digits, Windows-1252 letters in the region names, `-99` for a missing value, headers with spaces), `make_data.py` (the standard-library Python that wrote the file from a fixed seed, kept beside it so the file's origin is on record), `scripts/main.zeff` and `expected/stdout.txt` and `expected/stderr.txt`. The script is the data-cleaning path of the release end to end: `import` with `decimal:`, `thousands:`, `encoding:`, `na_values:` and `names: snake`; `where` with `is_missing`; `rename`; `add` with expressions and, under `by:`, a reducer evaluated region by region; `update` with `where:`; `sort` ascending and descending; `select`; `head`; `summary(by:)`; `mean(by:)`; `quantile` at three probabilities; `median`; `n_distinct`; `print`; and a shipped dataset twice, `dataset(sleep)` with its category printed by name and `dataset(wages)` summarised by `union` with its labels.

**How it is checked.** The conformance crate now describes each sample as a `Sample` (name, manifest, data files as bytes, script, stored output) and runs every entry of `SAMPLES` on an in-memory project, so the report carries `data_cleaning/stdout`, `data_cleaning/stderr` and `data_cleaning/exit_code` beside the first sample's `sample/*` cases, whose names are kept so the 0.1.0 report lines stay comparable; the four native targets and WebAssembly all check the new sample against the committed digests, and a unit test compares each in-memory run with the stored files. The command-line test runs the built `zeff` in both folders, compares both streams byte for byte and runs `zeff check` there. The stored output is regenerated with `zeff run > expected/stdout.txt 2> expected/stderr.txt` in the folder when a change is intended; both tests say so.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, section 1 (script tests, every push); the release row's "a data-cleaning script end to end, stored output, in the conformance report, identical on all four targets".

## 19 October 2026: Fuzzing in the nightly job

**Choice.** The fuzz targets live in `fuzz/`, a package of its own excluded from the workspace (`exclude = ["fuzz"]`), so the engine keeps its pinned stable toolchain and `cargo-fuzz` with a nightly toolchain is used only there, as the release plan rules. Four targets under libFuzzer (`libfuzzer-sys` 0.4.13, MIT or Apache-2.0, pinned): `lexer` (any text; every token must lie inside the text), `parser` (any text; the tree must also print as an s-expression), `checker` (any text through the parser and the checker against the engine's registry, built once) and `csv` (any bytes to the CSV reader, the first four bytes choosing the delimiter or its detection, the quote, the decimal mark with its grouping separator, the header and the lines to skip, so every option path is reached). Each must answer with a result or a diagnostic and never panic, which is what section 11 of the Language Reference asks of the parser and the checker at 0.2.0 and the testing handbook of the CSV import.

**The job.** A third job, `fuzz`, in `.github/workflows/scheduled.yml`, on the nightly schedule and by hand (`job: fuzz`). It installs the pinned toolchain and a minimal nightly one, `cargo-fuzz` through `taiki-e/install-action`, seeds each corpus from the repository (the two sample scripts and the specification's sample script for the three language targets; the twelve test datasets and the German staff file, each behind four option bytes, for the CSV reader), builds the targets and runs each for a fixed ten minutes with a twenty-second timeout per input. The run's summary page carries the note (runs, coverage, crash inputs), and the logs with any crash input are kept as an artifact. A crash input is to be copied into a regression test of the crate concerned (testing handbook, section 1, "every finding turned into a regression test"); the corpora themselves are not committed (`fuzz/.gitignore`), since they are rebuilt from the seeds every night. `fuzz/Cargo.lock` is committed so the job builds the same dependency versions.

**First runs.** Locally, each target ran 25 seconds and then 150 seconds on the Mac with no crash, from the seeded corpora.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 11 (the fuzzing row, 0.2.0); testing handbook, section 1 (fuzzing, nightly) and section 2.2; the release plan's ruling on `cargo-fuzz` and the nightly toolchain.

## 19 October 2026: The special-function kernel

**Choice.** `zeff_numeric::special` holds the functions the distributions need, in pure Rust on every target: `log_gamma`, `gamma`, `erf` and `erfc` from the `libm` crate like the elementary functions (musl's ports, a unit or two in the last place; `gamma` returns the exact factorial at the integers 1 to 171, where libm's value may be a unit off); `factorial` from a table of the 171 doubles nearest the exact values, written once by Python's exact integers; `choose` exactly while the integers fit in 128 bits, then one rounding per step, and `Inf` once `k` exceeds 600 (the result then exceeds the largest double whatever `n`); `log_beta` through the Stirling form, so that large arguments lose no digits to cancellation; the normal tails from `erfc` on each side, and the normal quantile by Halley steps on `erfc` from the Abramowitz and Stegun start, exact at one half; the regularised incomplete gamma function by its series below a + 1 and its continued fraction above (modified Lentz), the regularised incomplete beta function by its continued fraction on whichever side converges, each returning both tails with the small one computed directly (section 13: tails are never one minus the other side); and the inverses by safeguarded Newton steps with a bracket, on the smaller tail, from the Wilson–Hilferty and normal starts.

**The prefix terms.** The exponent of each prefix, a ln x − x − ln Γ(a) and a ln x + b ln(1 − x) − ln B(a, b), is the place where a large parameter loses digits: written naively it subtracts numbers of size a ln a. It is computed instead from the Stirling remainder S(x) = ln Γ(x) − [(x − ½) ln x − x + ln √(2π)] (the Bernoulli series from x = 10, the difference itself below) and the deviation from the mean: for the gamma function a·(log1p(d) − d) with d = (x − a)/a by its own series near zero, and for the beta function a log1p(d/a) + b log1p(−d/b) with one rounded deviation d = x(a + b) − a, so that the two terms' first-order rounding errors cancel (the derivative of their sum with respect to d vanishes at the mean). Far from the mean, where log1p would meet an argument at −1, the plain logarithm of the ratio serves, the result then being deep in a tail where the exponent's size bounds the error. Three attempts were needed to find the form that keeps both tails of the beta function to twelve digits at a = 500,000, and each wrong turn was caught by the exact reference, not by R, whose values at those points carry errors of the same order.

**The references.** `tests/reference/special.py` computes every value in Python's `decimal` module at 70 digits and rounds once: the gamma function by the Stirling series with exact Bernoulli numbers after a shift to 50, the error functions by the Maclaurin series up to 5 and the continued fraction beyond, the incomplete functions by the same series and continued fractions at 85 digits, the inverses by bisection (in log space for a lower tail, which may lie at 1e-100) followed by Newton steps with the bracket kept. `mpmath`, which the checklist named, is not in the standard library and the rules allow no installer for it; `decimal` suffices and runs in eleven seconds. `tests/reference/r/special.R` writes R's values on the same cases (`special_cases.csv`, exact hexadecimal floats) and CI compares them within 1e-12 (`check_r.py special`), since R's `pgamma` and `pbeta` differ between platforms in their far tails at that order.

**Tolerances found.** Against the exact reference: `log_gamma`, `gamma`, `log_beta` and the exact binomial coefficients to 1e-14; `beta`, `erf`, `erfc` and the normal tails to 5e-13 (a value through an exponential of a logarithm near −60 rounds by 1e-14; `erfc` at 20 and beyond carries 1e-13); the incomplete functions and their inverses to 1e-12, widened in a deep tail in proportion to the exponent's size (a probability of 1e-235 is exp(−541), and 1e-16 of 541 is 5e-14), and to 1e-10 for a parameter above 100,000, where the continued fraction's stopping rule cannot see below a unit in the last place and leaves an error of about 2e-11: the single departure from the class tolerance, recorded as a known issue of 0.3.0 and to be closed by the asymptotic expansions of Temme (as TOMS 708 does) in a later step or release; a t distribution with a million degrees of freedom is the case that meets it. Eight conformance series (`special/*`) hold the bits on the four targets.

**Tests.** `reference_special.rs` (the exact reference, 599 values), the special section of `reference_r.rs` (R), three property tests (the gamma recurrence; both tails are probabilities that sum to one, are monotone and mirror between I_x(a, b) and 1 − I_{1−x}(b, a); every inverse round-trips its function to 1e-11), and the unit tests of the domain edges and the deep tails.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.3 point 3 (one pure-Rust implementation, fixed order) and 13 (tails computed directly; the distribution class); testing handbook, section 1.1; the checklist's step 2.
