## 19 October 2026: The `Distribution` value, the `dist.` namespace and methods on a value

**The value.** `zeff_core::value::Distribution` is declared in `core` (section 8.1, rule 4) with three shapes: a family with its parameters named and every default filled in (`Family { name: "normal", params: [("mean", 0), ("sd", 1)] }`), a truncation of another distribution with its bounds, and a finite mixture with its components and their probabilities; the last two are shaped now so that steps 10's functions fill them without reworking the value. `Value::Distribution` prints as the owner decided (question 1): `normal distribution · mean: 0, sd: 1`, a truncation adding `· truncated to [lower, upper]` and a mixture listing `p × (component)` terms. The checker has `Ty::Distribution`, so a distribution given where a frame is wanted is Z0401 ("this is a Distribution") before anything runs.

**The namespace.** `dist.normal(...)` parses as a method call on the name `dist`; the checker, seeing a receiver that is the bare name of a namespace (`dist`, `power`, `spec`) and a callee of one segment, names the function `dist.normal` and drops the receiver, so the registry holds it under its full name, as the catalogue writes it (row 179), and `zeff help dist.normal` finds it. The three namespace words join the reserved names of `core`: `let dist = 3` is Z0105. An unknown family, `dist.gaussian`, is Z0103 with the help "`zeff help dist` lists the functions of the `dist` namespace". Methods on a `Distribution` need nothing new: the checker already picks a method by its receiver's type from the first parameter of its specification, so `pdf`, `cdf`, `quantile` and `draw` register at step 7 with a first parameter of type `Distribution` and dispatch at once; until then `dist.normal().pdf(1)` is Z0103.

**The package and its first function.** `packages/tier1/dist` (tier 1, order 4 of section 8.2, before `datasets` in the tier list) with `dist.normal(mean: Float = 0, sd: Float = 1)` and its complete page, so that the help build-check holds and the example runner prints the distribution; its row stays `planned` until the four methods make it whole at step 7. Each family declares its parameters with a default and a domain rule (any finite number; a positive number) in one table, and one function reads the arguments against it: a value outside the domain, or `NA`, is Z0413 at the argument with the help "`zeff help dist.normal` gives the domain of every parameter"; the code is new to the engine (its page `codes/Z0413.md`; section 4 of the Language Reference names it for a parameter outside its domain and a probability outside [0, 1]).

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/dist/tests/dist.rs`: printing with defaults filled in and through `print` and a list; a snapshot of the refusals (Z0413 at zero, a negative number and an `NA` computed from `sqrt(-1)`; Z0105 for `let dist`; Z0103 with the namespace hint; Z0401 for a frame method on a distribution and for text given to `sd:`); the check-time refusal of `dist.normal().head(3)`. The engine's registry test now lists the packages `core`, `data`, `dist`, `datasets`.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Namespaces", "Methods"), 3.8 (printing) and 4 (`Distribution`, Z0413); Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.1 (rules 4 and 6) and 8.2; the owner's decision on question 1; the checklist's step 3.

## 19 October 2026: Philox random streams and the run's seed

**The generator.** `zeff_numeric::random::philox4x32_10` is Philox4x32-10 exactly as the Random123 library defines it (the multipliers D2511F53 and CD9E8D57, the Weyl constants 9E3779B9 and BB67AE85, the key bumped between rounds), and its unit test holds the three published known-answer vectors (all zeros, all ones, and the π digits), so a draw means the same on every machine and in any other implementation of the same function. A `Stream` is keyed as section 8.3 fixes: the seed as the 64-bit key, the statement's ordinal within the run and the loop pass in the counter's high words, the block number in its low words; a uniform takes the top 27 bits of one word and the top 26 of the next, 53 bits in all, the combination the Mersenne Twister's `genrand_res53` uses, so every uniform is one of the 2^53 values in [0, 1) and the stream never depends on what was drawn before or on threads.

**The seed.** `Randomness`, one per run in the interpreter, holds the seed in force and whether a statement has drawn. A draw without a seed set chooses one from the operating system at that moment (a positive Int below 2^31, so that it reads back as an ordinary number), keeps it for the rest of the run, and prints the note "no seed was set, so N was chosen for this run; `seed(N)` at the top of the script repeats it" under that statement: the note is the run record of the seed until `.zeff/runs/` arrives. A `seed:` given to one call is a stream of its own, keyed with ordinal 0 and the given seed, so that the same `seed:` draws the same numbers wherever the call stands, as a researcher who writes `seed: 42` expects; the script-wide seed keys each statement by its ordinal, so two identical statements draw different numbers and inserting a statement changes the draws after it, as R and Stata behave. `seed(n)` itself, with Z0111 when it comes second, is the function of step 12 on this state. The loop pass is 0 until `for` arrives. On WebAssembly without a host, the standard library's randomness is fixed, so a run without `seed(n)` there would repeat; the browser will supply the seed from the host when that path is built.

**Tests.** The known-answer vectors; a property test that a stream is a pure function of (seed, ordinal, pass) and that every uniform lies on the 2^53 grid; the unit test of the run's seed (chosen once, noted once, an explicit seed standing alone, a scripted seed used as written); two conformance series (`random/philox`, `random/uniform`) holding the bits on the four targets. The message snapshot of the note follows at step 7 with the first `draw`.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.3 point 3 (random numbers) and 13 (random draws identical across platforms; the stochastic class); Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Random methods", `seed:`) and 11 (notes record the seed); the checklist's step 4.

## 19 October 2026: `zeff selftest`

**Choice.** The published report `crates/zeff-conformance/expected.txt` is compiled into the conformance crate (`PUBLISHED`), and `zeff_conformance::selftest()` runs every case of the build and pairs each digest with the published one. The command line depends on the conformance crate for it (a crate, not a package, so the tier rules are untouched) and `zeff selftest` prints the line of section 2.1, `conformant: 76 of 76 cases match the published results of Zeff 0.3.0-dev on this machine (ARM64)`, with exit code 0; or `not conformant: K of N cases differ ...`, each differing case on its own line with both digests, a request to report it with `zeff version --verbose`, and exit code 1. The target word follows the specification's example (`x86-64`, `ARM64`, `WebAssembly`). `--format json` gives one record per case (`case`, `published`, `actual`, `match`), and the usage text and the `--format` rule name the command. The environment variable `ZEFF_SELFTEST_FORCE_MISMATCH`, naming a case, flips that case's digest: a test hook like `panic_at_line`, so that the failing path is tested on every push without a build that really differs. The native identity jobs of CI build the command line in release mode on each target and run `zeff selftest`, so the four targets prove the command itself; WebAssembly runs the same cases through the conformance binary under Node, as before. `zeff doctor`, the launcher and the "unofficial build" mark stay at 0.9.0.

**A property test loosened.** The run's full suite caught `group_means_weight_back_to_the_grand_mean` (reducers2.rs) on a random case whose values sum to zero: the mean of the group means scattered back on every row came out as −4.4e-16 against a grand mean of exactly 0, and the test asked the two printed strings to be equal. Two routes through floating point cannot promise the last digit, so the property now holds them within 1e-12 of each other; the engine is unchanged and the failing case is kept in the crate's `proptest-regressions` file. This repeats the lesson recorded at 0.1.0: a property is written to what the design promises, not to what one run showed.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, sections 2.1 (`zeff selftest`, "Diagnosis and settings") and 8.3 point 3 ("Proof"); testing handbook, section 1 (cross-platform identity) and the 0.1.0 ruling on over-tight properties; the checklist's step 5.

## 19 October 2026: The first four distributions and the four methods

**The families.** `dist.lognormal(meanlog: 0, sdlog: 1)`, `dist.uniform(min: 0, max: 1)` and `dist.exponential(rate: 1)` join `dist.normal`, each built by the parameter table of step 3 (a domain rule per parameter, Z0413 at the argument) and, for `uniform`, a rule between parameters (`max:` must exceed `min:`, Z0413 at `max:`). `packages/tier1/dist/src/families.rs` holds each family's density, both tails of its distribution function and its quantile in closed form on the kernel: the normal and log-normal through `erfc` on each side and the inverse normal; the exponential's lower tail as −expm1(−λx) and its upper tail as exp(−λx), its quantile as −log1p(−p)/λ; the uniform's tails as (x − min)/(max − min) and (max − x)/(max − min). R agrees at six printed digits on grids reaching 1e-300 and 1e6 in both tails (`tests/reference/r/distributions.R`, compared within 1e-12 in CI like the special functions).

**The methods.** `pdf(x)`, `cdf(x, upper: false)`, `quantile(p)` and `draw(n, seed:)` are registered in `dist` as methods whose first parameter is of type `Distribution`, so the checker dispatches them by the receiver's type as it does frame methods; `quantile` thereby has two homes, the frame method of `data` and this one, picked by the receiver. `quantile` refuses `p` outside [0, 1] (Z0413); `draw` refuses a negative `n` (Z0401). A draw is the inverse CDF of a uniform of the run's stream (or of `seed:`'s own stream), the uniform shifted by half a grid step (2^-54) so that a draw never meets the quantile's endpoints (`normal_quantile(0)` is −Inf); the column is `Float`, and `Int` for the discrete families of step 9, as the owner decided (question 3); `draw(0)` is an empty column and `draw(1)` a column of one value.

**Two checker rules widened.** (1) The lift of a scalar function over a column, until now for functions of `core` only, also applies to a method on a value that is not a frame and returns a scalar, so `d.cdf(wages["z"])` and `wages.add(q = d.quantile(p))` work row by row with the distribution broadcast as a scalar; a method returning a column (`draw`) is not lifted. (2) A method's receiver written as a bare name inside a frame method's argument is the binding of that name when one exists (`f.add(q = d.quantile(p))` with `let d = dist.normal()`), since a column has no methods in this release and the run-time choice between column and binding of section 3.7 cannot apply to a receiver; the rule is recorded here so that it is revisited when columns gain methods.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/dist/tests/distributions.rs`: every value of R's file at six digits; the edges of each support (a log-normal or exponential below zero, a uniform outside its interval, the quantiles at 0 and 1, `NA` through); the refusals as a snapshot (Z0413 for `p` and the parameters, Z0401 for `n`, the wrong kinds of argument); columns row by row and inside `add`; draws equal under one seed, different under another and between statements, with the chosen seed noted once; and the stochastic class of section 13 on 100,000 draws of each family: the mean within five standard errors, the variance within five per cent, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance to the distribution function under the 0.1 per cent band 1.95/√n. Two conformance series (`dist/values`, `dist/draws`) hold the values and the first draws on the four targets. The eight catalogue rows (the four constructors and the four methods) are `implemented`.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Columns and scalars", "Methods", "Random methods") and 4; Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.3 point 3 and 13 (the distribution and stochastic classes); the owner's decision on question 3; the catalogue rows 179, 180, 187, 188 and 191 to 194; the checklist's step 7.

## 19 October 2026: The t, chi-square, F, gamma and beta distributions

**Choice.** `dist.t(df:)`, `dist.chi2(df:)`, `dist.f(df1:, df2:)`, `dist.gamma(shape:, rate: 1)` and `dist.beta(a:, b:)`, each on the kernel's incomplete functions: the chi-square and gamma distribution functions are P(α, λx) with Q computed directly, the F's is I_w(d₁/2, d₂/2) at w = d₁x/(d₁x + d₂), the beta's is I_x(a, b), and the t's is half of I_x(ν/2, ½) at x = ν/(ν + t²) on the side of t. The densities use the kernel's `gamma_density` and `beta_density` (the F's as the beta density at w times dw/dx), whose prefixes keep their digits for large parameters, and the t's density is written in logarithms with the beta function. Every quantile inverts on the smaller tail, the F's and the t's solving for 1 − w through the mirrored inverse when w would be near one. Degrees of freedom and shapes may be fractional, as in R, but must be finite: `dist.t(df: Inf)` is refused (Z0413) rather than read as the normal, since the specification gives `df:` the domain "positive" and nothing more. Above 400,000 degrees of freedom the t distribution uses the normal approximation R itself uses in `pt` (z = t(1 − 1/4ν)/√(1 + t²/2ν)), so the engine and the reference agree there exactly and the continued fraction's loss of digits at such parameters (the known issue of step 2) does not reach the t distribution; its quantile there is found by Newton steps from the normal quantile.

**Deep tails.** Three limits of double precision met on the way, each handled in logarithms. Past |t| = 1e150 the ratio ν/(ν + t²) lies below the smallest Float, so the t tail is its leading term, ½ x^(ν/2) / ((ν/2) B(ν/2, ½)) with ln x = ln ν − 2 ln |t| (a Cauchy tail at −1e300 is 3.18e-301, as R gives), and the deep-tail quantile inverts the same term; the normal approximation above 400,000 degrees of freedom is written as (1 − c) sign(t) / √(1/t² + 2c) so that a huge t does not become a ratio of infinities; and the kernel's inverse incomplete functions return the end of the interval outright when a tail's leading term lies below the smallest Float, instead of bisecting towards it for two hundred steps. R's `qbeta`, and so its `qf`, loses digits deep in a tail (`qf(1e-20, 3, 20)` returns a value whose `pf` is 1.02e-20, two per cent off, and at 1e-300 it returns 0 where the quantile is 7.9e-201); the test therefore holds a quantile that differs from R's to the round trip through the distribution function instead, within a few parts in a million of the printed six digits, and the engine's values pass it where R's do not.

**Tests.** R's `distributions.json` now holds fifteen more parameter sets (t at 1, 3, 24 and 1e6 degrees of freedom; chi-square at 1, 5 and 100; F at (3, 20), (1, 1) and (100, 1000); gamma at (0.5, 1), (2, 3) and (100, 0.1); beta at (0.5, 0.5), (2, 3) and (100, 100)), each on the grid of x from −1e300 to 1e6 and of p from 1e-300 to 1 − 1e-10, and every printed value agrees at six digits; the edges of each support (densities at zero infinite, one or zero as the shape decides; the t's median exactly zero and its quantile at zero −Inf); the refusals (Z0413 for a zero or negative parameter, a missing one Z0406); the stochastic class on 100,000 draws of each of the nine families; eight more parameter sets in the conformance series.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 4; Engine and Project Specification, section 13; the catalogue rows 181 to 183, 189 and 190; the checklist's step 8.

## 19 October 2026: The binomial, Poisson and negative binomial distributions

**Choice.** The three discrete families take whole numbers only: `pdf` at a value that is not a whole number is 0 (R's `dbinom` gives 0 with a warning; Zeff gives 0 without one, since the value is a legitimate point of the real line where the mass is zero), `cdf` counts up to the whole number below its argument, and `draw` gives a `Column<Int>` as the owner decided. The probabilities are computed in Loader's saddle-point form, exp(S(n) − S(k) − S(n − k) − D) / √(2πk(n − k)/n), with the kernel's Stirling remainders and a new kernel function `deviance(x, m)` = x ln(x/m) + m − x evaluated by its series near x = m, so that the probability of a thousand successes in a million trials is right to every digit where the logarithm of the binomial coefficient would lose nine; the Poisson uses the same form with one term, and the negative binomial is size/(size + k) times the binomial probability of `size` successes in k + size trials, which holds for a fractional size. The distribution functions are the incomplete beta and gamma functions with both tails direct (binomial I_{1−p}(n − k, k + 1), Poisson Q(k + 1, λ), negative binomial I_p(size, k + 1)). A discrete quantile is the smallest k with F(k) ≥ p, found from the normal approximation by widening a bracket and halving it, a few dozen evaluations of F however far the quantile lies; `quantile(1)` is `n` for the binomial and `Inf` for the others, as in R.

**Whole numbers with R's tolerance.** A value within one part in ten million (relative) of a whole number counts as that whole number in `pdf`, and `cdf` floors with the same tolerance, as R's `dbinom` and `pbinom` do, so that floating-point noise such as 2.9999999999 on a computed count does not turn a probability into zero; a negative value is below the support before any rounding, as in R, so `pdf(-1e-10)` is 0 where `pdf(1e-10)` is the mass at zero. The first version had neither rule and the R comparison caught both.

**Two parameterisations.** `dist.negbinomial` takes `size:` with `p:` or `mu:` with `size:`; both together are Z0410 (the provisional code of open decision #46 for options that exclude each other) and neither is Z0406; the value keeps the form it was given and prints it, converting with p = size/(size + mu) when it computes. The catalogue writes the two forms joined by ` or `, and the registry's reading of a usage now takes the union of the parameters of every form, which the help contract foresaw for `t_test`.

**Tests.** R's file holds nine more parameter sets (binomial at (10, 0.3), (1000, 0.5) and (1e6, 1e-3); Poisson at 2, 0.01 and 1000; negative binomial at (3, 0.4), (mu 4.5, size 3) and (0.5, 0.1)), every printed value agreeing at six digits; the edges (fractional and out-of-range arguments, the quantiles at 0 and 1, the point mass at `p: 1`, the Int draws); the refusals (a fractional `n` Z0401, a probability outside [0, 1] Z0413, both or neither parameterisation); the stochastic class on 100,000 draws of the three families, with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance taken at the distinct values, as a discrete distribution requires; three more parameter sets in the conformance series.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 4; Engine and Project Specification, section 13; the owner's decision on question 3; the catalogue rows 184 to 186; the checklist's step 9.

## 19 October 2026: `dist.truncated` and `dist.mixture`

**Truncation.** `dist.truncated(d, lower: -Inf, upper: Inf)` builds the `Truncated` shape of the value: with Z = P(lower ≤ X ≤ upper), the density is f/Z on the interval, the distribution function (F(x) − F(lower⁻))/Z and its upper tail (S(x) − S(upper))/Z, each from the inner tail on the same side so that a far tail keeps its digits, and the quantile the inner quantile at F(lower⁻) + pZ held inside the interval. For a discrete distribution the interval is closed at both ends (the mass at `lower:` is kept; the `truncdist` package drops it, its interval being open below), the reading a statistician gives "truncated to [a, b]". A bound not above the other, or an interval holding no probability, is Z0413. Near the inner centre the subtraction keeps about eleven digits, which the help page says.

**Mixtures.** `dist.mixture(parts, probs:)` builds the `Mixture` shape: density and both tails as weighted sums, the quantile as the smallest x with the mixed distribution function at or above p by halving a bracket set by the components' quantiles (landing on a whole number when every component is discrete), and a draw spending two uniforms of the stream, one to choose the component and one to invert through it, exactly as section 8.3 fixes. The probabilities must be 0 or more and sum to one within 1e-9 (Z0413), one per component (Z0401), `probs:` required (Z0406); they are normalised by their sum. `families::draw` now takes the stream rather than one uniform, so that a mixture can draw twice; its callers in the engine, the conformance report and the tests follow.

**The reference without `truncdist`.** The checklist named R's `truncdist` package as the reference for truncation. It is an R package and the rules allow no installer for one (R itself came through Homebrew), so `distributions.R` writes the truncated and mixed functions from base R's own: the formulas above, which are what `truncdist` computes, and `uniroot` for the mixture's quantile. The comparison allows a composite one part in a hundred thousand, since both sides subtract near-equal probabilities; a discrete quantile that differs from R's is held to the smallest-k property (F(k) ≥ p and F(k − 1) < p), where the R formula `qpois(F(a − 1) + pZ)` falls below the interval when pZ is lost in the addition.

**A correction found on the way.** The t distribution near its centre: the ratio ν/(ν + t²) rounds towards one and loses the digits of F(t) − ½, so for |t| < √ν the complement y = t²/(ν + t²) is used with I_x(ν/2, ½) = 1 − I_y(½, ν/2); the truncated t on [0, ∞) at 1e-10 showed it (0 where 7.6e-11 is right). The catalogue's usage of `dist.mixture` named no first parameter (`[d1, d2, ...]`, an example literal); corrected to `parts` and logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`.

**Two kernel properties made honest.** The full run caught two random cases of the kernel's properties. A beta quantile in an upper tail with a small second shape (a = 39, b = 0.1, p = 1e-12) has no double below one with so small a tail: the inverse now returns one when the leading term (p b B(a, b))^(1/b) lies below half a unit in the last place of one, and the round-trip property accepts the returned double when its two neighbours' tails straddle p, the honest statement where the function is too steep for the grid of doubles to hold a quantile whose tail returns p to eleven digits. The symmetry property I_x(a, b) = 1 − I_{1−x}(b, a) now allows 1e-9 instead of 1e-12: 1 − x is rounded, and a far tail moves by about a/x units in the last place when x does (a up to 2,000 and x near 0.005 in the case found).

**Tests.** The R comparison extended by four composites (a truncated normal on [−1, 2], a t with five degrees of freedom on [0, ∞), a Poisson on [1, 6], a mixture of two normals); a snapshot of their printing, edges and draws; the refusals; the stochastic class on 100,000 draws of the truncated normal and of the mixture against their exact moments; both in the conformance series. The two catalogue rows are `implemented`; the twelve families, the two constructions and the four methods of the release are complete.

**Reason.** The catalogue rows 425 and 426; Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.3 point 3 and 13; the checklist's step 10.

## 20 October 2026: `correlation` and `covariance`, the `stats` package

**The package and the tables.** `packages/tier1/stats` (tier 1, order 6, after `dist`, which it uses for the t distribution) holds `correlation` and `covariance` as frame methods on two or more numeric variables (Bool counted as 0 and 1; another type Z0401, a single variable Z0401). The tables follow the owner's decision on question 2: a square table of the variables with three decimals, titled `correlation · wages · pearson` or `covariance · wages`; `N = 1,139` on a second title line when every pair has the same N (always under listwise deletion); `p_values: true` adds a table `p-values` of the same shape, `<0.001` below a thousandth; and a table `N per pair` follows when pairwise deletion leaves the Ns different. To print several tables from one value, `Table` gained a field `more`, further tables printed after it separated by a blank line; every constructor sets it, and `summary` and `describe` are unchanged.

**The statistics.** `zeff_numeric::association` holds covariance and Pearson's r (two-pass, compensated, fixed order), ranks with ties averaged, Spearman's ρ as Pearson's on the ranks, and Kendall's counts over every pair in a fixed order (O(n²): 1,200 rows take a moment, 18,412 a few seconds; Knight's O(n log n) algorithm is a later improvement) with τ-b and the tie-corrected variance of S (Kendall 1970), as R's `cor.test` forms it. The p-values reproduce `cor.test` branch by branch: Pearson's t with n − 2 degrees of freedom; Spearman exact without ties up to n = 1,290 inclusive (R's `prho`: enumeration of the permutations up to n = 9, the Edgeworth series of AS 89 beyond, the statistic Σd² shifted by two for the lower tail as R does), otherwise the t approximation; Kendall exact without ties below n = 50 (R's `ckendall` recursion for the number of permutations with k inversions), otherwise the normal approximation. The exact enumerations and series live in the kernel beside the distributions. A constant variable has no correlation: `NA` with W0205 naming it.

**What the comparison with R showed.** Every estimate and p-value of 22 pairs (two from the large wages file; untied series of 5 to 1,291 observations across both exact boundaries; perfect, reversed and tied series) agrees with `cor.test` within 1e-12, with two allowances: R's Pearson estimate leaves a residue of 1e-17 where the exact answer is 0 (the estimate is compared with an absolute tolerance of 1e-15), and R's Edgeworth series clamps to 0 deep in a tail where the engine gives 1e-63 (a p-value below 1e-15 on both sides is one answer). The boundary of R's exact Spearman branch is n ≤ 1,290, not n < 1,290 as its documentation reads; the test at 1,290 and 1,291 fixes it. The five matrices (three methods × two deletions) and the covariance matrices on the large file print R's values at three decimals, and the N per pair equals R's.

**A platform residue.** The first CI run found R's Pearson estimate for the tied series exactly 0 on the Linux runner where the Mac's R left 6.5e-18, so `check_r.py` compares `association.json` with an absolute floor of 1e-15 beside its relative 1e-12, which a correlation in [−1, 1] can bear and the files of unbounded values do not get.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/association.rs`: the matrices and the N against R, the 22 pairs to twelve digits, and snapshots of the layout (p-values, the N line and the N table, a constant variable's warning, `NA` through) and of the refusals (one variable, a text variable, an unknown variable, an unknown method word, a method called without a frame). The two catalogue rows are `implemented`.

**Reason.** The owner's decision on question 2; Language Reference, sections 4 ("Matrix results are Tables") and 6; Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.2 and 13 (`cor`, `pwcorr`, `correlate`); the catalogue rows 167 and 168; the checklist's step 11.

## 20 October 2026: `seed`

**Choice.** `seed(n: Int)` in `core`'s program functions sets the run's seed on the `Randomness` of step 4 and returns nothing. It is refused with Z0111 in two cases, each with its own wording: after a statement has drawn ("comes after a statement that has already drawn random numbers", the help naming the seed those draws used, so that a run can still be repeated), and when a seed is set already ("set once per script"). A `seed:` given to one `draw` is untouched by it and leaves it untouched, and such a draw does not count as a use of the run's stream, so `seed` may still follow it. The code is new to the engine (its page `codes/Z0111.md`; the catalogue's row 63 names it). The page records the one difference from R's `set.seed` and Stata's `set seed`: a statement's draws are keyed by its position in the run, so inserting a statement that does not draw changes the draws after it (as in R and Stata) while a `seed:` given to one call does not move.

**Tests.** `packages/tier0/core/tests/seed.rs`: the same seed gives the same draws and no note, another seed or a shifted position gives other draws, a `seed:` of one call is its own stream; the refusals (a late seed naming the chosen seed, a second seed, a bound result Z0206, a Float seed Z0401) as a snapshot.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 3; the catalogue's row 63; Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Random methods") and 11; the checklist's step 12.

## 22 October 2026: the 0.3.0 sample project, and one stream for each drawing call

**The sample.** `samples/simulation` (no data file): one `seed`, draws from the normal, exponential, Poisson and a lognormal mixture into a frame, `describe`, `summary`, the Pearson table with p-values, a Spearman table, `covariance`, a z statistic with its one- and two-sided p-values from `cdf(..., upper: true)`, a far tail (P(Z > 8)), a t quantile, a truncated normal and the mixture's median and tail. Its stored output is in `samples/simulation/expected/`; it is the third sample of the conformance report (three new lines, no existing line changed) and of the command-line script test.

**A defect found by writing it.** The first run showed the four independent columns correlated at 0.9 and above. Every drawing call of one statement opened the same stream, (seed, statement, pass) with the draw number from zero, so `frame(a = d.draw(400), b = d.draw(400))` gave two columns made from the same uniforms. Section 8.3, point 3, keys a draw by seed, statement, loop pass and draw number, and two draws written in one statement must be independent. The fix: the second counter word, until now the high half of the block number, holds the index of the call within its statement (0 for the first); the run's randomness counts the calls of the statement being run. The first call of every statement keeps the stream it had, so no earlier result, stored output or conformance line changed; the second call and later ones of a statement now differ from before (none existed in a stored output). A block number stays below 2^32, which is 2^34 uniforms to a call. A `seed:` given to one call is still a stream of its own wherever it is written, so two such calls with the same seed in one statement repeat each other, as the help page says. Inserting a drawing call into a statement moves the later calls of that statement, as inserting a statement moves the later statements.

**Tests.** A kernel test (another call gives another stream, call 0 equals `new`), and `seed.rs`: two draws in one statement are uncorrelated (r = -0.007 on 2,000 each), and the first of two equals the draw made alone.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 3; the checklist's step 13.

## 22 October 2026: the nightly stochastic run and the distribution fuzz target

**The stochastic run.** `packages/tier1/dist/tests/nightly_stochastic.rs` (marked ignored, so the quick suite skips it; the nightly job runs it with `--ignored` in release mode and prints its note): each of the 14 distributions of the stochastic class (12 families, a truncated normal, a mixture) is drawn 100,000 times under each of 50 seeds, every family on a stream of its own, and compared with its exact mean (each within 5 standard errors, and the 50 errors not leaning one way: their summed z-score within 4.5), its exact variance (within 5 per cent) and its distribution function (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance below 2.6/√n, a tail probability near 3e-6 for one seed). The checklist's wording was "the 50-seed comparison with R": R's draws cannot be matched value for value (another generator), so the comparison is with the exact moments and distribution functions, which R's own functions agree with at six digits in the reference tests; this is what the handbook allows ("within Monte Carlo error"). The table of 14 cases is shared with the quick recovery test (`tests/common/mod.rs`). The first local run took 68 seconds in release mode; the first version drew every family from the same uniforms (same seed, same statement ordinal), which made the Kolmogorov–Smirnov column identical for nine families, so each family now has its own ordinal.

**The fuzz target.** `fuzz/fuzz_targets/distribution.rs`: raw bits become the parameters (NaN, infinities, subnormals, huge shapes, probabilities outside [0, 1]), a family, a truncation or a two-part mixture, and a script calls `pdf`, `cdf` (both tails), `quantile` and `draw` through the whole engine; an internal error (Z9001) fails. It is the fifth target of the nightly job (ten minutes), whose time limit goes from 60 to 75 minutes.

**What it found in its first minute.** A negative binomial whose mean lies beyond the largest Float (size 13,827, p 1.2e-321) made `draw` run for ever: the discrete quantile search started from an infinite mean and its bracket never moved; once started from the largest Float, the halving step could stall on neighbouring Floats more than 1 apart; and a start near 1e300 needed a thousand doublings of a step of 1, each an evaluation of the incomplete gamma function at its iteration limit. Now: the start is capped at the largest Float, the first step is the start times 2^-40 (at least 1), the halving stops when the middle is no longer strictly between the ends, and a quantile that no Float reaches is `Inf`. A discrete draw beyond the Ints is `NA` rather than the largest Int. The kernel's accuracy for a parameter above 100,000 stays as the known issue records; this only makes such a call return. A regression test is in `distributions.rs`.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, sections 1 and 2.2; the checklist's step 14.

**The nightly job** (run 39715853858) passed. The stochastic note: all 14 distributions inside their limits under 50 seeds (summed z-scores between -1.64 and +1.10 against a limit of 4.5; the worst Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance 0.0060 against 0.0082), the same figures to the last digit as on the Mac.

Repairs: `set -o pipefail` in the loop; and the discrete quantile search now ends with `NA` at the first `NA` of the distribution function, since parameters so large that the incomplete functions cannot be evaluated leave nothing to search (the quantile of a negative binomial with a mean beyond the Floats is therefore `NA`, no longer `Inf`; the regression test says so). The failing input from GitHub runs in under a second, and five minutes of local fuzzing found nothing further. Throughput on huge parameters is low (about 7 runs a second), which the ten minutes of the nightly job accepts.

## 22 October 2026: the second fuzz run, and a slow CSV header

**What happened.** With the job now failing on a failing target (`pipefail`), the second run (39722071331) failed on the CSV target, not on the distributions, which ran 16,447 inputs cleanly. A 34 KB input of delimiters took 19 seconds (18 KB took 5.6): the check of the column names compared every name with every earlier one, lower-casing both each time, so a header of tens of thousands of names cost the square of their number. A fault of release 0.1.0 that the earlier fuzz runs, blind to failures, never reported.

**The repair.** A map from each lower-cased name to its first position finds the first earlier column with the same name, ignoring case, in one step; it reports exactly what the pairwise loop reported (an exact repeat, a snake-case clash or a case clash, with the same positions). The 34 KB input now takes 0.7 seconds, the 18 KB one 0.25. A regression test reads a header of 40,000 names and checks that the first repeat and the first case clash are still the ones named. A remaining 0.7 seconds for 34 KB is linear-ish work on a very wide file and is left as it is.

## 22 October 2026: a review of the engine changes of steps 13 and 14 before the tag

**Why.** Steps 13 and 14 were built with the lighter model where the owner's convention names the stronger one for an engine step, so their three engine changes (the stream keying, the discrete quantile search, the `NA` rules for draws) were reviewed afresh before the release was tagged, with a probe of the distribution functions at large parameters against R 4.6.0.

**What the review found.** The three changes stood, with two small repairs: the stream's comment claimed 2^34 uniforms where 2^32 blocks hold 2^33, and past that the block counter wrapped silently (now an internal error); and a note that when loops arrive the per-call counter must start again at each pass. The probe found something worse that the reviewed changes had not caused: `dist.poisson(lambda: 1e9).cdf(1e9)` printed 0.50127 where 0.500008 is right. The kernel was innocent (Q(10⁹ + 1, 10⁹) agrees with R to 3.5e-13 when called directly); the `dist` layer floored the point x with a fuzz of 1e-7 *of x*, so at x = 10⁹ it added 100 and computed P(X ≤ 10⁹ + 100). The error grew with √λ: 2.5e-4 at 10⁷, 2.5e-3 at 10⁹, 2.5e-2 at 10¹¹, in the Poisson, binomial and negative binomial distribution functions alike (a wrong result without an error, S1). R's fuzz is an absolute 1e-7 (`floor(x + 1e-7)`), and that is the fix. Below 10⁷ nothing changes, since the fuzz stays below one; the conformance report is unchanged.

**A second defect, in the kernel.** The incomplete gamma series needs about 8√a terms near x = a; past its limit of two million terms (a shape of about 10¹¹) it returned the partial sum as if it had converged: 0.477 at 10¹² where 0.5000001 is right, 0.236 at 10¹³. The series and both continued fractions now return not-a-number when they run out of terms, so the gamma, Poisson and chi-square functions give `NA` there and a quantile or a draw that needs them is `NA`. The incomplete beta function still converges at 10¹⁴ but loses digits near its centre: 1.7e-12 at 10¹¹, 3.5e-10 at 10¹², 5.6e-10 at 10¹³ (measured against R). Both are in the known-issues list with these figures; Temme's expansions remain the later step.

**Two false alarms.** The probe first showed the beta far tail at a = b = 10⁵ as 0 against R's 1.9e-19, and the gamma upper tails off by 1e-9: both were the probe printing fifteen decimals, not digits. The kernel's values were right.

**Tests.** A kernel unit test (not-a-number past the limit; 10¹⁰ still within 2e-12; the beta near its centre at 10¹³ within 1e-9) and a `dist` test holding R's `ppois`, `pnbinom`, `pbinom` and their quantiles at 10⁷ to 10¹² (1e-10 on the gamma path, 1e-9 on the two binomial rows at 10¹², and `NA` where the series cannot converge). The grid and the R script used for the probe are not kept; the test carries the values.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, sections 2.4 (fixes only before a release) and 3 (an S1 bug is fixed first); the owner's question of 22 October 2026 on the model used for steps 13 and 14.

**The run.** The weekly mutation run of the numeric kernel (run 39756127163, on commit e72cf00, four shards) tested 1,877 mutants: 1,761 caught, 47 missed, 59 timed out, 10 unviable. The kernel lists 1,879 mutants today: the two more are the `delete !` mutants of the `if !converged` guards that the review of the same day added to `incomplete_gamma`, both caught by the run on the review's own lines. So every mutant of the kernel as it stood was tested. The owner asked for the release to wait until every survivor had a test or a reason and every timeout a verdict.

**The 47 survivors: 19 now caught by a test, 26 equivalent, 2 removed with dead code.**

Tests added (kernel unit tests, so that the kernel's own suite catches them in seconds):
- `covariance` and `pearson` refuse fewer than two pairs, series of different lengths and a series whose mean is not finite, and accept two pairs (eight guard mutants). Two mutants of the deviations in `covariance` survived because `Σ (a + x̄)(b − ȳ)` equals `Σ (a − x̄)(b − ȳ)` in exact arithmetic (the other series' deviations sum to zero); they differ in rounding, so two cases with values near 1e15 and 1e16, where the two-pass form is exact and a product with a raw value in it rounds at multiples of four, catch them.
- `ranks` is one-based with ties averaged (three mutants: a shifted or scaled rank is invisible to Spearman's correlation, which is affine-invariant, but not to the function's contract); `Kendall::has_ties` sees a tie in either series.
- `choose` is exact while the integers fit and rounded once after (C(50, 25), C(60, 30), C(100, 50) exactly), where a product of rounded ratios differs in the last digits; `log_beta` refuses a zero parameter; the gamma inverse refuses a shape that is not positive or not a number before answering the edges p = 0 and p = 1 (two guard mutants), and a corrupted underflow guard (`log(a) * lgamma(a)`) returned 0 for the median of a gamma with shape 0.01, where R gives 4.47e-31.
- `deviance`, which no kernel test called directly (the dist package's tests reached it, slowly), against seven values computed exactly in decimal arithmetic, one of them (x = 1,000,001, m = 1,000,000) where the plain form loses 2e-10 to cancellation, so the series branch must be the one taken.

Equivalent, with the reason, by site in today's numbering:
- `gamma` 61 (two) and 64: the clause refusing a negative integer is redundant with `libm::tgamma`, which returns not-a-number there (checked for −1, −2, −170, −171, −1e6, −1e300), and x = 0 is refused by the first clause; the clause stays because it states the rule.
- `choose` 96 (two): `k > 600` against `k == 600` or `k >= 600`: C(1200, 600) exceeds the largest Float, so the computed value overflows to `Inf` exactly as the early answer; a test now states it.
- `log_beta` 128: `a < b` against `a <= b` chooses the same pair when a = b.
- `deviance` 178 (two) and `beta_prefix` 473 and 478, `incomplete_beta` 557, `incomplete_gamma_inverse` 433 (the −745 boundary): a boundary between two formulas that agree wherever both are defined; the mutant moves the boundary by one exact value, or chooses the other valid formula, and changes a result only in rounding.
- Lentz guards in `incomplete_gamma` 374 and 378 (four) and `beta_fraction` 496, 512, 516, 523 (eight), and the convergence tests at 384 and 533: `|d| < 1e-300` against `==` or `<=`, `|delta − 1| < 1e-16` against `<=`: the guards protect the recurrence from an exact zero that no finite input of the references, properties or edges reaches, and equality with 1e-300 or 1e-16 is a value no input lands on; narrowing them changes no reachable result.
- `incomplete_gamma_inverse` 433 (two, `+ log(a)` to `− log(a)`): the underflow guard fires when the leading term of the lower tail lies below the smallest Float; the mutants move its threshold, but on either side of it the quantile is below the smallest normal Float, and the difference between returning 0 and a denormal is not a result the engine prints or compares. 440: a start of exactly 0 for Newton (`guess > 0` against `>=`) needs `1 − 1/(9a) + z/(3√a)` to be exactly zero, which no input does, and Newton converges from either start.
- Removed: `log1p_minus` kept a plain branch for |d| ≥ 0.1 that its one caller never reaches (it takes the logarithm of the ratio there), so the two survivors on it were in dead code; the branch is gone and a debug assertion states the caller's condition.

**The 59 timeouts: 54 now caught, 5 are hangs by nature.** A timeout means the mutated kernel ran the tests for five times their usual time. Rerunning every mutant of the affected sites against the kernel's own tests (354 mutants, 318 caught, 10 timed out, 24 missed as above, 2 unviable) showed the cause: 42 of them stop a continued fraction or series converging, so each call runs to its two-million-term cap before answering not-a-number; the kernel's exact reference rejects that in seconds, but two tests of the dist package make over a million kernel calls (the moments of 100,000 draws per distribution; R's grid of every family) and run for hours first. Those two tests are skipped by the weekly mutation job from now on (`cargo mutants -- -- --skip …`); CI still runs them on every push. The other 17 were hangs: the series of `deviance` and `log1p_minus` had no cap, so a mutant that stopped their terms shrinking never returned; each now gives up after 100 terms (nine and seventeen reach full precision) and returns not-a-number, which the new value tests reject, so twelve of them are caught. The five that remain are loops whose index no longer advances (`ranks` 67 and 73, `tie_groups` 151, `choose` 110 and 114): a test can only time out on them, and the job counts them as timeouts.

**Checks.** Format, clippy with warnings denied, all workspace tests (the kernel's unit tests 25 to 32), the tier and message checks and the conformance report, unchanged, pass; a rerun of every mutant of `deviance`, `log1p_minus` and `covariance` (85) caught 83 with no timeout. The final figures come from the twelve-shard weekly run on this commit, recorded in the release notes.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, sections 1 (mutation testing) and 2.4; the owner's instruction of 22 October 2026 to hold 0.3.0 until the survivors had tests and the timeouts verdicts.

Tests added, all kernel unit tests, so that the kernel's own suite catches them in seconds:
- Floored division and the remainder at infinite operands (an infinite dividend divides to itself; a remainder of infinities is not a number; a finite number divided by an infinity leaves itself, or the infinity's side of zero when the signs differ), and the signed zero of a zero quotient (−1 by −2 is +0 where the remainder is −1; until now only the command line's self-test noticed that one).
- The incomplete beta function, its density and its inverse refuse a zero shape before their edges x = 0, x = 1, p = 0 and p = 1 are answered; the density's values at the ends.
- Kendall: two pairs give an estimate; a tie group away from the start has its size; a pair tied in one series only counts as neither concordant nor discordant; the exact null distribution counts the permutations (1, 2, 2, 1 over 3! and 1, 3, 5, 6, 5, 3, 1 over 4!), and a q beyond the range answers 1, which also exercises the clamp that keeps the count inside its vector.
- The smallest probability a double holds has a finite normal quantile, a statement of fact beside the equivalent mutant below.

Equivalent, with the reason:
- `maths.rs`: `round` 135 and `round_significant` 199, the early return for a non-finite or zero x short-cuts a path that gives the same answer (Rust formats and parses not-a-number and the infinities as themselves, and a zero keeps its sign); `round` 143, a tie's even rounding never equals x; `away_from_zero` 189, a decimal point with no digits after it parses to the same number; `div_int` 219 and `mod_int` 237 (two each), `div_float` 253 (two) and `mod_float` 286 (two), a remainder of zero or a divisor of zero is excluded before the signs are compared; `div_float` 257, the sign of a product is the sign of the quotient; 261, the quotient lands a hair below the whole number, never a half; `mod_float` 271 (the second `||`) and 277 (two), with b not a number, zero or infinite the remainder arithmetic gives the guard's own answer.
- `special.rs`: `normal_quantile` 286, p = ½ is answered before the comparison; 294, the density underflows to zero only for a probability below the smallest double (the smallest one's quantile is −38.47, where the density is 6e-322), and an f of zero ends the loop by a zero step anyway; `incomplete_gamma` 330, a negative or not-a-number x makes the prefix not a number by arithmetic, so the guard only saves two million terms; 356, one iteration at exact equality. The 27 recorded in the first batch stand.
- `association.rs`: `tie_groups` 143, the loop bound's equality short-circuits before any index; `kendall` 164, a self-pair is skipped as a tie; 165, a product of ±1 signs equals their quotient; 169, the sign is never zero where it is compared; `kendall_exact_cdf` 199 (three), a scratch vector sized generously keeps zeros beyond the true maximum and every probability is the same.
- `order.rs` `quantile` 65 and 72: |h| equal to the fuzz exactly is unreachable, as is h = 1 (h lies in [−fuzz, 1 − fuzz)); the branch mirrors R's `quantile` and stays.

**Timeouts.** The run's six are the hangs by nature (`ranks` 67 and 73, `tie_groups` 146 and 151, `choose` 110 and 114) and nothing else.

**Tests (16).** Kendall's variance of S with the tie corrections of Kendall (1970), including the term for ties of three in both series, which the first cases had made zero; Spearman's exact tail at its maximum (the reversed ordering alone, one permutation in n!, which the guard's mutants `>=` and `==` answer as zero) and beyond it (zero and one, which `1 + pv` and `1 / pv` do not give); `is_tie` on halves and non-halves at negative digits; the weighted quantile's refusal of a probability outside [0, 1] and of a zero-weight value; `choose`'s symmetry to the bit; the beta inverse's upper tail of 1e-300 answering one (the deleted `!` had applied the lower guard to it), its lower tail of 1e-300 answering zero, and the median of a beta with shapes 0.01 and 1 (0.5^100), which two corrupted guards turned into zero.

**Equivalent (25).** Spearman's exact tail 228 (three): the guard's threshold n(n² − 1)/3 moved up still agrees with the enumeration and the series beyond the maximum, where both give zero; 248 and 251 (two): a permutation's elements are distinct, so equality and a self-pair never occur. `is_tie` 112 and 114: a subnormal is never a tie whichever sign its exponent is given, and bit 52 of the mantissa field is clear, so `|` and `^` agree. `quantile` 72 (`+` to `*`): the h = 1 branch is unreachable, as recorded for its sibling. `weighted_sum` 117: a total of zero with non-negative weights means every product is zero, and 0 × n / 0 is not a number either way. The beta inverse 607 (`+ log(a)` to `− log(a)`; `<` to `<=`): the guard moved to fire less, or at an unreachable equality, still returns a quantile below the smallest normal double; 612 (two): the upper guard's threshold moved by log(b)/b changes answers only at the last double below one; 620 (two): a start of exactly zero or one from the normal approximation needs an exact coincidence; 628 (three): Newton converges from an end of the interval, or never needs the fallback. `newton_with_bracket` 660: the derivative's sign is the same anywhere for a monotone function; 672: f = 0 ended the loop a line earlier; 679: an infinite slope needs the density at zero, where Newton never stands; 686: the expansion of an open bracket, which no test reaches (the gamma inverse's start never overshoots below its bracket in the references), a gap in coverage noted here; 693 (two): the step condition stops the loop on its own.

## 23 October 2026: The `zeff-kernels` crate

**Choice.** `kernel/zeff-kernels` is the linear-algebra module of section 8.1, rule 8: pure Rust, `unsafe` denied, no dependency. It holds a dense column-major `Matrix`; the reductions in the shape of open decision #47 (`reduce`: `LANES` independent accumulators, element i going to accumulator i mod `LANES`, each with Knuth's two-sum error term, the accumulators combined in lane order at the end, and the rotation carried across slices so that a sequence gives the same bits however it is cut; `sum`, `dot`, `sum_of_squares`, `norm`); matrix products whose every entry is such a dot product (`product`); Householder QR with LAPACK's reflector convention (`qr::r_factor`); the tall-skinny QR (`qr::TallSkinnyQr`), which re-cuts the rows it is given into blocks of `BLOCK_ROWS` = 65,536, factorises each block on its own and folds the block's R into the running one in block order, the shape of #48, so that a parallel version computing the block factors on several threads gives the same bits; the limited column pivoting of R's `dqrdc2` (`qr::pivoted_qr`: the columns factorised in order, a column whose remaining norm is below the tolerance times its own original norm moved to the end and left out, a zero norm counting as one so that a zero column is left out too, and columns beyond the pivot candidates transformed but never pivoted, so that the outcome rides along as the last column of `[X y]` and the residual sum of squares is the sum of squares of its tail); `qr::least_squares` on those, returning the kept R factor as well, from which (XᵀX)⁻¹ and the leverages follow; triangular solves and the triangular inverse (`triangular`); Cholesky with the first pivot that is not positive reported (`cholesky`); and the singular values by one-sided Jacobi rotations in a fixed sweep order, with the 2-norm condition number from them (`svd`). Inputs are finite and below about 1e150 in magnitude, which the model layer guarantees.

**Why 65,536 rows a block.** Section 8.3, point 10 allows up to a million; a block of a hundred columns then weighs 800 MB, where 65,536 rows weigh 52 MB, and the fold of a 2k × k stack per block costs nothing beside the block's own factorisation. The constant is part of the numerical definition of a fit and changes only with a release note.

**Why no intrinsics.** Section 8.3, point 3 names explicit 128-bit SIMD; what the contract needs is that the bits do not depend on the width, and the lane shape gives exactly that: the compiler may vectorise the lane loop or not, the operations and their order are the same. Intrinsics would need `unsafe` in the kernel; they are an optimisation for a later release if the benchmarks of #52 ask for one, and would change no bit. Two things the measurement of this step taught about the shape in Rust: the accumulators are copied to local arrays for the chunk loop, since through `&mut self` the compiler keeps them in memory; and the product loop takes the sum loop's form (the products of a chunk into an array, then one pass over the lanes), because a loop that zips the two chunks and enumerates the lanes compiles to code five times slower with the same arithmetic.

**Why recomputed norms in the pivoting.** `dqrdc2` downdates the column norms as it goes and recomputes one when the downdate loses accuracy; the kernel recomputes every remaining norm from the transformed column, which on the k × k factor the fit hands it costs nothing beside the QR of the rows and is deterministic by construction. The decisions agree with R's on every case of the reference; the order among the columns left out is that of the moves and means nothing.

**Tests.** 25 unit tests of exact small cases in the modules, so that a mutant dies in the crate's own suite in seconds (the lesson of the 0.3.0 close); `tests/properties.rs` (a sum cut into slices of any sizes gives the same bits; integer sums and dot products are exact; RᵀR is XᵀX within rounding; the blocked QR equals the block factors folded in order at any block size and any way of handing over the rows; a column scaled by a power of two scales its coefficient exactly and changes no other bit, since every operation of the factorisation commutes with such a scaling; a triangular solve inverts its product; the Cholesky factor reproduces its matrix; the singular values carry the Frobenius norm); `tests/reference_exact.rs` against `tests/reference/kernels.py`, which computes twelve least-squares cases in exact rational arithmetic with Python's `fractions` on the binary values of the inputs (columns at 1e7, 1e9 and 1e12, an exact duplicate, a near-collinear column dropped at 1e-9 and kept at 1e-5, a zero column, a wide matrix, an exact fit; the collinearity rule applied exactly), a triangular system with its inverse, a positive-definite system, and sums whose compensation matters; `tests/reference_r.rs` against `tests/reference/r/kernels.R` (R 4.6.0's `qr` with its limited pivoting and `qr.coef`, `qr.resid` and the leverages from `qr.Q`, the singular values, `backsolve`, `chol` and the solve through the factor; the same inputs as hexadecimal floats, read exactly). The tolerances scale with the condition number of the kept columns once each is scaled to unit norm, 1e-14 times it with a floor of 1e-12: on the case whose condition number is 3.3e5 the kernel and R each lie about 7e-11 from the exact solution, on opposite sides, which is what the condition allows. Six `kernels/*` series in the conformance report (the reductions, a 1,000 × 6 least-squares fit through four folded blocks with a duplicate column left out, its R factor, the inverse, the Cholesky factor of the kept Gram matrix, the singular values and the condition number) hold the bits on the four targets. The reference job of CI re-runs both scripts and compares R's file within 1e-12.

**Two things learnt about R.** `solve` (LU with partial pivoting) loses four digits on the positive-definite case, a matrix with a diagonal entry of 1e12 beside entries of order one, where the solve through the Cholesky factor keeps ten, so the script solves through `chol`, as the kernel does. And `qr` on an n × k matrix with k > n stops at row n and leaves the surplus columns where they are, while the kernel, which pivots the k × k factor, moves them to the end; the columns kept are the same.

**Reason.** Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.1 (rule 8), 8.3 (points 3 and 10) and 13; Language Reference, section 7.2 ("Collinearity"); open decisions #47 and #48 as the owner took them; the checklist's step 2.
