## 23 October 2026: The reduction shape measured, and N = 16 (open decision #47)

**The measurement.** `cargo bench -p zeff-kernels --bench reduction` (criterion 0.8.2, release profile): one sum and one dot product over ten million doubles in [−0.5, 0.5), the scalar Neumaier sum shipped in `zeff-numeric` since 0.1.0 against the two-sum lane shape at 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 lanes, with a plain uncompensated loop as the floor. On the owner's machine (Apple M2 Pro, ARM64, 128-bit NEON), the mean of twenty samples:

| Shape | Sum | Dot product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plain loop, no compensation | 8.61 ms | 8.59 ms |
| Neumaier, scalar (`zeff-numeric`; the dot as products into a vector, then its sum) | 10.81 ms | 13.40 ms |
| Two-sum, 2 lanes | 5.01 ms | 6.76 ms |
| Two-sum, 4 lanes | 3.08 ms | 6.14 ms |
| Two-sum, 8 lanes | 2.69 ms | 6.08 ms |
| Two-sum, 16 lanes | 2.56 ms | 3.11 ms |
| Two-sum, 32 lanes | 2.63 ms | 3.53 ms |

A plain loop is a chain of dependent additions, so it is no faster than the compensated scalar sum; the lanes break the chain. The dot product's dip at 4 and 8 lanes is a code-generation accident of those widths (the same arithmetic in a throwaway probe ran at 3.8 ms with 8 lanes), not a property of the shape.

**Choice.** `LANES` = 16: the fastest shape for both reductions on this machine, 4.2 times the speed of the scalar Neumaier sum and 4.3 times that of the scalar dot product. The figure is now part of the numerical definition of every reduction of `zeff-kernels` and changes only with a release note. The same benchmark on the x86-64 runner (GitHub-hosted, a baseline SSE2 build, as the official x86-64 builds are; run 39852353049) gave, for the sum, 9.45 ms plain, 15.10 ms scalar Neumaier, 9.55, 6.01, 5.69, 6.97 and 5.97 ms at 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 lanes, and for the dot product 9.58 ms plain, 24.84 ms scalar, 11.97, 8.72, 7.64, 6.20 and 6.53 ms: there 8 lanes is a fifth faster than 16 on the sum and 16 is the fastest on the dot product, four times the scalar. Sixteen is the best shape on the owner's machine for both reductions and the best or within a fifth of the best on the runner, so it stands.

**Consequence.** The owner's decision of 23 October 2026 moves the reducers of 0.1.0 to 0.3.0 to the shape at this release when the gain is a fifth or more; at fourfold it is, so the checklist gains step 2b, in which `zeff-numeric`'s sums move to `zeff_kernels::reduce` one routine at a time, with the changed last digits of the published conformance cases regenerated deliberately and listed for the release notes.

**Reason.** Open decision #47 as recommended and taken ("N fixed by that measurement and recorded once"); section 8.3, point 3; the checklist's step 2.

## 23 October 2026: The reducers of `zeff-numeric` on the reduction shape (step 2b)

**Choice.** Every sum over values in `zeff-numeric` is now the lane sum of `zeff-kernels` (a kernel crate may depend on a kernel crate): `sum` is `zeff_kernels::sum`; `mean` sums the values and then the deviations in that shape; the scaled two-pass variance behind `variance` and `sd` takes the sum of squares and the sum of the scaled deviations from it; `covariance` and `pearson` take the dot products and sums of squares of the centred series; the weighted mean, sum and variance already went through `sum` and moved with it, as did the weight totals of the column kernel and the `sum` statistic of `data`. The Neumaier accumulator is gone. Three loops stay sequential by nature and are not sums over rows: the running total of the weighted quantile (a prefix sum, where the order is the definition), the series and continued fractions of the special functions, and the small fixed sums over the components of a mixture distribution or the tie groups of Kendall's variance (exact integers in the latter case); the shape of #47 is for reductions over observations.

**The fallback.** The whole-slice functions of the kernel (`sum`, `dot`, `sum_of_squares`) keep the documented behaviour of the old `sum`: a result that is not finite is replaced by the plain left-to-right IEEE sum, which gives `Inf` for `Inf` alone, not-a-number for `Inf` with `-Inf`, and may still be finite where the lanes overflowed on the way (sixteen alternating values of ±1e308 sum to 0 in order and to not-a-number by lanes); the streaming accumulator, having no slice to return to, folds its lane sums plainly.

**What changed in the published results: nothing.** Every one of the 127 lines of the conformance report, the three sample projects' stored output, the exact and R references of 0.1.0 to 0.3.0 and every snapshot are unchanged by the move. That is what the arithmetic predicts: a compensated sum of some thousands of values is the correctly rounded exact sum except at rare boundaries (an independent check in exact rational arithmetic found the two orders equal, and both correctly rounded, in 200 of 200 series of 10,000 values), so two compensated orders agree to the bit. The release notes therefore list no changed digit for this step. A test in `zeff-numeric` holds each moved routine to the kernel's lane sums to the bit.

**Reason.** Open decision #47 as the owner took it (the shipped reducers move when the measured gain is a fifth or more; step 2 measured fourfold); the checklist's step 2b.

## 23 October 2026: Ordered categories, contrasts and comparisons on categories (step 3)

**The fields.** A Category column carries, beside its levels, an ordered flag and a contrast (`CategoryInfo` in the column kernel; `Contrast` is `treatment`, `sum`, `helmert` or `poly`), kept by `slice`, `take`, cloning and every table operation, and written to and read from the Arrow field metadata as `zeff:ordered` (`true` or `false`) and `zeff:contrast` (one of the four words), both written for every category field so that other tools see them; a stream whose key holds anything else is refused rather than guessed. They are fields of the type, as section 3.8's table places them, not keys of the nine-key store, whose list section 4.3 keeps closed. Ordering a category sets `measure` to `ordinal` (section 4.3: `category(ordered: true)` sets it); removing the order removes an `ordinal` entry and leaves any other reader's. The shipped `wages.arrow` is rebuilt with the two keys on `industry` (the CSV files and `sleep.arrow` are unchanged; `CHECKSUMS` follows).

**Value labels.** The `value_labels` entry is one JSON object of code to text, `{"0": "male", "1": "female"}`, written by `format_value_labels` and read by `parse_value_labels` in the column kernel: a reader of that one shape with JSON's escapes, `None` for anything else, and the store's `value_labels()` on top of it. The frame and table printers, `describe` and the dataset pages read through it, where each parsed the text by hand before and a label holding a comma would have broken them; `label` at step 6 writes through it.

**Comparisons.** In `core`'s operators, before the ordinary kind rules: a category column compares with text by its levels (`industry == "Retail"`, the text on either side, `NA` giving `NA`), with a text column by label row by row, and with another category by label whatever their levels; under `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` an ordered category compares by level position, against text that must be a level, against a text column every value of which must be a level (Z0216 naming the row otherwise), or against another ordered category with the same levels in the same order (Z0221 otherwise); an order comparison on a category without an order is Z0221, its help naming `category(x, levels: [...], ordered: true)`; text that is no level is Z0216 listing the levels (up to twelve, then the count); arithmetic, `&&`, `||`, `-` and `!` on a category are Z0221, no longer Z0304, which now names the `time` package of 0.6.0 for dates and times alone. An Int column with value labels compares as the number it holds: text against it is Z0216 with the code the label stands for in the help, written with the operator used (`write != 2`), or with the labels listed when the text is none of them. Z0216 is the code section 3.7 gives both conditions; its explained page is new.

**A fault found by the edge case.** A `where` that kept no rows lost a category's levels: Arrow's `take` with no indices returns an empty dictionary, so a later `== "Retail"` on the empty frame would have been refused as text that is no level. `Column::take` now gathers a category's codes itself and keeps the levels, since a level with no rows is still a level (section 4.2). Present since 0.2.0, found by this step's edge case before any script met it. The property's seed file (`kernel/zeff-columns/tests/categories.proptest-regressions`) records that case and is kept, by the rule of 0.1.0 that a seed file is committed when it records an engine fault the fixed test must keep catching.

**Tests.** `kernel/zeff-columns/tests/categories.rs`: the fields through slice, take and the Arrow round trip, the measure set and removed, a corrupted key refused, value labels with escapes and Unicode both ways and every malformed shape refused, and a property that every table operation and the round trip keep a column's whole store and fields. The operator rules at the column level in `core`: equality and order with text, with text columns and with categories, the sides flipped, every refusal, the labelled Int. `crates/zeff-engine/tests/categories.rs` on the shipped `wages` and `sleep`: the row counts of `where` with `==` and `!=` on either side, `NA`, a level with no rows, a Bool column from a comparison, and a snapshot of every message, both Z0216 wordings among them.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Comparison"), 3.8 (the Category row), 4.2 and 4.3 rule 3; Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 10; the checklist's step 3.

## 23 October 2026: `to`, `is` and `type_of` (step 4)

**Choice.** A new module of `core`, `types.rs`, for the family "Types and categories" (`category`, `levels` and `base` join it at step 5). `to(x, type)` and `is(x, type)` are methods on any value (their first parameter is `Any`, which the checker's method lookup accepts for every receiver, so `x.to(Int)` and `to(x, Int)` both read); `type_of(x)` is a function. `to` follows the table of section 3.7 and the conversions each column type declares (section 4.3, rule 1): numbers to text as the shortest text that reads back to the same number (a zero of either sign as `0`, the infinities as `Inf` and `-Inf`); text to a number when it is a whole decimal literal or a Float literal of the language with spaces around it ignored (`1_000`, `1,000`, `+5`, `.5`, `5.` and `0x10` are not numbers; `Inf` and `-Inf` read as the infinities); text to Bool from `true` and `false` in any case; Int to Bool from 0 and 1; Bool to Int and Float as 0 and 1; a Float to Int only when it is whole and within the Ints; text to Category with the distinct values in code-point order as levels, which needs a column; a category to text as its labels and to Int as its level positions from 1; a date or time to text in ISO form. A value that cannot convert is `NA` with W0203, which gives the count and up to three failing values, text in quotes; a number with a fraction or an infinity given to Int is `NA` with W0202, whose help names `round`, `floor` and `truncate`; `to(NA, T)` is `NA` with no warning. A type with no conversion to the target is Z0401 at run time, the help listing the conversions it has; `to(Category)` on a single value, a frame, a list or a record is Z0401 as well. Conversion to Date and DateTime is Z0304 naming release 0.6.0, as the catalogue's row 36 places it ("to Date from 0.6.0"), though the checklist's text for the step had assumed it; the catalogue is the authority. Given a column, `to` converts the whole column in its body rather than through the row-wise lift, since the warnings are counted over rows and `Category` needs every value; the result column carries no metadata (a derived column starts empty, section 4.3). `is` tests by the names of section 4: a scalar type name on a column tests what the column holds, so `wages["wage"].is(Float)` and `wages["industry"].is(Category)` are true, as is `.is(Column)`; an Int is not a Float; `NA` has no type and `is` gives `false` for it under every name but `Any`; `Failed`, `Result` and the other types no value has yet give `false`. `type_of` writes `Column<Float>`, `List<Float>` (Int and Float joining), `Mapping<Int, Str>` from the first pair, `Record`, `NA`, and `Type` for a type name given to it.

**The checker.** A new result rule beside `Join` and `Number`: `Typed` gives a call the type its `Type` argument names, as a column when the receiver is one (`Category` giving a column of unknown element type, since the checker does not track categories before the schema pass). The type names a script may write as values grew from the six scalar names to those of section 4 (`Category`, `Frame`, `Table`, `Column`, `List`, `Record`, `Mapping`, `Distribution`, `Result`, `Failed`, `Any`, `Type`; the result types join at step 12), and a bare name is read as a type name wherever a `Type` is expected before it could be a column of the enclosing frame method or a binding, so that `add(h = to(hours, Float))` works inside a frame method.

**The catalogue corrected.** Rows 36 and 37 wrote `x.to(Type)` and `x.is(Type)`, the parameter's type where every other row writes its name; corrected to `x.to(type)` and `x.is(type)` and logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`.

**Tests.** `packages/tier0/core/tests/types.rs`: against R 4.6.0 (`tests/reference/r/types.R`: `as.integer`, `as.numeric` and `as.logical` on twenty texts, `as.character` on thirteen numbers, the Bools) wherever the two sets of rules agree, the departures named in the test (R reads hexadecimal, a leading plus and a bare point, truncates a fraction to an integer, does not trim text given to `as.logical`, writes fifteen significant digits and `e+05`; its own reading of `1e300` is four units off, so its number rather than the literal is what the test converts; and `as.integer("NaN")` is the C cast of a NaN, 0 on one processor and NA on another, so that text is left out of the file); the edge-case datasets (all `NA`, no rows, one row, the Bool spellings, the infinities, the magnitudes to text and back, the Unicode labels to a category whose levels sort by code point, an Int beyond the Ints, spaces, `NaN`); the properties that a Float to text and back is the same Float to the bit (normal, subnormal and zero), that Ints and Bools round-trip, that a whole Float to Int is the Int, and that `type_of` and `is` agree with the column's type; a snapshot of `is` and `type_of` on every kind of value; a snapshot of every message. The milestone script of the conformance report gained six statements.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Conversion", "Words and types"), 4 and 5.6 (W0202, W0203); the catalogue rows 36 to 38; the checklist's step 4.

## 23 October 2026: The milestone case of the conformance report had failed silently since 0.2.0

**What was found.** The milestone script of the conformance report (`milestone/*`, the whole engine on one script of every construct) has carried the line `-a` since commit 7bcb2ed of 18 October 2026 (release 0.2.0, step 2, "expressions over values"), and the parser refuses a line that begins with an operator (Z0305, by design and in the known-issues list). The script therefore stopped at its check with exit code 1 and printed nothing, and the report recorded the digests of that failure, the empty text's for `milestone/stdout` and an exit code of 1, which every target reproduced alike through the identity checks of 0.2.0 and 0.3.0. The published report said so plainly (`# milestone/exit_code bits 3ff0000000000000` is 1.0) and nobody read it. The sample projects' cases, which also run the whole engine and whose test asserts exit code 0 and the stored output, were sound throughout, so the four-target identity of the engine was still proven; what was lost was the milestone's own coverage of the operators, mappings, records and columns.

**The repair.** The line is `print(-a)`, the milestone's three digests are regenerated (the only lines of the report that changed), and the conformance crate gains a test that the milestone script runs to the end with output and no error, as the samples had. Found at step 4 when the report did not change after statements were appended to the script.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, section 1 ("Cross-platform identity") and section 3 (a test that passes for the wrong reason is a bug of the suite); risk R2's mitigation, which rests on this report.

## 23 October 2026: `category`, `levels` and `base` (step 5)

**The levels.** `category(var)` takes its levels from the column when `levels:` is not given: a text column's distinct values in code-point order, which is the byte order of UTF-8 and the order R's `factor` gives in the C locale (the reference script sets `LC_COLLATE` to `C`; in any other locale R's order depends on the machine); an Int or Float column's distinct values in numeric order, each level the number's printed text (the shortest text that reads back, as `to(Str)` writes it), so that a level `16` matches a Float of 16 and `levels: [16, 12, 17]` reads against either; an Int with value labels gives its labels in the order of the codes, a code without a label keeping its number as its text, so that `levels:` can name it; a category keeps its own levels. `levels:` is a list of text or numbers, each once (a repeat is Z0401, as is an `NA`, a Bool or any other value among them), and sets both the levels and their order; a value that is none of them is `NA` and counted under W0203, the code a value that does not convert carries, since `category` with `levels:` is the Str-to-Category conversion of section 3.7 with the levels chosen; the message gives the count and up to three distinct values in quotes. With this step the warning of `to` lists distinct values too (it listed the first three failures, which were often one value three times). A Bool, Date or DateTime column is Z0401 with the help to convert it first. A level with no rows is a level; an all-`NA` column has no levels unless `levels:` gives them; no rows gives no levels.

**The fields and the result.** `ordered: true` and `contrast:` write the ordered flag and the contrast of step 3; the result carries no other metadata, as a derived column starts empty (section 4.3). More than 10,000 levels is W0602 (`MANY_LEVELS` in `types.rs`; the threshold of section 3.8), the warning saying that an identifier may have been categorised and its explained page showing a panel's row identifier.

**`levels` and `base`.** `levels(var)` is the `List<Str>` of the levels in the category's order; a column that is no category is Z0401 naming its type. `base(var, level)` moves the level to the front and keeps the others in their order, as R's `relevel` and Stata's `ib#.` do, the codes remapped and the ordered flag, the contrast and the whole metadata store kept; a level the category does not have is Z0216 listing the levels (as the comparison refusal of step 3 does), the help naming the nearest level by the diagnostics kernel's suggestion when there is one (`"Retial"` to `"Retail"`). Inside a formula both calls are read by step 7 and honoured by step 8; this step gives them their values and pages.

**Tests.** `packages/tier0/core/tests/category.rs`: against R 4.6.0 (`tests/reference/r/types.R` extended: `factor` on the Unicode labels and on the regions of `wages_large`, where the two forms of `café` are two levels on both sides because neither normalises; the codes; `relevel` to `Zürich`; `factor` on numbers; and the four `contr.*` matrices of four levels, stored for the model matrix of step 8); the edge-case datasets, the labelled `female` and `union` of `wages`, a subset of levels with its warning, `base` on a sum-contrast category, numeric levels on a Float column; a property that the levels of random texts are their sorted distinct values, that the labels read back, and that `base` keeps every level and every row's label; the identifier of a panel row categorised; every message. The three pages' examples run on a new fixture (`staff.csv`), where `add(dept = category(dept))` prints the note that it replaced the variable, as the page of `add` shows it.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7, 3.8, 4.2, 4.3 rule 3 and 7.1; the catalogue rows 40 to 42; the checklist's step 5.

## 23 October 2026: `label` and `recode` (step 6)

**The owner's decision.** Question 6 of the release, taken as recommended on 23 October 2026: `data.label(var, labels)` takes text for the variable label or a mapping of whole numbers to text for value labels, and the catalogue's usage is corrected (logged); `recode(var, [old => new, ...])` merges a category's levels with the merged level where the first of its old levels stood, maps the values of the other types by identity with `NA` allowed as a key, warns of a key that is no level or value, and on a labelled Int maps the codes with their labels following.

**`label`.** A new module of `data`, `labels.rs`. Text sets the `label` key of the column's store, trimmed; an empty text removes it, as Stata's `label variable x ""` does. A mapping sets `value_labels` on an Int variable only, replacing any it had, stored in code order through the one writer of the column kernel, so the same labels give the same bytes whatever the script's order; a code without a label prints as its number and a label may name a code no row holds, since labels are declarations. Value labels on a Float, text, Bool or category variable are Z0401, the help naming `category` for text and `recode` for a category's levels; an `NA` code or label is Z0401. The variable label prints nowhere in this release (section 10.2's `describe` has no column for it), so its test calls the body directly; Arrow files carry it, and Zemp's variable view and `save` will read it.

**`recode`.** The mapping's keys and values must be of the variable's kind, or `NA`: whole numbers for an Int, numbers for a Float (an Int key reads as its Float), text for a text variable or a category, `true` and `false` for a Bool; anything else is Z0401 naming the kind, with the help for a labelled Int given a label as a key (write the code, or `category` first). Values are matched by identity (section 3.7): `NA` matches the missing rows and `-0.0` is `0.0`, which `recode_floats` applies through the bits of the normalised value. The new values keep the variable's type, as `update` does; `add` is the way to another type. On a category: every old level maps to its target, itself when the mapping does not name it, and the new levels are the targets in the order of the old levels, each once, so a merged level stands where the first of its old levels stood, a renamed level keeps its place, `NA` as a value removes a level and makes its rows missing, and `NA` as a key gives the missing rows a level, appended when new, and adds nothing when no row is missing; the codes are remapped, the ordered flag, the contrast and the store kept. On an Int with value labels every labelled code maps to its target and the label of a target is that of the first of its old codes in code order, so `[0 => 2]` moves a label, `[1 => 0]` merges two codes under the first's label, and a swap swaps the labels; a labelled code mapped to `NA` loses its label, and a label whose code is not a number is kept as it is. A Date or DateTime variable is Z0304 naming 0.6.0 and the `time` package (as `update` now says too; its help had still named release 0.3.0, and for a category it now points to `recode`). A key that no row holds, or that is no level, is W0206, one warning naming every such key, the other keys applied; the code is new (the next of the W02xx family) and its row is added to section 5.6 and logged. A note after every recoding says how many rows changed, for a category how many levels remain (and from how many), and whether value labels moved.

**The checker.** `recode`'s mapping parameter is `Mapping`, which `Ty::parse` now reads as a mapping of any kinds, printed as `Mapping`, as `List` is a list of anything; and a mapping literal checked against an expected `Any` key or value type is typed from its own entries, where before the expectation `Any` was joined with the first entry's type and refused (`Any` joins with nothing), so no parameter could take a mapping of any kind.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/data/tests/labels.rs`: against R 4.6.0 (`tests/reference/r/frames.R` extended: `levels<-` merging two regions of `wages_large` into one, renaming one and merging one into an existing level, with the levels, codes and counts; `match` for the values of `educ` and `NA` to 0 in `hours` with the rows changed; and the rule for labels written out in base R for a move, a merge and a swap of `female`'s codes); the edge-case datasets (no rows, all `NA`, one row, Unicode levels, a Bool, `-0.0`, a level with no rows, the missing rows given a level, a level removed, a labelled merge and swap); frames, `describe` and `summary(by:)` printing labels set by `label`; the variable label through the body (set, removed, value labels replaced and stored in code order); a property that recoding there and back restores the values and the note counts the rows; every message, the date column included. The milestone script gained three statements.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Identity"), 4.2, 4.3 rule 3, 5.6 and 10.2; the catalogue rows 122 and 123; question 6 as the owner decided it; the checklist's step 6.

## 23 October 2026: Formula values and the checker's formula context (step 7)

**The value.** `Value::Formula` in `core` (Engine and Project Specification, section 8.1, rule 4): the outcome, the terms in the order written and the intercept flag. A term carries its written form, with canonical spacing, which is the name it keeps in results (section 7.2), and its structure: a variable, a range `x1..x9`, an interaction, a product, or an expression over the frame's variables kept as a tree of `core`'s own shape (`ColumnExpr`: variables, literals, words and type names, lists, the operators of section 3.3, and calls by package and name with their arguments in parameter order), which the model matrix of step 8 computes against a frame. The checker's IR has the same shape with typed sub-expressions (`ir::Formula`, `Term`, `TermStep`), and the interpreter converts the one into the other when the statement runs; `zeff-ir` sits below `core` and cannot name its types, so the two shapes are kept parallel and small.

**Lowering.** `~` anywhere builds a formula (section 3.3, level 10). The checker lowers the right side's `+`, `-` and `..` spine into steps: a term added, a term removed, the intercept switched by a literal `1`; a formula binding takes steps too, so `f + educ:female`, `f - female` and `f - 1` are new formulas, and `f + a + b` folds into one. Inside a formula a bare name is a variable of the frame the formula will be used with (section 3.7, "Resolution by parameter type"), never a binding, so after `let k = 2` the formula `y ~ k` names a variable `k`; the one exception is a binding that holds a formula, which is refused (Z0221) since it cannot be meant as a variable. Calls inside terms are checked as any call, every name a column (`category(industry, contrast: sum)`, `base(industry, "Retail")`, `log(wage)`); `interact` joins when step 8 registers it. The written form is a canonical printing of the syntax tree (`zeff_syntax::written`): spaces around every binary operator but `^`, `:` and `..`, brackets where they were written, so that `exper ^ 2` and `exper^2` are one term, `exper^2`.

**Ranges.** `..` binds more loosely than `+` (section 3.3) and does not chain, so `d + x1..x9 + z` parses as `(d + x1)..(x9 + z)`; the lowering reads the range as joining the nearest operand on each side, which gives the terms of section 7.1, and `f + x1..x9`, which parses as `(f + x1)..x9`, is read the same way from the formula at its far left. A second bare range is the parser's Z0314; a bracketed range, `(z1..z3)`, is read as the range. Open decision #54 records the question for 0.6.0.

**Arithmetic.** Inside brackets and calls every operator is arithmetic, and `(a + b)` or `(a + b)^2` is W0503 (section 7.2), the help naming `interact([a, b], order: 2)` and the interactions written out. A term must give a column or a number: `frame(...)` in a term is Z0401. `.` alone is Z0321 (a `.` that ends a line is the lexer's Z0312 first); a one-sided formula is Z0322, since no parameter of this release takes one; `as` stays the parser's Z0308; an interaction as the outcome is Z0401; a number other than `1` is Z0401 with the help for `- 1` and `y ~ 1`; an interaction inside a call is Z0306 with a help for the formula context.

**Operators on formulas.** `+` and `-` with terms only; `*`, `/`, `^`, `&&`, `||`, unary `-` and `!`, indexing and methods are Z0221 or Z0401 as for any type, `==` is Z0208 (a compound value), and a formula on the right of `+` is Z0221 with the help to put it first. `type_of` gives `Formula`, `is(Formula)` holds, lists of formulas join. `Terms` exists as a type name for `fe:` at 0.6.0; nothing takes it.

**Printing.** As written: the outcome, `~`, the terms joined by ` + `, then ` - 1` without the intercept; with no term, `y ~ 1` or `y ~ -1`. A removal that removes nothing is a note when the statement runs, since a binding's terms are known only then.

**Tests.** `crates/zeff-ir/tests/formulas.rs`: the lowering of every kind of term, canonical spacing, combination with a binding, names as variables, every refusal by its code, and the property that a formula written with or without spaces lowers to one structure whose printed form lowers to the same structure and prints as itself (the shape of the operator property of 0.1.0). `crates/zeff-engine/tests/formulas.rs`: binding, printing and combining through the engine, `type_of` and `is`, every message, and the specification's sample script checked against this release's registry, where no formula is refused and the diagnostics that remain are the functions and constructs of later releases. The milestone script gained four statements.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.3, 3.4, 3.7, 4, 7.1 and 7.2; the checklist's step 7.

## 23 October 2026: The model matrix (step 8)

**The owner's decision.** Question 5, taken as recommended on 23 October 2026: a category's indicator columns are named `var=level` under `treatment`, `sum` and `helmert`, naming the level each column codes (under `sum` the level whose deviation from the mean it carries; under `helmert` the level compared with the mean of those before it), and `var=linear`, `var=quadratic`, `var=cubic`, `var=degree4` and on under `poly`; the page of `category` shows R's names beside them.

**The packages.** `results` (`packages/tier1/results`, tier 1, order 5, before `stats`) holds the model matrix in `design.rs` and registers no script function yet; `regress` (`packages/tier2/regress`, tier 2, order 1), planned for step 10, is created now with `interact` alone, because the catalogue places `interact` in `regress` and the registry holds a function to its row's package. Both are in the workspace, the engine's registry and the tier check, whose lists already named them in the order of section 8.2.

**The design.** `Design::build(ctx, frame, formula, extra)` takes a frame value, a formula value and the names of further model variables (weights, a cluster), and gives the column names, the rows used, the rows dropped for `NA` with a count by variable, the notes, and the design in row blocks of the kernels' size (`BLOCK_ROWS`, open decision #48), each block a matrix with the block's outcome; `matrix()` gathers the whole for tests. Every variable or expression a term uses is evaluated once over the whole frame into a source, numbers with their missing rows or a category's codes with its levels and contrast, and a column of the design is the product of its parts, a number or the weight of the row's level, computed block by block, so that the memory held is the frame's own columns and the expressions' results, never n × k (Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 10). A category is read by its codes (integer-coded categories, the same point).

**Expansion and coding.** The rules of section 7.2 in its order. `a * b * c` gives the units, the pairs and the triples, in that order, as R does; `a * b:c` gives `a`, `b:c` and `a:b:c`; `interact([a, b, c], order: 2)` gives the variables and every interaction up to the order, as R's `(a + b + c)^2` (section 7.2 and the catalogue's row 427), and is read by the design, never evaluated; a range `x1..x9` is the frame's variables between them; a term written twice, `a:b` and `b:a` alike, is kept once with a note naming the kept form. A category is coded by its contrast when the term without it is in the model (the empty term counting as present), and by every level otherwise, which is R's marginality rule; without an intercept the first category met with more than one level is coded by every level (section 7.2, "Intercept"). The base, the level without a column, is the first level or the one `base()` moved first, under `treatment` and `sum` alike: Zeff's rule is one rule, where R's `contr.sum` omits the last level; `helmert` and `poly` have no base. The contrast weights are R's `contr.treatment`, `contr.sum`, `contr.helmert` and `contr.poly`; the polynomial ones are computed by Gram–Schmidt with reorthogonalisation over the centred, scaled positions, in a fixed order of pure IEEE operations, with a positive leading coefficient so that the signs are R's. A category of one level adds no column, with a note, where R stops with an error. The indicator columns of `category(x, ...)` and `base(x, ...)` are named by `x`; a level holding `=`, `:` or `+` is quoted inside the name (section 7.2); a variable's term name is its name as text, without backticks, as `m.coef("x y")` will write it.

**Rows.** A row with `NA` in the outcome, a regressor, an expression's result or an extra variable is dropped and counted, in all and by variable (section 4.1); an infinite value in any of them is Z0223 listing the rows, a code the specification did not give (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`), which a transformation's `log(0)` or division by zero also raises. Text in the model is Z0401 pointing to `category`; a category as the outcome is Z0401 until `logistic`; a date is Z0304 naming 0.6.0; a missing variable is Z0101 with the frame's variables. A term calls the functions of `core` only (`log`, `category`, `base`, the lifted scalar functions), through the function table of `core` and the row-wise call of section 3.7; a reducer in a term is refused by the checker's ordinary rules, and a call to another package's function is Z0401 with the help to compute it with `add` first. The messages of an operator's trouble and the warnings of section 4.1 now live in `core`'s `operators` module, worded once for the interpreter and the design.

**The checker and the values.** The formula value's calls carry whether they lift and their declared return, as the IR does; the engine's conversion of a lowered formula to its value is `zeff_engine::formulas`, which the interpreter and the test kit (`zeff_testkit::formula`) share.

## 23 October 2026: `interact` complete (step 9)

**Choice.** `interact([a, b, c], order: n)` stands for the variables and every interaction between them up to `order`, as R's `(a + b + c)^n` and the catalogue's row 427 say, so the main effects are included; the variables are any term parts, `category(x, ...)` among them, and a category is coded in each interaction as the product `a * b * c` codes it, since the two go through the same expansion. A variable listed twice, or a term the formula already has, is kept once with the notes of section 7.2. The rules of the order (two or more variables; 2 to their number) are checked by the model matrix, since the formula value is built before any frame is known; outside a formula `interact` is an error naming where it belongs, and the checker's ordinary rules refuse a list that is not one or an order that is not a whole number. ## 23 October 2026: The estimator trait, the OLS fit and the printed result (step 10)

**The owner's decisions.** Question 2, taken as recommended on 23 October 2026: CRAN packages are allowed for the R reference harness alone, `wooldridge` for the textbook data and `sandwich` for the robust and clustered errors, pinned and installed into a folder inside the repository that Git ignores, and by the runner in continuous integration, never linked into the engine or the apps; the installation itself comes with the first script that needs a package (step 11 for `sandwich`, step 14 for `wooldridge`), and if the owner has Stata, step 14 writes the `.do` file. Question 3 (a), taken as recommended: a regression without fixed effects prints the header `reg · formula`, the line `N = 18,184 (228 rows dropped for NA in model variables)`, the line `standard errors: classical` (or the kind used), the table of section 10.2, and the footer `R² 0.284 · adjusted R² 0.283`, with notes and warnings under it.

**The result value.** `Value::Fit`, declared in `core` (Engine and Project Specification, section 8.1, rule 5) and shared by reference: the kind (`RegFit`), the method, the formula as written, the terms with an estimate and the terms omitted as collinear, the estimates, standard errors, statistics, p-values and intervals, the variance matrix, the kind of standard error and the level, the rows used with the counts dropped, the residual degrees of freedom, the rows, residuals, fitted values and leverages, the fit measures, the condition number, the notes, and the printed summary as a `Summary` (lines before the grid, the grid, lines after), which `show` prints and a list or frame shows on one line as `RegFit · reg · formula`. `type_of` gives `RegFit`; `is(Result)` and `is(RegFit)` hold. The estimator trait in `results` has `fit`, `scores` and `bread`, with `Design::build` the design step every model shares; `results::variance::classical` is the first kind of the variance layer and `results::summary::linear_fit` assembles the value and its summary for every linear model to come.

**The fit.** Ordinary least squares in `regress`, on the kernels of step 2 as section 8.3, point 10 says: a first pass over the design's blocks for the column norms, accumulated by the kernel's lane sums across the blocks so that the design's block size changes no bit (a property test demands it); every column scaled to unit norm; the blocked Householder QR of [X y]; the pivoted QR of the k × k R with the tolerance 1e-7 of section 7.2, which drops a column collinear with the columns before it, named in a note (one note for all), and shown as `(omitted)` in the table in its place; the estimates by back substitution, unscaled; a second pass for y − Xβ row by row, the residual sum of squares by the lane sum, and the leverage from R; the bread (XᵀX)⁻¹ from R, unscaled; the exact condition number of the scaled R, W1001 above 1e8; the classical variance σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹ with σ² the residual sum of squares over n − k; the t table on n − k degrees of freedom, with the p-values and quantiles of the `dist` package's Student t; R² about the mean with an intercept and about zero without, as R; the adjusted R² and the Gaussian log-likelihood as R's `logLik`. An outcome without variation leaves R² undefined (`NA`), with a note, where R prints nothing useful. The self-check of section 11.1 after every fit: the residuals are orthogonal to the regressors to within the rounding of computing them (1e-8 of each column's norm times the sizes of the residuals and the outcome), a failure being Z9001. No row left is Z0801 (worded for an empty frame or for rows all dropped), no residual degrees of freedom or no regressor is Z0802; both codes are assigned by this step and logged. A level outside (0, 1) is Z0401; `se:` lists the four words of section 6 so that `robust`, `hc2` and `hc3` read, and any but `classical` is Z0304 until step 11.

**Printing.** The tables round half to even as section 3.8 says, through `display::fixed`, which also writes a number from 1e15 in exponent form, as the Float rule does, so that a degenerate t value does not print as eighteen digits; `p_value_text` gives `<0.001` below. The confidence column is headed `95% CI`, `90% CI`, `99.9% CI`. A term's written form keeps a Float literal in the shorter of its plain and exponent forms, `1e7` rather than `10000000.0`, so that `(educ * 1e7)` is a term's name.

**Tests.** `packages/tier2/regress/tests/reg.rs`: eleven fits against R 4.6.0's `lm`, `summary`, `confint` and `logLik` (`tests/reference/r/regression.R`) on the shipped `wages`, `wages_large` and the edge-case files, with categories under the treatment and sum contrasts, an interaction, no intercept, a collinear column, columns at 1e7 and 1e12, rows with `NA`, a level of 0.9, a text column made a category, and a fifth-degree polynomial, the terms matched by name (R orders them by degree, Zeff keeps the order written) and every statistic within 1e-10, p-values within 1e-8, counts exactly; the exact small cases of `kernels.py`, each a matrix with its rational solution, fitted on their own columns within rounding scaled by the condition number, the square and wide ones refused with Z0802; the summary and the edge cases through the engine (a sum contrast at level 0.9, no intercept, a collinear column, a constant regressor, a duplicate term, three rows with four terms, one row, an outcome without variation, every row dropped, an empty frame, a near-singular polynomial, a bad level, a standard error not yet available, text and a category as outcome and regressor, a bound formula with steps); the properties that doubling the outcome doubles every estimate to the bit and tripling it scales them within rounding, that rescaling a regressor by a million changes no t statistic, p-value or R², that reordering the rows changes no printed value, that a duplicate regressor is dropped with a note, and that any block size gives the same bits (whose first run found the column norms summed per block, now accumulated across them). ## 23 October 2026: The variance layer (step 11)

**The layer.** `results::variance` computes every kind of standard error from an estimator's scores and bread (Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 2), by the rulings of the release: `classical` is σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹ with σ² the residual sum of squares over N − k; `robust` is HC1, N/(N − k) times the sandwich B(Σ sᵢsᵢᵀ)B of the scores sᵢ = xᵢeᵢ; `hc2` and `hc3` scale each row's score product by 1/(1 − hᵢ) and 1/(1 − hᵢ)²; `cluster:` is CR1, the scores summed within each cluster (a dependence structure: the row pairs within a cluster weigh 1 and the others 0), with Stata's adjustment G/(G − 1) · (N − 1)/(N − k); the t table uses N − k degrees of freedom, or G − 1 when clustered, as Stata's `regress` and reghdfe do and as `sandwich::vcovCL(type = "HC1")` reproduces. The meat is accumulated block by block from the estimator's scores, so no n × k matrix is held; a cluster's scores are summed in one pass. The variance matrix is checked symmetric with no negative variance after every fit (section 11.1), a failure being Z9001.

**Weights.** `weights:` with `weight_type:` (frequency, analytic, sampling; sampling by default, as the catalogue says) enters the design: a row with `NA` weight is dropped with the others, a zero weight leaves its row out of the estimate and the count with a note, a negative weight is Z0224 listing the rows (a code the specification did not give; logged), and a frequency weight must be a whole number (Z0401). The design carries each row scaled by the square root of its weight, so the fit is weighted least squares on the same kernels and the fitted leverage is the weighted one; the residuals and fitted values the fit value keeps are unweighted. Under frequency weights N is the sum of the weights, the degrees of freedom their sum less k, and in the sandwich every row stands for its weight's worth of observations, each of leverage hᵢ/wᵢ, whose score products sum to the row's divided by its weight; analytic weights are scaled to sum to the rows (Stata's `aweight`), which makes the classical variance R's `lm(weights =)`; sampling weights are probability weights, with which `se:` defaults to `robust` and `classical` is Z0410, as section 6 says; `hc2` or `hc3` together with `cluster:` is Z0410 too. R² with weights is about the weighted mean, as R computes it. The summary's N line says when N is the sum of the weights and how many rows a zero weight left out, and a line `weights: hours (sampling)` names the weighting (an addition to question 3 (a)'s layout, which did not foresee weights).

**Clusters.** The cluster variable's values group the rows used by identity, whatever its type; one cluster is Z0802, since G − 1 is zero; clusters of one observation are counted in a note (section 6: "one-observation clusters are reported"); fewer than 30 clusters is W1002 (section 11.1).

**The warnings' rules.** W1003: the weights are extreme when Kish's effective sample size (Σw)²/Σw² is below a quarter of the rows used, which is a design effect above 4, the point at which the weights have cost three quarters of the sample. W1006: an observation drives a coefficient when its removal would move some estimate by more than one standard error, a DFBETAS beyond 1 (Belsley, Kuh and Welsch's 2/√n flags a share of any large sample; one standard error is a change a reader would notice), computed from the leave-one-out formulas with the row's residual and leverage in one pass over the design; the first five rows are named. Both thresholds are constants of `regress::reg`.

**The kept design.** A fitted design and its fit are kept for the run under the frame's table, the formula as written and the weighting, so that another `se:` or `cluster:` on the same frame and formula reuses the factorisation (section 8.3, point 10, "Reused model matrices"); the table itself is held so that its address cannot be reused by another frame. One entry, the most recent; a property test demands the same bits from the reused design as from a fresh one.

**The harness.** Question 2 as decided: `tests/reference/r/install.R` installs `sandwich` 3.1.1 from a dated snapshot of CRAN (packagemanager.posit.co, 2026-10-01) into `tests/reference/r/library`, which Git ignores and `renv.lock` records; the reference scripts put the folder first on their library path; CI runs the installer before the scripts. `regression.R` gained HC1 to HC3, clusters by worker and by industry, a category with clusters, and the three weightings, the frequency weights replicating rows in R and the sampling fit taking HC1 from `sandwich`.

**Tests.** `packages/tier2/regress/tests/reg.rs`: every reference case, now twenty-two, matched by name within 1e-10; the summary under each `se:`, clusters, the weightings, and every refusal (a weight that is text, a fraction in a frequency weight, a negative weight, one cluster, few clusters, extreme weights, an observation that drives a coefficient, `se: classical` with sampling weights, `hc2` with `cluster:`, `se: bootstrap`, a missing weight or cluster variable); the properties that clustering with every row its own cluster is HC1 to rounding, that the HC kinds stay close where the leverage is nil, and that the reused design gives the same bits as a fresh one. The conformance report gains a clustered and a weighted fit.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 4.1 ("Weights"), 6, 10.2 and 11.1; Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, points 2 and 10, and section 13; the rulings of release 0.4.0 on degrees of freedom and weights; the checklist's step 11.

## 23 October 2026: Results in the checker and the registry (step 12)

**The types.** `Ty::Result(Option<ResultKind>)` in the checker: `Result` is the interface every fitted model and test implements, and `RegFit` and `TestResult` are its kinds at this release; `Ty::Term` is a term name. A parameter of type `Result` accepts every kind and a parameter of a kind accepts that kind alone, so a method registered on `Result` dispatches on every result and one registered on `RegFit` on it alone (Engine and Project Specification, section 8.1, rules 5 and 6); two different kinds join to `Result` (Language Reference, section 3.7, "Joining types"), so `[m, t]` is a `List<Result>`, and an element of it may take only the methods every result has, with a help line saying so. `==` on a result is Z0208, as on every compound value. The kinds are listed once more in the registry crate (`RESULT_KINDS`), which a test of the checker holds equal to its own enum, so that a kind added later is added in both places or the build fails.

**One home per name per type.** The registry refuses, when it is built, two methods of one name whose receiver types overlap: the same type, or `Result` and one of its kinds (`RegistryError::OverlappingHomes`). That is the rule of section 8.1, rule 6, that made the instrument check `exclusion_check` rather than a second `check`; `summary` on frames and `summary` on results do not overlap.

**Term parameters.** A `Term` parameter takes a bare name or text (section 4). The checker lowers a bare name to the term of that name whatever else bears it, a binding included, and wraps text in the same `ExprKind::Term`; the interpreter turns either into `Value::Term` and, before the body runs, checks every term argument against the receiver's model matrix, the terms with an estimate and those omitted as collinear, so that no result method repeats the check. An unknown term is Z0414 (provisional, the next free code of the arguments family, logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`), listing the terms with a near name when there is one; a term asked of a test's result is Z0414 too, since a `TestResult` has no terms.

**The test value.** `core` declares `TestResult` (section 8.1, rule 4): the method, a title line, header lines, an optional table (the models `compare` sets side by side), the statistic with its name, value and degrees of freedom, the p-value, lines after the statistic, and notes. It prints as question 3 (b) recommends, provisionally until the owner decides the question at step 18: the title, the header lines, the table when there is one, then `F(1, 18,179) = 4.21   p = 0.040`, the statistic to two decimals, whole degrees of freedom as counts and fractional ones to one decimal (section 10.2 writes `df = 18,074.2`), p to three decimals and `p < 0.001` below. The statistic line is one function, so that a change of layout is one change. `type_of` gives `TestResult`, `is(Result)` is true, and a list of fits and tests prints its type as `List<Result>`.

**The Value section.** The registry generates the method list of a result type's Value section from the registered methods whose receiver is that type or `Result`, grouped as the catalogue groups them (`Result interface`, `Estimator interface`, `Result methods`), the groups in the order the catalogue first lists them and the names in catalogue order within each, printed as bullets under `Methods` after the page's written Value text. With no result method shipped the line reads `Methods: none in this release`, which `zeff help reg` prints at this step and a snapshot records; the page without the list stays as it was for the renderer's own tests.

**A fixture entry point.** `run::run_script_in` runs a script against a given registry and set of bodies, so that the engine's tests register fixture result methods beside the engine's own functions and exercise dispatch, `Term` arguments and Z0414 before step 15 ships the real methods.

**Tests.** `crates/zeff-ir/tests/results.rs` (the checker on a fixture registry: the binding types, both homes of `summary`, the join, every message); `kernel/zeff-registry/tests/results.rs` (the grouping, the Value section, the overlap refusal); `crates/zeff-engine/tests/results.rs` (`type_of`, `is`, lists of fits, `m.head(3)` refused, and with fixture methods the dispatch, the resolution of terms including an omitted column, Z0414 and the printed `TestResult`); `packages/tier0/core/tests/results.rs` (four shapes of printed test and the rounding of the statistic line); the CLI's `help_reg` snapshot.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7, 4 and 10.2; Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.1 (rules 4 to 6) and 9.1; question 3 (b) provisionally as recommended; the checklist's step 12.

## 23 October 2026: Word and LaTeX tables (step 13)

**The writers.** `results::export` holds both, as pure functions of the table, so that the bytes depend on the table alone and the four targets prove them identical. The input is `core`'s `Summary` (a title, lines above the grid, the grid, lines below), which a result's printed summary already is and a plain `Table` becomes with no lines; a table's further tables (`more`) follow it, each under its own title. The LaTeX form is a comment with the title, then a `tabular` whose columns are aligned as the printed table aligns them, `\toprule`, the headings, `\midrule`, the rows, `\bottomrule`, and the lines above and below the grid as full-width `\multicolumn` rows in `\footnotesize` under the bottom rule, so that the file needs `booktabs` alone and is meant for `\input` inside a `table` environment; `& % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \` are escaped, `<` and `>` set in maths mode, and the symbols the printed tables use (`²`, `·`, `−`, `×`, `≤`, `≥`, `…`) written as their commands, so the file compiles under pdfLaTeX. The Word form is a minimal WordprocessingML document, three parts in a zip container written by hand, `[Content_Types].xml`, `_rels/.rels` and `word/document.xml`, stored without compression under the fixed timestamp of 1 January 1980 with no extra fields, the CRC-32 computed here (no crate added, as the ruling says): the title in bold with `keepNext`, the lines above the grid as paragraphs, the table with a rule above and below it and under its headings, column widths from the widest cell, numbers right-aligned as the printed table has them, and the lines below the grid at 9 pt; no styles part, so the document takes the fonts of whatever opens it.

**The function.** `export(path)` is registered on `Table` now with a draft page, as `reg` was at step 10, and gains results at step 19 with the complete page; `size:` arrives with plots (0.7.0). The format comes from the extension, compared without regard to case; a path with no extension or an unknown one is Z0716 (provisional, the next free code of the paths family, logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`), listing the formats. The call prints nothing, as the `reg` page of the help examples shows for `report([m]).export("output/table1.docx")`. The catalogue row stays `planned` until step 19.

**Writes.** The `Files` interface of `core` gains `write`, with a default that refuses (Z0707) for runs without a project; the project's implementation resolves the path by the existing write rules (only under the project folder, never a data root or an absolute path, Z0707 otherwise), creates `output/` when it is missing and refuses any other missing folder with Z0707, so that a misspelt folder is caught rather than created, and replaces an existing file. A path with no folder is written under `output/`, which is section 2's "`output/` by default".

**Proof.** The sample table (the `wages` regression of `help/reg.md`, fixed in `export::sample`) is exported by three routes that must agree: the conformance report hashes both forms (`export/sample.docx`, `export/sample.tex`), so the identity jobs compare them across the four targets; `cargo run -p xtask -- export-samples` writes them to `tests/reference/exports/`, where the reference job rebuilds them, checks the Word file with Python's `zipfile` (every CRC, the three parts in order, stored, the fixed timestamp, well-formed XML, the title, headings, rows, notes and alignment) and the LaTeX file for its rules and escapes (`tests/reference/exports.py`), and compares both with the committed copies; and a test of `results` holds the writers to the committed bytes. A test reads the zip container back field by field and checks the CRC against the standard's check value.

**The Value section, corrected.** Step 12 printed a result type's methods as bullets under `Methods`; the `reg` page of `docs/spec/zeff_help_examples.md` writes them as sentences after the Value text (`Result interface: summary, estimates, …`), so the renderer now does the same, and with no method shipped ends the text with `No method applies to it in this release.` The two explained pages left out of the list at 0.3.0 (Z0111, Z0413) are listed, and a test now holds the list equal to the folder.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/results/tests/export.rs` (the two forms as snapshots, the container read back, the check value, the formats and escapes, a further table and a short row, the committed files); `crates/zeff-engine/tests/export.rs` (a table written under the project in both forms, `output/` created and a bare name written there, an existing folder taking a file, a file replaced, and every message); the registry's and the command line's snapshots of the Value section regenerated; the page's examples run by the example runner.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.8 and 10.2; Engine and Project Specification, section 2 ("Writes"), section 8.3, point 3 ("Proof"), and section 9.1; the help examples' `reg` page; the rulings of the release on exported files; the checklist's step 13.

## 23 October 2026: `reg` complete (step 14)

**The references.** Question 2 as decided: the `wooldridge` package (1.4-7, GPL-3, installed by `install.R` into the harness's own library and recorded in `renv.lock`; part of the R harness alone, never linked) supplies the textbook data. `regression.R` writes `wage1` and `wage2` beside the references as `tests/reference/data/wage1.csv` and `wage2.csv` (NA as empty cells), which the Rust tests fit, so that both sides see the same rows and continuous integration rebuilds and compares the files; the extracts are reference inputs of the test suite, not shipped data. Fourteen cases join the twenty-two: the textbook regressions of chapters 3 and 7 (`lwage ~ educ + exper + tenure`; the seven-regressor `wage2` model), Wooldridge's example 8.1 under HC1, HC2 and HC3, errors clustered by `numdep` and by `age`, a 99 per cent level, an interaction, analytic, sampling and frequency weights (`sibs`, with zero weights leaving rows out), rows with `NA`, and the helmert and poly contrasts of question 5 on `industry`; every one within 1e-10 of R. No Stata file was given, so the page keeps Stata's conventions in words alone.

**Truth recovery.** The shipped `wages` recovers its generating script's model: the pooled regression `log(wage) ~ educ + exper + exper^2 + female + union + industry + year` with errors clustered by worker (the worker effect makes the rows of a worker dependent) puts the return to schooling, 0.074, inside its 95 per cent interval and the other structural coefficients (experience, its square, female, union, the year trend) inside their 99 per cent intervals. The eleven industry effects share the base industry's sampling error (Agriculture has 3 per cent of the workers, Mining 1 per cent, and Mining alone lies 2.9 standard errors from its value), so they are judged together by the Wald statistic of their deviations under the clustered covariance against the 99 per cent point of χ² on eleven degrees of freedom; the nightly Monte Carlo of step 20 judges the coverage over fifty seeds.

**An engine fault found by the edge cases.** A regressor far from zero and barely varying, such as a calendar year, made every sandwich variance (robust, HC2, HC3, clustered) fail the symmetry self-check: B M B is symmetric in exact arithmetic, but its two triangles are summed in different orders, and the cancellation in an ill-conditioned bread magnifies the difference beyond the check's 1e-10. The variance layer now makes every matrix symmetric from its lower triangle after a check that the asymmetry is rounding, relative to each entry's scale √(Vᵢᵢ Vⱼⱼ) and to the condition number (1e-6, or a hundred units in the last place times the condition number), a larger asymmetry staying an internal error; `reg`'s own self-check is unchanged and now passes by construction.

**Dropped columns, by cause.** The first pass over the design records each column's largest size beside its sum of squares, so the notes tell the causes apart: a category level with no observations among the rows used (`industry=Mining` after `where(industry != "Mining")`), a column that is zero in every row, a column whose values are too small for their squares to be represented (the `tiny` column of the magnitudes file, below 1e-150, which R fits with an infinite standard error), and the rest collinear with the columns before them, as before. The `Fitted` value carries the zero and vanishing columns.

**An essentially perfect fit.** R's rule from `summary.lm`: a residual variance below 1e-30 of the fitted values' scale (their squared mean plus their variance) earns a note that the standard errors and t values say nothing; the numbers print as R prints them. An outcome without variation keeps its own note and `NA` for R².

**Bool variables and names.** A Bool outcome or regressor is coded 0 and 1 without a conversion, as section 7.2 codes a dummy; the term names of awkward columns are the names as written in backticks (`日本語`, `Gross Sales (total)`), the Unicode labels of the edge file appear in term expressions (`to(city == "東京", Int)`), and a level holding `=`, `:` or `+` keeps its quotes. The no-rows and all-`NA` files are refused with Z0801 in their two wordings, one row with Z0802.

**The page.** The description says what `se:`, `cluster:` and `weights:` do and where `fe:` arrives; the details add the dropped-column notes, the perfect-fit rule, the truth-recovery and the Wooldridge checks; the examples show classical, robust and clustered errors. The catalogue row is marked implemented. Risk R3: the edge cases of this step took one session with one engine fault found, within the allowance.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 6, 7.1, 7.2, 10.2 and 11.1; Engine and Project Specification, section 13; the testing handbook, sections 1.2 and 4; questions 2 and 5 as decided; the checklist's step 14.

## 24 October 2026: The result interface (step 15)

**The six methods.** `results::interface` registers `summary`, `estimates`, `std_errors`, `p_values`, `ci` and `n_obs` on every result (the receiver is `Result`, so a `RegFit` and a `TestResult` both answer them, as section 8.1, rule 5, asks), with questions 3 (d) and 4 as the owner decided them. `std_errors()` and `p_values()` give a `Mapping` from term name to value over the terms with an estimate, in the model's order, and one `Float` when a term is named; a term omitted as collinear gives `NA` by name and has no entry. `ci()` gives a `Table` of `term`, `lower` and `upper` titled with the level (`ci · 95%`), and `[lower, upper]` for one term, the intervals recomputed from the estimates, the standard errors and the fit's t table at any level, a level outside (0, 1) refused (Z0401). `n_obs()` gives an `Int`, the sum of the frequency weights under them. `estimates()` gives a `Frame` with `term`, `estimate`, `std_error`, `statistic`, `p_value`, `ci_lower` and `ci_upper` for the terms with an estimate, so that `m.estimates().where(p_value < 0.05)` reads as written. `summary()` gives the printed summary as a `Table`, `standardized: true` adding the column `beta` after the estimates (blank for the intercept and an omitted term) and `fit_measures: true` the line `log-likelihood … · AIC … · BIC …` under the fit measures, the three to one decimal with thousands separators. A test's result answers too: its single p-value from `p_values()`, `NA` from `std_errors()` and `ci()` (it has no terms and, at this release, no interval; the tests of `stats` add theirs at 0.7.0), its observations from `n_obs()`, one row from `estimates()`, and its printed form from `summary()`.

**Tables with lines.** `core`'s `Table` gains `before` and `after`, the lines a result's summary prints around its grid, and the separate summary type goes: a fit's summary is a `Table`, `summary()` returns it with its additions, `export` writes it with its lines, and every other table has empty lines and prints as before. A table without columns prints its lines alone, which is how a test's summary prints exactly as the test itself does.

**Standardized coefficients and criteria.** Each beta is the estimate times the standard deviation of its regressor's column over that of the outcome, the deviations computed at fit time over the rows used in two passes over the blocks with the rows unscaled by their weights: under frequency weights each row counts as its weight with divisor N − 1, as R computes them on the replicated rows; otherwise each row counts once, as R's `sd` of the model matrix does; a column without variation (the intercept) has none. AIC and BIC count the variance as a parameter, as R's `AIC` and `BIC` do: −2ℓ + 2(k + 1) and −2ℓ + ln(N)(k + 1), with k the terms with an estimate.

**A return type by use.** A method whose value depends on whether a term is named declares its return as `ByTerm<A, B>`, which the checker reads as A when a term is given or the receiver is a `TestResult` (one value), B otherwise, and unknown for a receiver of the interface type, whose kind is not known; so `m.std_errors(educ) + 1` and `m.std_errors()["educ"]` both check, and a mixed list's element is left to the run.

**The reference.** `regression.R` adds to every case the standardized coefficients (`coef × sd(column) / sd(y)` on the rows `lm` saw) and R's `AIC` and `BIC`; the interface's values agree with R within 1e-10 on all thirty-six fits (p-values within 1e-8; AIC and BIC except under analytic and sampling weights, where R's log-likelihood carries the weights' scale, as the fit's own measures already did).

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/results/tests/interface.rs`: every method against R on every reference fit, with `zeff-regress` as a test-only dependency (outside the tier rules, as the tier check says); the printed forms, both homes of `summary`, chaining into `where` and `export`, the omitted term, a clustered and a weighted fit, and every message. The engine's fixture tests cover a test's result; the six pages' examples run; the conformance report gains `regress/interface`; the catalogue rows 159 to 164 are marked implemented, and `zeff help reg` lists the six under its Value.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7, 3.8 and 10.2; Engine and Project Specification, section 8.1, rule 5, and section 9.1; questions 3 (d) and 4 as decided on 24 October 2026; the checklist's step 15.

## 24 October 2026: The estimator interface, part 1 (step 16)

**The six methods.** `results::interface` registers `coef`, `vcov`, `fit_measures`, `predict`, `residuals` and `fitted` on every result, with question 4 as decided: `coef()` a `Mapping` by term or one `Float` for a named term, `NA` for a term omitted as collinear; `vcov()` a `Table` over the terms with an estimate, titled with the kind of standard error (`vcov · clustered by worker (3,911 clusters, CR1)`), its cells the matrix the printed standard errors are the square roots of, written with six significant digits as a Float prints; `fit_measures()` a record `{log_likelihood, aic, bic, r_squared, adjusted}`; `residuals()` and `fitted()` columns of the fitted frame's full length with `NA` in the rows the fit dropped, so that `wages.add(res = m.residuals())` lines up, as R's `na.exclude` and Stata's `predict` fill them; `predict(newdata:)` a column of the new frame's length. A test's result gives `NA` from each, since it has no coefficients at this release.

**Prediction on new data.** The fit keeps its formula as a value, the levels of each category variable in the design's order and its frame's row count. `predict` rebuilds the design on the new frame from the formula without its outcome (so the outcome need not be present) through `Design::build_with`, which takes a plan of levels: a category column of the new frame is recoded by label into the fit's levels in the fit's order, a text column named in the plan is coded by the fit's labels, and a label the fit never saw is `NA` and counted by variable; contrasts and bases come from the formula as before, so an indicator or contrast column means what it meant in the fit. A variable the frame lacks is Z0101 as the design always raises it; a row with `NA` in a model variable predicts `NA`; the rows with an unseen level predict `NA` with W0207 (provisional, the next code of the W02xx family, logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`), the warning naming the variable and listing the fit's levels; `newdata:` is required (Z0406 without it, pointing to `fitted()`); a term omitted as collinear contributes nothing, as R's `predict` on a rank-deficient fit. No standard error of prediction at this release.

**The reference.** `regression.R` adds to every case the variance matrix in Zeff's names (classical from `vcov`, otherwise the sandwich already computed), `predict` on the first ten rows of the data as `predict` sees them before any replication under frequency weights, and the first twenty residuals and fitted values of the rows `lm` used; the coefficients, the matrix, the measures, the residuals, the fitted values and the predictions agree with R within 1e-10 on all thirty-six fits (the residuals and fitted values compared in length alone under frequency weights, where R's rows are replicated).

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/results/tests/interface.rs` gains the estimator comparison and a snapshot of the printed forms and every message: the mappings and the table, the record and its fields, the full-length columns added to the frame and their `NA` rows, predictions on the frame's head, on a frame written in the script with an unseen level and a missing value, under a sum contrast and a base, with an omitted term, and the refusals (no `newdata:`, a missing variable, a frame that is not one, text where the fit had numbers, an unknown term, a frame receiver). The engine's fixture tests cover a test's result; the six pages' examples run; the catalogue rows 240, 241 and 243 to 246 are marked implemented, and `zeff help reg` lists the estimator interface under its Value.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 4 and 7.2; Engine and Project Specification, section 8.1, rule 5, and section 13; question 4 as decided; the checklist's step 16.

## 24 October 2026: `r_squared` and `influence` (step 17)

**Where they live.** Both are methods of regression fits alone (receiver `RegFit`), registered by `regress` in `src/diagnostics.rs`, the module section 9.1 names for them, so that a test's result or a later model does not answer them; the Value section of `reg`'s page lists them under `Result methods`, the catalogue's group.

**`r_squared`.** The record of question 4, `{r_squared, adjusted}`, the two values the summary prints, `NA` when the outcome has no variation; the within and overall forms join it with fixed effects at 0.6.0.

**`influence`.** The frame of question 7, `leverage`, `cooks_distance` and `studentized`, of the fitted frame's full length with `NA` in the rows the fit dropped, so that a column of it adds to the frame; computed in one pass over the rows used from what the fit already holds (its leverage from the R factor, its residuals, σ and the residual sum of squares): Cook's distance (e / (σ(1 − h)))² h / k and the externally studentized residual e / (σ₍ᵢ₎ √(1 − h)) with σ₍ᵢ₎² = (RSS − e² / (1 − h)) / (N − k − 1), as R's `cooks.distance` and `rstudent`, with k the terms with an estimate and N the observations used (not the t table's degrees of freedom, which clustering changes). Under analytic and sampling weights the residual is weighted by √w, as R's `weighted.residuals`; under frequency weights a row stands for w observations, each with leverage h / w and the row's residual, which is what R computes on the replicated rows; a row of leverage one has no distance and no studentized residual. The fit now keeps the weights of the rows it used and their kind for this. The help of W1006 points to `influence` without the step number it carried.

**The reference.** `regression.R` adds the first twenty of `hatvalues`, `cooks.distance` and `rstudent` of the rows `lm` used to every case; the measures agree with R within 1e-8 on all thirty-six fits, the frequency-weighted ones compared replicate by replicate, and R² and its adjusted form within 1e-10.

**Tests.** `packages/tier2/regress/tests/diagnostics.rs`: the record and the measures against R on every reference fit, the frame's length and `NA` rows, and the printed forms with every message (the record and its field, the frame, its summary, a selection by Cook's distance, a column of it added to the frame, a weighted and a frequency-weighted fit, an outcome without variation, an exact fit, a frame receiver, a table receiver). The engine's fixture test no longer stands in for `r_squared`; the two pages' examples run; the catalogue rows 242 and 247 are marked implemented.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 4 and 11.1; Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 10, and section 13; questions 4 and 7 as decided (question 7 on 24 October 2026); the checklist's step 17.

## 24 October 2026: The estimator interface, part 2 (step 18)

**Expressions over the terms.** The restrictions of `test` and the definitions of `derive` are expressions whose bare names are coefficients of the fit, never columns or bindings (Language Reference, section 7.2). The checker carries this as a parameter type of its own, `Term<Bool>` for a restriction and `Term<Float>` for a definition (`Ty::TermExpr`), written in the registrations as the rest values of `test` and the rest definitions of `derive`: inside such an argument every bare name lowers to a `Float` variable, the expression is checked to give the inner type (Z0401 otherwise, with the shape of a restriction or a definition in the help), and it is kept as written (`ExprKind::TermExpr`). The interpreter does not evaluate it: it hands the function a `Value::TermExpr` holding the expression tree the formulas already use (`ColumnExpr`) and the source text, which the titles print. A term whose name is not an identifier is written in backticks, `` `exper^2` ``, `` `(intercept)` ``, as the lexer already allowed. A fit remembers the name a `let` bound it to, for the titles of question 3 (b) and (c); a fit never bound is named by its formula.

**`test`.** Each restriction is read as a linear form in the coefficients: constants, coefficients, their sums and differences, and products and quotients by a constant, on both sides of one `==`; anything else (a product or quotient of coefficients, a power, a function, `!=`, `<`, `&&`, an equality with no coefficient) is Z0415 with the help to use `derive`, and a term the fit lacks or dropped is Z0414 as the other result methods raise it. The statistic is the Wald F, (Rβ − c)ᵀ (R V Rᵀ)⁻¹ (Rβ − c) / q under the fit's own variance matrix (so robust and clustered errors carry through) on (q, the fit's residual degrees of freedom, G − 1 when clustered), its p-value from the F distribution of `dist`; the q × q matrix is factored by the kernels' Cholesky, and restrictions that repeat one another make it singular, which is Z0415 too. The result is a `TestResult` printing `test · m · educ == exper` and `F(1, 18,175) = 1748.67   p < 0.001`, as question 3 (b) decided; a single restriction gives the square of the term's t statistic.

**`compare`.** The two regressions must be on the same rows (the frame's row count and the rows-used mask compared; Z0416 otherwise, with the help to drop the rows with missing values first) and one nested in the other by its term names (the same terms, or each with a term the other lacks, Z0416); the receiver may be either model. Under classical errors the F test of the extra terms from the residual sums of squares, ((RSS_s − RSS_l) / q) / (RSS_l / df); under robust or clustered errors the Wald F of the extra coefficients under the larger model's variance matrix, as `test` computes it; the degrees of freedom are the larger model's. The result prints `compare · m2 against m1`, a two-row table of the models (N, RSS, R²) in the order given, and the statistic line, as question 3 (b) decided.

**`derive`.** Each definition is evaluated at the estimates with its gradient over the coefficients by forward-mode dual numbers over `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^` (a constant or a coefficient in the exponent) and the one-argument smooth functions of `core` (`log`, `exp`, `sqrt`, `log1p`, `expm1`, `log10`, `log2`, `abs`); any other call or operator is Z0417. The standard error is √(gᵀ V g) with V the full variance matrix; the t statistic and the interval use the fit's residual degrees of freedom and the fit's level, as Stata's `nlcom` after `regress`; a definition that is not finite at the estimates prints `NA` for its standard error, t, p-value and interval. The result is a `Table` titled `derive · m` in the coefficient table's columns, as question 3 (c) decided, so that `export` writes it as it writes the coefficient table.

**Codes.** Z0415 (a restriction `test` cannot use), Z0416 (two regressions that cannot be compared) and Z0417 (a definition `derive` cannot differentiate), provisional, the next codes of the Z04xx family, logged in `docs/spec_changes.md` and the reference's section-11 table, each with an explained page.

**The reference.** `regression.R` gains an `inference` block: ten fits (the shipped wages classical, HC1 and clustered by worker, each with its nested model without `female`; wage1 classical and with `exper^2` under HC3, each with the model on `educ` alone), fourteen Wald tests written out in base R with `solve` on the sandwich of each fit (one, two and three restrictions, with constants and scalings, on the intercept and on a backticked term), five comparisons (`anova` for the classical pairs, the Wald F of the extra terms otherwise) and forty-two delta-method quantities through `deriv` (ratios, exponentials, roots, logarithms in every base `derive` knows, powers of a sum, a product, a negation, the turning point of a quadratic). Zeff agrees within 1e-10 on every statistic, standard error and value, and the printed rows match R's numbers formatted the same way.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/results/tests/inference.rs`: the three against the reference; every linear shape of one restriction giving the same F and a single restriction the square of its t; the slope of every function `derive` knows and the gradient of a coefficient raised to another; the printed forms through the engine (restrictions in several shapes, the intercept and a backticked term, a bare name beside a binding, an unbound fit, a clustered, a robust and a weighted fit, the chaining of `derive` into `where`, an omitted term, a definition that is not finite) and every message (each shape `test` refuses, each refusal of `compare`, each of `derive`, the checker's own, a test's result or a frame as the receiver). The engine's result tests call the real methods instead of fixtures, and the checker's tests type a restriction and a definition. The three pages' examples run; the catalogue rows 249, 250 and 428 are marked implemented; `zeff help reg` lists the three under the estimator interface.
