**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7, 4, 7.2 and 11; Engine and Project Specification, section 13; questions 3 (b) and (c) as decided on 24 October 2026; the checklist's step 18.

## 24 October 2026: `report` and `export` on results (step 19)

**The table.** `report([fits], stats:, digits:, stars:, labels:, title:)` in `results::report` builds a `Table` in the layout of section 10.2: a first column of term names with no heading, one column per fit headed `(1)`, `(2)`, …; for each term two rows, the estimate with its stars and the standard error in parentheses; a rule; the rows `SEs`, then `N`, `R²`, `AIC` and `BIC` as `stats:` asks (`[n_obs, r_squared]` unless given; `r_squared_within` and the `Fixed effects` row join at 0.6.0 with fixed effects, so the word is not accepted before then); the legend `* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001` and the footer after the grid. The terms are the union of the models' terms in order of first appearance, those with an estimate before those dropped; a model without a term leaves its two cells empty, a model that dropped it as collinear prints `(omitted)`. Estimates and standard errors are rounded to `digits:` decimals (three unless given, as section 3.8 says; 0 to 10, Z0401 outside); R² keeps three decimals, AIC and BIC one, N is a count. The `SEs` row says `classical`, `robust`, `hc2`, `hc3` or `cluster worker`, shortened from the fit's standard-error line.

**The alignment of esttab.** The stars hang to the right of the estimates in a tail of three characters, and the parentheses of the standard errors and the column headings hang into the same tail (two spaces after `(0.004)` and `(1)`), so that right alignment lines the numbers up on their decimal points with the stars beside them, exactly as section 10.2 draws it; without stars the tail is one character for the closing parenthesis. The statistics under the rule take the full column width.

**The rule.** `Table` gains `rules`, the indexes of the rows above which a rule is drawn: a line of `─` across the block when printed, `\midrule` in LaTeX and a top border on the row's cells in Word. Every table built so far has none. A table without a title (a `report` without `title:`) now prints from its grid, with no empty line above it.

**The footer.** Every note of a fit (a dropped term) and every statistical warning it raised (W1001 to W1006, section 11.1) is listed under the legend, numbered as the fit's column is: `(2) warning[W1006]: 1 observation drives a coefficient…`. For this the fit now keeps its warnings as printed (`Fit.warnings`), which `reg` fills as it raises them.

**`labels:`.** A record of term names and text, `labels: {educ: "Years of schooling"}`; a key that is a term of none of the fits is Z0414, a value that is not text Z0401. A record key is an identifier, so a term such as `industry=Retail` or `(intercept)` keeps its name at this release; a text key in records is a syntax question for a later release, not settled here.

**`export` on results.** The receiver of `export` is now `Table | Result`: a regression exports its summary table (the title, the lines above and below the grid as notes), a test's result exports its title and header lines with the models' table and the statistic line under it when it has a table (`compare`), or one row of the statistic, its degrees of freedom and its p-value otherwise. The registry reads a receiver written with several types (`receiver_types`) when it lists the methods of a result type and when it checks that two homes do not overlap; the checker already accepted a union receiver. The catalogue's usage parser reads a list parameter written in brackets, `report([fits], …)`, which it skipped before.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/results/tests/report.rs`: every cell of a two-model table against R's numbers of the reference cases (classical and HC1 on the shipped wages), rounded and starred as the table rounds and stars them, with the `SEs`, `N`, `R²`, `AIC` and `BIC` rows; the stars' thresholds and the standard-error labels; the printed layout through the engine with three kinds of errors, every option, a dropped term, a term a model lacks, weighted fits, a small file whose fit warns, the export of a report, of a fit and of two tests' results, and every message (an empty list, a test's result in the list, `digits:` out of range, a label for no term or not text, a fit not in a list, a word not a statistic, a word not in a list, a frame or a number as the receiver of `export`, an extension `export` does not write). The export tests cover the rule in both formats and a test's result as a table. The shared helpers of the results tests moved to `tests/common/mod.rs`. The two pages' examples run; the catalogue rows 165 and 166 are marked implemented; `zeff help reg` lists `export` under the result interface.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.8, 6, 7.2, 10.2 and 11.1; Engine and Project Specification, sections 2 and 13; the checklist's step 19.

## 24 October 2026: The sample project, its script test and the truth-recovery Monte Carlo (step 20)

**The sample.** `samples/regression` is the fourth sample project: a regression analysis end to end on the shipped wages read from the `zeff:` data root (so it holds no data file), in the shape of section 10.1: load and clean (`add` with `log`, `category` with a sum contrast, `recode`, `label`), describe, four fits of one model (classical, robust and clustered errors, hours as sampling weights), the result interface on the clustered fit (`summary` with standardized coefficients and fit measures, `estimates` filtered, `coef`, `ci` at 90 per cent, `r_squared`, `fit_measures`), `test` twice, `compare` of a nested model with union and the industry deviations, `derive` of the turning point of the experience profile and the return to a decade of schooling, `influence` sorted by Cook's distance, `predict` on a frame written in the script, and `report` of the four models printed and exported to `.docx` and `.tex`, with one model's summary exported on its own. Its stored output is `expected/stdout.txt` and `expected/stderr.txt`, compared byte for byte by the command-line script test and by the conformance report on every target; the files it writes to `output/` are ignored by Git (`/samples/*/output/`), because every run makes them afresh.

**The exported files in the report.** `sample_run_with_outputs` runs a sample on the in-memory file system and lists what it wrote under `output/`; the conformance report hashes each file as a case (`regression/output/table1.docx`, `table1.tex`, `model5.tex`), so the four targets prove the Word and LaTeX writers give the same bytes on real output, not only on the fixed sample of step 13.

**The truth-recovery Monte Carlo.** `packages/tier2/regress/tests/nightly_truth.rs`, marked ignored and run by the nightly job in release mode: fifty seeds of 400 rows under three designs with known coefficients (`y = 1 + 0.5 x1 − 0.25 x2 + 0.3 d + e`, `x1` standard normal, `x2` uniform, `d` an indicator with probability 0.4), the error standard normal (homoskedastic), scaled by `0.5 + |x1|` (heteroskedastic), or the sum of a cluster effect and an individual one with `x1` sharing a cluster component, forty clusters of ten rows (clustered). The data come from the engine's own generator of 0.3.0 (`Stream::new(20261024 + seed, design, 0)` through `dist`'s draws), so the run repeats exactly. Each seed is fitted by `reg` with classical, HC1, HC2, HC3 and CR1 errors. Two checks: the bias of each coefficient, the Monte Carlo mean against its truth, within four standard errors of the mean; and the coverage of the 95 per cent intervals, pooled over the four coefficients and fifty seeds (200 intervals), between 0.89 and 0.995 for the standard errors that suit the design (all five under homoskedastic errors; HC1 to HC3 and CR1 under heteroskedastic errors, which cluster-robust errors also cover; CR1 alone under clustered errors), the others reported for the record. The band leaves room for the Monte Carlo error of 200 correlated intervals (a standard deviation of about 1.5 points when independent) without passing an estimator that is wrong. The nightly note prints each design's biases in standard errors of the mean and the coverage of every kind; the job keeps the log.

**The first nightly run** (run 40055938738, started by hand on 24 October 2026) passed, and its note reads the same as the local run, as a deterministic generator promises. Bias in standard errors of the Monte Carlo mean: homoskedastic (intercept) −1.25, x1 +0.51, x2 +1.08, d +0.84; heteroskedastic −1.51, +2.28, +1.00, +1.23; clustered −0.39, +1.14, −0.48, −0.14. Coverage of the 95 per cent intervals: under homoskedastic errors classical 0.965, HC1 0.950, HC2 0.950, HC3 0.955, CR1 0.955; under heteroskedastic errors HC1 0.955, HC2 0.955, HC3 0.955, CR1 0.940, and classical 0.910 as expected of an estimator that ignores the heteroskedasticity; under clustered errors CR1 0.965, and classical and HC1 to HC3 0.860 to 0.865, the under-coverage that clustering produces when the errors share a cluster component. The long property runs and the stochastic class passed in the same run.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, sections 1 (script tests; truth-recovery tests) and 2.2; Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.5 and 13; Language Reference, section 10.1; the checklist's step 20.

## 24 October 2026: The benchmark suite, the formula fuzz target and the weekly job's new crates (step 21)

**The suite.** `tools/zeff-bench`, a tooling crate outside the engine (its only addition is `criterion` 0.8.2 as a development dependency, already in the workspace for the reduction micro-benchmark of open decision #47; MIT or Apache-2.0), holds the suite of the testing handbook's new section 6: `import` of a CSV, `summary` of three variables by a group of twenty, `mean` by that group (the grouped case until `aggregate` arrives) and `reg` of three regressors with classical errors, at ten thousand, a million and ten million rows. The data come from the engine's generator under a fixed seed, written with six decimals, so the file is the same bytes everywhere; the cases run through the package bodies on a frame parsed once, so that each time is the operation's alone. Each case's result is checked against a digest stored in the crate before it is timed: BLAKE3 of the frame's every cell (bit for bit) for `import`, of the printed table for the grouped cases, and of the printed summary with the bits of the estimates, standard errors, variance matrix, residual sum of squares and log-likelihood for `reg`. The digests at ten thousand rows are a test on every push; the larger sizes are checked when the suite runs (and by an ignored test in release mode, which regenerates them after a deliberate change). Criterion takes ten samples per case, over ten seconds (twenty at ten million rows), so the suite finishes in minutes; it runs in the nightly job after the Monte Carlo, with the processor and each case's time in the summary and the log kept, and reports only (open decision #52): the release notes record and judge the times, and the targets of open decision #30 are set from these first measurements.

**The formula fuzz target.** `fuzz/fuzz_targets/formula.rs`, the sixth target: the bytes choose a frame of one to twelve rows of five variables (missing values, zeros, ones, extremes, repeated values, three labels), one to four terms from a menu of sixteen (variables, a square, a logarithm, interactions, categories under each contrast, an arithmetic term, a duplicate, the intercept removed) and one of eight option sets (robust, HC2, HC3, clustered by a label or an indicator, analytic and frequency weights); the script fits `reg`, prints the fit, predicts on the frame, asks for its influence measures, a test and a derived quantity. Any diagnostic is a fine answer; a Z9001 in the messages, or a panic the engine does not catch, fails the target. It joins the nightly fuzz job's ten-minute runs and its corpus folder.

**The weekly job.** Mutation testing now covers the estimator and variance code as the handbook asks: `zeff-kernels`, `zeff-results` and `zeff-regress` beside `zeff-numeric`, each crate's mutants shared among runners in proportion to their number (at this step 1,838, 368, 1,043 and 288 mutants, about 150 a shard: twelve, three, seven and two shards, twenty-four runners), the options and the two skipped long tests as before; a sample of regress mutants ran at about ten seconds each on this machine, so a shard fits well inside the 340-minute limit. The coverage table lists the estimators (`results`, `regress`) after the kernel crates and applies the handbook's 80 per cent threshold to their total as well as the kernel's.

**Eleven engine faults the formula target found in its first minutes**, each now a regression test. (1) An outcome far below one (1e-300) made the orthogonality self-check fail: the sums of squares of the residuals and of the outcome underflowed to zero, so the check's bound vanished while the products of residuals and regressors did not. The check now computes both norms at the scale of their largest value (`scaled_norm`), which neither underflows nor overflows; the slope of such a fit is recovered to a part in a million. (2) An outcome above about 1e154 in size left the residual sum of squares infinite and the variance matrix full of infinities, which the symmetry self-check reported as an internal error. `reg` now refuses an outcome above 1e150 in size with Z0803 (provisional, logged in `docs/spec_changes.md` and the reference's table, with its page), before anything is squared, telling the user to rescale; a regressor of that size, whose sum of squares overflows, is scaled to zero so that the pivoting drops it, and is reported with a note as a regressor below 1e-150 is (the `Fitted` value carries these `oversized` columns beside the zero and vanishing ones; the design keeps its outcome's text for the message). The thresholds mirror each other at 1e150 and 1e-150, well inside the range where a square is representable.
(3) An observation alone in a cell of the design (a category level with one observation under a model without an intercept) has leverage one, so HC2 and HC3, which divide by one minus the leverage, produced infinities and the same internal error. The variance layer now counts the observations whose leverage is within 1e-8 of one (per observation under frequency weights, as the factors are computed) and refuses HC2 and HC3 with Z0802, naming the count and pointing to HC1, which keeps those rows; the reference's row for Z0802 gains the condition (logged). R's `sandwich` returns infinities in that case.
(4) An interaction of two finite but huge values overflowed to infinity inside the design column (the factors themselves pass the design's check of each variable), and the column, scaled to zero, put a not-a-number into the QR. The design now checks the product of every column with more than one part over the rows it keeps and refuses an overflow with Z0223, the code the reference gives an infinite value in a model variable (section 4.1), naming the column and the rows; the two earlier rulings stand: an infinite value in a variable is Z0223, never a silent drop.
(5) A robust variance whose meat has rank one (two rows sharing the one design pattern with a nonzero residual, the third fitting itself exactly) has a variance and covariances that are exact zeros in arithmetic and rounding residue in floating point; the symmetry check measured their difference against their own vanishing scale and reported a fault. The check now lends every entry the matrix's largest variance as a floor of scale (a difference eight orders below it is never a fault), which leaves a wrong product, an error of order one, as detectable as before.
(6) A perfect fit under sampling weights (two identical rows and a third, every residual rounding residue) gave a sandwich that was nothing but cancellation, and the floor of the previous ruling, a share of the largest variance, was residue too. The check now also bounds each entry's asymmetry by the sum of the sizes of the terms that made it, |B| |M| |B| times the adjustment, which is what the rounding of a sum is bounded by however much it cancels; a wrong product, whose error is of the order of the terms themselves, stays detectable. R prints such a fit's figures without comment.
(7) A sampling weight of 1e300 beside ordinary ones made the weighted design overflow (the rows carry the square root of their weight), while analytic weights, scaled to average one, were safe. Sampling weights are now scaled the same way: every estimate and the HC1 variance are invariant to the scale of such weights (the bread shrinks by the factor, the meat grows by its square), so nothing a user sees changes, as a test of the same fit under weights a thousand times larger shows; frequency weights stay as given, being counts.
(8) A robust variance with an exact zero on its diagonal (the rows with a nonzero residual sharing one design pattern, so a coefficient's scores cancel) came out as a negative residue, which the self-check against a negative variance reported as a fault. Within the same bound as the symmetry check (the sizes of the terms, or a share of the largest variance) a negative diagonal entry is now zero; beyond it, it stays an internal error. The printed table then shows a standard error of zero and the t and p of a degenerate fit, as R prints them.
(9) One category variable written twice with different contrasts (`category(c, contrast: helmert) + category(c, contrast: sum)`) passed the duplicate check, which compared the terms' sources, and produced two sets of columns under the same names, which the summary's bookkeeping could not tell apart (an assertion in debug builds; wrong rows in release). The duplicate check now compares what the sources stand for, a category variable by its name whatever its contrast, so the second coding is a duplicate kept once, with the usual note naming both spellings.
(10) A weighted design column can overflow where its factors are finite (a product of 1e308 times the square root of its row's weight), and the oversized column, scaled to zero, put zero times infinity, a not-a-number, into the factorisation. A column whose scale is zero is now zero outright in the factorisation, so it is dropped and reported as oversized and nothing undefined reaches the arithmetic.
(11) Weights hundreds of orders of magnitude apart (a sampling weight of 1e300 beside ones near 1) scaled the ordinary rows to shares near 1e-300 of the fit, whose products underflow into denormal numbers, where rounding is of order one; the sandwich came out as noise that no bound on exact arithmetic explains. The design now refuses weights more than 1e150 apart (the largest positive against the smallest) with Z0224, naming both, since a row that small a share of the fit is a share of nothing; the Weights row of section 4.1 gains the condition (logged). The sampling-weight scaling of ruling (7) stays, for weights that are large but close.
**A correction the weight scaling uncovered.** The log-likelihood of a fit under analytic or sampling weights was not R's: the step-16 comparison had left the fit measures of weighted fits out, and the two kinds disagreed with each other (analytic weights were scaled to average one, sampling weights were not). The log-likelihood now follows R's `logLik` for a weighted `lm`, which takes both kinds as precision weights: half the sum of the logarithms of the weights (as scaled, which leaves R's value unchanged since R's is invariant to their scale) less half N times (log 2π + 1 + log of the weighted residual sum of squares over N); under frequency weights the rows stand repeated and the formula is unchanged. The comparison with R now covers every weighted fit's log-likelihood, AIC and BIC within 1e-10, and the printed fit-measures line of a sampling-weighted fit changed accordingly.

After these eleven the target ran 442,306 random frames and formulas in five minutes on this machine without an internal error or a crash; the nightly job runs it for ten minutes beside the other five targets, and any input it finds becomes a regression test in `packages/tier2/regress/tests/reg.rs` as these eleven did.

**The first measurements** (this machine, an Apple M2 Pro, ARM64, release mode, the median of criterion's ten samples), which open decision #30 makes the first targets, to be tightened at each release:

| Rows | `import` | `summary` by group | `mean` by group | `reg` |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 10⁴ | 4.26 ms | 0.99 ms | 0.66 ms | 4.17 ms |
| 10⁶ | 484 ms | 94.7 ms | 65.9 ms | 390 ms |
| 10⁷ | 4.87 s | 970 ms | 677 ms | 3.91 s |

Every case scales linearly from a million to ten million rows; `import` parses about two million rows a second and `reg` fits three regressors on ten million rows in under four seconds, both within the engine's single thread. The first nightly run (run 40762764342, started by hand on 29 October 2026, the nightly job green in thirty minutes) gives the x86-64 runner's times, GitHub's `ubuntu-latest`, between 20 and 50 per cent slower than this machine, with every digest matching:

| Rows | `import` | `summary` by group | `mean` by group | `reg` |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 10⁴ | 5.44 ms | 1.36 ms | 0.82 ms | 5.99 ms |
| 10⁶ | 596 ms | 128 ms | 82.3 ms | 579 ms |
| 10⁷ | 6.34 s | 1.69 s | 982 ms | 5.77 s |

The same run's truth-recovery note reads exactly as the first (the generator is deterministic), and the release notes of 0.4.0 will carry both tables.

**The weekly job's first run.** The coverage job of the same run failed in its instrumented test run on an old property of the regression tests, that HC2 and HC3 standard errors stay within a factor of two of HC1's at zero leverage: a random draw with a row of high leverage, where HC3's factor 1 / (1 − h)² is large, showed the claim false (it had passed by luck on every push so far). The property is now the exact one: rows of zeros in a model without an intercept have no leverage and zero scores, so HC2 and HC3 give the same standard errors with and without them, and HC1's change by its factor N / (N − k) alone, each to a part in 1e12; the coverage job was run again by hand after the fix and passed (run started 29 October 2026): line coverage of the kernel 92.6 per cent of 6,874 lines (`zeff-columns` 90.2, `zeff-dates` 98.6, `zeff-diagnostics` 95.0, `zeff-hash` 100, `zeff-kernels` 98.3, `zeff-numeric` 97.7, `zeff-registry` 80.1), of the estimators 91.8 per cent of 4,384 lines (`results` 92.1, `regress` 90.6), both above the handbook's 80 per cent; the engine crates sit between 84.9 (`zeff-cli`) and 98.7 per cent, and the only crate below 80 is `xtask`'s tooling at 55.1. The fuzz job of the same run passed with the formula target among its six: ten minutes each, lexer 1,462,062 inputs, parser 526,564, checker 90,923, CSV 552,989, distribution 66,616, formula 357,501, no crash and no timeout. The nightly job passed in 30 minutes: the long property runs, the stochastic class, the truth-recovery Monte Carlo with a note identical to its first run's (recorded at step 20), as a deterministic generator promises, and the benchmark suite, whose times are the x86-64 table above.

**The mutation shards of the first run.** Twenty-three of the twenty-four finished, in 68 minutes (`zeff-kernels` 0 of 3) to four hours (`zeff-numeric` 2 of 12, whose mutants stop the enumerations of the exact tails and wait for the timeout); the runner of `zeff-results` 1 of 7 was shut down by the service after 110 minutes (exit code 143, "the runner has received a shutdown signal", with every test passing until then and nothing of ours in it), and that job alone was run again on the same commit, as attempt 2 of the run; its outcome is recorded below when it finishes. The twenty-three tested 3,462 mutants: 3,138 caught, 214 missed, 10 timed out, 100 unviable.

- `zeff-numeric`, twelve shards, 1,838 mutants: 1,738 caught, 82 missed, 8 timed out, 10 unviable. The 82 missed are the number recorded as equivalent at 0.3.0 and sit in the same functions (`maths.rs` 19, `special.rs` 46, `association.rs` 13, `order.rs` 4; the largest groups `beta_fraction` 11, `incomplete_beta_inverse` 9, `incomplete_gamma` 7), and the sixteen given tests then are caught now; the timeouts are the hangs by nature (`ranks` 56 and 62, `tie_groups` 135 and 140, Spearman's exact tail 242 twice, `choose` 110 and 114). The match line by line against the 0.3.0 record is part of step 22.
- `zeff-kernels`, three shards, 368 mutants: 335 caught, 11 missed, 2 timed out, 20 unviable. Missed: the `Debug` formatting of a matrix (`matrix.rs` 182); `TallSkinnyQr::cols` returning 0 or 1 (`qr.rs` 132) and a sign in the room left in a block in `push_rows` (160); two comparisons and a product in the pivoted QR's test of a column's remaining norm (243, 245); four conditions in the lanes of the reductions, the wrap of the lane index and the filling of a partial block (`reduce.rs` 68 twice, 75, 110). Timed out: two operators of the pivoted QR's loop that stop it advancing (248, 263).
- `zeff-results`, six shards of seven, 949 mutants: 811 caught, 80 missed, 58 unviable, none timed out. Missed, by function: `symmetrised` 21 (`variance.rs` 88 to 125: the tolerance, the scales of the symmetry check, the bound of the diagonal residue and the mirroring of the triangle), `variance` 6 (196 to 217: the one-cluster guard, the sign of the clustered score sums, which cancels in their products, and the sizes of the rounding bound), `observation_leverage` 3 (259, the frequency-weights branch), `term_magnitudes` 2, `effective_sample_size` 1; in `design.rs`, `weighted_outcome` 7 (440, 444), `orthonormal_polynomials` 6 (1439 to 1441), `weighted` 2 (288, 307: the spread check and the scaling to mean one), `has_outcome` 2, `source_of_column` 2, `expression` 2, `column_expr_text` 3, `category_levels`, `matrix` (427, the root weight) and `evaluate` (729, the negation of a column) one each; in `inference.rs`, `linear` 6 (135 to 153: the negation, the sums, differences and quotients of linear forms), `scaled` 1, `restriction` 1; in `summary.rs`, `deviations` 6 (309 to 320: the standard deviations of the terms and the outcome), `linear_fit` 1 (89), `level_heading` 1; in `interface.rs`, `ci`, `level_text` and `standardized` one each; `export` 1 (`export.rs` 83).
- `zeff-regress`, two shards, 307 mutants: 254 caught, 41 missed, 12 unviable, none timed out. Missed: `reg` 24 (`reg.rs` 128 to 519: the level's bounds, the condition and few-clusters warnings, the symmetry and negative-variance self-checks, the extreme-weights share, the count of driving rows, the perfect-fit rule), `Ols::fit` 10 (`ols.rs` 67, 200, 213 to 217: the oversized outcome, the cross-products of the self-check and its bound), `scaled_norm` 5 (290, 294), `measures` 2 (`diagnostics.rs` 64, 69: the guards of Cook's distance and the studentised residual).

Each shard's full report (`caught.txt`, `missed.txt`, `timeout.txt`, `unviable.txt`) is the run's artifact `mutation-reports-<crate>-<shard>`, and its summary page lists the survivors in full; the job's log keeps only the last forty lines of the run, so the longer lists are read from the artifact. Every survivor is given a test or a recorded reason, and every timeout a verdict, at step 22, as the checklist says. The estimators' survivors come first there: most name arithmetic and guards that the reference fits do not pin (the weighted outcome returned empty, the root weight in the design matrix, the negation and the constants of a restriction, the frequency-weights branch of the leverage), though some will prove equivalent (a sign that cancels in a product, a comparison at an unreachable equality, a rounding bound that no test's data strain).

**The shard that killed its runner.** `zeff-results` 1 of 7, run again as attempt 2 of the run, died the same way after 102 minutes and left no log (the service keeps none when the machine itself goes). Its 159 mutants all lie in `design.rs`, twenty-two of them in `next_combination`, the walk through the combinations of a formula's terms; the one that turns `chosen[i] += 1` into `chosen[i] *= 1` leaves the combination where it is and returns `true` for ever, so `interactions_up_to` pushes the same term without end. Run alone on this machine under a watchdog, that mutant took the two `zeff` processes of the self-test tests past 4 GB within seconds of their start, where the watchdog killed them and the tests failed, the mutant caught; on the runner nothing stood between that growth and the machine's memory, and the service shut the runner down before any test timeout could act. The mutation job now runs every test process under an address-space limit of 8 GB (`prlimit --as`, applied by Cargo through its runner setting for the Linux target and inherited by the processes a test spawns), so that such a mutant aborts in its test with an allocation failure and is caught; and a `shard` input of the scheduled workflow runs one shard by hand, written as `package k/n`, the other twenty-three skipping their steps, so that a shard can be repeated without the whole weekly job. The shard's third run, under that limit and alone on its runner (run 40817137357), died the same way after 105 minutes, a `zeff` process still alive when the service stopped the machine. The limit was the wrong size: the tests run four at a time on the runner's four processors, each self-test with a `zeff` process of its own, and two such processes under an 8 GB limit may take between them the machine's whole 16 GB, so that the machine failed before any one of them reached its limit. Nor was the `*=` mutant the only one of its kind: deleting the `!` before the loop's break test, and making `next_combination` answer `true` whatever its argument, leave the loop without end as well, and the first of the three in the shard's order, mutant 120 of 159, falls at about a hundred minutes at the pace of the sister shards, where each run died. Two measures replace the first. The loop in `interactions_up_to` now runs exactly as many times as there are combinations, a count a new `combinations` function gives in exact integer arithmetic, so that no fault in the stepping can make it run on, and `next_combination` advances the combination in place without a result for the loop to trust; the behaviour is unchanged, the test with `a * g * c` catches any wrong count of terms, and the conformance report and every test are as before. And the limit on each test process is now 2 GB on the memory it may allocate (`prlimit --data`, which counts the heap and the anonymous mappings and not the binary's own image or the allocator's reservations): the whole suite's largest process on this machine reaches 157 MB, so the limit is thirteen times the need, and four processes at the limit together take 8 GB of the runner's 16. The `shard` input now takes several shards separated by commas, so that shards 1 and 2 of `zeff-results` run together: the edit moves the last mutants of shard 1 into shard 2, and both must be seen once. The fourth run (40828889355, on ec0784f), shards 1 and 2 together under the 2 GB limit, passed: shard 1's 160 mutants in 2 h 17 min, 143 caught, 9 missed, 8 unviable, none timed out; shard 2's 160 in 2 h 43 min, 132 caught, 18 missed, 10 unviable; the baseline suite passed under the limit in 18 seconds, and the 156 mutants that both runs tested gave the same outcome both times. The loop's thirty mutants are caught, the three that ran without end among them, all but one: `m - size + i` turned into `m / size + i` in `next_combination` (1349) survives for step 22 with shard 1's other eight, the deletion of the interaction arm of `expand` (897) and the `&&` and `||` of its guards for `interact` and a power (911, 920), `>=` in place of `>` in `refuse_infinities` (1153) and `refuse_infinite_products` (1185, 1200 twice), and the bound of `list_rows` (1301); shard 2's eighteen are the eighteen of the first run. The crate now has 1,114 mutants, six more than before the edit (the eight of `combinations`, less the two the rewrite removed); 1,113 have an outcome from one run or the other, 958 caught, 89 missed, 66 unviable, none timed out, and the one without, the first of the old shard 1, which the edit moved to the end of shard 0, deleting the `Value::Column` arm of a binary operand (782), was run on this machine with the same cargo-mutants and options and caught in 59 seconds. Over the whole weekly job, then, 3,627 mutants: 3,286 caught, 223 missed, 10 timed out, 108 unviable.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, sections 1 (benchmarks; fuzzing; mutation testing on estimator and variance code; coverage of the kernel and the estimators), 2.2, 2.3 and 6; open decisions #30 and #52; Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 10; the checklist's step 21.

## 29 October 2026: the pre-release routine split into six sub-steps

**Choice.** Step 22 of release 0.4.0 is replaced in the checklist by 22a to 22f: the survivors of `zeff-results` (89), of `zeff-regress` (41), and of `zeff-kernels` with its two timeouts (13), each a test or a recorded reason confirmed by local reruns; the numeric kernel's 82 survivors and 8 timeouts matched against the 0.3.0 record; the runs on the four targets and the scheduled jobs by hand on the finished commit, with the sample projects read by eye; and the documents (reference versions, known issues, the risk register's figures, the open decisions, the sample pins) with the report to the owner.

**Reason.** At 0.3.0 the routine took two days and three mutation runs in one step; this release has 143 survivors in three new crates besides the kernel's record, and the standing rule is that a step too large for one session is split in the checklist, not pushed through. The order puts the tests first, since they change the code the final runs must cover, the runs next on that commit, and the documents last.

## 29 October 2026: the survivors of `zeff-results`, each a test or a reason (step 22a)

**The list.** The 89 surviving mutants of the results package from the weekly runs of step 21 (by function in the record of step 21 above: 33 in the variance layer, 36 in the design, 8 in inference, 8 in the summary, 3 in the interface, 1 in export). Each has a test, a removal or a reason below: 50 tests, 11 removed with the dead code they sat in, 28 equivalents. The batches were confirmed by rerunning their mutants on this machine with the same cargo-mutants, the outcomes under *Reruns* below.

**Tests (27 new, catching 50).** The variance layer, 24 of its 33: eight unit tests of the symmetry check inside `variance.rs` itself, the first unit tests in this package's sources, since the check is private (a difference beyond rounding is a fault and the lower triangle is the one kept; the condition number widens the tolerance; the entry's scale is the geometric mean of its two variances; an entry without a scale of its own borrows a hundred-millionth of the largest variance; entries at the edge of the floating range are accepted when they agree; the bound is inclusive; a negative residue within the bound is zero and a larger one is kept for the caller to refuse; a residue without any scale is zero); in the regression tests, two clusters are enough (the one-cluster guard's boundary), a perfect fit under clustered errors with an ill-conditioned bread passes the symmetry check (the case the check once refused; the condition number carries it, so the test pins the scenario and no mutant), and frequency weights give the standard errors of the data written out row by row for HC1, HC2 and HC3 (a property, which pins the leverage a row shares among the observations it stands for); and Kish's effective sample size is zero without weights, not a division of zero by zero. The design, 15 of 36: analytic weights are scaled to mean one in the matrix and frequency weights are not; weights exactly 1e150 apart are accepted and wider apart refused; the category levels kept for `predict` list every category variable; a term may negate a column; `a * b:c` expands as R does; `interact` refuses an order below two at the design (the formula lets it through); `interact` of five at order 2 gives the ten pairs in R's order; an item written as an expression is named by its text, a power without spaces; messages list ten rows and count the rest, for an infinite value, an overflowing product and a negative weight. Inference, 7 of 8: every linear form of a restriction (a coefficient scaled by a constant on one side, negated, shifted by a constant, divided by a constant, and a shifted coefficient scaled or divided, which scales its constant too) gives the Wald F of its row and constant, checked by hand from the estimates and the variance. The summary, 1 of 8: without an intercept, R² under frequency weights weights the squared outcomes. The interface, 2 of 3: a constant regressor in a model without an intercept has no standardized coefficient, nor has any regressor of an outcome without variation; a level of exactly one is refused. Export, 1 of 1: a path ending in a dot has no extension, not an extension Zeff does not write.

**Removed (11).** `Design::has_outcome` and `Design::weighted_outcome`, and the builder's `used` list of the variables used, had no caller anywhere in the workspace (the blocks carry the weighted outcome themselves); eleven of the survivors sat in them, and dead code is removed rather than tested.

**Equivalents (28), with the reasons.** The variance layer, 9: `value < 0.0` turned into `<=` differs only in the sign of a zero, which nothing prints or uses; `i > j` turned into `>=` is taken after the diagonal's own branch; the sign of the clustered score sums, and of their sizes, cancels in their products (two); the sizes left at zero (one), their products (two) and the adjustment of the term magnitudes (two) change the rounding bound alone, which no data strains, the asymmetry of a sandwich lying ten orders below it. The design, 10: the guard that names `category` and `base` columns by their variable (two forms): no other call yields a category column in a formula at this release, a text result being refused before the name is used; the `interact` guard's `&&`: no other call carries the `regress` package in a formula; `parts.len() > 1` in the product check: a single-part column with an infinite value is refused by the infinity check that runs first; the centring and scaling of the polynomial positions (six): an affine change of the positions with a positive scale leaves the orthonormal basis unchanged, signs included, in exact arithmetic, and the bits of the mutated basis differ by rounding alone, which no test should pin to a mutation. Inference, 1: the guard on comparison operators in a restriction sees no other operator, since the checker admits only Bool restrictions. The summary, 7: the standard deviations of the terms and of the outcome enter the results only as a ratio, in the standardized coefficients, so a change of their common divisor (four forms, among them the guard on a single observation, which Z0802 makes unreachable) cancels; the sign of a difference inside the outcome's square (two): Σ c (y + m)(y − m) equals Σ c (y − m)² in exact arithmetic, since Σ c y is m Σ c; and the rounding test of a level heading at exactly 1e-9 (here and in the interface's title, 1) is a boundary no level reaches.

**Reruns.** The batches were first rerun as the weekly job runs them, against the whole workspace's tests with its limits: the 33 survivors of the variance layer with their 13 caught neighbours at the same positions, then the other 73 mutants by description. Most timed out: cargo-mutants 27.1.0 times its baseline on the mutated package alone (17 seconds here) and runs each mutant against the whole workspace (about 100 seconds on this machine), so the five-fold limit, floored at two minutes, falls short as soon as anything else runs; 29 of the 46 and 5 of the first 29 were killed in the middle of another package's tests, none inside a test of their own, and one catch rested on the CSV reader's timing test alone, which gave way under the load. The conclusive outcomes were kept (17 and 19 caught, 5 missed) and the 73 inconclusive mutants rerun against the tests of the results and regress packages, which hold every new test, with a ten-minute limit, two at a time: 22 minutes, 49 caught, 24 missed, none timed out; the mutant with the spurious catch, rerun alone, missed. That rerun exposed four survivors the first draft of the tests did not reach: a scaled restriction's constant (`inference.rs` 112) and the standardized coefficients of an outcome without variation (`interface.rs` 253), which got a case and a test and were caught on a last rerun; and the sizes of the clustered scores (`variance.rs` 208, two forms), re-read as equivalents, as above. The final tally over all the reruns: of the 78 survivors still in the code, 50 caught, each by one of the new tests (the failing tests read from the logs), 28 missed, exactly the equivalents, none timed out. A local rerun therefore passes `--timeout 600` or tests only the packages holding the tests; the weekly job's ten timeouts (`zeff-kernels` 2, `zeff-numeric` 8) may be the same artefact where a package's own tests are quick, to be read in steps 22c and 22d.

**Checks.** Format, clippy with warnings denied, all workspace tests, the tier and message checks, the conformance report (unchanged) and the export check pass.

## 29 October 2026: the survivors of `zeff-regress`, each a test or a reason (step 22b)

**The list.** The 41 surviving mutants of the regression package from the weekly runs of step 21 (by function in the record of step 21 above: `reg` 24, `Ols::fit` 10, `scaled_norm` 5, `measures` 2). Each has a test or a reason below: 23 tests, 18 equivalents, nothing removed. The batch was confirmed by rerunning the 41 on this machine against the package's tests with a ten-minute limit, the lesson of step 22a, the outcome under *Rerun* below.

**Tests (11 new, catching 23).** `reg`, 13 of 24: every form of a level at the ends of the open interval (an integer 0 or 1, a float 0.0 or 1.0) is refused (three mutants: the integer arm and the two bounds); sixty rows in thirty clusters draw no few-clusters warning and twenty-nine do (the bound of W1002); thirteen rows with one weight of 14 among ones, whose effective sample size is exactly a quarter of the rows (3.25, that is 26² over 208, exact under the mean-one scaling too), draw no extreme-weights warning and a weight of 15 does (the bound of W1003); forty rows on a line with five, then six, rows far out on alternate sides and lifted by fifty, each moving an estimate by more than its standard error (DFBETAS of 1.3 and more, the configuration found by search), so that the driving-rows warning lists five rows and counts the rest from the sixth (the two mutants of the count); and R's rule for an essentially perfect fit measured at its threshold, 1e-30 of the fitted values' squared mean plus their variance, by three fits placed on either side of the line by construction (six mutants: the mean as a remainder, the squared deviation's two divisions by the mean, its doubling, and the variance's guard on one row in two forms): an intercept alone on 1.25 with residuals of five units in the last place, a line through 10 + 40x with residuals of 4e-14, and the same line with residuals ten times larger, which is not perfect. `Ols::fit`, 3 of 10: an outcome of exactly 1e150 in size is accepted (the bound of Z0803); an outcome of zeros fits with estimates of exactly zero, its residuals orthogonal within a bound that is zero too (the strict comparison of the self-check in both its mutated forms, which fire at the equality of two zeros). `scaled_norm`, 5 of 5: the package's first unit tests, inside `ols.rs`, since the norm is private: nothing has norm zero, a zero vector too, an infinite value is its own norm and a NaN propagates; and 3 and 4 give 5 at scale 1e-200, where the plain squares underflow, and at 1e200, where they overflow. `measures`, 2 of 2: a single residual degree of freedom leaves no Cook's distance and no studentized residual, whatever the leverage; and a row whose removal leaves a perfect fit (three zeros and a four on an intercept alone, every quantity dyadic) has an error variance without it of exactly zero, so no studentized residual, while its Cook's distance is exactly one.

**Equivalents (18), with the reasons.** `reg`, 10: the condition-number warning at exactly 1e8 is a boundary the scaled design's columns cannot produce (one); the variance arrives from `symmetrised` with one triangle copied, so the asymmetry self-check compares equal numbers whatever its tolerance or comparison (four), and no sound sandwich carries a negative or undefined variance to the other self-check, whose `||` and `&&` then agree (one); `n > 0` before the extreme-weights share, and `df > 0` with a non-empty fitted vector before the perfect-fit rule, hold already, since Z0802 refuses a model without more observations than regressors (three); and (f + m)(f − m) summed over the fitted values equals Σ(f − m)² in exact arithmetic, since Σf is nm (two). `Ols::fit`, 7: the orthogonality self-check's accumulation `+=` turned into `-=` changes a sign that its absolute value drops, and into `*=` leaves it at zero so that the check never fires, as it never fires on a sound solver (two); the slack and the bound of the same check loosened (a slack of ten or more, the column norm added rather than multiplied, the norms' sum added) or reshaped within the norms' sum, which no test's data strains (five).

**Rerun.** The 41 rerun on this machine against the package's tests, the eleven new ones among them, two at a time with a ten-minute limit, in nine minutes: 23 caught, each by one of the new tests (the failing tests read from the logs), 18 missed, exactly the equivalents, none timed out. The rerun corrected one reading: the self-check's comparison turned into an equality (`ols.rs` 217) does fire, at the equality of two zeros, which the outcome of zeros produces, so it counts among the caught.

**Checks.** Format, clippy with warnings denied, all workspace tests, the tier and message checks, the conformance report (unchanged) and the export check pass.

## 29 October 2026: the self-check under large frequency weights (a finding of the fuzz job, step 22e)

**The finding.** The fuzz job of step 22e (run 40903554955) failed on the formula target after 96,764 inputs: the frame `y,a,b,c,d / 1e-300,1e300,1e300,,0 / 1e-300,1e-300,1e300,,0` with `reg(y ~ a, weights: b, weight_type: frequency)` answered Z9001 ("the residuals are not orthogonal to the regressors"), the regression's self-check of section 11.1 of the Language Reference. Reproduced by hand; class S2 (an internal error for a valid script); the same answer from ordinary data under equal frequency weights of about 1e15 and more, so the fault was not the frame's extremes.

**The cause.** The self-check bounds Xᵀe by the slack times the column's norm times the sum of the residuals' norm and the outcome's norm. The columns and the residuals it uses are the weighted ones (each row times the square root of its weight), but the outcome's norm came from the design's unweighted outcome. Analytic and sampling weights are scaled to average one, which keeps the two within the spread of the weights; frequency weights are counts and are not rescaled, so under weights of w the bound was too small by about √w, and from w near 1e15 the rounding of Xᵀe, which grows with w, crossed it.

**The fix.** The outcome's norm is accumulated in the second pass from the weighted outcome the fit uses, at its own scale (the squares of the values divided by the largest, times the largest, as `scaled_norm` does), so the three quantities of the bound are measured alike. No estimate, standard error or printed value changes: the self-check is the only reader.

**The sibling.** Reading the fit of the frame by eye after the fix showed the N line printing 18,446,744,073,709,551,615, the largest 64-bit count, for a weight total of 2e300: the total is a floating-point sum cast to a count, and the cast saturates. Frequency weights whose total exceeds 2^53 (9,007,199,254,740,992), the largest count the arithmetic holds exactly, are now refused with Z0224 (the weights' code), naming the total and saying it is more observations than can be counted exactly, with the help that frequency weights count the observations a row stands for; below the limit every total is exact and prints exactly. Other sibling checks read: the perfect-fit rule and the influence measures divide the residuals and fitted values by the root weights before use and need no change; the leverage h/w under frequency weights is the recorded choice of 23 October (the variance layer); the `Inf` t value of a constant outcome whose estimate is not exactly zero is the same with or without weights and is not part of this finding.

**Tests.** `packages/tier2/regress/tests/reg.rs`: the fuzzer's frame answers Z0224 and never Z9001; equal frequency weights of 1, 1e8, 1e12 and 3e15 give the unweighted estimates (−1 and 1 on an exact line); a total of exactly 2^53 prints as `N = 9,007,199,254,740,992`; a total just beyond is refused. Run once with the self-check fix set aside, the test fails with the fuzzer's Z9001 at the 3e15 weights, so it guards the fix. The crash input replayed through the formula target on this machine runs clean.

**Checks.** Format, clippy with warnings denied, all workspace tests, the tier and message checks and the conformance report (unchanged) pass. The fuzz job is run again by hand on this commit for the record of step 22e.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, section 3 (handling each bug: reproduce, classify, the failing test first, the fix, the siblings, the record) and section 2.4 item 2; Language Reference, section 11.1 (the self-checks after every fit).

## 30 October 2026: an outcome too small to compute with (the fuzz job's second finding, step 22e)

**The finding.** The fuzz job run by hand on commit 6d0c5bb (run 40940333841) failed on the formula target: the frame `y,a,b,c,d / -0.0,1e8,0.5,z,0 / 1e-300,1e-300,3.25,z,0 / 1e-300,1e-300,-1e300,x,1` with `reg(y ~ a^2 + b, se: robust)` answered Z9001 from the self-check on the residuals. Reproduced through the target on this machine; class S2.

**The cause.** The column `b` is oversized and dropped; the fit of an outcome of 1e-300 on the intercept and `a^2` (1e16 in its first row) has a slope near 1e-316, below the smallest normal number (2.2e-308), where a double keeps a few significant digits only. The fitted value of the first row, 1e16 times that slope, is wrong in its seventh digit, so its residual is about 1e-307 where the self-check expects 1e-316, and the check, which allows for ordinary rounding, fires. The arithmetic is at fault, not the check: no solver recovers digits a subnormal estimate does not hold.

**The fix.** A fit whose estimates include one below the smallest normal number (2.2e-308, and not zero) is refused with Z0803, the code of the outcome too large (24 October): the outcome is too small against its regressors to compute with. The first draft refused every outcome below 1e-150 in size, the mirror of the rule above 1e150; the test of step 21 that an outcome of 1e-300 against regressors of ordinary size fits (its slope 6.4e-301 is a normal number) refused that draft, rightly, so the rule reads the estimates, where the harm is. The message names the outcome and the estimate's size, the help says to multiply the outcome by a power of ten and read the estimates in those units; an outcome of zeros still fits with estimates of zero. The code's declared text, its explained page and its row in the Language Reference name the second condition (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Siblings read.** A regressor below 1e-150 in size was already dropped with a note (step 21); the estimates are checked before the second pass computes anything from them, so no fitted value, residual, leverage or standard error is formed from a subnormal number; a subnormal product of a normal estimate and a normal regressor is a value below the outcome's own scale and harmless.

**Tests.** `packages/tier2/regress/tests/reg.rs`: the fuzzer's frame answers Z0803 and never Z9001; an outcome of 1e-300 on a regressor of 1e6 (slope 1e-306, normal) fits and on one of 1e16 (slope 1e-316, subnormal) is refused; the tests of the tiny outcome and the outcome of zeros stand. Both crash inputs of this release's fuzz runs replay clean through the formula target on this machine. The help snapshot of `reg` follows the code's new text.

**Checks.** Format, clippy with warnings denied, all workspace tests, the tier and message checks and the conformance report (unchanged) pass. The fuzz job is run again by hand on this commit.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, section 3 (handling each bug) and section 2.4 item 2; Language Reference, section 11.

R2: the identity check of 107 conformance cases showed no cross-target difference on any push; the reduction shape of #47 (sixteen lanes, `zeff_kernels::reduce`) and the blocked kernels of #48 (the tall-skinny QR in blocks of a million rows, every sum through the lane accumulators across blocks) were built at steps 2 to 3 and are proven in three ways: identical digests on Linux x86-64 at the baseline and at v3, Linux ARM64, macOS ARM64 and WebAssembly; the nightly stochastic figures identical to 0.3.0's to the last digit; and the mutation run's outcomes identical mutant by mutant between the x86-64 runner and this ARM64 machine. R3, at its first test: the R harness matched 36 regression cases within 1e-10 and the inference block (ten fits, fourteen Wald tests, the delta method through `deriv`) at the same tolerance, and the edge cases did cost: the formula fuzz target found thirteen engine faults over the release (eleven in its first minutes at step 21, two at 22e), each fixed with a test within the release, none a wrong result on ordinary data (infinities, underflow, subnormal estimates, singular sandwiches, a weight scaling); the mitigation's extreme-parameter rule and the fuzz target did their work. R6: no dependency upgraded during the release; `arrow` stays at 60.0.0 behind the column store; `criterion` 0.8.2 (Apache-2.0 or MIT) joined as a development dependency of the kernel and the benchmark tool only. R7: a clean release build of the engine takes 67 seconds on this machine (23 at 0.1.0) for a 9.1 MB binary, CI's identity jobs run in two minutes each, and the weekly mutation run spent 2,994 runner-minutes over 25 jobs in 3 hours 45 minutes of wall time. R9: the free GitHub-hosted runners carried every job of the release, the fifty runner-hours of the weekly run and the ARM64 targets included, at no cost. R4, not named by the step but measured on every push: the compressed bundle is 1,337 kB (brotli; 1,151 at 0.3.0) against the 5 MB warning level, and the cold start 639 ms against 1,000 ms (140 at 0.3.0), of which the first call takes 620 ms, a rise to understand before the next release adds to it.

## 30 October 2026: `if` and `case` (release 0.5.0, step 2)

**Choice.** Blocks, `if` and `case` are lowered by the checker into the typed IR (`Block`, `ExprKind::If`, `ExprKind::Case`, and `Statement::Expr` for an expression statement inside a block) and run by the interpreter. Six rulings on what the text leaves open:

1. *Only the script's own statements print.* Inside a block, an expression statement that is not the last is evaluated for its effects (a `warn`, a `print`) and its value discarded; the last expression is the block's value (section 3.1, "Value of a block"), and it reaches the page only where the block's value does: an `if` with `else` used as a statement prints its value, an `if` without `else` prints nothing (its type is `Nothing`, section 3.7). This is how R treats a loop body and how Rust treats a block, and it keeps `let reps = if c { 5000 } else { 1000 }` from printing 5000 on the way.
2. *A branch without a value makes the `if` a statement.* When one branch of an `if` with `else` ends in a `let`, or an `else if` chain has no final `else`, the whole `if` has type `Nothing` and no message is given; binding or passing it is Z0206, whose help says that every branch must end in a value. Two branches whose types do not join are Z0214.
3. *`case` chooses its mode from the values.* The arms are checked in order; while every condition is a single Bool, the first true arm wins and its value alone is evaluated, so an arm not chosen may hold anything (`[1, 2, 3][9]`). The first condition that is a column turns the rest row by row: each later condition is evaluated over every row, each arm's value only when it supplies at least one row, and the first true arm wins in each row; a scalar condition `true` takes every row still unmatched, a scalar value stands for its value in every row. Over the rows, every arm's expression is evaluated on the whole frame, as R's `ifelse` evaluates both branches, so a warning such as W0205 may count rows the arm does not supply; a per-row evaluation that kept the reducers (`mean(x)` inside an arm) over all rows is an optimisation for a later release, not a change of result.
4. *The values a `case` combines are the computable scalar types of this release.* Bool, Int, Float and Str cells are combined row by row; a Category column is refused (Z0214) rather than turned into its labels unasked, since section 3.7 forbids implicit conversion and `to(x, Str)` is one call away; a Date or DateTime column is refused with Z0304 until the types become computable at 0.6.0. A `case` whose every row is `NA` gives a column of the first column value's type, or a scalar `NA` when no arm gave a column.
5. *W0301 is raised for a literal `true` that is not the last arm*, the one always-true condition a checker without constant folding can see; `_` out of place stays the parser's Z0316, and an empty `case { }` is the parser's Z0301, since the grammar requires an arm.
6. *W0208 is the provisional code of the rows no arm matched* (W02xx, the next free number after W0207; logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`), with the count over the rows and, over one value, "no arm matched".

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.1, 3.7 and 5.1, and the checklist's step 2; the printing rule follows from section 3.1's "Value of a block" read with section 3.7's `Nothing`; the evaluation over whole columns keeps every reducer inside an arm computed over the frame it names.

## 30 October 2026: `for`, `[for ...]`, `break` and `continue` (release 0.5.0, step 3)

**Choice.** Loops are lowered to `Statement::For`, `ExprKind::ListFor`, `Statement::Break` and `Statement::Continue`; a binding now carries its kind (`let` or loop variable), and a term may be `Bound` to a loop variable. Six rulings:

1. *A jump travels as a flag.* `break` and `continue` set a pending jump on the interpreter; every block returns at once after a statement that set it, and the loop the jump belongs to takes it. The checker lets a block that jumps stand only where a statement may (its value is `Nothing`), so no expression is left half-evaluated by a jump.
2. *The loop pass in the random key.* The run's randomness keeps a pass counter that the interpreter resets at each statement and raises at every pass of every loop within it, nested loops included, so that `(seed, statement, pass, call)` is unique and a draw inside a loop differs by pass and repeats on a re-run; the draws of a statement outside a loop keep pass 0 and the published digests of 0.3.0 and 0.4.0.
3. *A loop variable holding a variable stands for it everywhere.* In a formula (`y ~ educ`, `log(y)`, `y:female`) the term is resolved when the statement runs and takes the variable's name, so the printed header and the result's term names read `log(hours)`; as a `Var` or `Vars` argument the binding is passed and the function resolves it; inside `add` and the other column arguments the column of the variable it holds is read. A loop over `vars(x1..x9)` is refused (Z0221), since a range is expanded only against a frame.
4. *A loop variable named like a column is Z0106*, whether the name is read as a column argument or as a variable argument of a frame method, checked when the statement runs against the receiver's columns (section 3.7, rule 2); outside a frame method there is no clash.
5. *What a loop runs over*: a List (a Range is one), or Vars; anything else is Z0221, with the help that a frame's rows are not looped over. The body of `[for ...]` must end in a value (Z0206 otherwise); a `let` that reuses a loop variable's name is W0302.
6. *`vars` moved from step 13 to this step*, because a loop over variables cannot be tested without it; its page and row are done here, and step 13 keeps `any`, `all` and `seq`.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7, 5.2 and 6; Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 3; the checklist's step 3.

## 30 October 2026: spreads in calls and records (release 0.5.0, step 4)

**Choice.** `..opts` in a call and `..r` in a record run from this step. Five rulings:

1. *A spread is evaluated once, where it stands.* In a call the IR keeps the spread as its own slot in the order of evaluation (`Slot::Spread`), with the parameters its fields fill decided by the checker from the record's type; the parameters it fills carry a placeholder (`FromSpread`) that is never evaluated. An argument written out overrides the spread's field wherever it stands, before or after it, in silence; the same field from two spreads is Z0405, a field that names no parameter Z0404 (with the nearest name), the receiver Z0404, a field of the wrong type Z0401, and a spread of anything but a record whose fields are known Z0401. A spread counts as a named argument, so a positional argument after it is Z0408.
2. *In a record, the fields keep the order written*, a spread's fields in its place; a field written out overrides a spread's field and keeps the spread's position; a field written twice, or supplied by two spreads, is Z0222, whose row in section 11 gains the condition (logged).
3. *Option records hold words.* Section 3.1 writes `{se: robust}` as an option record, and a bare word has no meaning outside an argument (section 3.7); inside a record literal, a bare name that is no binding and that some registered parameter accepts as a word is that word, typed as the one-word list, which the parameter's word list accepts when the record is spread. A name no parameter accepts stays Z0101, with the nearest word in its help. So a typo such as `{se: robst}` is caught where it is written.
4. *A one-word type reads as the word in messages* (`the word \`robust\``), and a list of words accepts any of its members, which the type checker did not say before because no value of a one-word type existed.
5. *No identity case*: a spread adds no numeric path; the checker's and the engine's tests compare a spread call with the call written out, bit for bit through the printed fit.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.1 ("Definitions"), 3.4 (`arg`, `field`) and 3.7 ("Arguments"); the checklist's step 4 and its ruling that the spreads arrive at "Language complete".

## 30 October 2026: the `Failed` type and `attempt` (release 0.5.0, step 5)

**Choice.** `core` declares the `Failed` value (the error's code, message and line) and the type; `attempt(expr)` is lowered by the checker to a node of its own, typed as `expr`, and the interpreter evaluates the expression under a catch. Seven rulings:

1. *What is caught.* A script error (Z01xx to Z08xx) becomes a `Failed` value; an internal error (Z9xxx) is a bug, not the script's failure, and stops the run as before. The warnings and notes raised before the failure stay, since they happened. The failure's line is the line of the error's primary label, so a failure inside a loop names the statement in the loop body.
2. *Where a failed value may stand.* In a list, and as the argument of the functions that look at it (`is`, `type_of`, `print`) or skip it (`report`; `len` from step 11). Anywhere else, as an argument, inside a list given to any other function, in arithmetic or a comparison, in a record or a mapping, it is Z0220, found when the statement runs and reporting the failure it holds. A failed value in a definition of `add` or `frame` is the argument case.
3. *The guard warning is W0209*, the next free code of the W02xx family (logged): a method called on a binding whose value came straight from `attempt`, unless the call is guarded. The checker narrows by the two forms of section 3.7: inside `if !x.is(Failed) { }`, and after `if x.is(Failed) { }` whose block ends in `continue`, `break` or a call to `error` (and `return`, at step 6), for the rest of the enclosing block; a `[for]` body that starts with `if m.is(Failed) { continue }` is the common case. `is`, `type_of` and `print` never warn.
4. *The static type of `attempt(e)` is `e`'s*: a failed fit is still a `RegFit` to the checker, so arithmetic on it is the checker's Z0221, and only a failure whose type admits the use reaches Z0220 at run time. A list's run-time type ignores its failed items, as section 3.7 says.
5. *`report` skips failed fits with W0801*, naming how many of how many failed and up to three distinct causes (`Z0801 at line 3`); a list whose fits all failed is Z0406 with the causes, since the table would have no column.
6. *The printed form* is the owner's: `failed · Z0801 at line 3: message`, on one line, in a list and alone.
7. *The registry entry of `attempt`* carries the page and the signature; its Rust body is never reached and reports Z9001 if it is, so the help contract's build check holds for it as for every function.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Failed values", "Narrowing"), 4, 5.4 and 5.6; the checklist's step 5 and question 3 (a).
