## 1 November 2026: dates and times as computable types (release 0.6.0, step 2)

**Choice.** `core`'s value type gains `Date` (days since 1970-01-01) and `DateTime` (microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC), the two scalars the column kernel has held since 0.1.0 and no expression could hold; they print in ISO 8601 (`2026-10-16`, `2026-10-16T09:30:00`, a fraction of a second to the microsecond), compare chronologically, are identical by their counts, and sort after text and before `NA` in the order of section 3.7. The operators follow section 3.7, "Dates": `Date - Date` is Int days, and every other arithmetic on a date is Z0221 naming the function meant (`add_days` and `add_months` for a date beside a number, `days_between` for two DateTimes, which have no difference until a Duration type arrives), in the checker and in the row-wise operators alike; a date against text is Z0210, numbered by section 3.7 and new to the engine, whose help names `to("2020-01-01", Date)` and `date()` of the `time` package. `to` reads text as a Date or DateTime from ISO 8601 or from the format written with the type (`Date("%d/%m/%Y")`, checked by Z0409), an ISO date without a time given to DateTime being midnight as a Date converted to DateTime is, a DateTime to Date dropping the time, an impossible date `NA` with W0203, and date-and-time text with `Z` or an offset converted to UTC and counted (W0702, the reader's code and wording); `is`, `type_of`, the lists, `sorted`, `unique`, `is_in`, `equal`, `first`, `last`, `coalesce`, `fill_missing`, `is_missing`, `min` and `max` (a Date or DateTime beside Floats in their signatures, the earliest and latest by count) take dates; a `case` may give a date column or a date arm; `add` and `update` define date columns and `update` keeps a date variable's type; `recode` maps dates to dates by identity; the frame literal holds dates. Every "arrives with release 0.6.0" message that named dates is retired; Z0304 keeps the opaque columns.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Dates", "Comparison", "Identity", "Order", "Conversions"), 3.8 ("Time", the printing table), 4 and 4.1; the step's definition in `docs/releases/0.6.0.md`; the dates kernel's decision of 18 October 2026 (ISO 8601 strict, formats in `strftime` notation, four-digit years under `%Y`, hours 0 to 23), which the reference test records as the two departures from R (`01/02/26` under `%Y` is no date; `24:00:00` is no time).

**Tests.** The R reference `tests/reference/r/dates.R` (base R: `as.Date` with and without a format, day counts, comparisons and differences, `as.POSIXct`, offsets, midnight and the dropped time, `sort`, `unique`, `min`, `max`; exact, the calendar's ends kept as day counts because R prints years below 1000 differently between platforms); the engine's `dates.rs` (the reference, the types in expressions and frames, every message as a snapshot, and the property over the whole calendar that every day round-trips through its text, differences are day counts and sorting dates is sorting their counts); the conformance case `control/dates`; the pages of `to`, Z0221, Z0304 and the new Z0210.

## 1 November 2026: the `time` package, part 1 (release 0.6.0, step 3)

**Choice.** A new package crate, `packages/tier1/time` (`zeff-time`), first in tier 1 as section 8.2 orders it, depending on `core`, the dates kernel, the diagnostics and the registry only, registered with the engine before `data` and loaded at start by rule 7. Its eight functions are scalar functions that the checker lifts over a column row by row: the lifting rule of section 3.7 ("every built-in scalar function of `core`, `text` and `time` applies row by row") was written for `core` alone at 0.2.0 and now names the three packages. `date(s, format:)` and `datetime(s, format:)` read ISO 8601, or the format given in `strftime` notation (Z0409 at the call for a text that is not a format), a date alone given to `datetime` being midnight, `Z` or an offset applied to reach UTC (W0702) and text that does not read becoming `NA` with W0203; the warnings are worded without the failing text, so that the rows of a column count as one warning (`to(s, Date)` names the values). The date parts `year`, `month`, `day`, `weekday` (ISO: Monday 1 to Sunday 7), `quarter` and `week` (ISO 8601: the week of the Thursday, 1 to 53) take a Date or a DateTime, whose day they read, and return Ints; the kernel gains `weekday_of`, `quarter_of` and `iso_week`, proved for every year of the calendar against R at 1 January and 31 December. The catalogue rows 67, 68 and 71 to 76 are marked implemented; the conformance report gains `time/parts`.

**Reason.** Catalogue rows 67, 68 and 71 to 76; Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.1 (rules 3, 7 and 8), 8.2 and 9.1; Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Columns and scalars") and 3.8 ("Time"); the owner's decision of 1 November 2026 that the references stay in base R: `as.Date`, `as.POSIXct` and `format` with `%Y`, `%m`, `%d`, `%u` and `%V`, and `quarters`, which give every value exactly; the two departures of the dates kernel from R (a two-digit year under `%Y`; hour 24) stand as recorded at step 2.

**Tests.** The R reference `tests/reference/r/time.R` (the parts on a grid of thirty dates, at every year boundary from 1 to 9999 packed as text, and on times); the crate's `time.rs` (the references, including every boundary through the kernel and every 97th year through the engine; the edge cases and the column forms as a snapshot; every message as a snapshot; the property that every day reads back through `date`, the weekday advances by one per day, 4 January is in week 1 and the parts rebuild the day); the eight pages' examples through the examples runner; the conformance case `time/parts`. The bundle and cold-start figures with `time` loaded at start are read from the continuous-integration run of this commit and recorded at the next step.

## 1 November 2026: the `time` package, part 2, and the run's clock (release 0.6.0, step 4)

**Choice.** `add_days` and `add_months` take a Date or a DateTime and an Int and return the type they were given (the registry's `Same` return rule, which a lifted call now wraps in a column once rather than twice), the time of day kept on a DateTime; `add_months` clamps to the last day of the target month and is therefore not reversible at a clamped day, which the page says; a result outside years 1 to 9999 is `NA` with W0203. `days_between` is `end − start` in days on dates and the whole days between two instants truncated towards zero on times, a date beside a time refused at the call with Z0401 since the checker admits either type for each argument; `months_between` is the largest `m` with `add_months(start, m)` at or before `end`, negative and symmetric backwards, the days alone counting on times. The clock is an interface, never read by the engine: `Files` of `core` and `FileSystem` of the engine gain `now()`, microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 with no zone, `None` by default; the in-memory file system takes a fixed clock (`set_clock`), which the examples runner, the crate's tests and the conformance case set to 2026-11-01 09:30:00 so that `today()` and `now()` print one value on every target; the command line wraps the machine's file system with the local wall-clock time read through `chrono` 0.4.45 (MIT or Apache-2.0), which was already in the dependency tree through Arrow and is now a direct dependency of `zeff-cli` alone, with only its `clock` feature, so the engine and the browser build carry nothing new. `today()` and `now()` print W0703 as a note with the value at each use; `--deny-warnings`, among the options of a later release, refuses it when it arrives, and the run record of 0.11.0 records it. A run without a clock (a test's bare `Files`) answers `today()` with an internal error, never a guess. The catalogue rows 69, 70 and 77 to 80 are marked implemented; the conformance report gains `time/arithmetic`. One test of `iterate` named a script function `now`, which the built-in now captures (Z0109, as section 3.6 says); the test's function is renamed.

**Reason.** Catalogue rows 69, 70 and 77 to 80; Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Dates", "Effects": Z0110 for `today` and `now` in a function, built at 0.5.0), 3.8 ("Time": month arithmetic, differences, `today()` and `now()`, exit code 3 under `--deny-warnings` when that option arrives), 3.6 ("Built-in names"); Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3 (point 4: never cached) and the dependency rules of the standing instructions.

**Tests.** The R reference `time.R` extended with days and months added (the clamping written out in base R, which R's `seq` lacks), the differences in days and whole months over every pair of ten dates, and the whole days between four pairs of times, exact (R's proleptic calendar has a year 0 and years beyond 9999, which the engine refuses: the test reads those as `NA`); the crate's `time.rs` (the references; the clock under a fixed instant with its notes as a snapshot, Z0110 inside a function and the internal error without a clock; the edge cases and the column forms; every message; the properties that moving by days and counting them agree, that a month forward and back returns to the day or an earlier one, and that the months between a day and its move are the move); the six pages' examples; the conformance case `time/arithmetic` under the fixed clock.

**The figures of step 3, read from its continuous-integration run (41322024807).** The compressed browser bundle is 1,466.7 kB with `time` loaded at start (1,457 at the close of 0.5.0) against the 5,000 kB warning level, and the cold start 93.6 ms (the module's load 25.5 ms, the first call 68.0 ms, a one-line script, the median of five fresh processes) against 1,000 ms; the whole conformance report takes 1,665 ms with 154 cases, for information. Both limits hold; the first call's growth from 48 to 68 ms is the registry's two added crates and is noted for the review of R4 at the close.

## 1 November 2026: `format`, and the `text` package (release 0.6.0, step 5)

**Choice.** A new package crate, `packages/tier1/text` (`zeff-text`), second in tier 1 after `time` as section 8.2 orders it, with one function at this release and twelve to follow at 0.7.0; registered with the engine between `time` and `data`, so that `data`'s functions written in Zeff may call it. `format(x, digits:, big_mark:, pattern:)` takes an Int, a Float, a Date or a DateTime and gives text: a number without options as section 3.8 prints it; with `digits:` to that many decimal places (0 to 20), half to even on the exact binary value as `round` decides a tie, trailing zeros kept and the plain form used whatever the size (the tables' `fixed` switches to the exponent form at 1e15, which a formatted number should not); `big_mark:` between every three digits of the whole part, any text but the empty one; a date or time without a pattern in ISO 8601, with `pattern:` as the dates kernel prints it, which gains `format_with` and the printing directives `%a`, `%A` and `%j` beside the parsing ones, the English names whatever the locale. An option that does not fit the value is Z0401, `pattern:` beside `digits:` or `big_mark:` is Z0410, and a pattern that is not one is Z0409, as the reader's formats are. `format` is lifted over columns by the rule of step 3. The catalogue row 95 is marked implemented and the conformance report gains `text/format`.

**Reason.** Catalogue row 95; Language Reference, sections 3.8 ("Printing": `format(x, big_mark:)`; "Text": the unit of `format`) and 3.7 ("Text": `format` builds text from values); Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.1 (rule 3) and 8.2; the ruling of the checklist that `digits:` means decimal places, as `round(x, digits:)` and `report(digits:)` mean it.

**Tests.** The R reference `tests/reference/r/format.R` (`sprintf` to zero to six places over twenty numbers, which R and the engine both take from the correctly rounded decimal expansion, so the texts agree exactly, R's `-0` excepted; `formatC` with a comma and a space on whole numbers; `format` of dates and times by ten and four patterns in the C locale); the crate's `format.rs` (the references; the edge cases and the column forms as a snapshot; every message; the properties that the decimals are the count asked, the text reads back within half a unit of the last place plus the number's own spacing, the separators come out to the plain text and the ISO pattern is the ISO text); the page's examples; the conformance case `text/format`.

## 1 November 2026: a scalar call lifted at run time when a column shadows a binding (a bug found after step 5)

**What was found.** The owner's request for sample scripts of the release exposed a defect older than it: with `let d = date("2026-10-16")` in scope, `sales.add(d = date(sold)).add(y = year(d))` stopped with an internal error (Z9001). Inside a frame method the variable wins over a binding of the same name, with W0102 (section 3.7, "Name lookup"), and the interpreter did use the column; but the checker, which does not see a frame's columns before the schema pass (step 20), had typed `d` as the binding, a scalar, and so had not marked the call for row-by-row application, and `year`'s body received the whole column. The same clash since 0.2.0 made `sqrt(x)` on a shadowed `x` give `NA` and the misleading error Z0219 ("`y = NA` has no type"); no wrong number was printed, so the severity is S2 (an internal error) with an S3 sibling (a wrong message).

**Choice.** Every call carries, beside the checker's `lifted` mark, whether the function may apply row by row at all (the rule of step 3: a scalar function of `core`, `text` or `time`, or a scalar-returning method on a value that is not a frame) and which of its parameters and further values take one row's scalar; the interpreter lifts a call whose scalar parameter receives a column at run time, with the same row-by-row machinery and the same counting of warnings. A built-in written in Zeff already chose its form from the values it was given, so it needed nothing. The failing test was written first (`crates/zeff-engine/tests/shadowing.rs`: `sqrt`, `year`, `min` with a further value, `round`, and the Zeff-written `clamp`, each over a column that shadows a binding). The schema pass of step 20 will let the checker type the name as the column in the first place; this run-time rule stays as the guard for the steps the checker marks "checked at run time".

**Reason.** The testing handbook, section 3 (the failing test first; siblings sought: the reducers take a `Var`, not a value, and the operators already work on columns at run time, so no other path shares the fault); Language Reference, section 3.7. The conformance cases `time/parts` and `time/arithmetic` of steps 3 to 5 carried the same clash, so their published hashes had been taken from runs that stopped at the internal error; both are republished from the correct output, read by eye (every date part and every move printed as the pages say), which is the lesson that a new case's text is read before its hash is published.

## 1 November 2026: shared columns and selection vectors (release 0.6.0, step 6)

**Choice.** A frame made by `where`, `sort` or `drop_missing` (and `sample` when it arrives) no longer copies its rows: each of its columns is a slot holding either a gathered column or a pending source, the parent's column (whose Arrow buffers it keeps alive) with the row positions, gathered into a compact buffer the first time the column is read and the source let go then. The slots are shared by reference between the frames a verb derives without touching the rows (`select`, `drop`, `rename`, `add`, `update`), so a column is gathered once for all of them; a selection of a selection composes the row positions and keeps naming the original parent, so a chain of `where`s gathers once; a selection that keeps fewer than half of the parent's rows is gathered at once and the parent let go, as section 6 says; `head` and `tail` gather, since a slice needs the buffer. Models, `save`, the IPC writer and `frame(x = ...)` read through the same accessors and so always work on compact columns. The kernel's eager `take_rows` stays as the oracle of the lazy form. Every column reader goes through the slot, so nothing a script prints changed: the conformance report and the benchmark digests are byte for byte what they were.

In `zeff run`, a `let` of the script's top level is freed after the last top-level statement that reads it, found by one pass over the typed IR (`liveness`); a use inside a loop or a block counts for the statement that holds it, so a binding read in a loop lives to the loop's end, and a binding never read goes right after its `let`. When a frame is freed, every frame still bound gathers what it still read from it (`release`, matched by a token that names the parent table), so the parent's buffers go with it; a session keeps every binding until shadowed, as the console runs with freeing off. The interpreter records what each frame held when bound (its own bytes and the parent bytes kept alive, as Arrow counts them) and when a binding was freed with how many columns were gathered from it; `zeff run --verbose` prints the record, which is the reported size of section 8.3, point 7 until Zemp's object panel shows it.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 6 ("Memory", the whole table; "Row order", unchanged); Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.1 (rule 8: column store and selection vectors), 8.3 (points 7 and 10); open decisions #48 and #49 (the block interface the verbs adopt at 0.6.0; option B of 23 October 2026). The parent is named by a token, the table's address, rather than held, so that a selection keeps alive only the columns it still needs and not the whole parent; the token can only be matched while the parent lives, so a stale match can at worst gather early.

**Measurement.** The five-step chain of section 6 (`import` of the million-row benchmark file, `where` keeping 80 per cent of the rows, `add`, `select`, `sort`, `head`) on this machine (Apple silicon, release build, five runs, the machine otherwise idle): peak memory 689 to 691 MB after against 695 to 697 MB before, with the import alone at 449 MB in both; wall time 0.76 to 0.78 s in both. The gain is small on this chain because it reads four of the file's five columns and the import's own buffers set the peak; the saving grows with the columns a chain leaves unread, and with `where`s that keep most rows. The benchmark suite's times at a million rows, before and after, are in the progress entry; the digests are unchanged.

**Tests.** The kernel's `selection.rs` (a large selection pending until read and a small one gathered at once, with the bytes own and kept; a selection of a selection composing its rows and `release` gathering what is pending; a `select` sharing the slot; the property over generated tables and chains of selections that the lazy form equals the eager `take_rows` column for column, read in any order or compacted, with its own bytes never above the eager form's); the engine's `memory.rs` (bindings freed after their last use, a loop keeping its binding, a never-read binding freed at once, a session keeping everything, and a frame from a freed frame answering from its own buffers, each as the memory record); the command line's `--verbose` record as a snapshot with the byte counts masked; the whole suite unchanged, the published conformance report and the benchmark digests byte for byte.

## 1 November 2026: the panel declaration and its index (release 0.6.0, step 7)

**Choice.** `data.panel(unit:, time:)` writes the declaration into the frame's metadata store, which the IPC round trip and the shipped `wages` have carried since 0.2.0, and the header has printed as `panel worker × year`; what this step adds is the function with Stata's checks and the rules by which the declaration travels. `time:` is an Int or a Date (a Float or text is refused with the conversion to write), `NA` in either variable is refused with the rows counted, and a unit observed twice at one time is refused naming the first repeated pair and how many more repeat, each as Z0601, the next free number of the data family, with `duplicates([firm, year])` named for when it arrives at step 11; a unit of any computable type is accepted and an opaque one refused; `unit:` and `time:` are written as options, so a missing one is Z0406 at the call. The index, the stable sort of the rows by unit then time, is built once at the declaration and kept with the table in a cell the derived frames that keep the rows share (`select`, `rename`, `add`, `update`); a selection builds its own when a panel function first asks (`panel_index()`), which `lag`, `lead`, `diff`, `fill_forward`, `by:` on the unit and `fe:` on the unit will read. The declaration survives every verb that keeps both variables unchanged (`where`, `sort`, `head`, `tail`, `drop_missing`, `add` of other variables, `update` of other variables, `label`, `select` with both among them) and `rename` of either, which renames the declaration; it is dropped with a note naming what the verb did when `select` or `drop` leaves one out, or `add`, `update` or `recode` replaces or changes one, through one helper every such verb calls; `aggregate` and `to_wide` drop it at their steps, and `merge` on other keys keeps it at its step. The function prints nothing: the header says what was declared.

**Reason.** Catalogue row 120; Language Reference, sections 6 ("Panels"; the "Panels" row of the task table; "Row order"), 4.3 (rule 3: the frame's store), 10.2 (the header); Engine and Project Specification, sections 8.3 (point 10: panel indexes) and 8.7 (the `zeff.panel` key); the checklist's rulings on the declaration and on provisional codes (Z0601 in section 11's table, logged).

**Tests.** The data crate's `panel.rs`: the header and the rows keeping their order; the index on a fixture, built once and shared by a verb that keeps the rows, rebuilt by a selection; survival through fourteen verbs as a snapshot with every note; the edge cases (one unit, one time, a Date time, the shipped `wages` declared again and a one-year slice of it); every message; the property over generated panels that the index is a permutation sorted by unit then time and that a verb keeping both variables keeps the declaration with the same index. The page's examples; the conformance case `panel/declare`; the kernel's existing round trip of the declaration through IPC.

## 1 November 2026: the panel column functions (release 0.6.0, step 8)

**Choice.** `lag`, `lead`, `diff` and `fill_forward` stand inside `add` or `update` of a declared panel and take the frame from the enclosing verb: the declaration's index gives each unit's rows in time order, and a two-pointer walk down each unit finds, for every row, the row exactly `n` periods away, so a gap in the periods gives `NA` as Stata's `L.` and `F.` do and the row order of the frame plays no part. `diff` is written in Rust rather than in Zeff: a Zeff body `x - lag(x)` has no handle on the enclosing frame whose panel `lag` needs (the catalogue's row 127 now says so, logged; the shape of such bodies is open decision #69). `fill_forward` carries the last value present forward within the unit in time order when the frame is a panel and down the rows as they stand otherwise, and `by:` splits the rows first either way. Outside a panel, outside `add` and `update`, with a column of another frame, or with `n:` below 1, each is refused: Z0602 (a provisional code in section 11's table, logged), Z0602 with its own help, Z0217 and Z0401. The kernel's `Column::take_optional` gathers rows by optional index in one Arrow `take`, which keeps every column type, categories included.

**Reason.** Catalogue rows 125, 126, 127 and 139; Language Reference, section 6 ("Panels": the period rule, the gap rule, "Row order"); the checklist's rulings on the index and on provisional codes. The exact period rule is the one statisticians expect of a panel: dplyr's `lag` takes the previous row, which is wrong after a gap.

**Tests.** The data crate's `panel_functions.rs`: R's values on a generated unbalanced panel with gaps and `NA`s and on a slice of the shipped `wages` (`tests/reference/r/panel.R`, registered with `check_r.py` and the CI job; the difference, the one computed value, written with 17 significant digits since 15 round the last bit of a subtraction away), exactly, both frames shuffled; the edge cases as a snapshot (a one-row unit, a gap of exactly `n`, a text column lagged, a Date time, `fill_forward` with and without a panel and with `by:`, `diff` on Ints); every message as a snapshot; the property that `lead(lag(x))` and `lag(lead(x))` are `x` where both exist, that `diff` is `x - lag(x)` row by row, that `fill_forward` leaves no `NA` after a unit's first value and that a reordering of the rows changes nothing. The conformance case `panel/lags` is published. The four help pages' examples run under the examples runner.

## 2 November 2026: the column functions running_sum, running_product, rank and bin (release 0.6.0, step 9)

**Choice.** The four read one column in its current row order and need no frame of their own: under `by:` the verb hands each group's rows to the definition, so the running values restart and the ranks begin again in each group, and `sort` first fixes the order. `running_sum` keeps an Int column Int, with Z0211 naming the row where the sum leaves 64 bits, and sums Floats as a plain double in row order; an `NA` makes the rest `NA`, as R's `cumsum`. `running_product` is always Float, as R's `cumprod`, since Int products overflow within a few dozen rows. `Inf - Inf` in a sum and `0 * Inf` in a product give `NA` with W0205 and the rest `NA`. `rank` sorts once through the kernel's `sort_rows` (the order of section 3.7, stable, `NA` last) and gives each run of equal values its ranks: a Float under `ties: average`, since a tied rank may end in a half, and an Int under `min`, `max` and `first`; `NA` stays `NA` as R's `na.last = "keep"`; an unordered category is refused with Z0221, as `<` refuses it. `bin` is R's `cut`: the breaks sorted, compared as doubles, `(a, b]` by default and `[a, b)` under `closed: left`, an ordered category whose levels are the intervals, labelled as R's `formatC(breaks, digits = 3, width = 1)` labels them, with more digits while two neighbouring breaks print alike, and R's quirk of a leading space before `Inf` kept so that the labels match character for character; a value outside every interval becomes `NA` with W0210, a provisional code in section 11's tables, logged. The kernel's `Key::of` became public so that a package can order rows by the kernel's own key. `rank`'s declared result is the union `Column<Float> | Column<Int>`, which the checker already parses, so a comparison after it checks.

**Reason.** Catalogue rows 128, 129, 130 and 132; Language Reference, sections 3.7 ("Numbers": `running_sum` on Int stays Int, Z0211; "Identity" and "Order"), 4.1 (`Inf` as open ends; an `NA` makes the rest `NA`) and 4.2 (categories); the checklist's rulings on order, `NA` and the category `bin` returns. The three closed-form rows carry References to R's documentation, as the page contract asks of a statistical method.

**Tests.** The data crate's `column_functions.rs`: R's `cumsum`, `cumprod`, `rank` under the four tie rules and `cut` with its labels (`tests/reference/r/running.R`, registered with `check_r.py` and the CI job), exactly; the values summed and multiplied are integers to 1e12 and dyadic fractions, whose sums are exact in a double, so that R's long-double accumulator on x86-64 and the engine agree bit for bit on every platform. The edge cases as a snapshot (an `NA` first, one row, ties throughout, `-Inf` and `Inf` only, Int sums staying Int, `by:` groups, ranks of dates, text, Bools and an ordered category, values on the breaks under both closures, labels at four digits); every message as a snapshot (Z0211 near 2^63, W0205 twice, Z0406, Z0401 for each refused list, Z0221, W0210); the properties that `running_sum` of ones is the row number within its group, that `rank` under `ties: first` is a permutation of the values present, and that `bin` gives each value the interval its definition names under both closures. The unit test of the label formatting against R's printing. The conformance case `panel/running` is published.

## 2 November 2026: quantile_group and winsorize (release 0.6.0, step 10)

**Choice.** `winsorize(x, at:)` is written in Zeff, as planned: `clamp(x, quantile(x, at), quantile(x, 1 - at))` on a frame of the column, with the quantile of type 7, so that it agrees with R's `pmin(pmax(x, quantile(x, at)), quantile(x, 1 - at))` to the bit; a share outside 0 to 0.5 is refused by `assert` inside the body (Z0001, the only voice a body has until open decision #70). `quantile_group(x, n:, type:)` is written in Rust instead of the planned Zeff: a body in Zeff cannot build the probabilities 1/n to (n − 1)/n exactly, since `/` does not apply to a list, nothing maps over a list, and `seq` with a fractional step reaches each probability within a rounding of i/n rather than at it, which could move a cut point against R; the catalogue's `layer` is corrected and logged, and the missing piece is open decision #79 (a `map` over lists, or arithmetic lifted over lists, recommended for 0.7.0). The Rust body takes the kernel's `zeff_numeric::order::quantile` on the values present, the same bits as `quantile` gives, and each row's group is one more than the number of cut points strictly below its value: a value equal to a cut point falls in the group below, so tied values share a group, as R's `cut(include.lowest = TRUE)` places them; when two cut points coincide (fewer distinct values than groups) the groups between them are empty and the numbering is kept, as Stata's `xtile` keeps it, where R's `cut` would refuse repeated breaks; the page says so. `NA` stays `NA` without a warning, as `rank` treats it, while `winsorize` carries the reducers' warning for the rows skipped, once per quantile, as `iqr` does.

**Reason.** Catalogue rows 131 and 138; the `quantile` row's nine definitions; Language Reference, section 3.7 ("Columns and scalars"); the checklist's layer ruling: in Zeff where the language expresses the function, in Rust otherwise with the column corrected and logged and the missing piece an open decision.

**Tests.** The data crate's `quantile_group.rs`: R's `findInterval(x, quantile(x, probs, type), left.open = TRUE) + 1` for six group counts under the nine definitions, which the R script checks against `cut(include.lowest = TRUE)` wherever the cut points are distinct, and `pmin(pmax())` at six shares (`tests/reference/r/quantile_group.R`, registered with `check_r.py` and the CI job), exactly, on eight vectors with `NA`, ties, one value, all equal and values to 1e12; the edge cases as a snapshot; every message as a snapshot; the properties that the group never falls as `x` rises (checked with `lag` over a panel of the sorted rows), that the group counts differ by at most one more than the number of tied values, that `winsorize` changes nothing between its cut points and nothing under `at: 0`, and that `NA` goes where `x` is. The conformance case `functions/quantile_group` is published.

## 2 November 2026: distinct, duplicates and sample (release 0.6.0, step 11)

**Choice.** `distinct(vars)` and `duplicates(vars)` group the rows through the kernel's groups under the identity relation (`NA` with `NA`, `-0.0` with `0.0`), so that one rule serves `sort`, `by:` and these two; `distinct` keeps the first row of each group in the current row order, as a selection over the parent's columns, and says in a note how many repeats were dropped (nothing when none). `duplicates` is written in Rust rather than the planned Zeff, since neither `aggregate` (step 12) nor `table` (row 530) exists yet at this step; the catalogue's `layer` is corrected and logged with the note that a Zeff body can replace it once both exist. Its table is the one of question 5 (a): `duplicates · firm, year`, the key columns left-aligned as the grouped statistics print them and `copies` right-aligned, one row per repeated value in key order; when nothing is repeated the empty table prints with the note. The keys are a category's levels in level order, the order of section 3.7, so a category sorts as the engine sorts it and not as text. `vars` is required, as the catalogue's usage writes it. `sample` takes `n:` or `frac:` (both Z0410, neither Z0406), `frac:` rounded to the nearest whole number of rows as Stata's `sample` rounds; without replacement a partial Fisher–Yates over the row positions, one uniform per kept row; with replacement `n` uniforms; the kept positions sorted so that the rows come back in their original order as a selection, which keeps the panel declaration and every column's metadata; `with_replacement: true` on a panel drops the declaration with a note when a row repeats, since the unit would then have two rows at one time. The note gives the count and the seed, the run's seed when `seed:` is absent, after the run's own note on the seed it chose. The registry's reader of the catalogue's usage learnt that a bar between two `name: Type` pieces, `n: Int | frac: Float`, lists both parameters, while the bars of a word list or a type union list none, so the catalogue's notation stands.

**Reason.** Catalogue rows 112 to 114; Language Reference, section 6 ("Rows"; "Row order": the first occurrence kept), 3.7 ("Identity"), 4.3 (opaque columns, refused as keys with Z0401 until they have an identity); Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 3 (the random stream) and 13 (`sample` stochastic); question 5 (a) and (c); the checklist's rulings on the stream, on `n:` with `frac:` and on the selection.

**Tests.** The data crate's `distinct.rs`: R's `!duplicated` and the table of repeated keys (`tests/reference/r/distinct.R`, registered with `check_r.py` and the CI job) on the shipped `wages` to worker 50 and on a frame with `NA` keys, exactly, the kept rows checked as a set and a count since a printed column stops at twenty values; the edge cases as a snapshot (no repeats, every row equal, `NA` keys, `-0.0`, a panel through both verbs, `frac: 1`, `n: 0`, the rounding of `frac:`, an empty frame, the same seed twice); every message as a snapshot, the run's own seed normalised; the properties that `distinct` keeps the first occurrences and is idempotent, that `duplicates` finds nothing after it, that one seed gives the same rows twice and that no row repeats without replacement. The stochastic class for `sample`, `nightly_stochastic.rs`, fifty seeds of a sample of a fifth of 5,000 rows without and with replacement, the draws per block of a hundred positions against the uniform within Monte Carlo error and the distinct rows with replacement against n(1 − (1 − 1/n)^k), joins the nightly job. The conformance cases `verbs/distinct` and `verbs/sample` are published.

## 2 November 2026: aggregate (release 0.6.0, step 12)

**Choice.** `data.aggregate(name = expr, ..., by:)` reuses the machinery `add` has under `by:`: the interpreter evaluates each definition once per group on the group's rows and hands the verb each result spread back over the rows, and the verb regroups the rows through the kernel's groups, keeps the first row of each group of every definition and of the key columns, and builds the frame with the keys first, in key order with `NA` last, then the definitions in order; without `by:` the frame is one group and the result one row. A definition that gives a column is refused at check time: the registry's definitions type for `aggregate` is the scalar types alone, the checker opens the frame's scope for every definition of a frame method whatever that type (before, only when it admitted columns), and a definition of such a verb that gives a column is Z0401 with the message naming it; the verb refuses the same at run time should a column reach it. A later definition names an earlier one as the value it gives, not as a column: the checker keeps the list of an `aggregate`'s definitions checked so far, scoped to that call and visible inside the reducer and `sqrt` calls within its definitions, so that `se = spread / sqrt(n())` checks; at run time the earlier definition arrives as a column holding its one value in every row of the group, which the verb reads as that value. The keys keep their metadata through `take`; a definition starts empty; the panel declaration is dropped with a note, always, since the rows are summarised. The reducers' warnings are counted once per statement as `summary` counts them: the interpreter collects every group's messages of each definition of an `aggregate` (instead of keeping distinct texts, as `add` does), sums the rows with `NA` in a variable over the groups within a definition, and keeps one warning per variable across definitions, the largest count, since the rows with `NA` in a variable are the same rows whichever reducer skipped them; every other message is kept once. The benchmark suite gains `aggregate` by a group (`mean`, `sd` and `n` over twenty groups) at the three sizes, run as the engine runs it, each group's reducers on the group's rows then the verb; a frame's digest is every cell, since its printed form stops at ten rows.

**Reason.** Catalogue row 119; Language Reference, section 6 (the opening example; "Statistics as methods and reducers"; "Row order"; "Panels"), 3.7 ("Definitions in one call"; "Identity"), 4.3 (rule 3), 4.1 ("Groups"); Testing, section 6; the checklist's ruling on definitions.

**Tests.** The data crate's `aggregate.rs`: R's grouped statistics on the shipped `wages` by industry, by industry and year and by year, and on the Wooldridge `wage1` by education and by sex and marriage (`tests/reference/r/aggregate.R`, registered with `check_r.py` and the CI job), the exact reducers (`median`, `min`, `max`, `n`, `n_distinct`, `mad`) exactly and the closed-form ones (`mean`, `sd`, `variance`, `sum`, `skewness`, `kurtosis`, the interpolated `quantile` and `iqr`) within a relative 1e-12; `wage1` taken from the package in R, since R's own CSV reader is not correctly rounded in the last bit, where the engine's is; the edge cases as a snapshot (no `by:`, a `by:` column of all `NA`, an empty frame, a group of one row, `n()` alone, constants, a definition naming an earlier one, the labels of a key, the panel note, the merged warnings); every message as a snapshot; the properties that `aggregate(m = mean(x), by: g)` is `add` then `distinct` on `m`, that the groups come sorted with `NA` last and that the row count is `n_distinct` of the keys. The conformance case `verbs/aggregate` is published and the benchmark digests at the three sizes stored.

## 2 November 2026: merge, with firms and wages.firm (release 0.6.0, step 13)

**Choice.** `wages` gains `firm`, its eleventh variable, by the rule the owner took on 1 November: the workers of each industry, in order of their number, cut into firms of 3 to 40 workers, most of them small (3 + 37 u⁴ for a uniform u), by draws taken after every draw the file already used, so that the ten columns of release 0.2.0 are byte for byte what they were (checked against the committed file) and every published number on `wages` stands; 397 firms in all. `firms` ships beside it, written by `generate/firms.py` from the wages file (firm, industry, the count of distinct workers as `size`, and `founded`, a date drawn with its own seed over 1950 to 2009), with three firms without workers, its Arrow file carrying the labels, the `industry` category with the levels of `wages` and the `founded` Date, its page, and the CI job regenerating both. Since both frames carry `industry`, which agree by construction, the pages merge them on `[firm, industry]`; merging on `firm` alone is the page's example of Z0604. `merge` indexes the right frame's rows by their key values (compared by value, a category by its label, `-0.0` as `0.0`, `NA` matching nothing), lists the pairs in the left order and the right order within one left row, appends a full join's unmatched right rows last in the right order with their own key values (a category keeping the left's levels and taking any level of the right's the left lacked), and notes the matched rows and the rows of each side that nothing matched, whatever the join keeps. `relation:` is checked on the whole of each frame before joining; without it the merge is refused only when a key repeats on both sides, with the counts of repeated keys on each side as section 11's example shows; the help names `duplicates` on the frame when it is bound and the bare function otherwise. A shared non-key column is Z0604 unless `suffixes:` names two texts, the first for the left's column and the second for the right's. The left frame's metadata is kept, and its panel declaration too unless the merge repeated or added rows. Z0603 and Z0604 gained their rows in the table of codes (logged) and their explained pages.

**Reason.** Catalogue row 115; the merge page of the help examples; Language Reference, section 6 ("Combine"; "Row order"; "Panels"), 4.1 ("Merge keys"), 3.7 ("Resolution by parameter type"), 11 (Z0603's example), 4.3 (metadata); Engine and Project Specification, section 8.5; the owner's answer to question 3.
