## 5 November 2026: a property test that failed by chance had decided mutants in the weekly records (found at step 24b)

**What was found.** The weekly run on the commit of step 24a (run 42013171412 on 80b026d) listed two survivors in `is_tie` of `zeff-numeric` (`maths.rs` 112 and 114), a crate the step had not touched, which the run on 1b31366 had counted as caught. One of the two cannot change a result (below), so its "catch" was not a catch. The logs show what failed: `a_common_shift_of_treat_and_time_changes_nothing` and `relabelling_the_units_changes_nothing` in `packages/tier2/regress/tests/event.rs`, on the generated panel `units = 6, periods = 4, seed = 263`, with Z0802 ("no regressor remains: every one is absorbed by fe: unit + time"). The engine is right and the test was wrong: the generator drew each unit's cohort at random, and for 2 of the 27,944 panels the properties can draw (six units, four periods, seed 263; six units, seven periods, seed 360) every unit is treated at the same period, so the leads and lags are the time effects themselves and there is no fit to compare. A property run draws 40 cases on a runner, so each of the two properties met such a panel about once in 350 runs.

**Why it hid mutants.** A failing case is written beside its test (`event.proptest-regressions`) and replayed first on every later run. The mutation tool tests every mutant of a shard in one working copy, so after the first chance failure in a shard the saved panel failed again under every later mutant that had passed the tests run before `event.rs`, and that mutant was counted as caught there: a true survivor instead of missed, and a mutant that a later test (those of `zeff-stats`, say) would have caught for the wrong reason. Which of the two a given mutant is, these records cannot say. In the run of 3 November on 1b31366 (41592468329, the record of step 24a) this happened in seven shards (`zeff-numeric` 2, 3 and 4; `zeff-regress` 2; `zeff-results` 2, 3 and 9) and decided 63 mutants (35 of them in `spearman_exact_tail`, 15 in the leverage and sample-size helpers of `variance.rs`); no shard records a survivor after its first chance failure. In today's run it happened in three of the thirty shards read (`zeff-regress` 2, `zeff-results` 1 and 9) and decided 52. The step-24a record's sentence that eight old survivors of `zeff-numeric` are "caught now" is no longer relied on: three of that crate's shards are among the seven, and the clean run decides. No other property test shows the pattern (the same failing case under unrelated mutants) in either run. On an ordinary push the same chance made the test job fail about once in 175 runs; none of this release's pushes met it.

**Choice.** (1) The generator of `event.rs` makes its first unit never treated and its second treated from period 2, whatever the draws, so every panel has a control and a treated unit; a new test, `every_generated_panel_has_a_control_and_a_fit`, checks that over all 27,944 panels and fits every panel of six units under unit and time effects. The panel of units all treated at once stays what it was, an edge case with its own snapshot. (2) The mutation job sets `PROPTEST_RNG_SEED`, so the unmutated baseline and every mutant draw the same cases and a failure under a mutant is the mutant's own; the ordinary and nightly jobs keep fresh seeds, which is where chance should find a wrong test. (3) `maths.rs` 112 (the exponent of a subnormal with its sign dropped) is a true gap in the tests of `is_tie` and gets its case: the smallest subnormal is a tie at 1,073 digits and at no other count; the mutation, applied by hand, fails it. `maths.rs` 114 (`|` for `^` when the hidden bit is set) is an equivalent: the mantissa's field never holds bit 52. (4) The weekly job is run again in full on the commit of this correction, and its records, not those of the two runs above, are the ones matched for the release; the survivors it shows that the chance failures had covered are resolved as step 24a resolved the others, before step 24b is ticked.

**Tests.** `event.rs`: six tests pass, the new one in 4.5 seconds (the fits of all 27,944 panels were run once, 65 seconds, all fitted; under the old generator the same loop gave the two panels above and no other). `maths.rs`: the subnormal cases. The workflow file parses.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, sections 1 (property tests; mutation testing) and 3 (handling each bug); the decisions of 22 and 23 October (what counts as a catch); the checklist's steps 24a and 24b.

## 6 November 2026: the runs and the samples of 0.6.0, on the commit of the correction (step 24b)

**The commit.** Every run below is on 19ea819, the commit of the correction of 5 November, except where a figure is said to be read on 80b026d. The two commits build the same engine: the difference is the workflow file, two documents, a test file (`event.rs`) and three assertions inside the test module of `maths.rs`.

**The suite on the four targets.** CI run 42078724621: every job green at the first attempt (test, reference, lint, tiers, words, build, and the identity check on macOS ARM64, Linux ARM64, Linux x86-64, Linux x86-64-v3 and WebAssembly with their comparison). On this machine before the commit: 190 test programs, none failing. (That run took three hours instead of forty minutes: the operating system scanned each newly linked test program for half a minute to over a minute before letting it start, one at a time; nothing in the repository causes it and nothing was changed for it.)

**The scheduled jobs, by hand** (run 42078736108 with `job=both`, run 42078742467 with `job=bench`; all green). Nightly, 52 minutes: 193 test programs in release mode, none failing; the stochastic class of `zeff-dist` and `zeff-data` and the truth-recovery class of `zeff-regress` passing; the benchmark suite, at one million rows: `import` 484 ms, summary by group 110 ms, mean by group 69 ms, aggregate by group 245 ms, `reg` 568 ms, `reg` with two-way fixed effects 506 ms, a column chain 1.19 s; at ten million: 5.01 s, 1.78 s, 945 ms, 3.10 s, 5.68 s, 4.87 s and 12.4 s. Fuzzing, ten minutes a target, no crash: lexer 1,447,031 inputs, parser 515,400, checker 127,247, CSV 466,571, distributions 68,259, formulas 147,834. Coverage: kernel 93.8% of 7,859 lines and estimators 93.5% of 5,854 (threshold 80% each); language tooling 92.0% of 13,727 and the other packages 90.3% of 15,748 (reported). The reduction benchmark on x86-64, ten million: sums, plain 9.52 ms, scalar compensated 6.44 ms, sixteen lanes 6.91 ms; dot products, plain 9.84 ms, scalar compensated 53.3 ms, sixteen lanes 7.42 ms. The run on 80b026d drew a faster runner (4.49, 4.10 and 4.41 ms; 4.53, 38.3 and 4.25 ms); on both the sixteen-lane compensated reduction costs no more than the plain one, which is the shape the benchmark exists to watch. The hosted runners differ by a factor of two between runs, so the absolute times are for the shape and the order of magnitude only.

**The weekly mutation job, clean.** All 34 shards finished, in 74 to 201 minutes each, with the fixed seed: 4,136 mutants, 3,830 caught, 162 missed, 18 timed out, 126 unviable; by crate, `zeff-numeric` 1,838 (1,739 caught, 81 missed, 8 timed out, 10 unviable), `zeff-kernels` 544 (510, 7, 5, 22), `zeff-results` 1,324 (1,200, 42, 5, 77) and `zeff-regress` 430 (381, 32, 0, 17; five mutants more than on 1b31366, from the range lines rewritten at step 24a). No log of the run shows either property of `event.rs` failing, and a failing case that recurs within a shard recurs only under mutants of the one file it tests.

**The records matched** (by file and mutation, as at step 24a). The missed are the records and nothing else. `zeff-numeric`: the 82 of 0.5.0 less one, `is_tie` line 112, which the subnormal case of 5 November now catches; so the six of `kendall`, `kendall_exact_cdf` and `tie_groups` and the one of `is_tie` line 114 that the run on 1b31366 had counted as caught were chance catches, as the entry of 5 November supposed, and their recorded reasons stand. `zeff-kernels`: the one of 0.5.0 and the six equivalents of step 24a. `zeff-results`: the 30 of 0.5.0, `inference.rs` 195 among them (the "caught now" of step 24a was a chance catch too; its 0.5.0 reason stands), and the twelve equivalents of step 24a. `zeff-regress`: the 29 of 0.5.0 and the three equivalents of step 24a. Every survivor that step 24a resolved with a test is caught in this run (thirteen in `demean.rs`, thirteen in `absorb.rs` and `interface.rs`, thirteen in `reg.rs`). So the chance failures hid no survivor that lacks a record: the 63 mutants they decided on 1b31366 are, in the clean run, either caught by a test of their own or among the recorded equivalents. The timeouts are the records too (the eight of `zeff-numeric`; the two of `pivoted_qr`, the two hangs of `without_singletons` and the `ordered` mutant that the rerun of step 24a caught when given its time; the four loops of `effect_values`), and one more: `sums[g] += …` as `-=` in `effect_values` (`absorb.rs` 437), which the run on 1b31366 caught after 215 seconds of tests when the self-test failed, and which this run cut off at its 240-second limit with `selftest_says_this_build_is_conformant` already failed in its log. It is of the kind recorded at step 24a, item (15): a loop that then runs to its cap of ten thousand sweeps on every fit, slow rather than hung and wrong where it ends; the tests catch it when the runner is quick enough, and no test is added.

**The faults of the runners, for risk R9.** On 80b026d the test job's first attempt lost four links at once to a bus error in the linker before any test ran, and passed when run again; one mutation shard of the superseded weekly run on that commit (`zeff-numeric` 8 of 16) lost its runner. On 19ea819 no job was run twice.

**The samples and the self-test.** The six sample projects were run on 80b026d and each printed output and saved file read by eye: all byte-identical to the stored output; one wart, already a known issue tied to open decision #70 (`winsorize` warns twice, naming `value`). On 19ea819 the test that runs every sample to its stored output passes on every target, and `zeff selftest` on this machine reports 194 of 194 cases conformant (ARM64).

**The bundle and the cold start (risk R4), with `time` and `text` loaded at start** (read on 80b026d; Node 22.23.4, the median of five fresh processes). The bundle is 9,603.4 kB raw, 1,653.2 kB with Brotli (2,359.0 kB with gzip) against the 5,000 kB warning level; 1,466.7 kB at this release's step 3 with `time` alone. The cold start is 106.9 ms (the module's load 28.5 ms, the first call 75.4 ms) against 1,000 ms; 93.6 ms at step 3. The whole conformance report takes 1,903.6 ms with 194 cases, for information. Both limits hold with a wide margin; the rating is for the register's review at step 24c.

**The `import` times, judged against open decision #51.** At one million rows `import` takes 484 ms on the runner (468 ms on this machine) beside 568 ms for `reg` and 506 ms for the two-way fixed-effects fit (390 and 387 ms here); at ten million, 5.01 s beside 5.68 s and 4.87 s. Reading a panel costs about as much as one fit of it, and a script of panel work fits more than once, so `import` is not the bottleneck of panel work and the decision's recommendation stands: the chunked reader stays at 0.11.0. Nothing is changed in the register; the figures go to the release notes.

**Reason.** Testing handbook, section 2.4 items 2 and 3; Engine Specification, section 8.3; open decision #51; risk register R4 and R9; the decisions of 22 and 23 October (a timeout is not a catch; a loop that its cap ends) and of 5 November (the correction); the checklist's step 24b.

**The risk register's figures, for the review at the release.** R1: the release's 27 steps were built between 1 and 6 November 2026, the sixth release within its cadence; the early warning was not seen. R2: the identity check of 194 conformance cases (148 at 0.5.0) showed no cross-target difference on any push, and the bytes `save` writes are part of it; no identity job failed in the release's 51 CI runs. R3, at its first model release since 0.4.0: the fits under `fe:` and the event study match fixest within 1e-7 on estimates, errors, intervals and the four R² forms and exactly on the terms, N, singletons and degrees of freedom; the data verbs, the dates and `format` match base R exactly. Three findings, each a matter of the reference and not of the engine, recorded on 2 November: R reads a seventeen-digit literal differently on the two platforms (the `format` reference now writes it in hexadecimal), the `aggregate` reference is compared within its tolerance, and the event panel is rounded to six decimals. R4: the compressed bundle is 1,653 kB (1,457 at 0.5.0) against the 5,000 kB warning level and the cold start 106.9 ms (67.1) against 1,000 ms, with `time` and `text` loaded at start. R5, with the schema pass: 127 diagnostic codes (114 at 0.5.0), every one from the diagnostics-as-data path with its snapshot (785 files) and its explained page, checked on every push; the language tooling is covered at 92.0 per cent of 13,727 lines (`zeff-syntax` 95.8, `zeff-ir` 92.7, `zeff-engine` 89.5; 11,328 lines at 0.5.0), the checker's fuzz target, extended to the new verbs' arguments, found no fault, and the JSON output carries the schema pass's two marks for the language server of 0.7.0, which is still to come. R7: a clean release build of the engine takes 78 seconds on this machine (69 at 0.5.0) for an 11.1 MB binary (9.8 MB), with two package crates more; the weekly mutation run spent 4,634 runner-minutes over 34 shards (3,583 at 0.5.0) in 3 hours 21 minutes of wall time, the longest shard 201 of its 340 minutes (284 at 0.5.0). On this machine the full test suite, forty minutes as a rule, took three hours twice on 5 and 6 November while the operating system scanned each newly linked test program before its first start; a cost of the machine, not of the build, and to be watched. R9: the free runners carried every job. Two faults of the runners (a bus error in the linker on one test job, a mutation shard that lost its runner), each passed or superseded on a second run. And one fault of the test suite that the mutation job exposed, recorded on 5 November: a property test failing by chance had decided mutants in two weekly runs; corrected, the seed fixed, and the clean run matched the records.

**The red checks of 1 and 2 November, found while reading the release's CI history.** Twenty-seven of the release's 51 CI runs failed, all between the opening of the release and the evening of 2 November. The `reference` job failed on every one of them, for the cause recorded on 2 November (the `format` reference, then the `aggregate` tolerance and the event panel's decimals). Behind it, unnoticed in the records, the `test` job failed on seven pushes: (1) at step 9, a property test of `bin` drew values that were all missing or outside every interval, so its column of expected labels held only `NA` and the frame was refused (Z0219); a chance failure of the test's own data, corrected in the next commit (the first value is fixed inside an interval); (2) at step 14, the command-line test of `zeff help`, which names functions that are yet to arrive, named ones the step had just shipped; corrected four minutes later in the next commit; (3) on the five pushes from step 18 to step 20, the regress crate's `diagnostics` test built the arguments of `reg` by position without the new `fe:` slot and failed on its first weighted fit; corrected at step 21. The third broke the rule that no commit carries a failing test, and it went unseen because the run was already red for another reason. No result of the engine was wrong in any of the three, and every run since the evening of 2 November is green (one at its second attempt, the linker's fault above). The lesson, kept as practice from here: a red run is read job by job before the next push, whatever its known cause, and the local count of failing tests is read from the line `test result: FAILED`, not from a tally of names.

**A leftover branch and folder, removed at the owner's word.** While reading the samples' pins a working copy made by the desktop tool on 2 November was found inside the repository's directory, with its branch here and on GitHub, both named by the tool under a word of the forbidden list. The branch was the head of pull request #1 (the `format` reference correction), merged into `main` that day; its content is identical to the merged commits, and no commit message, tracked file, file name or pull-request text carries a forbidden word. The hooks and the words job check files and messages, not branch names, and the folder was hidden by the owner's global ignore. Told of it, the owner said to remove both: the working copy and its two empty folders are removed, the branch deleted here (the ordinary delete) and on GitHub, and only `main` and the five tags remain. The page of pull request #1 keeps the old branch name, which GitHub does not let an owner change. From here the work stays on `main` in the main checkout, and the branches and working copies are listed before a push.

**Open decisions due at 0.6.0.** #14, #26, #51, #54, #67 and #72 were taken on 1 November 2026, each as recommended, and are built or stand: `event` (row 252), Zemp at 0.7.0, the chunked reader at 0.11.0 (its condition read at step 24b: `import` is not the bottleneck of panel work), one bare range per formula, `ci()` at the fit's level, and `table` (row 530); none remains due. Due at 0.7.0 by the register's table: #24 (the Zemp interface framework, after the two-week trial that #26 placed in a Zemp session during this release; this repository holds no record that it was run, which is for the owner to say), #68 to #71 and #79 (the pieces the Zeff-written built-ins lack), #76 and #77 (the traceback and the schema-aware completion), #80 (`each`, whose text is to be written before 0.7.0 opens) and #83 (the sentence of section 3.7 on bare words); #73's trial of the typesetting engine is planned beside the plot renderer of 0.7.0, its decision due at 0.8.0. Rows #12, #15 and #16 still show 0.7.0 in the table though the status paragraph of 16 October records them as taken; the status line is brought up to date at the release.

R3 passed its first model release since 0.4.0 on the edge cases it names and stays at Medium for the models still to come; R5 stays at Medium until the formatter and the language server of 0.7.0; under R7 the time of the full suite on this machine (three to four hours on each run of 5 and 6 November, against forty minutes) is an item to watch and to measure again at 0.7.0; the chance failure that decided mutants and the red `test` job read late are named under R9 as faults found and corrected, not as a new risk, so that the next review asks whether they recurred. ## 6 November 2026: Release 0.7.0 opened

**Choice.** The owner said "go" to the checklist of `docs/releases/0.7.0.md` (44 steps) and took its eight questions as recommended. (1) The open decisions due: #68, #69, #70 and #79 (option B) adopted and built at steps 3 and 3b, #71 at step 30, #76 and #77 option A, #83 option A; #24 waits for its trial, run in a Zemp session during this release; #73's trial is a tool-only step beside the plot renderer. (2) `each` (#80): option B, built after the tests. (3) The R reference library gains `car` and `nortest` in the step that first needs each; Hedges' g and Cohen's d by their formulas in base R; `dist.tukey` against a 70-digit quadrature in Python, R's `ptukey` as a second check at its own accuracy. (4) The definitions, as R: the exact Wilcoxon distributions below 50 observations without ties; Royston's 1995 algorithm for Shapiro–Wilk; `ks_test` exact below 100 without ties, `estimated: true` for the normal only by Dallal–Wilkinson; `fisher_test` with the conditional odds ratio and interval for 2 × 2 and the p-value alone above; partial eta squared in factorial `anova`; `posthoc` after Welch's ANOVA as Tukey's HSD on the pooled variance with a note, and pairwise Welch tests under `bonferroni` and `holm`. (5) Every test prints in the form of the `t_test` page; `tabulate` with counts, percentages, `NA` as its own row and a total; each form shown to the owner before its commit. (c) #83's correction was written after trying the engine, not from the register's wording: a word in a record is accepted, a misspelt one is refused where it is written, and a bare variable name in a record is refused (Z0101), a variable travelling only through a binding that holds a `Var` (a loop over `vars(...)`); a `Vars` of one variable is refused by a `Var` parameter (Z0401). The GitHub organisation stays open with `zeff-lang` recommended.

**Reason.** Open decision #31, due before 0.9.0, because the launcher carries the key list's address and it cannot move; `zeff.dev`, the specification's placeholder, was found registered by others in the public DNS on 6 November 2026, and `zeff-lang.dev` had no record. `.dev` was preferred to `.io` for the country code's uncertain future and to `.org` by the owner's choice; `.dev` serves only HTTPS.

## 6 November 2026: The pragma and `--deny-warnings` (release 0.7.0, step 2)

**Choice.** `// zeff: allow(CODE) reason` is read after parsing (`zeff-syntax`, `pragma.rs`): the lexer keeps each `// zeff:` comment with whether it stands alone on its line, the parser lists the span of every `use`, `fn` and statement at every depth, and each pragma is placed against that list. Alone on a line it belongs to the next statement, with only blank lines and comments between; after code it belongs to the outermost statement that begins on that line. A `fn` begins at its `///` lines, so a pragma for a function stands above them. The engine (`zeff-engine`, `pragmas.rs`) adds the one check that needs the list of codes: a code with no explained page is no warning's.

**What a pragma covers.** The whole statement: a warning of the check that points inside it, and every warning raised while it runs, whatever it calls (a function of the script, a module, a built-in written in Zeff). The interpreter takes the allowed warnings out as each statement ends, at every depth, so a pragma inside a loop or a function works where it stands and a pragma on the statement that calls covers the call. It silences a message by its code, a warning or a note (W0703 prints as a note). A warning of `warn` has no code and cannot be allowed until `code:` arrives (step 3).

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) A pragma that silences nothing is passed over: a warning of the run depends on the data, so its absence is no mistake. (b) A pragma that cannot be applied is always Z0317, never an ordinary comment (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`); in a file that does not parse, only what the pragma says is checked, the syntax error being the one to put right. (c) One code to a pragma; two pragmas stand on one statement. (d) Every warning silenced is kept (`Output.allowed`: code, file, line of the statement, reason, the message as it would have printed), for the run record of 0.11.0; until then `zeff run --verbose` lists them by statement with their count and reason.

**`--deny-warnings`.** On `zeff run` and `zeff check` (`zeff test` takes it when it arrives, step 32). It refuses every warning that no pragma allows and every note that carries a warning's code (section 3.8: it refuses `today()` and `now()`); a note without a code is not refused. In a run, a warning of the check is shown as an error and the run does not start; a warning of the run is shown as an error after its statement, whose output stays, and the run stops there; a statement that fails stops the run with its own error and exit code 1. Each refused warning prints as `error[W0204]: … (line 9)` with a help line giving the pragma that would keep it. `zeff check --deny-warnings` reports every refused warning as an error, in the text and in the JSON records, with exit code 3 when they are the only errors and 1 beside an error of the script. Exit code 3 is as section 3.8 gives it.

**Open decision #45.** The owner's decision of 18 October holds a warning's code back from the line under a result "until the pragma arrives at 0.7.0". The pragma is here, and a user needs the code to write it; printing it changes every snapshot and page that shows such a line, so it is its own step, 2b, added to the checklist.

**The checklist corrected.** Step 2's "Done when" named a pragma line of the sample script; `docs/spec/zeff_samples.zeff` has none. It now names the example of section 11.1, which is tested.

**Tests.** Syntax: 15 tests (what a pragma says, its statement at every depth, the edge cases, twelve message snapshots). Engine: 23 tests and one property (pragmas change the messages and never the output; under `--deny-warnings` a run passes exactly when every warning is allowed), four message snapshots. Command line: one test through the program with two snapshots. Conformance: `control/pragma` and `control/pragma_denied`, four digests added and none changed.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.1 ("Comments"), 3.8 ("Exit codes"; `today()` and `now()`) and 11.1 ("Deliberate exceptions"); Engine and Project Specification, section 2 (`zeff run`); open decision #45; testing handbook, section 4.

## 7 November 2026: The code of a warning under a result (release 0.7.0, step 2b)

**Decision.** A warning or a note that carries a code prints it under the result in the form of an error, `warning[W0204]: log of zero gave -Inf (line 4)` and `note[W0703]: …`; a message without a code (`warn(message)`, the note of a format or a seed) prints as before. The short form of a message in the diagnostics kernel does this for every message, so the denied warnings of `--deny-warnings` and the warnings of the run print alike. `--color always` paints `warning[W0204]` as one word, as it paints `error[Z0101]`.

**Reason.** Open decision #45, option B, due when the pragma arrives: the pragma of step 2 needs the code, and a user who has to look it up in `--format json` or the run record would not write the pragma. Errors have printed their code since 0.1.0, so the layout is already the reader's.

**The phrase list of `check-messages` retired.** `xtask check-messages` proved that a code is tested by a snapshot that holds its text in brackets or by a phrase of a table kept in the tool; the table is gone, since every coded message now prints its code and a snapshot that shows the message proves the code.

**Method.** The stored expectations (38 help pages, five sample scripts' standard error, 23 explained pages of codes, 53 lines of test sources, 94 snapshot files) were rewritten by rule from the phrase table and from the examples run, and the full suite then found the 25 lines whose phrase the table lacked (the special functions W0204, the dates W0203, the regression W1006), each read and accepted as a code insertion only, and the one line where a `warn()` of a Zeff-written function (`kurtosis`) carries no code and prints plain, kept so. The conformance digests of standard error of 22 cases changed and no digest of a result.

**A kernel helper corrected on the way.** The random property test of the reductions (`the_short_path_matches_the_lanes`) found a short slice whose sum overflows, `[-1.62e308, -1.41e308]`: the short path of `sum` gave not-a-number where the lanes give `-Inf`, because the error term of a two-sum is not a number past an overflow and only the lanes' `value()` fell back on the plain sum. The short path now falls back the same way. No result changes: `sum` already replaced a result that is not finite by the plain sum of the slice, so both paths gave `-Inf` through it; the correction is to the helper the test compares, and the case is kept among the fixed tests and in the proptest regression file.

## 7 November 2026: A note, a coded warning and a variable's name (release 0.7.0, step 3.1)

**Decision.** `note(message)` and `name_of(v)` join `core` in Rust (rows 534 and 535); `warn` and `note` take `code:`. The code is written bare, `code: W0205`, or as text, and a new checker type `Code` carries it: where a parameter is typed `Code`, a bare name of the shape `W` or `Z` and four digits is that code as text, and text is accepted as it is. Whether the engine raises the code is checked when the statement runs, not by the checker, which does not know the engine's pages: the body raises the coded message, and the interpreter, which knows the pages, replaces a message whose code has no page by Z0401 at the call ("no warning has the code `W9999`"); an error's code is refused by the body itself (Z0401, "an error's code"), since a warning cannot carry one. A coded message from `warn` or `note` is then one the pragma allows and `--deny-warnings` refuses, as the engine's own, with no new rule. `name_of` gives `NA` for `NA`, so an optional variable left out reads as `NA` in a message.

**Reason.** Open decision #70, option A, the pieces step 4 needs to move `drop_missing`, `skewness` and `summary` into Zeff. The code is checked at run time because the explained pages live in the engine crate, above the checker and the packages; a check at build time exists for the one place it matters at build time, a built-in written in Zeff, whose page declares the codes its body gives `warn` and `note` and whose build fails on a code without a page.

**Step 3 split.** The step's three pieces (#70, #68, #69) are three engine pieces, each a commit of its own: 3.1 to 3.3 in the checklist.

**The catalogue's usage of `warn`.** `warn(message, code: Code?)`, since the registry requires the usage to list every parameter.

## 7 November 2026: The local routine on every step is the handbook's five-minute one; CI is the full run

**Decision.** From step 3.1 of release 0.7.0, a step is checked locally with format, clippy with warnings denied, the tier and message checks, and the test programs the step touches together with those that read the catalogue, the specification and the conformance digests, the command-line tests, whose help listings count the functions of a package, and the test programs of the built-ins written in Zeff, whose pages list what their callees declare (about ten minutes; the first use of the routine missed those two kinds, and CI caught a count and a snapshot); the whole suite runs on CI, on the four targets in parallel, and a step is ticked only when CI is green. A CI failure is fixed in a follow-up commit before the next step begins. The full local run stays where the handbook puts it: before each release (section 2.4) and after a change to a kernel crate or the registry that every program depends on.

**Reason.** The owner's decision of 7 November, asked when a step's local run had grown to three hours and more: the suite is about 130 test programs, macOS inspects every rebuilt program before it runs, and the catalogue is compiled into the registry, so every function step rebuilds nearly everything. The testing handbook's routine on every change (section 2.1) is the five-minute one, with the four-target check on CI; the full local run had been the sessions' habit, not the handbook's rule, so the handbook is unchanged. The cost accepted: a commit may reach `main` that CI then fails, for the twenty minutes until the fix follows.

## 7 November 2026: A parameter of several types in a built-in written in Zeff (release 0.7.0, step 3.2)

**Decision.** The grammar is unchanged: `x: Bool | Int` already parses as a list of words, and the checker reads a list whose every word begins with a capital as a union of types when the file is a built-in's (`builtin_file` on the checker, set by `check_builtin`), and refuses it in a project (Z0101, with a help naming the rule). The forms of a built-in are the product of one type per such parameter and the column choices of the scalar parameters, each form a lowering of its own, as the column forms were: `BuiltinForm` carries `chosen`, the type taken for each parameter. A choice whose types do not join is skipped when the result is `Join`, since the call-site rule (Z0214) lets no call reach it; the forms are capped at 256 (Z0323). `Join` and `Same` as a return type are rules, not types: under each form the checker resolves them from the parameters' types (the join of all, or the first's), wrapped in `Column` when the form has a column, so the body's result is checked against a concrete type, while the registry keeps the words for the call site, which already knows them. The interpreter picks the form by the arguments: columns as before, then the chosen types, exactly first (an Int takes the Int form) and then by acceptance (an Int where only Float is offered), `NA` fitting any.

**Reason.** Open decision #68, option A: one signature language for Rust and Zeff built-ins, the body still checked before any script runs. Forms rather than a dynamic check keep the checker's guarantee that a built-in ships clean under every type it accepts. The cap of 256 is generous for the catalogue (`fill_missing` needs 24) and keeps the build bounded. The conformance case named by the checklist (`control/several_types`) waits for step 4, when `fill_missing` becomes the first shipped built-in to use the piece; a fixture is not shipped and the conformance digests describe the product.


## 7 November 2026: The enclosing frame of a built-in written in Zeff (release 0.7.0, step 3.3)

**Decision.** The spelling of open decision #69 is `data: Frame = enclosing`: the grammar is unchanged, since a default is an expression and `enclosing` a name, and the type the body sees stays written as `Frame`. The checker (`zeff-ir`, `check.rs`) reads the mark in a built-in's file only, on the built-in's own `fn` line, on its first parameter, typed `Frame` exactly (Z0323 otherwise, each with a help saying where the mark goes); the parameter is never optional and its "default" is not evaluated. The registry (`zeff-engine`, `registry.rs`) leaves every marked parameter out of the signature it derives, so the usage line, the page's Arguments and the catalogue's usage check see the arguments a call gives, and declares the Z0401 of a call outside a frame method on the page's "Warnings and notes" (the generated list now starts from what the function declares of its own, then the codes its body gives `warn` and `note`, then its callees'). The interpreter (`interpreter.rs`, `run_zeff`) binds the first parameter to the current frame of the innermost receiver, the group's rows under `by:`, before the arguments, or stops with Z0401 ("`f` reads the frame around it and stands inside a frame method such as `add` or `aggregate`", "no frame here") when no frame method encloses the call.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) The page has no entry for the enclosing frame: a `data:` line is refused (Z0323) with a help to say in the description that the function stands inside a frame method, since Arguments lists the usage line's parameters. (b) In a project function `= enclosing` is Z0101 ("nothing is called `enclosing` here") with a help naming the rule, unless a binding of that name is in scope, when it is that binding as any default. (c) A function of the script called inside a definition sees no frame, as `n()` sees none there (section 5.3, "Scope"; the interpreter takes the receivers out for a user call), so a Zeff built-in called from its body is refused as `n()` is; the Rust row functions behave the same today. (d) The frame is the receiver's current frame, which is what a Rust body reads from `CallContext::frame`: the original frame outside a definition, the extended one inside `add`, the group's rows under `by:`. (e) The message of the Z0401 is one for every such built-in and differs from the Rust row functions' ("reads the variables of a frame and stands inside `add` or `update`"); step 4 decides whether the conformance digest of a row function's refusal may change, and the `control/enclosing` case refuses through `n()`, whose message is fixed.

**Tests.** Engine: `tests/enclosing.rs`, two fixtures of `data` (`fixture_rows`, a Zeff `n()`; `fixture_mean_here`, a reducer over a variable beside the frame): the usage and page leave the frame out (page snapshot), the examples run, the frame supplied inside `add`, `add` under `by:`, `aggregate`, `aggregate` under `by:`, `update` and `where` (run snapshot), the fixtures agreeing with `n()` and `mean` in each place, a project function seeing no frame, the refusal outside a frame method, and every message as a snapshot (outside a frame method, through a function, a project function marking a parameter, the mark on a helper, not first, not a `Frame`, a page entry). Conformance: `control/enclosing`, two digests added and none changed.

**Reason.** Open decision #69, option A: the body is ordinary Zeff over a frame it was given, `data.add(...)` and the reducers included, and the registry's usage stays `row_mean(vars, ...)`, so that `row_mean`, `row_sum` and `diff` can return to Zeff at step 4; Engine and Project Specification, section 9.1; testing handbook, section 4.

## 7 November 2026: A function literal, with `map`, `filter` and `reduce` (release 0.7.0, step 3b)

**Decision.** The grammar (`zeff-syntax`) gains `fn(params) expr` as a primary: `fn` followed by `(` starts a literal in an expression, while `fn` at the start of a top-level line stays a definition and inside a block stays Z0309. The checker (`zeff-ir`, `fn_literal`) accepts a literal only where the expected type is `Fn(...)`: each parameter takes that type's type at its position unless one is written, which must agree (Z0205 either way, as a named function that does not match); the body is one expression checked with the parameters pushed on the scope in sight, so it reads the enclosing bindings, and is lowered as a function of the program named `fn(i)` (a name no call can write) whose value carries the ids of every binding in scope where it stands. The interpreter copies those bindings' values into the function value when the literal is evaluated and puts them back in sight before the body runs, so a literal passed into a built-in written in Zeff, whose body runs with the script's bindings hidden, still sees what it was written over. `map`, `filter` and `reduce` are registered in `core` beside `iterate` with bodies that are never reached: the checker matches their arguments on its own (`list_function`), reading the list first, `start` second for `reduce`, and typing `f` by them, `Fn(T) -> ?` (what `f` gives is the item type of the result), `Fn(T) -> Bool` and `Fn(S, T) -> S`; the interpreter applies `f` item by item in order, as it applies `iterate`'s functions. `Ty::accepts` treats an unknown return type in the wanted function type as any, which only `map`'s expected type produces.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) A literal's body is one expression, not a block: a longer body is a named function. (b) A literal stands only where a parameter takes a function; `let f = fn(x) ...` is Z0205 with a help naming the rule (the overview keeps closures bound to a name after 1.0). (c) The literal captures, by value when it is made, exactly the outer bindings its lowered body reads, found by the walk over the typed IR that the engine's liveness pass already made (moved from the engine to `zeff-ir`, `uses.rs`, so the checker and the pass share it); the pass counts the captures as reads, since the engine frees a binding after its last use and a literal's use comes where the literal is made, not where its name is written. (d) `filter` refuses `NA` from `f` (Z0203) as `if` and `iterate`'s `done` do, with a help to decide the missing case in the function. (e) A list holding a `Failed` item is refused at the call (Z0220), as every list given to a built-in is unless the function is one that skips failures (`report`, `len`); `attempt` around the call keeps the failure. (f) `map` over an empty list is an empty list, `reduce` over one is `start`. (g) The three functions take the method form, `xs.map(f)`, as any function does on its first argument. (h) A literal may call `today()` and the other script-only functions where the script may, since it is checked as part of the statement it stands in, not as a function of its own.

**Tests.** Syntax: the literal's tree. Engine: `tests/list_functions.rs` (the run, the edge cases, every message as a snapshot, the property that `map` keeps the length and the order). Conformance: `control/map`, two digests added and none changed; the help examples of the three pages.

**Reason.** Open decision #79, option B: every computation over a list becomes expressible in a built-in written in Zeff, so that `quantile_group` returns to Zeff at step 4 with its probabilities i/n computed exactly; Language Reference, sections 3.4, 3.7 and 5.3; testing handbook, section 4.

## 7 November 2026: `fill_missing` back in Zeff; `n_missing` stays in Rust (release 0.7.0, step 4.1)

**Decision.** `fill_missing` is `functions/fill_missing.zeff` of `core`: `fn fill_missing(x: Bool | Int | Float | Str | Date | DateTime, value: Bool | Int | Float | Str | Date | DateTime) -> Join { coalesce(x, value) }`, checked under 32 forms (the eight choices of types that join, each under the four column choices), its page carried in the `///` lines. The Rust body and `help/fill_missing.md` are removed. `n_missing` stays in Rust with the reason in its catalogue row: a list holding failed values reaches it, where they are skipped and counted (W0801), and no function of the language takes such a list apart, since every list function refuses a failed item at the call (section 5.6); `len` is the only other function that accepts one, and a count of `NA` cannot be built from `len` alone.

**A run-time gap closed on the way.** The interpreter ran the written form of a Zeff built-in when no form fitted the arguments, which the comment called impossible; it is possible when a column's type is not known before the run and its values do not join with another argument (`fill_missing(d["x"], "none")` with `d` a frame literal), and then the body ran under types it was never checked for and `coalesce` spoke in its own name. The interpreter now refuses such a call with Z0214 in the built-in's name, worded as the checker words it, and treats any other unfitting call as a bug (Z9001). Closing the gap showed that the form matcher compared every argument's column-ness with the form's column mask, which marks only the scalar parameters a form reads as columns: a parameter declared as a column (`winsorize`'s `x: Column<Float>`) never matched and had been running on the fallback; the matcher now asks, parameter by parameter, whether the form's type is a column exactly where a column is given. One snapshot of `missing_in_zeff` changes by its last words: "(row 1)" is gone, since the whole column is refused at once rather than at its first offending row.

**Step 4 split.** Nine functions in five groups, 4.1 to 4.5 in the checklist, each a commit of its own; the known-issues entries on them are resolved at 4.5.

**Tests.** The existing programs of `fill_missing` unchanged but for that snapshot; its page's examples; the conformance case `control/several_types` (every scalar type, `NA` typed and bare, Int with Float both ways, the column forms, the join inside `add`), two digests added and none changed, `control/missing` among them.

**Reason.** Open decision #68 and the checklist of 0.7.0, step 4: a function moves to Zeff where the adopted pieces express it and stays in Rust, with the reason recorded, where they do not.

## 7 November 2026: `row_mean`, `row_sum` and `diff` stay in Rust (release 0.7.0, step 4.2)

**Decision.** None of the three moves to Zeff, and the reasons are recorded in their catalogue rows, the register and `diff`'s page. `row_mean` and `row_sum` take the values present in a row and reduce them with `zeff_numeric::sum` and `zeff_numeric::mean`, the kernel's compensated reductions, as every sum and mean of the engine does (Engine and Project Specification, section 8.3, point 3). A body written in Zeff has `+` over columns as its only row-wise arithmetic, a plain left-to-right sum, and `/` by a count for the mean: on the `rows` conformance case (1e12 beside 1.5 and 2.5) and on the wages data the results differ in the last bits, so the digests would move, which step 4 forbids, and the help's promise of the compensated summation would be broken. Building the row through `to_long` and `aggregate(mean(value), by: row)` would reach the kernel but at the cost of a reshape per call and the reducers' warnings in the caller's output. `diff` is `x - lag(x, n)`, and `lag` reads the panel of the frame around the call from the interpreter's receiver stack, which `run_zeff` empties while a body runs (section 5.3, "Scope": a function sees its parameters only); the enclosing frame reaches the body as a value, not as a context its callees read.

**What the enclosing frame is for.** The Zeff-written functions over a frame's variables that need no kernel reduction of their own and call nothing that reads the frame for itself: `drop_missing` (step 4.3), and the later verbs that read several variables and return the frame or a count.

**Tests.** Nothing changes but the texts; the conformance digests are unchanged and `diff`'s page prints its new sentence.

**Reason.** The checklist of 0.7.0, step 4: a function the pieces still do not express stays in Rust with the reason recorded; open decision #69.

**Decision.** The four `warn` calls of `skewness` and `kurtosis` for too few values take `code: W0205`, the code the owner's answer to question 5 of 0.5.0 gave them (open decision #70): the warning prints `warning[W0205]: skewness needs at least three values for the adjusted form: the result is NA`, a pragma allows it, `--deny-warnings` refuses it, and the two pages list W0205 under "Warnings and notes" from the codes the bodies raise. ## 7 November 2026: `quantile_group` back in Zeff; pragmas in a built-in's file; the loader's column guard (release 0.7.0, step 4.4)

**Decision.** `quantile_group` is `data/functions/quantile_group.zeff`: `fn quantile_group(x: Column<Float>, n: Int?, \`type\`: Int = 7) -> Column<Int>`. The cut points are `frame(value = x).quantile(value, p: map(seq(1, n - 1), fn(i) i / n), type: \`type\`)`, the kernel's sample quantiles at probabilities each computed as the one division; each row's group is `1 + reduce(cuts, fn(acc, c) acc + to(c < x, Int), below)`, with `below` a column of zeros that is `NA` where `x` is (`case { is_missing(x) => NA, _ => 0 }`), so that `n: 1` and an all-`NA` column come out as the Rust form had them. The parameter `type` is written in backticks in the `fn` line, as a column of that name is, since `type` is a reserved word; the page and the usage line read `type:` as before. `x: Column<Float>` accepts a column of Ints (Float accepts Int, item by item). Every result and every conformance digest is unchanged, the R agreement and the property tests among them.

**Three pieces built on the way.** (a) A reducer whose `p:` takes a Float or a list of them (`quantile`) is typed at the call by what it is given: a list of probabilities gives `List<Float>`, which `reduce` and `map` take; before, the checker typed the call `Float` whatever `p` was. (b) The pragmas of a built-in's file travel with its body: the checker returns them with the lowered forms, the registry refuses a code no warning has (Z0317 at the build), and the run adds them to its table under the file's name, so that a pragma inside the body silences a warning where it stands, as in a script. `quantile_group` uses one to take out the reducer's W0201 for the rows with `NA`, which the Rust form never raised and the digests must not show. (c) The loader checks a parameter declared as a column against the column it is given at the run, since a frame literal's column is not typed before the run: a `Column<Str>` to `x: Column<Float>` is Z0401 in the checker's words, where before the body ran and the inner `quantile` complained in its own name; `between` given a text column gains the same message in place of its operator's (one snapshot of `scale_in_zeff`), and `quantile_group` moves to its place among the Zeff-written functions in the `zeff help data` listing (one snapshot of the command line).

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) The argument errors of the body are `error(message)`, so they print as Z0001 at the call where the Rust form gave Z0406 and Z0401 with a label on the argument; the precedent is `winsorize` (0.6.0), and the question of a coded error from a built-in's body is raised as open decision #89, deadline 0.8.0. (b) The messages keep the Rust wording and gain the hint that the Rust help carried, since a Z0001 has no help line. (c) `n: Int?` rather than a required `n`, so that the usage line stays `quantile_group(x, n: Int, type: Int = 7)` and a call by position, `quantile_group(x, 4)`, stays refused as before.

**Tests.** The package program `quantile_group` (R agreement under the nine definitions, the edge cases, the properties) unchanged but for the message snapshot, which shows the three Z0001 messages and the column guard's wording; the examples of the page; the conformance digests unchanged, `functions/quantile_group`, `panel` and the samples among them.

**Reason.** Open decision #79, the owner's definition of done for step 3b (`map(seq(1, n - 1), fn(i) i / n)` exactly), and the checklist of 0.7.0, step 4.

## 7 November 2026: `text`, part 1 (release 0.7.0, step 5)

**Decision.** The eight functions live in `packages/tier1/text/src/basics.rs`, one module for the family, each a scalar function over one text that the lifting rule applies row by row, `join` apart. `upper` and `lower` map each scalar value through its simple case mapping, taken from the standard library's full mapping where that gives one value and the value itself where it gives more (`ß`, `ﬁ`, `ŉ`), so the length never changes (section 3.8) and no table is added; the mapping is per value, so a capital sigma lowers to `σ` wherever it stands, the final form being a rule of words. `trim` removes the characters with the Unicode `White_Space` property (`char::is_whitespace`), wider than R's `trimws`, which removes ASCII white space only. `starts_with` and `ends_with` compare scalar values, case-sensitively. `slice(s, start:, len:)` counts from 1 and gives what is there past the end, `len: 0` the empty text; `start:` below 1 and `len:` below 0 are Z0401, and either left out is Z0406 from the body, since the catalogue writes both as options. `pad(s, width:, fill: " ")` pads on the left (right-justified, as R's `formatC` and Stata's string formats) with one character, never cuts, and refuses a negative width or a fill that is not one character (Z0401). `join(list, sep: "")` takes a `List<Str>`, writes an `NA` item as `NA` as R's `paste` does, and gives the empty text for an empty list; a list of numbers is refused by the checker with the usage line, the caller formatting them first.

**The R reference.** `tests/reference/r/text.R` writes `text.json` from `toupper`, `tolower`, `trimws`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `substr`, `formatC` and `paste` on fifteen strings (accented, a combining mark, `ß`, `ﬁ`, Greek, Cyrillic, CJK, emoji, a flag, white space, the empty text), thirteen affix pairs, twelve slices, six paddings and six joins; every value is exact and the comparison exact, so `check_r.py` lists `text` among the files compared exactly and the CI job regenerates it. The JSON writer of `common.R` escapes no tab, so a tab stands in the Rust edge cases rather than in the reference strings; the Unicode spaces `trim` removes and R's `trimws` does not are there too.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/text/tests/basics.rs`: the five groups against R, the edge cases (`NA`, the empty text, Unicode white space, a slice past the end, a fill of two characters or none, a list that is not text), the column forms inside `add` and `where`, every message as a snapshot, and the properties that the length never changes under `upper` and `lower`, that `trim` is idempotent and that a slice of the whole is the whole, on random printable text. The conformance case `text/basics`, two digests added and none changed. The eight pages, with their examples run.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 3.8 ("Text"); the catalogue rows 83 to 85, 87, 88 and 92 to 94; the testing handbook, section 4.

## 7 November 2026: `drop_missing` stays in Rust; open decision #90 (release 0.7.0, step 5b)

**Decision.** `drop_missing` is not rewritten, `join` notwithstanding. A body could keep the complete rows by folding `where(!is_missing(f[name]))` over the names and write the note with `join`, `format(n, big_mark: ",")` and `name_of`; what it cannot do is see the variables a range names. A `Vars` value holds the names as written, a range as the one token `id..z`, which the Rust verbs resolve against the frame (`resolve_vars`), and no function of the language resolves it: `split` arrives at step 6, and a search of `data.variables()` by position in every body would reimplement the engine's rule. ## 8 November 2026: hypothesis and decision lines in test output; open decision #91 applied (release 0.7.0, before step 7)

**Decision.** The owner raised and decided #91 on 8 November 2026: every `TestResult` prints `H0:` and `H1:` under its header, as statements about the population in words and standard symbols, and a `decision at α` line beside the p-value; `alternative: two_sided | less | greater` joins the shared arguments for `t_test`, `wilcoxon_test`, `proportion_test` and `fisher_test` (2 × 2 only); α is `1 − level`, or 0.05 for a test without `level:`, revisited with #15 at 1.9. The two gaps the entry exposed he settled the same day: `shapiro_test` refuses more than 5,000 non-missing observations, as R does; a group variable without value labels prints `female=0` and `female=1`.

**Rulings taken in applying it.** The `H0:` and `H1:` lines are indented two spaces, as the tables are (rule R1 of the entry); the decision line stands flush with the statistic lines it follows, as the existing example of section 10.2 prints them, rather than indented as the owner's draft showed. A one-sided interval prints as R gives it, `[0.136, Inf)`. The two refusals (`alternative:` on a Fisher table larger than 2 × 2; `shapiro_test` above the cap) receive their codes at steps 13 and 14, the release's ruling being that a provisional code is numbered at the step that raises it, with its row, its explained page and its log entry. The `TestResult` fields `h0` and `h1` hold the sentences, not the symbols, so that Zemp's hover text and `report()`'s table notes read as prose.

The testing handbook's definition of done now asks, of every function returning a `TestResult`, a snapshot of the block for every form in the entry's table, with one `less` and one `greater` case; step 7 adds the shared machinery, each test step its snapshots.

**Reason.** The specification freeze allows a normative change only to correct an error found while coding or by the owner's decision recorded in the register; adopting the layout before the first test ships means no shipped layout ever changes, which section 3.7's stability rule would otherwise forbid within an edition.

## 8 November 2026: `text`, part 2, on the `regex` crate (release 0.7.0, step 6)

**Dependency.** `regex` 1.13.1 (MIT or Apache-2.0), pinned exactly in the workspace and used by `zeff-text` alone, with its default features (Unicode classes, the performance features; the full DFA is not among them). It is the engine's one dependency on a result-bearing path besides the kernels, and it is what section 3.8 names: Unicode classes, no back-references or look-around, matching in linear time, identical on every platform. Its transitive crates (`regex-syntax`, `regex-automata`, `aho-corasick`, `memchr`) carry the same licences; all were already in the lock through the test tools.

**Decision.** The four functions live in `packages/tier1/text/src/patterns.rs`. `contains(s, pattern, regex: false, ignore_case: false)` looks for the text itself unless `regex: true`; `ignore_case: true` folds case by the crate's simple case folding in either mode (the literal pattern escaped into an expression under `(?i)`), so `ß` folds to itself and not to `ss`, as section 3.8 says. `replace(s, from, to, regex: false)` replaces every occurrence with `to` as plain text in both modes (`NoExpand`: a `$` or a backslash in `to` stands for itself); an empty literal `from` is Z0401, as R refuses it; under `regex: true` an expression that matches the empty text inserts `to` between the characters and at both ends, the crate's rule. `extract(s, pattern)` is the first whole match, `NA` when there is none. `split(s, sep)` keeps every piece, a trailing empty one included, so that `join(split(s, sep), sep: sep)` gives `s` back where R's `strsplit` drops the trailing piece; a pattern that matches the empty text splits between the scalar values with the empty pieces left out, so `split("abc", "")` is the three characters, as R gives them. A pattern the crate cannot read is Z0419 at the pattern, naming look-around and back-references when they are the cause, and is refused even where the text is `NA`. Compiled expressions are kept in a thread-local table of up to 256, so a call lifted over a column compiles its pattern once.

**The lifting rule tightened.** A function of `core`, `text` or `time` lifted over a column whatever it returned, so `split(d["s"], ",")` gave a column of `NA`s in silence, each row's list having no cell to go in. A call now lifts only when its result is one row's value (a scalar type, or a return word resolved at the call such as `Number`, `Join` or `Same`); `split`, whose result is a list, takes one text and refuses a column as any parameter does (Z0401). No shipped function other than `split` returns a list from scalar arguments, so nothing else changes.

**The R reference.** `tests/reference/r/text_regex.R` writes `text_regex.json` with `perl = TRUE` wherever a pattern is read, on patterns PCRE and the crate read alike (classes, anchors, alternation, groups, repetition, escapes, `\d` and `\s` on ASCII); 360 `contains` cases over ten texts, thirteen replacements, ten extractions and nine splits, compared exactly. A trailing separator, an empty match and an empty literal `from` are the Rust program's, where R's conventions differ or R refuses.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/text/tests/patterns.rs`: the four groups against R, the edge cases, the column forms, every message as a snapshot (Z0419 for an unclosed group, look-around, a back-reference, a repetition with nothing to repeat), and the properties that splitting and joining round-trip on a literal separator, that replacing a text by itself changes nothing, that a text contains every slice of itself and that a class replacement equals the three literal ones. The conformance case `text/patterns`, two digests added and none changed.

**The bundle.** CI's measurements of the two commits: before, 9,851.0 kB raw, 1,710.9 kB under brotli, 2,439.7 kB under gzip, cold start 62.0 ms; after, 10,977.8 kB raw, 1,927.3 kB under brotli, 2,821.1 kB under gzip, cold start 75.8 ms. The crate costs 216 kB of compressed bundle (13 %) and about 14 ms of cold start, for the Unicode tables and the matching engines section 3.8 asks for; the early warning of risk R2 is a compressed bundle past 5 MB, so the rating stands.

**Reason.** Language Reference, sections 3.1 (raw strings) and 3.8 ("Text"); the catalogue rows 86 and 89 to 91; the checklist of 0.7.0, step 6; the dependency rule of the standing instructions (a permissive licence, pinned exactly, recorded here).

## 8 November 2026: `TestResult` and the shared arguments of the tests (release 0.7.0, step 7)

**Decision.** The value stays where it was declared, `zeff_core::value::TestResult` (section 8.1, rule 4: every package reads one value), and grows the pieces section 4 and open decision #91 name: `hypotheses` (H0 and H1 as sentences, with their symbolic forms where a standard one exists), `alternative`, `estimate` and `effect` (each a label, a value, an interval and the decimals it prints to), `level`, `alpha` (the α of the decision line, `None` to print none) and `dropped`. The printed form (`zeff_core::display`) follows section 10.2's example: the title; the hypothesis block, `H0:` and `H1:` indented two spaces, each sentence padded to the longer and its symbols six spaces after, sentences alone where no symbolic form exists; the header lines; the table; the estimate with its interval; the statistic line; the effect size with its interval; `decision at α = …: reject H0 (p …)` or `fail to reject H0`; the lines after. One source gives these lines to the printer, to `summary` and to the table `export` writes. `stats` gains `testing.rs`, what every test will share: `level` (0.95 unless given, Z0401 outside (0, 1)), `alternative` (two-sided unless given), `alpha` (`1 − level` free of the subtraction's rounding), `weights` (frequency or analytic weights taken; sampling weights, the default kind, refused with Z0411), `two_groups` (the two groups of `group:` with their labels and rows, Z0412 for one level or more than two) and `complete_rows` (the rows with a value in every tested variable, the note `228 rows with NA in educ or exper dropped`). The result interface answers for a test: `estimates` gives one row with the estimate and its interval, `ci` the intervals of the estimate and the effect size at the test's level (another level is refused, since a test's intervals are made once), `p_values` and `n_obs` as before; `report([t1, t2])` sets tests side by side (estimate, statistic, df, p value, effect size, N) with each test's hypotheses in the footer, as rule R11 allows. Z0411 and Z0412 have their explained pages and their rows in section 11 (logged).

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) A `t` statistic with one degree of freedom prints `t = 20.42   df = 18,074.2   p < 0.001`, as the example of section 10.2 does; the other statistics keep their brackets, `F(1, 18,179)`, `chi2(3)`. (b) `test` and `compare`, the two results shipped before #91, print no hypothesis block and no decision line, since the decision's table gives no sentence for them and rule R10 keeps shipped layouts; the owner may add their sentences. (c) The blank line the engine prints after every grid stays, as `compare` has printed it since 0.4.0; the example of section 10.2 runs the estimate line straight after the table, and that one blank line is corrected in the example when `t_test` ships (step 9) rather than making the tests' tables print unlike every other. (d) A group without a value label prints as `female=0`, as the owner ruled; a text variable's groups print their texts; the two groups are ordered by their codes, numerically where both are numbers. (e) `ci` on a test at another level is Z0401 with a help to run the test with `level:`; the fit's `ci` recomputes, a test's cannot without its data. (f) The decision line prints `p` as the statistic line prints it, so `p = 0.050` at α = 0.05 reads `fail to reject`, the comparison being on the value, not the printed text.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/test_result.rs`: a hand-built Welch `t_test` and a one-sided signed-rank result print (snapshots), export as a table and LaTeX (snapshot), report side by side (snapshot), and answer `summary`, `estimates`, `ci`, `p_values` and `n_obs`; the shared arguments with their defaults and refusals (Z0401, Z0411, Z0412, Z0101); `complete_rows` with its note; and the fields the types table of section 4 names, read from the Language Reference's row. The core program's statistic-line expectation follows ruling (a); the snapshot of the hand-built results in `core` follows it too.

**Reason.** The checklist of 0.7.0, step 7; Language Reference, sections 4, 6 and 10.2; open decision #91, rules R1 to R11; the help contract's definition of done for a `TestResult` (testing handbook, section 4).

## 8 November 2026: `tabulate` (release 0.7.0, step 8)

**Decision.** `tabulate` is a Rust frame method of `data` (`packages/tier1/data/src/tabulate.rs`), `data.tabulate(vars, percent: row | col | total)`, returning a `Table` as `summary` and `describe` do, with no message of its own. One variable gives a table of its values, `N` and `%` (of all rows) and a `Total` row under a rule; two variables give a cross-table with the first variable's values down the side, the second's across the top, a `Total` column and a `Total` row under a rule, and with `percent:` a row of percentages under each row of counts (of its row, of its column or of every row), the `Total` row and column showing the matching marginal percentages. The values are the groups of the column kernel (`Groups::by`, the order of section 3.7, `NA` last as its own value), so only the values present appear, a labelled variable prints its labels and a Category its levels in position order. Counts print with thousands separators, percentages with one decimal (`fixed(x, 1)`), `NA` where the frame has no rows.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) `percent: row` and `percent: col` with one variable are refused (Z0401): a one-way table's percentage is always of the total, and `percent: total` is accepted as that default. (b) A Category's unused levels are not shown with a count of 0 (Stata's behaviour; R's `table` shows them), since every other grouping in Zeff lists the values present; a ruling the owner may overturn. (c) Weights wait for open decision #53 (1.1). (d) More than two variables is Z0401; the checker's Z0402 covers a `percent:` word outside the three. (e) The title names the frame and the variables, `tabulate · wages · female × union · row %`, so that a saved table says what it counts.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/data/tests/tabulate.rs`: the reference `tests/reference/r/tabulate.json` (R's `table(useNA = "ifany")` and `prop.table` by row, column and total on the shipped wages, `industry`, `year`, `educ`, `industry × female`, `educ × union`, and on a small frame with `NA` among the values), counts exactly and percentages within half a unit of the printed decimal, rows matched by their printed value and the labelled columns by position; the edge cases (an empty frame, Float, Date and Bool variables, labels, the three refusals, Z0101 and Z0102); a property on random frames with `NA` (every value listed once in order, the counts summing to the rows, the percentages to 100 within rounding, the two-way corner 100.0); snapshots of every form of question 5 and every message; the conformance case `verbs/tabulate`. The comparison script's tolerance for `tabulate.json` is a relative 1e-12 under the generic walker.

**Reason.** The checklist of 0.7.0, step 8 and its question 5 as the owner took it; catalogue row 154; Language Reference, section 6 ("Look", "Row order"); the help contract's definition of done.

## 8 November 2026: `t_test` (release 0.7.0, step 9)

**Decision.** `t_test` is a Rust frame method of `stats` (`packages/tier1/stats/src/t_test.rs`), not the Zeff body the checklist planned: a body written in Zeff can neither build a `TestResult` nor raise Z0411 and Z0412, recorded as open decision #92 (deadline 0.8.0, with #89). One registration carries the three forms, chosen by the arguments: `mu:` alone is the one-sample test, `group:` the two-group test (Welch's unless `equal_var: true` pools the variances), a second variable with `paired: true` the paired test, which is the one-sample test on the differences; a mixture of forms is Z0401 naming the clash. The second variable `b` is a positional parameter with a default (`NA`), which the checker now treats as omittable for Rust-registered functions as the table of section 3.4 already says of defaults (`crates/zeff-ir/src/check.rs`); the usage line reads `data.t_test(var, b, mu: Float = 0, …)`. `alternative` joins the registry's shared table, where the Language Reference's section 6 already lists it. The statistics are the kernel's weighted mean and variance (frequency weights replicate rows, N = Σw; analytic weights scale to n) and the t tail of `dist`, each side on its own; a one-sided alternative gives a one-sided interval, printed `[x, Inf)` or `(-Inf, x]` (`estimate_line`). The effect size of the two-group form is Cohen's d on the pooled standard deviation or Hedges' g = d · (1 − 3/(4(n₁ + n₂) − 9)), with the large-sample interval of Hedges and Olkin (1985), since the engine has no noncentral t (open decision #93, deadline 0.8.0); the one-sample and paired forms print no effect size, as the help example shows.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) Fewer than two values in a sample (after the rows with `NA` are dropped) is Z0401 naming the count, and a standard error of zero is Z0401 "the values of x are all equal, so the t statistic is undefined", as R refuses essentially constant data. (b) The printed forms: the two-group form's table of `group`, `N`, `mean` and `sd` at three decimals; the one-sample header `N = …   mean = …   sd = …`; the paired header `N = 10 pairs   mean(a) = …   mean(b) = …   sd of differences = …`; the difference at three decimals and the effect size at two; a blank line between the hypothesis block and a header line, as the help example prints and as a table already had (`test_result_before`), which moved the signed-rank snapshot of step 7 by one line. (c) The H1 of a one-sided two-group test reads "the population mean of x is less in g1 than in g2". (d) The example of section 10.2 already carries the blank line ruling (c) of step 7 expected to correct, so nothing in the specification changes at this step.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/t_test.rs`: the reference `tests/reference/r/t_test.json` (R's `t.test` in the three forms on the shipped wages with `lwage = log(wage)`, by `female` and `union`, one-sided and at other levels; R's own sleep data for the paired form; one frequency-weighted case by replication; the effect sizes in base R) within a relative 1e-6 through the package's own function; the edge cases of the checklist and every refusal; two properties (shifting both groups leaves t, p, the difference and g; scaling scales the difference and its interval and leaves t, p and g); snapshots of every form and every message; the conformance case `tests/t_test`. The comparison script holds `t_test.json` to a relative 1e-6.

**Reason.** The checklist of 0.7.0, step 9; catalogue row 169; Language Reference, sections 4, 6 and 10.2; open decision #91, rules R1 to R11; the help example of `t_test`; the testing handbook's definition of done for a `TestResult`.

## 8 November 2026: `proportion_test` and `chi2_test` (release 0.7.0, step 10)

**Decision.** Both are Rust frame methods of `stats` (`packages/tier1/stats/src/proportion_test.rs`, `chi2_test.rs`), for the reason recorded at step 9 and in open decision #92. `proportion_test` counts a Bool, or a variable of 0 and 1 (any other value is Z0401 naming it); its statistic is the uncorrected z of Stata's `prtest`, the signed square root of the chi-squared of R's `prop.test`, with Yates's correction on `correct: true` bounded as R bounds it; `ci:` chooses Wilson's score interval (as `prop.test` computes it, widened by ½/n under the correction), Wald's, or the exact Clopper–Pearson interval of `binom.test` from the beta quantiles, and for a difference of two proportions Wald's interval of `prop.test` or Newcombe's hybrid score interval (1998, method 10, or 11 under the correction), `exact` being refused there (Z0401, pointing to `fisher_test`). `chi2_test` is Pearson's test on the cross-table of two variables (the values present, in the order of section 3.7, after the rows with `NA` are dropped) or of one variable's frequencies against `p:`, which must hold one positive proportion per value and sum to 1 (R rescales only when asked; refusing is safer); the correction applies to a 2 × 2 table only and never exceeds the smallest |O − E|, as `chisq.test`; an expected count below 5 is W0211, the next free number of its family, with its two rows in the Language Reference, its explained page and its entry in `docs/spec_changes.md`. Both take frequency weights and refuse analytic weights (Z0401: a count cannot be scaled), sampling weights by the shared rule. `chi2_test` takes no `level:` and prints its decision at α = 0.05 (open decision #91, option A).

**A kernel fault found and corrected.** The bracketed Newton solver of `zeff-numeric` (`newton_with_bracket`, which every continuous quantile uses) read the direction of the function from the sign of its derivative at the midpoint of the bracket; for a beta distribution concentrated far from one half (a = 5,857, b = 12,557, the exact interval of the wages' union share) the density at ½ underflows to zero, −0 ≥ 0 read as "increasing", and the bracket was tightened towards the wrong end, so the quantile at 0.975 or 0.99 came out as 2 × 10⁻⁶¹ where R gives 0.3248 and 0.3261. The solver now reads the direction from the function's values at the ends of a finite bracket, then from its slope at the starting point, and only then from the midpoint; a unit test holds the beta inverse at these parameters to R's digits. The conformance digest `special/incomplete_beta_inverse` changed with the fix: six of its 160 values, all at a = 500,000 and b = 0.5, had been wrong (the median came out as 6 × 10⁻⁶¹, and the quantiles at 0.1 to 0.975 as 1 − 4 × 10⁻¹⁶), and every value of the grid now agrees with R's `qbeta` to 5 × 10⁻¹⁵ or better; no other digest moved, and the R reference files had no case this concentrated, which is why the reference job never saw it. The digest's new value is the corrected result, recorded here as the conformance rules require.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) The printed forms: one proportion prints `N = …   successes = …` and `proportion (Wilson) = 0.318   95% CI [0.311, 0.325]`, naming the interval; two proportions print a table of `group`, `N`, `successes` and `proportion` and `difference (g1 − g2, Newcombe) = …`; `chi2_test` prints the observed cross-table with a `Total` row and column (as `tabulate` does) or, for goodness of fit, the values with observed and expected counts and the proportions; no estimate line. (b) A one-sided interval of a proportion is bounded by 0 or 1, of a difference by −1 or 1, as `prop.test` gives them. (c) The title says `· continuity-corrected` when the correction was applied. (d) A proportion of 0 or 1 is not refused: Wilson's and the exact interval stay informative there, and Wald's collapses to a point, its known flaw, which the page does not hide.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/counts.rs`: the reference `tests/reference/r/counts.json` (`prop.test` uncorrected and corrected, one- and two-sided, at other levels, on the wages' union share by female and on small counts; `binom.test`; Newcombe's limits computed in base R from Wilson's; `chisq.test` on `industry × female`, `union × female` with and without the correction, a 3 × 2 table with an empty cell, and two goodness-of-fit cases) within a relative 1e-6 through the packages' own functions; proportions of 0 and 1; every refusal; properties (swapping the groups flips the sign of z and the interval; the cross-table's statistic is symmetric in its variables; frequency weights of k scale chi-squared by k); snapshots of every form and every message; the conformance case `tests/counts`; the beta-inverse unit test in `zeff-numeric`.

**Reason.** The checklist of 0.7.0, step 10; catalogue rows 173 and 175; Language Reference, sections 4, 6, 10.2 and 11; open decision #91 (the sentences of the four forms, α for a test without `level:`); the help contract's definition of done.

## 8 November 2026: the exact Wilcoxon distributions and `wilcoxon_test` (release 0.7.0, step 11)

**Decision.** The two exact distributions live in the numeric kernel (`kernel/zeff-numeric/src/wilcoxon.rs`), counted in integers: the signed-rank statistic as the subset sums of a rank vector and the rank-sum statistic as the sums of m of the N ranks, both by the recurrence over the ranks in `u128`, which holds every count a sample below 50 in each group can give (2⁴⁹ subsets, C(98, 49) ≈ 2.5 × 10²⁸). Tied ranks, multiples of one half, are doubled to integers, so the same recurrences give the permutation distribution over the tied ranks; a probability is a count over the total, so the probabilities of a distribution sum to one exactly, and R's rule for a tail at `q` (every value below `q + 1e-8`) is kept so that `q − ¼` excludes the value itself. `wilcoxon_test` is a Rust frame method of `stats` (`packages/tier1/stats/src/wilcoxon_test.rs`) in the three forms of `t_test`, reproducing R 4.6.0's `wilcox.test`: V from the ranks of the absolute differences (a zero difference keeps its place among the ranks in the exact test and is set aside from the sum; it is dropped before ranking in the approximation), W from the pooled ranks less m(m + 1)/2; the exact two-sided p-value twice the smaller tail, at most one; the approximation with the continuity correction by the alternative (`correct: false` drops it) and the tie terms in the variance; the Hodges–Lehmann estimate as the median of the Walsh averages or of the pairwise differences; the interval from the order statistics at the exact quantiles (R's adjustment of the quantile by one when the tail at it is already within α), searched among the Walsh averages by the exact tail when there are ties or zeros, and in the approximation from the shifts at which the standardised statistic meets the normal quantile, including R's widening of the level where the data cannot reach it and its check at α/2 in the one-sided "less" branch. Frequency weights repeat rows; analytic weights are refused (Z0401); sampling weights by the shared rule.

**A ruling on question 4 (a), for the owner.** The plan's recommendation, taken as "as R does", reads "exact p-values when n is below 50 and there are no ties, otherwise the normal approximation with the continuity correction". That describes R before 4.5. R 4.6.0, the reference version pinned by the project, gives exact p-values below 50 observations whether or not there are ties or zeros, from the permutation distribution over the tied ranks, and applies the continuity correction in the approximation whether or not there are ties. The function follows R 4.6.0, since the step's definition of done is that the exact p-values equal R's to the last digit and the recommendation's intent was to match R; the older rule is one line to restore (`exact.unwrap_or(n < 50 && !ties && zeros == 0)`), and the page says which rule holds. The owner may overturn this.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) The estimate is the median of the Walsh averages (or differences) in every case, including the approximation, where R returns the root of a statistic that is exactly zero over the whole interval between the two middle Walsh averages, so that R's value depends on where its root finder happens to stop; the bounds, which lie at discontinuities, are R's to within its root tolerance of 1e-4. (b) The printed form follows the hand-built result of step 7: `N = 12` (or `N = 10 pairs`, or a table of `group`, `N` and `median`), the estimate line `pseudomedian = …` (`pseudomedian of differences (a − b) = …`, `location shift (g1 − g2) = …`), `V = 61.00   p = 0.023`, the decision line, then a line saying how the p-value was computed: `exact p-value, no ties`, `exact p-value, over the tied ranks, 3 differences of 0 set aside`, `normal approximation with continuity correction, ties`.
