(c) The sentences of open decision #91 for the three forms, with "shifted by mu" added to the rank-sum sentences when `mu:` is not 0. (d) All differences equal to `mu` is Z0401, where R returns a p-value of 1 from an empty rank vector. (e) The shared helper `testing::weights` (step 7) printed a weight error in its debug form (`NotWhole { rows: [1], count: 1 }`); it now gives the sentences the reducers give, which this function was the first to reach.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/wilcoxon.rs`: the reference `tests/reference/r/wilcoxon.json` (R 4.6.0's `wilcox.test` with `conf.int = TRUE`: the signed-rank test on a fixed series for every n from 2 to 60, exact and approximate, the alternative rotating; the rank-sum test on ten pairs of group sizes up to 60 in each of three alternatives, exact and approximate; eleven cases with ties and zeros; the paired form), statistics, exact p-values, estimates and exact intervals within a relative 1e-12, approximate p-values within 1e-10 (a normal tail at z ≈ 4) and approximate bounds within 2e-4 (R's root tolerance); the kernel's distributions sum to one exactly and are symmetric for every n to 60; the rule of exactness and every refusal; frequency weights against the replicated frame; a property (negating the data mirrors V, the p-value, the estimate and the interval; shifting data and `mu:` together moves the estimate alone); snapshots of every form and every message; the conformance case `tests/wilcoxon`.

**Reason.** The checklist of 0.7.0, step 11 and its question 4 (a); catalogue row 170; Language Reference, sections 4, 6 and 10.2; open decision #91; R 4.6.0's `wilcox.test` and its `.wilcox_test_*` helpers, read from the owner's installation.

## 8 November 2026: `kruskal_test` and `p_adjust` (release 0.7.0, step 12)

**Decision.** Both functions are written in Rust in `stats` (`packages/tier1/stats/src/kruskal_test.rs`, `p_adjust.rs`), the checklist's "written in Zeff" set aside for the same reason as the tests of steps 9 to 11 (open decision #92, due 0.8.0): a Zeff-written test would need a constructor of `TestResult` that does not exist, and a list adjustment written in Zeff would run the four recurrences row by row through the interpreter for no gain in clarity. `kruskal_test` ranks the pooled sample with average ranks, forms H = 12/(N(N + 1)) Σ R_g²/n_g − 3(N + 1) over the tie correction 1 − Σ(t³ − t)/(N³ − N), and takes the upper tail of chi-squared with k − 1 degrees of freedom from `dist`, as R's `kruskal.test` does; a grouping variable with fewer than two groups among the rows kept, or a variable whose values are all the same (the correction is zero), is Z0401. Two groups are allowed, where H is the square of the uncorrected rank-sum z. The decision line uses α = 0.05, since the test has no `level:`. The printed form follows step 11's rank-sum table (`group`, `N`, `median`) with the statistic line `H(2) = 0.77   p = 0.680` and an after-line saying "chi-squared approximation over 3 groups" and whether ties were averaged and corrected. `p_adjust` reproduces R's `p.adjust`: `NA` keeps its place and does not count, n is the number of p-values present, Holm is the running maximum of (n + 1 − i)·p₍ᵢ₎ from the smallest, Bonferroni n·p, Benjamini–Hochberg the running minimum of (n/i)·p₍ᵢ₎ from the largest, Benjamini–Yekutieli the same with the factor Σ 1/i, every result capped at 1; a numeric column is accepted beside a list. The checker refuses a mixed list (Z0214) and an unknown method word (Z0402) before the body, so the body's own guards for them are defensive only and not declared.

**The shared group helper.** `testing::two_groups` of step 7 is now built on a general `testing::groups`, itself on the kernel's `Groups::by`, so that the groups come in the order of section 3.7 (codes ascending, texts by code point, a category's levels in their order) and a Category variable is accepted: the sample script's `anova(lwage, group: industry)` needs it, and so does `kruskal_test`. The labels are unchanged (value labels, then `var=value` for codes, the text itself for Str and Category); Date, DateTime and opaque variables are still refused with the same message, now naming Category among the accepted kinds. Every existing snapshot of `t_test` and `wilcoxon_test` is unchanged, which confirms the order.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/kruskal.rs`: the reference `tests/reference/r/kruskal.json` (R 4.6.0's `kruskal.test` for 2 to 6 groups of unequal sizes, heavy ties, a group of one, `NA` in the variable and the groups, text groups, 300 rows; `p.adjust` under the four methods on eight vectors with ties, zeros, ones, `NA`, a single value and all `NA`), statistics and p-values within a relative 1e-12 and every adjusted value within 1e-12; the properties that an adjusted p-value is never below the raw one nor above 1, that `NA` keeps its place, that a larger raw p-value never gets a smaller adjusted one, that Bonferroni ≥ Holm ≥ BH and BY ≥ BH, that H ignores the order of the rows and that frequency weights equal the rows written out bit for bit; the two-group identity with the rank-sum z; the refusals; the Category and labelled groups of `wages`; the snapshots `kruskal__forms` and `kruskal__messages`; the conformance case `tests/kruskal`. `tests/reference/r/kruskal.R` is on the CI's reference list with tolerance 1e-12.

**Reason.** The checklist of 0.7.0, step 12; catalogue rows 172 and 178; Language Reference, sections 4, 6 and 10.2; open decisions #91 and #92; R 4.6.0's `kruskal.test` and `p.adjust`, read from the owner's installation.

**Addendum, 9 November 2026 (the cross-platform check of the R reference).** The first CI run of step 12 failed in the reference job alone: R's own `kruskal.test` statistic differs between the Linux runner and the macOS machine that wrote `kruskal.json` by about 1.6e-12 relative on the two cases with the smallest H (0.09 and 0.14), because R computes H as a difference of two numbers near 3(n + 1) and the last bits of that subtraction depend on the platform's maths library. The engine's agreement with the committed values (the Rust test, 1e-12) was never in doubt; only the R-against-R check across platforms needs room. `tests/reference/r/check_r.py` now compares `kruskal.json` within a relative 1e-9, which still detects any real change of R's answer.

## 9 November 2026: `fisher_test` (release 0.7.0, step 13)

**Decision.** `fisher_test` is written in Rust in the `stats` package, on the shared helpers of the tests. A 2 × 2 table gives the exact p-value for the alternative asked, the conditional maximum-likelihood estimate of the odds ratio and its 95% interval, each as R's `fisher.test` defines them (question 4 (d) of the release plan, "as R does"); a larger table gives the exact p-value alone.

**The 2 × 2 kernel.** The conditional distribution of the first cell is built by the recurrence of its probability ratios from its mode, at any odds ratio ψ, and normalised; no factorial and no logarithm of one is formed, so the probabilities near the mode are exact to a few units in the last place and the far tails underflow harmlessly. The estimate solves mean(ψ) = x, the bounds solve P(X ≤ x) = α and P(X ≥ x) = α, each by a bracket grown from 1 and bisection on the logarithmic scale until the ends of the bracket agree to the last digit. R's `fisher.test` solves the same equations with `uniroot` at its default tolerance, about 1e-4 of the root, so the two differ in the fourth digit of the bounds (up to 0.7% on a wide interval); the reference file therefore carries both R's printed values and the same quantities re-solved in R to 1e-12 ("tight"), and the engine is held to the tight values within 1e-9 and to R's within R's own tolerance. The two-sided p-value counts the outcomes whose probability is at most the observed one's times 1 + 1e-7, R's rule, so that outcomes equal in probability are counted together. The p-values agree with R within 1e-12.

**The larger table.** The tables with the observed margins are enumerated column by column, the last column forced, the probability of each from a table of ln i! accumulated once with the engine's own logarithm; the p-value sums those no more probable than the observed table under the same 1e-7 rule. The enumeration stops at one million tables (`TABLE_LIMIT`) and the test is then refused (Z0401) with `chi2_test` suggested, as question 4 (d) says; the limit is a count of tables, so the same table is always accepted or always refused. R's network algorithm reaches further (and R itself refuses the twelve industries by sex of `wages` for want of workspace); a faster enumeration is a later improvement, not a change of result. The count of tables is printed under the result.

**Rules.** A value with no rows, possible only through frequency weights, is left out of the table and named under the result: it has no place in the conditional distribution, and R's p-value for a table with a row of zeros is that of the table without it. Frequency weights must give whole counts (Z0401), since the exact distribution is one of counts. `alternative: less` or `greater` on a table larger than 2 × 2 is refused with the new code Z0420 (open decision #91 announced it; `docs/spec_changes.md`); `two_sided`, the default, is accepted on any table, since the engine fills an omitted option with its default and the two-sided test is what the larger table computes. The test takes no `level:` and its decision line is at α = 0.05, as the owner's ruling on open decision #91 fixes it. `less` means an odds ratio below 1, where the odds ratio is the odds of the first value of `b` among rows with the first value of `a` relative to rows with the second, in the convention of the shared argument; the directional H1 sentences read "the odds of b = … are lower among a = … than among a = …", a wording for the owner to review.

**Printing.** Fisher's test has no statistic, so `statistic_line` in `core` now prints `p = 0.486` alone for a `Statistic` with an empty name and no degrees of freedom; the estimate line reads `odds ratio (conditional MLE) = 6.408   95% CI [0.212, 626.244]`, with `Inf` at an open end.

**Shared code.** The cross-table of two variables (complete rows, values in the order of section 3.7, counts with frequency weights, the two Z0401 refusals) moved into `testing::cross_table`; `fisher_test` uses it and `chi2_test` keeps its own copy of the same lines until a later tidy, so that this step changes nothing `chi2_test` prints.

**Tests.** Reference (`tests/reference/r/fisher.R`: thirteen 2 × 2 cases including empty cells, the three alternatives and the union-by-sex table of `wages`; nine larger tables including a row of zeros and a symmetric table whose outcomes tie in probability), properties (the conditional distribution sums to one and its tails meet; the p-value is unchanged when rows and columns are swapped or reversed; a transposed 2 × 2 table keeps its odds ratio; the one-sided p-values overlap at the observed cell), edge cases (empty cells, a balanced table, the table limit on either side), snapshots of every form and every message, the conformance case `tests/fisher`. The cross-platform check of the R reference compares `fisher.json` within 1e-3, since R's `uniroot` roots may move within their tolerance between maths libraries.

**Reason.** The step asked for the 2 × 2 odds ratio with its interval, the larger table's p-value and the size limit; building the distribution by recurrence and solving to the last digit makes the engine's numbers reproducible across targets (section 8.3, point 3) and more accurate than the reference, which the tight re-solution in R lets the tests verify.

## 9 November 2026: a `TestResult` read as values (release 0.7.0, step 12b)

**Decision.** Six methods in `results`, on a `TestResult` alone (the receiver's type is `TestResult`, so the checker refuses a fit with Z0401 before the script runs, and the body refuses one at run time too): `statistic()` (a Float; `NA` for a test without a statistic, which the value carries as NaN), `df()` (a list of one or two Floats in the statistic's order; `NA` where it has none), `effect_size()` (a Float or `NA`), `h0()` and `h1()` (the printed sentences; `NA` for `test` and `compare`, which print none) and `alternative()` (the word as text: `"two_sided"`, `"less"`, `"greater"`). `estimates()` gains `df` and `df2` after `statistic` on both receivers: a fit's rows carry the residual degrees of freedom of their t statistics; a test's first row carries the statistic's degrees of freedom, the second of two (an F) in `df2`; and a test with an effect size gains a second row, named by the effect's label, with its value and interval and the other columns `NA`. The help of Z0213 names the methods when the value is a result (the test's methods on a `TestResult` or on a result of unknown kind, the fit's by-term methods on a fit), in the checker and in the interpreter alike; the explained page shows the case. The catalogue gains rows 539 to 544, the engine specification's count of `results` rises from 18 to 24, and the `Result` row of the types table is reworded (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) The decision says "a `df` column"; a statistic with two degrees of freedom needs two, so `df2` was added rather than a list in a cell or a column missing on an F, and the fit's frame carries both so that the frame has one shape whatever the result. (b) "A row for the effect size, `NA` where a test has none" is read as: the row exists where the test has an effect size; a test without one has no such row, since a row of `NA`s would need a label the test does not have. (c) `alternative()` gives text, not a word: a word is an argument's form, and text joins into sentences. (d) The refusal on a fit is Z0401, the code of a receiver of the wrong kind throughout `results`; no new code. (e) The `Value` paragraph of every test's help page names the six methods, as the help contract wants the ways of reading a value on its page.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/results/tests/fields.rs`: the six methods on hand-built results (a Welch t with everything, an F of two degrees of freedom without hypotheses, an exact test without a statistic); the shape of `estimates()` on each and on a fit; the refusal on a fit and on a number; a snapshot of every method through the engine on `t_test`, `chi2_test`, `kruskal_test`, `test` and `fisher_test`, the sentence of the definition of done with `format` and `join`, and the refusals (a fit, Z0213 on a result). The conformance case `tests/fields`. The stats test of the `Result` row reads the new wording.

**Reason.** Open decision #94 (B, decided 9 November 2026); the checklist's step 12b; Language Reference, section 4; the help contract of the testing handbook.

## 9 November 2026: `shapiro_test` (release 0.7.0, step 14)

**Decision.** `packages/tier1/stats/src/shapiro_test.rs` carries Royston's (1995) algorithm AS R94 as R's `swilk.c` carries it, constant for constant and in the same order of summation: the coefficients of the upper half from the normal quantiles at (i − 3/8)/(n + 1/4), the first two corrected by the polynomials in 1/√n and the rest rescaled; W as 1 − (1 − W) through the squared-correlation form that keeps its digits near 1; the exact p-value at n = 3, the transformation of log(1 − W) with constants in n for 4 to 11 values, and with constants in log n for 12 to 5,000, referred to the standard normal. The kernel `shapiro(sorted)` is public for the tests and answers `None` outside its conditions; the body `shapiro_test(ctx, args)` reads the frame and the variable, drops the rows with `NA` through the shared helper, sorts, and builds the `TestResult` with the hypotheses of open decision #91, the header `N = …`, no table, the statistic `W` without degrees of freedom, α = 0.05 and a line naming the source of the p-value. The elementary functions are the kernel's own (`zeff_numeric::maths`), the quantile and the tails those of `zeff_numeric::special`.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) More than 5,000 non-missing values are refused with Z0421, the next free number of its family, as the catalogue row announced; the help names `qq_plot` and `ks_test` as the catalogue row asks. (b) W prints to four decimals where every other statistic prints two: W lies in (0, 1] and departs from 1 in its third or fourth decimal, and the example of open decision #91 prints `W = 0.9997`; the rule is keyed on the method in `test_result_after`, through a new `statistic_line_to(statistic, p, decimals)` of which `statistic_line` is the two-decimal case, so no `TestResult` gains a field. (c) The header carries `N = …` alone; the rows dropped go in the shared note, as every other test prints them, rather than in the header as the illustrative example of #91 drew them. (d) Constant data are refused only when the range is exactly zero (Z0401), where R refuses a range below 1e-10 absolute: the algorithm scales every value by the range, so a small positive range is a legitimate sample, and a threshold in the data's own units would be arbitrary. (e) An infinite value is refused (Z0401) rather than carried into W as not-a-number. (f) Bool, Int and Float variables are accepted, as `kruskal_test` accepts them. (g) Fewer than three values after dropping `NA` is Z0401, with the count after dropping in the label. (h) The reference is held to a relative 1e-9 on W and on the p-value, and `check_r.py` compares the regenerated `shapiro.json` to the committed copy within 1e-9, since the p-value passes through the platform's log and exp in R.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/shapiro.rs`: the reference (`tests/reference/r/shapiro.json`, written by `tests/reference/r/shapiro.R`: n = 3, 4, 5, 11, 12, 50, 2,000 and 5,000 on normal quantiles, a skewed transform, values rounded to one decimal so that they tie, and a smooth non-normal series, with `NA` in one case); the kernel's bounds (fewer than three, more than 5,000, constant, infinite, and the closed forms at n = 3: W = 1 and p = 1 for equally spaced values, W = 3/4 and p = 0 for two of three equal); the property that W lies in (0, 1], p in [0, 1], and both are unchanged by a change of location and scale and by any order of the rows; the edge cases (Int and Bool variables, an infinite value, the wages of one year, the whole dataset refused); snapshots of every form and every message. The conformance case `tests/shapiro`; the help page's three examples through the engine.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 14; the catalogue row 176; open decision #91 (the sentences and the code's family); Royston (1995), as R and Stata implement it, so that a reader can check a value against either.

## 9 November 2026: `ks_test` (release 0.7.0, step 15)

**Decision.** `packages/tier1/stats/src/ks_test.rs`: D as the largest of F(x₍ᵢ₎) − (i − 1)/n and i/n − F(x₍ᵢ₎) over the sorted values, F being the distribution value's own `cdf` (so any family, truncated or mixed, is accepted, the step's "any `dist` family"); the exact distribution of D by Marsaglia, Tsang and Wang's (2003) matrix power, written as R's `pkolmogorov_two_exact` writes it (the same matrix, the same scaling by powers of ten, the same integer powers by repeated squaring), used below 100 values without ties as question 4 (c) rules; the limiting Kolmogorov distribution otherwise, both of its series summed to convergence rather than to R's tolerance of 1e-6 (the theta form below 1, the alternating form from 1, each tail computed directly so that a small p-value keeps its digits). `estimated: true` is Lilliefors' form against the normal family alone, with the sample mean and standard deviation and Dallal and Wilkinson's (1986) approximation, Stephens' form above 0.1, constant for constant as `nortest`'s `lillie.test`; any other distribution is refused (Z0422). The kernels are public for the tests; the elementary functions are the kernel's own.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) The asymptotic p-value is summed to convergence, not truncated as R truncates it: R's value can differ from the true limit in the fourth decimal near x = 1, and the fisher step set the precedent of holding the engine to the exact value and R within a looser tolerance; the help says so. (b) Ties are warned about with W0212, the next free number of its family, giving the count of values that share their value with another, in both forms of the test (R warns in `ks.test` alone, but Lilliefors' approximation assumes distinct values just the same); with ties the limiting distribution is used whatever the size, as R does. (c) Under `estimated: true` the parameters written in the distribution value are ignored, and the header prints the estimates with "(estimated from the data)"; the hypotheses are the sentences of open decision #91 for that form. (d) A distribution is named in a hypothesis as a phrase, "the normal distribution with mean 3 and sd 0.5", built from the value's parameters, since the value's own printed form (`normal distribution · mean: 3, sd: 0.5`) does not read as a sentence; the title keeps the printed form. (e) D prints to four decimals by the rule set for W at step 14, keyed on the method. (f) One value is enough for the plain test, as R allows, and five for Lilliefors', as `nortest` requires; a constant variable under `estimated: true` is Z0401. (g) Discrete families are accepted, their ties warned about, and the help says the test is conservative for them. (h) The reference holds D within 1e-10, the exact and Lilliefors p-values within 1e-9, the asymptotic ones within 1e-9 of the limit summed to convergence in R and within 1e-3 of R's own value; `check_r.py` compares the regenerated `ks.json` within 1e-9; `nortest` 1.0-4 joins the harness's packages in `install.R` and `renv.lock`, GPL code used by the harness alone.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/ks.rs`: the reference (`tests/reference/r/ks.json`, written by `tests/reference/r/ks.R`: the normal family at n = 1, 2, 7, 25, 60, 99, 100, 250 and 1,000 on data drawn from it and from shifted and scaled neighbours, ties at 40 and 300 values, `NA`, the nine other continuous families and the Poisson each at an exact and an asymptotic size; Lilliefors at n = 5, 6, 20, 50, 100, 101, 250 and 1,000 on five shapes, with `NA`); the kernels' closed forms (P(D₁ ≤ d) = 2d − 1, Marsaglia, Tsang and Wang's published value at n = 10, K(1) and K(2), the two series agreeing where they meet, both tails summing to one, D of the cell midpoints against the uniform, the exact-or-asymptotic rule, the count of ties, Lilliefors' bounds); the property that D lies in [1/(2n), 1], p in [0, 1], the exact p-value equals one minus the exact distribution function, and the answer is the same under any order of the rows and under a common shift of the data and the distribution; the edge cases (ties warned, an infinite value and `estimated: true` on the exponential refused, both forms on the wages of one year); snapshots of every form and every message. The conformance case `tests/ks`; the help page's three examples through the engine.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 15; question 4 (c) of the release; the catalogue row 177; open decision #91 (the sentences and the codes' families); R and `nortest` as the references the step names.

## 10 November 2026: `anova`, one-way (release 0.7.0, step 16)

**Decision.** `packages/tier1/stats/src/anova.rs`, in Rust as the tests of steps 9 to 15 (open decision #92): Welch's (1951) F as R's `oneway.test` computes it, the groups weighted by nᵢ/sᵢ² and the second degrees of freedom from the dispersion of the weights, unless `equal_var: true` asks for the classical F on the pooled within-group variance, as R's `aov`; the p-value is the upper tail of `dist.f`, computed directly. Both forms share one `TestResult` with the group table (N, mean, sd) of `t_test`'s two-group form, F with its two degrees of freedom, eta squared as the effect size and the decision line; the classical form adds the table of sums of squares (source, df, SS, MS, with a rule above the total) as a further table of the result's table, and the test-result printer, `summary()` and `export` now carry a result's further tables, which no earlier test had. The kernels (`welch`, `classical`, the `GroupSummary` they read and the `Undefined` reasons they return) are public for the tests. The weighted sample of `t_test` (values, weights and their kind; N, mean and variance by the kernel's weighted functions) moved into `stats::testing` as `Sample`, so that both tests of means read a group the same way.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) Eta squared is the sum of squares between the groups over the total sum of squares in both forms, from the ordinary decomposition (the Welch weights play no part in it), printed to three decimals without an interval: the interval of an F effect size needs the noncentral F, which `dist` does not have (the reasoning of open decision #93), and the help says so. (b) Welch's form refuses a group of fewer than two values and a group whose values are all equal, each with Z0401 naming the group and pointing to `equal_var: true` or `where` (R stops with "not enough observations" and gives `NaN` for the second); the classical form admits both, printing `NA` for the standard deviation of a group of one, and refuses no degrees of freedom within the groups and a pooled variance of zero. (c) The title names the variant as `t_test` does, `anova · Welch one-way · lwage by industry` and `anova · classical one-way · …`, and the line after the decision says how F was computed and what eta squared is. (d) The symbolic hypothesis of open decision #91, `μ₁ = μ₂ = … = μ_k`, writes every mean out for two or three groups and the ellipsis beyond, with k in subscript digits (`μ₁₂`); H1 is `not all equal`. (e) Two groups are allowed, as in `kruskal_test`: Welch's F is then the square of Welch's t and the classical F the square of the pooled t, which the kernel tests check. (f) Weights as in `t_test`: frequency weights count rows and analytic weights scale each group's variance by the kernel's convention, N being the rows under analytic weights. (g) The degrees of freedom print as every statistic line prints them, `F(11, 3,489.4)`, the form of the specification's own example. (h) The catalogue row 171 stays `planned` until the factorial form of step 17 ships, its notes saying that the one-way form shipped at this step; the help page describes the one-way form alone. (i) The reference holds F, both degrees of freedom, the p-value, the sums of squares and eta squared within a relative 1e-9; the classical values come from `aov`, since `oneway.test(var.equal = TRUE)` refuses a group of one, and the script checks that the two agree wherever both run; `check_r.py` compares the regenerated `anova.json` within 1e-9.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/anova.rs`: the reference (`tests/reference/r/anova.json`, written by `tests/reference/r/anova.R`: 2 to 6 groups of unequal sizes and variances, ties, a group of one, `NA`, text groups, 300 values, groups far apart with a p-value near 1e-20, and two groups twice); the kernels' closed forms and refusals; the properties (F is never negative, p and eta squared lie in [0, 1], the answer does not depend on the order of the rows or on a common shift and scale of the values, frequency weights repeat rows, in both forms); the edge cases of the checklist through the engine; snapshots of every form, including the result read as values and `summary()`, and every message. The conformance case `tests/anova_oneway`; the help page's four examples through the engine.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 16; question 4 (e) of the release; the catalogue row 171; open decisions #91 and #92; R as the reference the step names.

## 10 November 2026: `anova`, factorial (release 0.7.0, step 17)

**Decision.** `packages/tier1/stats/src/anova_factorial.rs`, in Rust as the tests of steps 9 to 16 (open decision #92). `anova` takes the factorial form when its first argument is a formula: the parameter `var` is registered as `Var | Formula` and `type: Int = 2`, and the function checks at run time which form was written, each form refusing the other's arguments with Z0401 (`group:` and `equal_var:` with a formula; `type:` with a variable; a `type:` other than 1, 2 or 3). The model matrix is the formula engine's (`Design::build` of `results`, with its notes on dropped rows), every category recoded by deviations over the levels the rows used hold (`Design::sum_coded`, new, with `Design::terms`, which names the columns of each term). The matrix `[X y]`, X scaled to unit column norms as the least-squares fit of `reg` scales it, is factorised once by the blocked QR of the kernels; every entry of the table is then read from a pivoted QR (tolerance 1e-7, the collinearity rule of `reg` and of R's `lm`) of that small triangular factor with its columns reordered: for type 1 the terms in order, for type 2 the terms that do not contain the tested term first, then the term, for type 3 every other column first, then the term. No pass over the rows is repeated and no cross-product matrix is formed. Frequency and analytic weights give the weighted least-squares table, the weights scaled as `Design::weighted` scales them; the observations are the total of the frequency weights or the rows; sampling weights are refused (Z0411) by the shared rule. The result is the `TestResult` of the one-way form with a new part `terms` (a `TermTest` for each row: its F, its two degrees of freedom, its p-value and its partial eta squared), so both forms share one result type as the step requires.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) Sum coding is applied under all three types, whatever contrast a category carries: types 1 and 2 do not depend on the coding, and type 3 is meaningful only under it, which is what the checklist's "type 3 with sum contrasts" asks; the help says so. (b) The rows of the table stand in the order of the terms' degree (main effects, two-way interactions and so on, the written order kept within a degree) under every type, as R orders the terms of a model; under type 1 that is also the order of adjustment, so `y ~ a * b + x` adjusts `a:b` for `x`, as `anova(lm())` does. (c) Type 3 is refused (Z0401) when a column of the model is determined by the others, an empty cell or a repeated term: car refuses it too, the test "adjusted for every other term" has no meaning there, and the message names `type: 2` and `tabulate` where two categories meet, or the repeated term where none do. Types 1 and 2 give the table, the aliased columns carrying no degree of freedom, with a note; a term left with no degrees of freedom keeps its row with blank cells and a note. (d) A formula without an intercept is refused (Z0401): every type adjusts for the grand mean, and R's tables without an intercept answer another question. (e) No row for the intercept under type 3, which car prints: the table tests the terms, and its total is the corrected total. (f) The table prints a row for the whole model, the terms, the residual and the total, with `source, df, SS, MS, F, p value, partial eta squared`; the result's own figures (`statistic()`, `df()`, `p_values()`) are the whole model's F, as Stata's `anova` heads its table, and `estimates()` gives a row for each term followed by its partial eta squared. There is no single hypothesis, so `h0()`, `h1()`, `effect_size()` and `ci()` are `NA` and no decision line is printed. Reading one term's row by name (`p_values("dose")`) is open decision #100; until it is decided a term named on `p_values` is Z0414, whose message for a result with terms now points to `estimates()`, and the three methods of a test's own take no argument (Z0407). (g) The conditions of a fit use the codes of `reg`, as the Language Reference's section 11 defines them for any fit: Z0801 (no row remains), Z0802 (no residual degrees of freedom, or a model that reproduces the outcome exactly, judged by R's rule of a residual mean square below 1e-30 of the fitted one), Z0803 (a value too large to square, above 1e150). (h) A model with no category is allowed with a note that each row tests a slope and that `reg` gives the estimates; a category with one level among the rows used and a constant outcome are refused (Z0401). (i) Partial eta squared is SS / (SS + SS residual), printed to three decimals without an interval, for the reason of the one-way form. (j) Under analytic weights the factorial form is weighted least squares with the weights scaled to sum to the number of rows, as Stata's `anova [aweight]` and R's `lm(weights =)`, while the one-way form of step 16 scales each group's variance: the two can differ on the same data. Flagged for the owner in `docs/progress.md`.

**Dependencies and tooling.** `zeff-stats` now depends on `zeff-results` (the formula engine's design) and `zeff-kernels` (the QR), both lower in the tier order, so the tier check holds; no new crate. The reference needs car: `tests/reference/r/install.R` installs car 3.1-5 with its dependencies from the dated snapshot of the lock file (on Linux from the snapshot's binaries, so that CI does not compile them), `renv.lock` records it, and the installer's comparison of versions, which read `3.1-5` and `3.1.5` as different, was corrected.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/stats/tests/anova_factorial.rs`: the reference (`tests/reference/r/anova.json`, key `factorial`, written by `tests/reference/r/anova.R`: `anova(lm())` for type 1 and `car::Anova` for types 2 and 3 on fifteen cases, balanced and unbalanced, the terms in both orders, a covariate alone and in an interaction with a factor, three factors, an empty cell, rows with `NA`, frequency and analytic weights), each figure compared before rounding within a relative 1e-9 and again through the function; the properties (the three types agree on a balanced layout; the type 1 sums of squares add up to the model's, and the model's and the residual to the total; types 2 and 3 do not depend on the order of the terms; frequency weights repeat rows); the edge cases (every refusal and every note); snapshots of every form and every message. `packages/tier1/results/tests/design.rs` gains the test of `terms` and `sum_coded`; the module has unit tests of the kernel (an unbalanced two-by-two layout against R, a balanced one, and each reason a table cannot be computed). The conformance case `tests/anova_factorial`.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 17; open decision #98 (every type of sums of squares R and Stata give) and question 2 of #99 (the covariate); the catalogue row 171; open decision #91 (the family of the codes); R and car as the references the step names.

## 10 November 2026: `effect:` on `anova` (release 0.7.0, step 17b)

**Decision.** `anova` takes `effect: eta | omega | epsilon = eta` in both forms (the owner's ruling on question 2 of open decision #99, "Yes, add them."), one option on the one function (open decision #97). The option is registered as a fixed list of words, read as `alternative:` is read: the checker refuses any other word with Z0402 before the function runs, so the function declares no refusal of its own. One-way, from the unweighted decomposition under either F: omega squared is (SS between − (k − 1) MS within) / (SS total + MS within) and epsilon squared is (SS between − (k − 1) MS within) / SS total, the adjusted R² of the regression on the groups. Factorial, for each term and for the row of the model: partial omega squared is (SS − df × MS residual) / (SS + (N − df) × MS residual) and partial epsilon squared is (SS − df × MS residual) / (SS + SS residual), N the number of observations (the sum of frequency weights; the rows used under analytic weights). The kernels compute all three measures in every call (`OneWay` and `Row` carry them), and the function prints the one asked for: the effect-size line and `effect_size()` in the one-way form, the last column of the table and the rows of `estimates()` in the factorial form, each named for the measure.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) A negative estimate is printed as it is (the owner's ruling, "Print as it is."), and `effect_size()` and `estimates()` return the same figure. A note says why: in the one-way form that F is below 1 (after Welch's F, the classical F of the same sums of squares is named with its value, since Welch's own F may be above 1); in the factorial form one note names every row concerned, the model first and then the terms in the order of the table. (b) After Welch's F the two measures come from the same unweighted decomposition as eta squared, so the three stay comparable and the choice of F changes none of them. (c) No interval, for the reason of open decision #93. (d) A term without degrees of freedom keeps `NA`, as it does for eta squared.

**What R and Stata do.** R's `effectsize::omega_squared()` and `epsilon_squared()` use the ruled formulas and replace a negative estimate by 0 (read in the package's source on 10 November 2026). Stata's `estat esize, epsilon` uses the same formula for partial epsilon squared. Stata's `estat esize, omega`, and R's `effectsize::F_to_omega2()`, compute partial omega squared from the F of the term alone, (SS − df × MS residual) / (SS + (df residual + 1) × MS residual), which equals the ruled formula in the one-way form, for a model of one term and on the row of the model, and is slightly farther from zero for a term of a model with several terms (checked on the example of Stata's manual, `regress bwt smoke i.race`: Stata 0.0716 and 0.0806, the ruled formula 0.0709 and 0.0802). The step builds the ruled formula; the help page states both differences; whether Stata's figure becomes a further word on `effect:` is open decision #101, for the owner.

**Tests.** The reference (`tests/reference/r/anova.json`, regenerated by `tests/reference/r/anova.R` with the earlier figures unchanged) gains omega and epsilon squared for every one-way case and for every row of every type of every factorial case, computed from the tables of base R and car by the formulas above: `effectsize` is not in the library, and its truncation at 0 would hide the sign in any case. `packages/tier1/stats/tests/anova.rs` and `anova_factorial.rs`: each figure before rounding within a relative 1e-9 and again through the function; closed forms in F for two and three groups and for F = 0; the properties (epsilon squared never above eta squared, omega squared never farther from zero than epsilon squared and of the same sign, the sign that of F − 1, invariance to a shift and a scale, frequency weights as repeated rows, the model's row equal to R² and the adjusted R², one category equal to the one-way form); the edge cases (the notes of a negative estimate in both forms, the value returned as it is, a word outside the list); snapshots of both forms under each measure. The conformance cases `tests/anova_oneway` and `tests/anova_factorial` gain calls under `effect:`; the help page gains three examples run through the engine.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 17b; question 2 of open decision #99 and the ruling on negative estimates; open decisions #97 and #98; the catalogue row 171.

## 10 November 2026: The debug build folder, and no debugging information in development builds

**What was found.** By 10 November `target/debug/deps` held 1,340,137 entries and `target/debug` about 110 GB; 99.1% of the entries were object files (`*.rcgu.o`). On macOS a development build keeps its object files beside the build so that a debugger can read them, each rebuild writes its object files under new names, and nothing removes the earlier ones. Every start of the compiler reads that folder, and listing it took 96 seconds: the lint check took 24 minutes and the full local routine over four hours, where CI takes about six minutes. The owner's second session diagnosed it; this one had reported the long runs as normal.

**The clean-up.** `cargo clean --profile dev`, which removes `target/debug` and nothing else (the benchmark results in `target/criterion`, the release build and the WebAssembly build stay), after a dry run that listed no path outside that folder: 1,670,145 files removed, 111 GB freed. The full local routine from the empty folder then took 6 minutes 39 seconds and left 15,840 entries.

**The measurement.** One source file of `zeff-stats` touched and its tests rebuilt, twice, under four settings of the development profile, each in a build folder of its own:

| Setting | Entries after the first build | Left behind by each rebuild | Time of a rebuild |
|---|---|---|---|
| as it was (full debugging information) | 15,840 (after the whole routine) | 1,767 object files | 3 s |
| `debug = "line-tables-only"` | 4,023 | 1,767 object files | 2 s |
| `split-debuginfo = "packed"` | 344 | none | 9 to 10 s |
| `debug = false` | 332 | none | 3 s |

**Choice.** `debug = false` in `[profile.dev]`, which the test profile inherits. It removes the cause, gives the fastest build and the smallest folder, and means the same on every target, where `split-debuginfo = "packed"` would also change how the Linux builds are made. Under it the full local routine takes 5 minutes 16 seconds from an empty folder and leaves 1,274 entries with no object file, and a rebuild leaves the count unchanged. No result depends on the setting and the release profile is untouched. The file and line of a failed assertion or of a panic are printed as before; what is given up is the line numbers inside a backtrace and the use of a debugger, and one run with `CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=true` in the environment brings both back (clear the folder afterwards).

**The rule from now on.** Before the full local routine of a step, count the entries of the folder (`ls -f target/debug/deps | wc -l`, instant on a healthy folder); above 10,000, run `cargo clean --profile dev` first. Builds made under earlier settings, dependencies or toolchains still accumulate, far more slowly, because cargo removes nothing by itself. A local routine that takes many times what CI takes is a fault to look into, never a duration to report.

**Reason.** An engineering decision under the standing instructions; it adds to "Build profile and lints" of 18 October 2026, which stands otherwise.

## 11 November 2026: `dist.tukey`, the studentized range (release 0.7.0, step 18)

**Decision.** `dist.tukey(groups: Int, df: Float)` is the thirteenth family of `dist`; its values come from a new module of the numeric kernel, `kernel/zeff-numeric/src/tukey.rs`, which holds the lower tail, the upper tail, the density and the quantile. `groups:` is a whole number of 2 or more and `df:` a finite number of 1 or more, whole or not; anything else is refused with Z0413. R's `ptukey` and Stata's `tukeyprob()` need 2 degrees of freedom or more; the checklist's grid starts at 1, the integral exists there, and the reference confirms the values, so 1 is accepted. A `df:` of 1e30 or more gives the range of the normal values themselves (a known standard deviation).

**The method.** P(Q ≤ q) = ∫ P(W ≤ qs) f(s) ds, where W is the range of k standard normal values and f the density of S, with νS² chi-squared on ν degrees of freedom. Both integrals are trapezoidal sums over the whole line, carried in logarithms, the outer one in t = ln s. For integrands of this kind the trapezoidal rule gains digits geometrically as the step shrinks (Trefethen and Weideman 2014), so no table of nodes is needed and the error is seen directly: the step is divided by three, which gives three interleaved sums, until the three agree. The upper tail and the density have integrals of their own, so that a far tail keeps its relative accuracy and the density is not a difference of two probabilities. R's `ptukey` (Copenhaver and Holland 1988) sums fixed Gauss–Legendre rules of 12 and 16 points and is the less accurate for it; the kernel takes nothing from it.

**The constants.** The first step is 0.8 of the integrand's standard deviation (`FIRST_STEP`), a sum stops when a term falls below 1e-17 of the total (`NEGLIGIBLE`), the three sums must agree to 1e-6 (`AGREEMENT`, which by the geometric convergence leaves the next refinement right to the last digits), and past a range of 60 the upper tail of the range of normal values is below the smallest double, so the lower one is 1 (`WIDEST`). They were tuned on the 279 reference cases by counting evaluations of the inner integrand: a first step from 1.1 down to 0.7 standard deviations gave the same worst error, 8.03e-15, at 18.2 down to 8.8 million evaluations; the values chosen need 7.8 million and 3.5 seconds for the 279 cases. A value costs about 5 milliseconds, about 35 on 1 or 2 degrees of freedom.

**The quantile.** Solved in ln q on the smaller tail: a bracket found by doubling, then false position with the Illinois safeguard, stopped when a step moves the point by less than a few units in its last place, since the iteration gains digits faster than one for one. About twenty values of the distribution function, so about a tenth of a second, more on 1 or 2 degrees of freedom. The `quantile` method of a `Distribution` takes the lower probability only, so the family passes that; the kernel also solves from the upper probability, which `posthoc` may use. `draw` goes through the quantile as for every family and is slow for a large `n`; the help page says so.

**Accuracy reached.** Against the exact reference the worst relative error over the 279 cases is 8.03e-15 (the upper tail at q = 30 for 4 groups on a million degrees of freedom), and a probability returned by the quantile comes back within 3.9e-15. The class of 1e-12 holds on the whole grid, wider than the checklist asked: 2 to 200 groups, 1 to 1e12 degrees of freedom, tails down to 1e-98.

**The reference.** `tests/reference/tukey.py` (Python's `decimal` at 70 digits, the standard library only) computes the same probabilities by the same outline and shares no detail with the kernel: two changes of variable in the outer integral that the kernel does not make, a normal tail from a 95-digit `erfc` carried between the points of a lattice by its Taylor series, an exponent range wide enough for the weight of a million million degrees of freedom far from its peak, and nothing taken from a float except places to start looking, rounded to six digits so that no platform's C library can move a node. Before writing, it checks itself to 1e-20 against the two cases with a closed form (2 groups on 1 and on 2 degrees of freedom) and checks that the two tails, each summed on its own, add to one. 252 cases on a grid and 27 chosen ones, written to `tests/reference/tukey.json` with the list of cases in `tests/reference/data/tukey_cases.csv`. It runs on at most four processes and takes about 45 seconds on four, about three minutes on one.

**R as the second check.** `tests/reference/r/tukey.R` records `ptukey` on the same cases and `qtukey` on 36. Measured against the exact reference, the worst absolute error of `ptukey` is 4.6e-3 on 2 degrees of freedom, 3.1e-5 on 5, 9.6e-8 on 20, 3.8e-8 on 120 and 2.1e-6 on a million, where R switches to the range of normal values; the tail above 50 for 10 groups on 5 degrees of freedom comes out at 9.35e-6 where the true value is 4.71e-6. `qtukey` agrees to about four digits, is out by up to a fifth on 2 degrees of freedom, and fails to converge (NaN) for a probability of 0.05 or 0.1 on 30 groups; its grid therefore starts at 5 degrees of freedom and at the median. The test holds `ptukey` to an absolute 1e-2 below 5 degrees of freedom, 1e-4 below 20 and 1e-5 from 20, and `qtukey` to a relative 1e-4. In CI, `check_r.py` compares the regenerated R file with the committed one at a relative 1e-9 with a floor of 1e-12, since a far tail of `ptukey` is one minus a sum of which only the rounding is left.

**Tests.** `kernel/zeff-numeric/tests/reference_tukey.rs`: all 279 cases at 1e-12, the quantile on 48 of them (every tail below 1e-3 and one in six of the others), and R at its own accuracy. `tests/properties.rs`: both tails in [0, 1] and ordered in q, one more group never raising the lower tail, the density equal to the slope of the smaller tail, and the quantile's round trip. They run 24 and 12 cases where other properties run hundreds, because every value is a double integral; both held over 960 and 480 cases once. Package tests with real output, four refusals in the snapshot, and a series `dist/tukey` of the conformance suite, kept apart from `dist/values` so that the published digests of earlier releases stand.

**Considered and not adopted.** Optimising `zeff-numeric` in the development profile, to shorten the tests: measured at 5.3 seconds against 6.1 for the reference test, not worth a second profile rule. R's `nranges` argument, the largest of several independent ranges, is not in the catalogued usage and is open decision #102.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 18; the catalogue row 494; Engine Specification section 8.3, point 3 (one pure-Rust implementation, fixed order of summation: the sums run in a fixed order and use the kernel's own elementary functions).

## 11 November 2026: four further methods of `p_adjust` (release 0.7.0, step 18b)

**Decision.** `p_adjust` takes `method: holm | bonferroni | hochberg | hommel | bh | by | sidak | none = holm` (the owner's ruling on question 2 of open decision #99, "Yes, add them."), one option on the one function (open decision #97). The four words of step 12 keep their order and the default stays `holm`; `hochberg` and `hommel` follow `bonferroni`, and `sidak` and `none` close the list, which is the order in which step 19 lists the words `posthoc` shares. The option stays a fixed list of words, so the checker refuses any other word with Z0402 before the function runs; the function's own refusal (Z0401) is reached only by a direct call. With n the number of p-values that are not `NA` and p₍₁₎ ≤ … ≤ p₍ₙ₎: Hochberg gives the smallest of (n + 1 − j)·p₍ⱼ₎ over j ≥ i, one pass from the largest p-value with a running minimum. Hommel gives the largest Simes p-value among the sets of hypotheses that hold the one adjusted, the closed test with Simes's rule; it is computed by Wright's (1992) pass over the set sizes m = n, …, 2, 1, each size contributing the smaller of m·p₍ᵢ₎ and the Simes value of the m largest p-values, written from that definition (the module's comment derives it) and not from R's source. Šidák gives 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ as −expm1(n·log1p(−p)) with the kernel's own two functions, so that a p-value of 1e-20 keeps its digits where 1 − p would lose them. `none` returns the values given. `Method` gains `Hochberg`, `Hommel`, `Sidak` and `Unadjusted` (the word `none` read as a Rust name would collide with the absent option), with `Method::WORDS` and `Method::from_word` as the one list the function, its message and the tests read.

**Rulings where the text is silent.** (a) `sidak` is the single-step form, as the checklist says and as Stata's `mtest(sidak)` computes it. The step-down form of Holland and Copenhaver (1987) is in neither base R nor Stata and is not offered. (b) With one p-value present Šidák returns it exactly, without passing through the logarithm, as every other method leaves a single p-value alone. (c) A p-value of 0 gives a plain zero under every method and a p-value of 1 gives 1; the reference script sets Šidák's zero itself, because the sign R gives it depends on the platform's `log1p`. (d) For two p-values Hommel's method is Hochberg's; R switches methods there, and the pass over set sizes gives the same figures without a branch. (e) `none` returns a `List<Float>` like every other method, also when a column is given, with `NA` in place. (f) R's second name for Benjamini–Hochberg, `"fdr"`, is not a word: one word for one method. (g) `n:`, the number of comparisons when it exceeds the p-values given (R), is not built: the review of #99 classed it B, and it waits on question 3 of that decision, due at 0.8.0.

**What R and Stata do.** R's `p.adjust` has `"holm"`, `"hochberg"`, `"hommel"`, `"bonferroni"`, `"BH"` (also `"fdr"`), `"BY"` and `"none"`, and no Šidák. Stata's `test, mtest()` has `bonferroni`, `holm`, `sidak` and `noadjust`, and `pwcompare, mcompare()` has `bonferroni`, `sidak` and `noadjust` among its words (from the manuals as remembered; Stata is not installed). The help page gives both sets of names.

**Cost.** Hommel's pass takes time proportional to n². Measured on the owner's machine: 20,000 p-values take 0.3 seconds with the compiler's optimisation on, as in a released build (5 seconds in the development build), against 3.9 seconds for R's `p.adjust`; 100,000 take 6.5 seconds. The other methods sort once. A linearithmic algorithm exists (Meijer, Krebs and Goeman, 2019) and was not adopted: the families `posthoc` and an analyst adjust are small, and the quadratic pass is the one that can be read against the definition. The help page states the cost.

**Tests.** The reference (`tests/reference/r/kruskal.json`, regenerated by `tests/reference/r/kruskal.R` with every earlier figure unchanged) gains `hochberg`, `hommel` and `none` from `p.adjust` and Šidák's formula written beside them, for the eight cases of step 12 and six new ones: two p-values in descending order, three and four close together so that Hommel differs from Hochberg and Hochberg from Holm, two ties at the top, `NA` with 0 and 1 and a tie, and forty p-values. `packages/tier1/stats/tests/kruskal.rs`: the eight methods on the fourteen cases within a relative 1e-12, `none` bit for bit; Šidák by hand on four lists, one with a p-value of 1e-20; the properties over lists with `NA`, ties, 0 and 1 (every adjusted value between the raw one and 1, the order kept, equal p-values adjusted equally to the last bit, `none` returning its input, Bonferroni ≥ Holm ≥ Hochberg ≥ Hommel, Bonferroni ≥ Šidák, and Hommel equal to the closed test computed by visiting every set of up to eight hypotheses); the edge cases (one p-value, an empty list and all `NA` under every method, 0 and 1, three tied p-values with their values by hand, two p-values, a word outside the list by a direct call); the snapshots of every form and of the message, whose refused word is now `tukey` since `hochberg` is a method. The conformance case `tests/kruskal`, added at step 12 of this release and not yet published, gains five calls and its output digest changes; no digest of a released version changes. The help page is rewritten with the eight methods, the names R and Stata use, the conditions under which each holds, nine references and six examples run through the engine.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 18b; question 2 of open decision #99; open decisions #97 and #98; the catalogue row 178.

## 11 November 2026: `posthoc` after a one-way `anova` (release 0.7.0, step 19)

**Decision.** `fit.posthoc(method: tukey | bonferroni | holm | hochberg | hommel | bh | by | sidak | scheffe | none = tukey)` is built on the result of the one-way `anova`, in Rust like the other tests of `stats` (open decision #92). The step as first written said "after either form of `anova`". What is compared after the factorial form is defined by no normative text, and R's `TukeyHSD` gives other figures than R's `emmeans` and Stata's `pwcompare` in an unbalanced design, so the step was split in the checklist: step 19 is the one-way form with all ten methods, step 19b the factorial form, which waits on open decision #104. Until then `posthoc` after an `anova` given a formula is refused with Z0401, whose help names the one-way form.

**How it is built.** The `anova` leaves what `posthoc` needs on its result, so nothing is read from the frame a second time: `TestResult` gains `follow_up`, an optional shared record that for the one-way form holds the names of the outcome and the grouping variable, the groups in printed order with their size, mean and variance at full precision, and whether F pooled the variances. A weighted `anova` passes on its weighted sizes, means and variances. The comparisons are a kernel inside `stats` (`posthoc.rs`) over those summaries: the differences, the pooled or Welch standard errors and degrees of freedom, t, and the p-values and limits by `dist.tukey`, `dist.f`, `dist.t` and the adjustments of `p_adjust`, all through the numeric kernel's own elementary functions. The result is a `TestResult` of several rows: a row of a test (`TermTest`) gains an optional estimate with its interval and an optional standard error, and `estimates()`, `ci()` and `export` of `results` read them, so a comparison's difference, standard error and limits reach a frame, a table and a file as a fit's do.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) A comparison is the first group minus the second, in the order (1, 2), (1, 3), …, (2, 3), the groups as `anova` prints them; `t_test` already writes its difference so. R's `TukeyHSD`, `DescTools::ScheffeTest` and Stata write the second minus the first, and the help page says that the signs are therefore opposite. (b) Intervals are printed for the single-step methods, `tukey`, `scheffe`, `bonferroni`, `sidak` and `none`, whose intervals match their p-values; the step-wise methods print none, and `ci()` on such a result is `NA` (open decision #105 holds the alternative of `emmeans`, Bonferroni's intervals). (c) The intervals are at 95% and `posthoc` takes no `level:`, since the catalogued usage has none; `ci(level:)` at another level is refused with a message saying so (#105). (d) The `df` column is printed only when each pair has its own degrees of freedom, after Welch's `anova`, with one decimal; on the pooled variance the one figure stands in the line beneath the table. (e) `tukey` and `scheffe` pool the variance whichever F the `anova` computed, by question 4 (f); after Welch's F a note says so and names `method: holm`. (f) `statistic()`, `df()` and `p_values()` on the result give the F of the `anova` followed, as step 17 ruled for a result of several rows; `h0()`, `h1()` and `effect_size()` are `NA` and no decision line is printed, a set of comparisons having no single hypothesis (a dated note on open decision #100 records it). (g) After `equal_var: true` a group of one value is compared with the others on the pooled variance; Welch's comparisons need what Welch's `anova` already requires. (h) With two groups every method gives the p-value of the t-test of the two. (i) No p-value exceeds 1. (j) Stata's `snk`, `duncan` and `dunnett`, class B in the review of #99, and the Games–Howell comparison (#85) are not built; the help page says so. (k) The result of any other test, of `kruskal_test` among them, is refused with Z0401; pairwise rank tests after `kruskal_test` are a class B item of #99.

**Accuracy.** Closed form. Against R the differences, standard errors, t, degrees of freedom, and the p-values and limits of every method but Tukey's agree within a relative 1e-9. Tukey's p-values and limits come from `dist.tukey`, accurate to a relative 1e-12 against the exact reference of step 18, while R's `ptukey` and `qtukey` are not: the tests hold R's Tukey p-values within 1e-6 on 20 or more degrees of freedom and 1e-4 below, and R's limits within a thousandth of the standard error. The help page states this.

**The reference packages.** `DescTools` 0.99.60 (for `ScheffeTest`) and `emmeans` 2.0.4 (for Šidák's p-values and the intervals on the pooled variance) join the pinned R library as the checklist's step 19 names them, with the 34 packages they depend on, 36 entries in `tests/reference/r/renv.lock` from the dated snapshot of 1 October 2026. Licences: `DescTools` GPL (>= 2), `emmeans` GPL-2 | GPL-3, `estimability` GPL (>= 3), `mvtnorm` GPL-2, `Exact`, `gld`, `expm`, `rootSolve` and `e1071` GPL, `lmom` Common Public License 1.0, `data.table` MPL-2.0, the others MIT. They are R code run by the test harness alone and nothing of them is linked into the engine or the apps. The committed `tests/reference/r/posthoc.json` was written on the owner's machine from his own R library, which holds `emmeans` 2.0.3, because no package is installed there without his word; its header says 2.0.3. The continuous integration installs the pinned 2.0.4 and regenerates the file, and the comparison is of the numbers within tolerance, the header being left out, so the two versions are checked against each other on every run. Whether 2.0.4 is installed into the project's ignored library folder on his machine is his to say.

**Tests.** Reference: `tests/reference/r/posthoc.R` on the fifteen sets of groups of `anova.R` (2 to 6 groups, unequal sizes and variances, ties, a group of one, `NA`, text groups, a large sample, two groups) and on hours by industry of the shipped `wages` (12 groups, 66 comparisons), each with `TukeyHSD`, `ScheffeTest`, `pairwise.t.test` pooled and not under each method of `p.adjust`, Šidák from `emmeans` and by its formula, and the intervals of the single-step methods; `check_r.py` gains the series `posthoc`. Unit: the kernel against its closed forms and its refusals. Property: every figure in range, each interval centred on its difference and excluding zero exactly when its p-value is below 0.05, the order of the methods comparison by comparison (Bonferroni ≥ Holm ≥ Hochberg ≥ Hommel ≥ `none`, Bonferroni ≥ Šidák ≥ `none`, Benjamini–Yekutieli ≥ Benjamini–Hochberg ≥ `none`, Hochberg ≥ Benjamini–Hochberg, Scheffé ≥ Tukey ≥ `none` on the pooled variance), `none` after Welch's `anova` equal to `t_test` of each pair in its t, degrees of freedom, p-value and interval, no dependence on the order of the rows, and frequency weights equal to the rows written out. Edge cases: two groups under every method, unequal sizes, a group of one, everything that is not a one-way `anova`. Snapshots of every printed form and every message. The conformance case `tests/posthoc` (two digests, 235 of 235 in `zeff selftest`). The help page runs its six examples.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 19; question 4 (f) of the release; question 2 of open decision #99; open decisions #92, #97, #98 and #100; the catalogue row 195; the testing handbook, section 4.

## 11 November 2026: the plot value, the scene and `points` (release 0.7.0, step 20)

**Decision.** The package `plot` is a new crate of tier 1, `packages/tier1/plot` (`zeff-plot`), which depends on the kernel crates and `core` alone. A plot is a value declared in `core` (section 8.1, rule 4): the frame, the mappings of the aesthetics and the layers, in the order the script wrote them, with its printed form. The package makes and extends it and derives the *scene* from it, a pure function of the plot value: the marks in the units of the data, the scales with their limits, breaks and labels, the axes, the layout and the notes. The writers of step 21 and Zemp read the scene alone. At this step `data.plot(x:, y:)` maps variables, `p.points(data:, alpha:, size:, jitter:)` adds a layer, and a printed plot is its scene read as text. The type `Plot` joins the checker's types.

**The split.** The step as first written held the eight aesthetics "with variables, expressions and constants". It was split in the checklist rather than pushed through: step 20 is the two positions as variables, with everything the scene needs; step 20b is expressions in `x:` and `y:`; step 20c is the six other aesthetics with their constants and the content of the legend. The catalogue's row 461 (`points`) is `implemented`; row 460 (`plot`) stays `planned` until 20c, because its usage is not yet built as written. The help page of `plot` is complete for what is built and is reopened at 20b, 20c and step 21 (`export`).

**One name on two types.** The catalogue has `plot` twice in the package `plot`: `data.plot(…)` on a frame (row 460) and `fit.plot()` on a fit (row 227), which rule 6 of section 8.1 allows. The registry looked a function's row up by package and name and took the first. `Catalogue::find_for` now takes the receiver the usage is written on as well, and where a package has several rows of a name the row written on that receiver is the one meant; a test of the registry holds both cases.

**The linear scale** (section 7.6, whose defaults "follow Observable Plot"). (a) The domain of an axis is the extent of the values its layers draw, after any jitter; before a layer is added, or when the layers draw nothing, it is the extent of the variable in the plot's frame. (b) The limits lie 5% of the extent beyond it on each side, so that no mark sits on the edge of the panel; ggplot2 does the same, Observable Plot insets the panel instead. (c) An extent of one value v is widened by the larger of 0.5 and 5% of |v|; with no value the limits are 0 and 1. (d) The breaks are the multiples of a step of 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten that lie within the limits, the step chosen so that the limits span about five steps: the rule of D3 and Observable Plot. A break is read from its decimal text, so that 0.3 is the double nearest 0.3; no logarithm or power is computed on the way, and the elementary functions of the platform are not touched. Limits too close for round numbers between them are their own breaks. (e) The labels are the numbers as tables print them, to six significant digits (section 3.8); where two neighbouring breaks would share a label, every label is the number in full. (f) Limits are never rounded outward to a break ("nice" limits), which would move with the data less predictably.

**The scene.** (a) Version 1, written `"zeff_scene": 1`: `layout` (rows and columns of panels), `scales` (each with an identifier, its kind, title, limits, breaks and labels), `guides` (the axes, each naming its scale and its side, and the legends, empty until 20c), `panels` (each with its place counted from 1, the scales it uses and its layers from the bottom up) and `notes`. A layer of points holds its `x` and `y` in data units with its size and opacity. (b) A scene has no size in pixels, no fonts and no colours of the theme; they belong to the writer, so the same data give the same scene on every target. (c) The JSON is written by the package itself, the engine linking no JSON library: keys in a fixed order, a number in the shortest form that reads back to the same double. A reader must round correctly; the tests read the numbers back with the standard library, because the default reader of `serde_json` may be one unit out in the last place. (d) The version rises when a reader of the earlier version would misread the new one.

**Rows not drawn.** A row with `NA` in a mapped variable is dropped and counted in a note, as section 7.6 requires. A row with an infinite value, which no axis can hold, is counted in a note of its own. A plot carries each note once: a later layer whose note would read the same does not repeat it, and a layer with its own frame raises its own. The note is raised when the layer is added, at the line of the mark.

**`points`.** (a) It needs both `x` and `y`; with one of them unmapped it is refused (Z0401) with a message naming what to add. (b) `size:` is the diameter in points of 1/72 inch, 4.5 when not given, which is the default of Observable Plot (a radius of 3 pixels at 96 to the inch). (c) `alpha:` lies in [0, 1], `size:` is above 0 and finite, `jitter:` is 0 or more and finite; each refusal is Z0401. An option written `NA` takes its default, as on every other function. (d) `jitter:` is one share for both axes, in units of the smallest gap between two different values on each axis (1 when all are equal), the resolution ggplot2 uses; a point at x is drawn at x + (2u − 1)·j·r. The draws come from the run's seeded stream at the statement of the mark, one for `x` and then one for `y`, point by point in the order of the rows, so the layer holds its stream and the scene can be derived again without drawing anew. Without a seed the usual note names the one chosen. (e) `data:` names a frame for the layer, which must hold the variables the plot maps, as numbers (Z0101, Z0102 and Z0401 otherwise); the titles of the axes stay those of the plot's frame. (f) A layer does not override a mapping: the catalogued usage has no option for it, although section 7.6 says a layer may. That is open decision #106, due before step 23.

**The printed form**, a layout the owner may change. A header, `plot · w · wage against educ` (the frame's name left out when the frame has none); a grid of the axes, with the title, the kind of scale, the limits and the breaks of each; a grid of the layers, with the mark, the frame, the number of marks drawn and the settings; or the line "no layer yet" before a mark is added. `core` prints it without knowing the package (rule 5). A long title or long breaks make the grid wrap as any wide table does. In messages a frame without a name is "this frame", and in the grid of layers "the frame" or "its own frame".

**Variables that are not numbers.** A Bool is placed as 0 and 1 and an Int as its value. Text, categories and dates are refused with Z0401, whose message says that their scales are not built yet; the categorical position scale comes with `bars` at step 24 and the date scale at step 25, and the wording is to be changed there. The edge-case files `empty.csv` and `all_na.csv` are read as text by `import` and so meet this refusal.

**A defect found: the seed noted for a run does not repeat it.** While the jitter was tested, the assertion that an unseeded run and the same script with the noted seed at its top draw alike failed. The cause is in the engine since 0.3.0 and not in this step: a draw is keyed by the place of its statement among all the statements of the run, so the line `seed(N)` itself moves every later draw, and so does any inserted statement that draws nothing. The random-numbers rule of section 8.3 says that inserting a statement that draws changes the draws after it, the help page of `seed` says that one that does not draw never does, and the engine's note says that `seed(N)` at the top repeats the run; the code agrees with none of the three. It is corrected as step 20a, after this step and before 20b, by keying a draw by the place of its statement among those that draw from the run's stream. Every figure drawn under a script-wide `seed` then changes, in the tests, the help examples and the conformance digests, and the release notes must say so. The jitter test of this step asserts what is true today (one seed repeats, another differs, the note is raised) and gains the full assertion at 20a.

**Dependencies.** None new. The package's tests use `insta`, `proptest` and `serde_json` at the versions already pinned and recorded, as dev-dependencies. The conformance crate now depends on `zeff-plot` and `zeff-datasets`; it is not a package, so the tier rule is not concerned, and `plot` itself does not depend on `datasets`, which stands after it in the order of tier 1.

**Tests.** Unit: the scale (margins, one value, no value, the widest doubles, the breaks and their exact decimals, the labels) and the JSON writer. Scene: four snapshots of the JSON (a small scatter, no layer, two layers of which one jittered and one with its own frame, one variable and none), the JSON read back value for value, and the edge cases (one point, a constant variable, only missing values, no rows, an infinite value, whole numbers and truth values, the largest numbers). Property: the same data give the same scene; reordering the rows changes only the order of the marks; every break and every mark lies within the limits; jitter moves a point by no more than its share of the gap. Script: the printed wages scatter, with its limits, counts and note checked against R 4.6.0 on the shipped file (18,412 rows, 18,201 drawn, 211 dropped; 26 wages above 100); every shape of a printed plot; the thirteen edge-case files of `tests/datasets/`, each with what it prints, notes or refuses; all twenty refusals with their messages; the plot as a value that adding a layer does not change; the notes; the jitter under a seed. Conformance: the case `plot/points` (the printed output, the messages and the scene's JSON of the wages scatter with jitter), `zeff selftest` at 238 of 238 with no earlier digest changed. Both help pages run as examples. Two snapshots of the engine that check the sample script of the specification were renewed and read: they list what the sample asks for that this release does not have yet, and the list changed as it should. `plot` and `points` are no longer unknown functions; `plot` is now refused for its `color:` argument (step 20c), and `export` is refused on a Plot (step 21). The engine's own test of the packages shipped now names `plot`.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 20; sections 7.6 and 3.8 of the Language Reference; sections 8.1 (rules 4, 5 and 6) and 8.3 (points 3 and 5) of the Engine and Project Specification; the catalogue's rows 460 and 461; the testing handbook, section 4.

## 11 November 2026: the seed noted for a run repeats it (release 0.7.0, step 20a)

**Decision.** A draw from the run's stream is keyed by the ordinal of its statement among the statements that draw from that stream: the first that draws has ordinal 1, the next 2, and so on. Until now it was keyed by the statement's place among all the statements of the run. `Randomness` (in `core`'s `runtime`) gains a counter, `drawing`, raised when a statement draws from the run's stream for the first time; the place of the statement, which the interpreter still passes, is kept only to tell one statement from the next. Nothing else of the stream changes: the generator, the key, the loop pass, the call within the statement, the 53-bit uniform, and the stream of a call with its own `seed:` (ordinal 0, the same wherever it stands).

**Why this is a fault of the code and not a change of the rule.** Section 8.3, point 3, of the Engine and Project Specification keys a draw by "the ordinal of the drawing statement within the run" and says that inserting or removing "a statement that draws random numbers" changes the draws after it, as in R and Stata. The help page of `seed` has said since 0.3.0 that a statement that does not draw never changes the draws after it, and the engine's note for an unseeded run says that `seed(N)` at the top of the script repeats it. The code did none of the three: `seed(N)` is itself a statement, so writing it at the top moved every later draw by one place and the run was not repeated. The test of `seed` in `core` held the fault in place with an assertion that contradicted its own comment; it now asserts what the comment says. No normative sentence changes, so `docs/spec_changes.md` has no entry beyond the one of step 20.

**What counts as a statement that draws.** (a) A top-level statement in which at least one call takes the run's stream, however many calls and however many passes of a loop: a loop is one statement, its passes kept apart by the pass number as before. (b) A call with a `seed:` of its own is not counted and does not make its statement one that draws, as it already did not count for Z0111. (c) `seed(n)` and every statement that draws nothing are not counted. (d) A draw inside a function written in Zeff belongs to the calling statement, as the step 3 ruling of 0.6.0 says. (e) A plot layer with `jitter:` above 0 takes the stream when the layer is added, so the statement that adds the layer is the one that draws; `jitter: 0` draws nothing.

**What changes for a user: every figure drawn under a script-wide `seed(n)`.** A script that begins `seed(n)` and then draws now gives the numbers that the same script would have given before with `seed(n)` removed and the seed supplied otherwise, that is, other numbers than it gave under 0.3.0 to 0.6.0. Draws with a `seed:` of their own are unchanged. This is a breaking change for the notes of 0.7.0 (material for step 40c): results that depend on `seed(n)` are equally valid draws from the same distributions but are not the same numbers as before, and there is no rewrite that restores the old ones.

**Outputs renewed, each read.** (1) The help example of `seed` (now five draws rather than three, since the first three under the page's seed happen to lie close together and would mislead a reader about what normal draws look like; 100,000 draws under another seed were summarised as a check: mean 0.001, standard deviation 1.000). (2) The second example of `points` (limits moved in the third and fourth significant digit, as jitter does). (3) The stored output of the sample project `simulation`: 400 draws from each of four families, read against the truth (scores 99.2 and 14.6 against 100 and 15; waiting times 2.04 and 2.04 against 2 and 2; visits 3.09 against 3; the mixture's mean 17.31 against 17.27; the six Pearson correlations within 0.1 of zero; the z statistic recomputed by hand from the printed mean and standard deviation). The draws of that script under `seed: 7` did not move. (4) Two snapshots of the plot's printed form with jitter (`printing__wages`, `printing__edge_case_datasets`): only limits and breaks of the jittered layers moved. (5) One figure in the test that two draws of one statement are uncorrelated (0.012, p = 0.586, where it was −0.007). (6) Three conformance digests, exactly the three cases that draw under a script-wide seed: `control/for_draws/stdout`, `plot/points/stdout` and `simulation/stdout`; the other 235 are unchanged, `plot/points/scene.json` among them, and `zeff selftest` stands at 238 of 238.

**Tests.** Unit (`core`, the run's stream): the two statements that draw give the same numbers at places 1 and 2, 2 and 3, 4 and 9 and 0 and 1; they are the streams of ordinals 1 and 2; a drawing statement between them moves the later one; calls with their own `seed:` are not counted; two calls of one statement draw apart; the passes of a loop draw apart and the statement after a loop has ordinal 2. Script (`core`, the tests of `seed`): four scripts run without a seed and again with the noted seed at the top print the same figures (plain draws, draws among statements that draw nothing, a loop, two draws in one statement); statements that draw nothing change no draw wherever they stand, one that draws moves those after it; the passes of a loop differ from one another and from the statement after it. The plot's jitter test now also runs the unseeded script again under the noted seed. The help pages of `seed` and `draw` say the rule as it now holds.

**Dependencies.** None.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 20a; section 8.3, point 3, of the Engine and Project Specification; the catalogue's row 63; the help page of `seed`.

## 11 November 2026: expressions in `x:` and `y:` (release 0.7.0, step 20b)

**Decision.** `x:` and `y:` of `data.plot(…)` take a bare variable name or an expression over the variables of the frame, as the catalogue's row 460 already types them (`Var | Expr`) and as section 7.6 of the Language Reference says in the row "Data and aesthetics". `w.plot(x: educ, y: log(wage))` computes `log(wage)` row by row on the plot's frame, and again on the frame of each layer that names its own with `data:`. The axis is titled by the expression as the script wrote it. A result that is `NA` or infinite is dropped and counted in the same notes as for a variable, the name in the note being the expression (`211 rows with NA in educ or log(wage) dropped`). The counted warnings of the row-by-row kernels (W0204, W0205 and the others) are raised once for the plot and once for each layer that computes on its own frame. No normative sentence changes.

**How a name inside the expression is read: frame scope, not formula mode.** The expression is lowered as the arguments of `add` are (section 3.7, "Name lookup"): a name is a variable of the frame when the frame has one; otherwise a binding of the script; otherwise Z0101.
