The preview of macOS crops a figure wider than its window; that is the preview, not the file.

**Tests.** `crates/zeff-engine/tests/export.rs`: a plot written at each size, to `output/` by a bare name, with and without its notes, the same plot twice to the same bytes, a plot with no layer, a file replaced, nothing of the frame in a file; a snapshot of twenty-five messages (`every_message_of_a_plot`), each leaving nothing written. `packages/tier1/plot/tests/layout.rs`: the notes under a figure (as printed, wrapped, at the foot, their room taken from the panel, none without the option) and the writer of the package against the layout and the SVG writer, with its two refusals. The type parser's tests cover the mixed type. The help pages of `export` and `plot` describe the figure and run three more examples. The conformance set: `plots/stdout`, `stderr`, `exit_code` and the six figures.

**The specification.** F7 enters the table of defaults of section 7.6; the usage line of catalogue row 165 gains `List<Float>` for `size:` and `notes: Bool = false`; both logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's steps 21 and 21d; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Sizes", "Rendering and export"); open decision #118 (F7); section 8.1 of the Engine Specification, rules 2, 5 and 6.

## 12 November 2026: the journal theme frozen (release 0.7.0, step 22)

**The owner's decision.** The six figures of `samples/plots` (step 21d) were sent to the owner with the list of what was proposed in them. Asked "Step 22: are the six figures right as they are, so that I freeze the theme?", he answered "Yes, freeze it". No change was asked for. What follows is frozen: it changes only by a decision of his, and the test `the_journal_theme_and_the_sizes_are_as_the_owner_froze_them` fails if any of it is changed.

**The sizes.** `one_column` 89 by 66 mm; `two_column` 183 by 110 mm; `slide` 254 by 143 mm; one column when `export` is given no `size:`.

**The journal theme.** A white page (#FFFFFF). Text, axes and ticks in #222222. Major gridlines alone, #E3E3E3, 0.35 point wide. The two axes as lines of half a point, their ticks 3 points long outside the panel; no frame round the panel or the legend. Labels of breaks and of legend keys in 8 points and titles of axes and legends in 9, in IBM Plex Sans Regular, 1.25 of the size from one line to the next. A margin of 4 points round the figure; 3 points between a tick and its label and between a key and its label; 5 between the labels of an axis and its title; 10 between the panel and the legends. A mark with no colour of its own in #222222, 4.5 points across; the largest mark of a scale of sizes 18 points across; the bar of a continuous colour 8 points wide and 72 long. The legends at the right.

**With it.** The three faces (Sans Regular for labels, Sans SemiBold for titles, which no figure draws yet, Mono Regular for code and aligned digits); no ligatures; an outline shape and a shape of lines stroked 0.9 point wide; a mark at the edge of the panel cut by it; no text below 8 points and no panel below 36 points each way.

**What is not frozen by this.** Questions 1, 3, 4 and 5 of open decision #110 (where a scale of sizes starts, sizes of 0 and below, `group` and `label` before a mark reads them, shapes of equal area) stay in the register with their deadline, before step 25: the figures show them as built, and the owner was not asked about each. `theme(minimal | slide)` and the options of `theme` are step 26. A title of a plot is drawn from step 26, in the SemiBold face.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 22; question 6 at the opening of the release ("the journal theme is drawn on six figures, read by the owner and then frozen").

## 12 November 2026: step 22b split (release 0.7.0, opening of step 22b)

**The split.** Step 22b (the PDF and PNG writers) is too large for one session and is split in the checklist into four: 22b1, the PDF writer; 22b2, the rasteriser and the PNG writer; 22b3, `export` in the three formats, the layer flag `raster` and the six figures in each; 22b4, the tool-only trial of the typesetting engine of open decision #73. The step as first written stays above them and is ticked when the four are.

**What is settled before any code**, as engineering. (a) A PDF carries its text as text in the embedded fonts, as section 7.6 of the Language Reference now says, and carries each font file whole: no subsetter is written at this release, at the cost of about 0.1 MB a face in a file. (b) The content of a PDF and the pixels of a PNG are compressed by the DEFLATE method; the crate for it is chosen and recorded at step 22b1 with its licence and its exact version, and its output must be the same on the four targets or the engine's own encoder takes its place. (c) The PDF is checked by a pure-Rust parser and the PNG by an independent decoder, both test dependencies alone.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 22b; the standing instruction that a step too large is split in the checklist.

## 12 November 2026: the PDF writer (release 0.7.0, step 22b1)

**Decision.** `plot::pdf::write` turns a drawing into the bytes of a PDF file of one page as large as the drawing, and is a pure function of it. The file uses nothing newer than PDF 1.4 and the plain layout every reader takes: a header, the objects in a fixed order (the catalogue, the pages, the page, what the page draws, five objects for each face used, one for each shape written once, one for each image, and what the file says of itself), a cross-reference table and a trailer. It says of itself `Producer (Zeff)` and nothing else: no date, no version, no path. Its identifier, which some programs ask for, is the first sixteen bytes of the BLAKE3 hash of the file up to the table, given twice, so it is made from the bytes and never at random. `plot::pdf::write_plain` gives the same file with its streams not compressed, for reading and for the tests.

**The page.** The axes are turned over once at the start, so that every place is written as the drawing has it, from the top left. A length is written by `drawing::length`, to a thousandth of a point; a colour as three shares of one to three decimals, which give back each of the 256 steps (tested). The corners of lines are cut at four widths, as an SVG reader cuts them, so that the two formats of one drawing look alike. Opacity is a graphics state of the page for each value met, and the page is then marked as blended in the colours of a screen. A clip region is a clipping rectangle. An arc of an ellipse is drawn as cubic curves of at most a quarter turn each, by the engine's own sine, cosine and arctangent. A rectangle with round corners and a circle are four curves. A path that does not begin with a move begins where it first goes; a colour that cannot be read is black; an opacity outside 0 to 1 is brought inside.

**Text.** Text is text. Each face used is a font of glyphs by number (Type 0 with `Identity-H`, a `CIDFontType2` under it, `CIDToGIDMap` the identity), with the whole TrueType file carried in it, the advances of the glyphs used, and what describes the font taken from the font itself (its box, its heights, its lean, whether it is of one width; the thickness of its stems by a rule of thumb from its weight, which a reader uses only to stand in for a font that is missing). The words are set glyph by glyph in one array for each span, with a number wherever step 21a sets two glyphs closer or farther than the advance, so that every glyph stands where the SVG draws its outline; the tests rebuild the place of every glyph from the file and compare. The turn of a text is written to six decimals and a quarter turn exactly. The map from glyphs to characters gives each glyph the first character, in the order of Unicode, that the face draws with it; a character no face has is the face's empty box and maps to nothing. The faces are named `F1` (Sans), `F2` (Sans SemiBold) and `F3` (Mono) whichever of them a file uses.

**Marks.** A sample figure holds about 18,000 marks. A shape of one size met three times or more (`SHARED`) is written once as a form and placed by a translation where each mark stands, a short line for each; a shape met less often is written where it stands. Neighbouring marks of one colour, opacity and kind share their paint. Each mark is painted by itself, so that marks that are not opaque darken each other where they overlap, as in the SVG. The first sample figure is 171 kB as PDF and 846 kB as SVG; the figure with a size for each mark has 768 shapes written once and is 421 kB.

**Cells.** A grid of cells is an image of the cells, flagged not to be smoothed, with each cell repeated until a dot is no wider than a three-hundredth of an inch (at most 64 times each way, and never past four million dots in all). Rectangles side by side show hairlines between them in programs that soften edges, and an image of one dot to a cell is blurred by programs that smooth images whatever the file says; repeating the cells leaves both sharp. Fewer colours than cells: the whole rows as one image and the cells of the next row as another.

**What is not carried.** The names of the items of a drawing (`axis:x`, `layer:1`) are groups of an SVG and nothing in a PDF; section 7.6 says so of the SVG alone. The notes of a drawing are not in the file unless `notes:` laid them out, as for SVG. No row, no binding (F2).

**The font reader** gains what a PDF asks of a font: the box that holds every glyph (`head`), the PostScript name (`name`, record 6), the weight and the permission to embed (`OS/2`), the lean and whether the face is of one width (`post`), and the first character of a glyph. Each is compared with the independent reader of step 21a. The three faces set no limit on being carried in a document.

**Dependencies.** `miniz_oxide` =0.9.1 (MIT OR Zlib OR Apache-2.0), with its default features off but `with-alloc`, compresses the streams by DEFLATE at a fixed level of 9; it is linked into the engine and brings `adler2` 2.0.1 (0BSD OR MIT OR Apache-2.0). It is pure Rust, and in the engine's build no part of it is written for one processor. A compressor is real work to write and to test, and the PNG writer of step 22b2 needs the same method. Its output must be the same on the four targets: the conformance set holds the sample figures twice, `plot/pdf/plain` with the streams as they are and `plot/pdf/figures` compressed, so that a difference between two machines says whether it lies in what is drawn or in how it is compressed; if the compressed bytes ever differ, the engine's own encoder takes the crate's place. `zeff-hash`, a kernel crate, becomes a dependency of `plot` for the identifier. `lopdf` =0.47.0 (MIT), default features off, is a test dependency of `plot` alone, the independent reader the checklist asks for; it brings thirty crates into the lock file and into no build of the engine: `aes`, `block-buffer`, `block-padding`, `cbc`, `cipher`, `const-oid`, `cpubits`, `crc32fast`, `crypto-common`, `digest`, `ecb`, `flate2`, `hybrid-array`, `inout`, `md-5`, `rangemap`, `sha2`, `stringprep`, `thiserror`, `thiserror-impl`, `typenum`, `unicode-bidi`, `weezl` (each MIT OR Apache-2.0), `nom` and `simd-adler32` (MIT), `alloc-no-stdlib` and `alloc-stdlib` (BSD-3-Clause), `brotli-decompressor` (BSD-3-Clause OR MIT), `unicode-properties` (MIT OR Apache-2.0, with Unicode-3.0) and `zlib-rs` (Zlib). In a build with the tests, that reader's own compression crate turns on a faster checksum inside `miniz_oxide`; the checksum is the same number however it is computed, and the routine shows it, since the digests recorded by the engine's build are compared again in the build with the tests.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/pdf.rs`, nine: every primitive of the closed set, kept as a snapshot of the file with its streams as text and the length and hash of the compressed file; a shape met often written once and placed; a grid of cells as an image, its dots read back; text set with the kerning of the font, centred, ending at its place, turned, in the face of one width, with a letter and its mark written apart and a character no face has; a small figure kept whole, its words also found by the reader's own extraction; the seven sample scenes of the shipped wages at the three sizes, each read back and kept as its size and hash; nothing of the rows, the frame or the notes in a file; brackets, a backslash and letters beyond ASCII found as written; and a property over 120 frames. What is read back from every file, by `lopdf`: one page of the size of the drawing; a table at the end that says where each object stands; each face carried whole, byte for byte, under its own name; the advances the file lists; the words of every text through the map from glyphs to characters; every glyph at the place the font sets it; one mark for each mark; no type below 8 points; nothing said of the day. `packages/tier1/plot/src/pdf.rs`, eight unit tests (colours, numbers, the circle, the arc against half and three-quarter circles worked by hand, a path with no start, round corners, an empty page). `packages/tier1/plot/tests/common/mod.rs` now holds the frames, scenes and the drawing of every primitive that the tests of the SVG and PDF writers share; the SVG snapshots did not change. `packages/tier1/plot/tests/fonts.rs`: what a PDF asks of a font.

**Checked by hand on the owner's machine**, outside the routine. Ghostscript 10.05.1 reads the 21 sample files and the file of every primitive with `-dPDFSTOPONERROR` and says nothing, and its own text extraction finds the titles and labels; Ghostscript and the macOS renderer both draw the pages as the SVG of the same drawings is drawn.

**Left for later, on purpose.** (a) The faces are carried whole, about 88 kB each after compression; a subsetter would bring a small figure from 91 kB to a few, and is not written at this release (decision of the split, above). (b) No structure for screen readers and no PDF/A. (c) Some readers refuse a page wider or taller than 14,400 points (5.08 m); `export` should refuse such a size for PDF with a plain message, which belongs to step 22b3, where the sizes of the three formats are checked. (d) A figure with a size for each mark writes a form for each size met three times; one form scaled for each mark would be smaller for filled shapes, at the cost of a second rule.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 22b1; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("a PDF carries the fonts inside it"; "a figure's SVG and PDF bytes are identical on every machine"); open decision #118 (F1, F2); section 8.3 of the Engine Specification, point 3.

## 12 November 2026: the rasteriser and the PNG writer (release 0.7.0, step 22b2)

**Decision.** `plot::raster::render` turns a drawing into a picture in dots at a number of dots to the inch, 300 for a figure, on a white page, and `plot::png::write` turns a picture into the bytes of a PNG file. Both are pure functions and both are the engine's own: no crate draws, and none writes the file but for the compression.

**How many dots.** A length in points times the dots to the inch over 72, with what is left of a dot cut, as R's `png()` cuts it. Checked against R 4.6.0 on the owner's machine: 89 by 66 mm is 1051 by 779 dots in both, 183 by 110 mm 2161 by 1299, 254 by 143 mm 3000 by 1688, 120 by 75 mm 1417 by 885. A picture of more than forty million dots is refused (`RasterError::TooLarge`), and a page that leaves no dot (`NotASize`); `export` words the two at step 22b3.

**Edges.** A dot takes the colour of a shape in the measure in which the shape covers it, and the measure is the area, worked out from the straight edges of the shape: each edge adds to every dot of its rows the area of the dot to its right, and the sum along a row gives how often the shapes wind round each dot, weighted by area. A path is filled where it winds round (`min(|w|, 1)`), a polygon with holes where it winds round an odd number of times (the sum folded at 1), as the SVG and the PDF fill them. A curve is first made of straight lines no farther than a twentieth of a dot from it. A region that clips, and the page itself, cut the edges themselves: what lies above or below is left out and what lies to the side is moved onto the side, which leaves the winding of every dot inside as it was, so a cut edge is as exact as any other. The tests hold this to nine decimals against shapes cut by hand.

**Lines.** A line is the shape of its ink: a rectangle along each straight piece and a wedge at each corner, drawn out to a point within four widths and cut flat beyond, its ends cut square, as the other two writers have it. The pieces of one line are one shape (their shares are added and held at one), so a line that is not opaque is no darker where its pieces meet. Where two pieces lie over each other inside one dot at the edge of the line, on the inner side of a corner, the sum can be above the true share by a part of that dot; elsewhere it is the area.

**Cells.** A dot over a grid of cells takes the mean of the colours of the cells under it, each by its share of the dot, and is laid on once, so no seam shows between cells. A rectangle with its sides along the axes is laid on by its width covered times its height covered, which is its area.

**Colour.** Each part of each dot is kept to one in 65,535 while the page is drawn and laid on by whole-number arithmetic, so that 18,000 marks that are not opaque lose nothing to rounding; the picture has 256 steps. Paint is laid over what is under it in the measure of its opacity, in the numbers of the colours as written (those of a screen), as a browser shows the SVG of the same drawing. The letters are the outlines of the embedded fonts, placed as the SVG writer places them, without hinting, which 300 dots to the inch does not need.

**The file.** Eight bits each of red, green and blue, no transparency, rows in order; a chunk that says the colours are those of a screen (`sRGB`), one that gives the dots to the metre (`pHYs`, 11,811 at 300 to the inch) so that a program placing the figure gives it its size, the dots in one chunk, and nothing else: no date, no text. Each row is written by the one of the five rules of the format that leaves the smallest numbers, the first where two tie; the rows are compressed by `miniz_oxide` at level 6. The check of each chunk is the engine's own.

**The question left open at the opening of the release** ("whether its bytes are held identical or only its scene is"): the bytes are held identical on the four targets, as those of the SVG and the PDF. The reckoning uses addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and the square root of 64-bit numbers, the engine's own sine and cosine, and whole numbers for the colours, and draws in the order of the drawing; nothing in it depends on the machine. The conformance set holds the sample drawings of one column and of 120 by 75 mm twice, `plot/png/dots` (the dots) and `plot/png/figures` (the files), so that a difference between machines says whether it lies in what is drawn or in how it is compressed. Taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026 ("If at any point any decisions to be taken by me, I will go by your recommended decisions"); the sentence of section 7.6 that names the SVG and the PDF gains the PNG once the identity jobs have agreed.

**One path for three writers.** The moves, lines, curves and closings of a path, with the arc of an ellipse as curves, the circle and the round corners, moved from the PDF writer to `plot::trace`, which the rasteriser shares; the bytes of every PDF are as they were (the snapshots and digests of step 22b1 did not change).

**Dependencies.** None added to the engine. `png` =0.18.1 (MIT OR Apache-2.0) is a test dependency of `plot` alone, the independent reader the checklist asks for; it brings `fdeflate` 0.3.7 (MIT OR Apache-2.0) and, for that reader's own use, a second `miniz_oxide`, 0.8.9 (MIT OR Zlib OR Apache-2.0), so the files are decompressed by code other than what compressed them.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/png.rs`, fourteen. Every primitive drawn at 300 dots to the inch, with dots that must have a given colour (the page, the inside of marks, a half-opaque mark, the line of an outline shape, a polygon and its hole, a round corner, the ink of an axis, the head of an arrow, each cell, the box behind a text) and the picture and its file kept as size and hash; a clip region (a quarter of a disc, a dot cut in half, regions inside each other); marks that darken each other and a bent line that does not; cells without a seam; the letters of each face against the area of their outlines as the independent reader of fonts gives them, upright, turned a quarter and turned by 30 degrees, to one part in a hundred; pages refused; a small figure and the seven sample scenes at the three sizes, each file decoded by the independent reader and compared dot for dot; and five properties: the shares of the dots sum to the area of a shape inside the page, and each dot holds the area of the shape inside it (400 shapes, to nine decimals); two halves of a shape cover what the whole does; the ink of a straight line is its length times its width; a picture is given back dot for dot by its file; every figure is drawn the same twice. `raster.rs` has eight unit tests and `png.rs` four (the check of a chunk against the value every description of CRC-32 gives, the rules of a row).

**Checked by eye on the owner's machine.** The picture of every primitive and two sample figures, beside Ghostscript's rendering of the PDF of the same drawings: the same shapes, joins, opacity, cells and letters.

**Left for later, on purpose.** No transparent page and no 16-bit file; nobody has asked. Colours are mixed in the numbers as written, not in light; that is what every browser does with an SVG, and changing it would make the PNG differ from the other two. The layer flag `raster` (a layer drawn in dots inside a vector file) is step 22b3 and will call `render` on the items of the layer.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 22b2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("PNG at 300 dpi"); the opening of the release, on the identity of PNG bytes; section 8.3 of the Engine Specification, point 3.

## 12 November 2026: step 22b3 split, and `export` by the three extensions (release 0.7.0, step 22b3a)

**The split.** Step 22b3 is split in the checklist into 22b3a, `export` writing SVG, PDF or PNG by the extension with the six sample figures in each, and 22b3b, the layer flagged `raster` drawn in dots inside a figure drawn with lines. The second needs the grid of cells of a drawing to hold its colours as numbers and a picture placed inside an SVG, which is a step of its own; the first is what a script sees.

**Decision.** `p.export(path, size:, notes:)` writes `.svg`, `.pdf` or `.png`, the extension compared without regard to case; the format travels in `FigureRequest` to the writer the plot value carries (`plot::figure::write`), which lays the scene out once and hands the drawing to `svg::write`, `pdf::write`, or `raster::render` at 300 dots to the inch and `png::write`. `size:` and `notes:` mean the same in the three. The refusal of `.pdf` and `.png` as "not written yet" (step 21d, ruling (b)) is gone, with its two messages.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn, taken under his standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) A page longer than 5080 mm on a side is refused for a PDF (Z0401): that is 14,400 points, the longest side some readers of PDF take, and a file that one reader opens and another does not is worse than a plain refusal; the message offers `.svg`, which has no largest page. A page of exactly 5080 mm is written (tested). (b) A page of more than forty million dots is refused for a PNG (Z0401), with the number of dots it would have and the offer of `.pdf` or `.svg`; that is about 535 mm each way. (c) A PNG has a white page and no transparency, at 300 dots to the inch whatever its size; no option changes either at this release. (d) The help of every refusal of a path now names the three formats and recommends `.pdf`.

**The specification.** The sentence of section 7.6 on bytes identical on every machine names the three formats, as decided at step 22b2 and confirmed by the identity jobs of that step's commit; the note of catalogue row 165 says PDF and PNG are written. Both logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`.

**The sample project.** `samples/plots` binds each of its six plots to a name and exports it three times; the six SVG files are byte for byte what they were (their digests in the conformance set did not move), which shows that a plot bound to a name and one exported from a chain draw the same marks. Its messages carry new line numbers. The conformance set gains the twelve new files, 321 lines in all.

**Tests.** `crates/zeff-engine/tests/export.rs`: a plot written as PDF and as PNG, by a bare name and under `output/`, with the extension in capitals, at three sizes, with and without its notes, twice to the same bytes, with no layer, and at the largest page of a PDF; the size of each PDF page read from the file and the size and density of each PNG from its chunks; nothing of the day or of the frame in a file. The snapshot of messages has twenty-nine: the two of "not written yet" left it, and a table format in capitals, a page too small in each of the two new formats, too large for a PDF, of too many dots for a PNG, and of no size for a PNG joined it. The examples of the help page of `export` run with the three formats.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's steps 22b3 and 22b3a; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("`export` writes SVG or PDF (vector) or PNG at 300 dpi (raster), chosen by the extension"); the standing instruction that a step too large is split in the checklist.

## 12 November 2026: a layer drawn in dots inside a figure of lines (release 0.7.0, step 22b3b)

**Decision.** A layer of the scene flagged `raster` (open decision #118, F4) is laid out as a picture and not as marks. `plot::layout` draws the panel as it stands with that layer on it (the page, the gridlines and the layers under it, with the layer's own marks) by the rasteriser of step 22b2 at 300 dots to the inch, and puts the picture in the place of the layer's marks as a grid of cells, a cell to a dot, under the layer's name. A picture cannot let through what is under it, so it holds it; what was under stays in the file as lines and is covered. The axes, the labels, the legends and every layer not flagged stay lines and text. No script of this release can set the flag (the marks gain the option after 1.0); the tests set it by hand on the scene.

**The picture.** It starts where the panel starts and is as many whole dots as cover the panel; its last dots are drawn whole and the edge of the panel, which is a line in the file, cuts them. `raster::render_part` draws a part of a page from a place on: every corner is counted from that place, and so are a clip region and a grid of cells. A part that starts on a dot is, dot for dot, the picture of the whole page there (tested).

**In each format.** In a PDF the grid is an image, as since step 22b1, one dot of the file to a dot of the picture. In an SVG a grid of more than 4,096 cells (`MOST_RECTANGLES`) is no longer rectangles but a PNG held inside the file as text (base64, the engine's own encoder, in an `image` element whose link is the data itself); a file with such a picture names the `xlink` way of holding one, and no other file does, so every SVG written before this step is byte for byte what it was. Nothing outside the file is named. In a PNG a figure is dots throughout: `figure::write` clears the flag, and the layer is drawn once like any other. A panel of more dots than a picture may have (forty million) keeps its marks as lines.

**Cells as numbers.** The cells of a grid in a drawing were text, `#RRGGBB`; they are now three numbers, so that a picture of half a million dots is a megabyte and a half and not fifteen. The text of a drawing (`describe`) and every file written from one are unchanged: the snapshots and the digests of steps 21b to 22b3a did not move. A cell that is no colour can no longer be written.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026, each of which he may overturn. (a) The picture holds what is under the layer in the panel, as above, in place of a picture with transparency. (b) The picture is at 300 dots to the inch whatever the size of the page, as a PNG figure is. (c) An SVG shows the picture as a program shows any picture: smoothed when enlarged; no instruction to show its dots as squares is written.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/png.rs`: a part of a page against the whole, a part that starts between dots, a clip region and cells inside a part; a flagged layer laid out as one picture under the marks of the layer over it, its dots the panel drawn directly, everything outside the panel as it was; the layer over flagged instead, and both; a panel too large; the PNG of a drawing with a picture in it against the PNG of the drawing without. `tests/pdf.rs`: the image read back by the independent reader, its size and its dots those of the picture, its place inside the clip of the panel, six marks left as lines, the same words. `tests/svg.rs`: the picture taken out of the file, turned back from text to bytes by a decoder written in the test, decoded by the independent reader of PNG and compared dot for dot; its place and its group; the words; a grid of 64 by 64 cells as rectangles and one of 65 by 64 as a picture. Unit tests: the text of 64 letters against the seven examples of its definition; a PNG figure as the picture of its drawing. The conformance set gains `plot/svg/picture` and `plot/pdf/picture`, 323 lines.

**Checked by eye.** The PDF, read by Ghostscript without a message, and the SVG, drawn by the macOS renderer: the large half-opaque marks as a picture with the gridlines in it, the small marks, the axes and the labels sharp over it.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 22b3b; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("A layer may also be flagged `raster`, to be drawn as a grid of pixels inside a vector figure"); open decision #118, F4.

## 12 November 2026: the trial of the typesetting engine, as a tool only (release 0.7.0, step 22b4; open decision #73)

**What was done.** Typst 0.15.0, already installed on the owner's machine by Homebrew, was run as a program on files Zeff wrote. Nothing was linked into the engine, nothing added to the repository or to its dependencies, and nothing downloaded for the tool; the trial's files are outside the repository, in `~/dev/handbook/typst-trial-0.7.0/` (`report.typ`, `report.pdf`, and the table and the figure Zeff wrote). The document holds one regression table (`m.export("model.tex")`) and one plot written by `p.export` as SVG, PDF and PNG and placed three times, set in IBM Plex from the three font files of the engine and no font of the system. The decision on #73 stays due at 0.8.0 and stays the owner's; what follows is what was measured for it.

**1. The licence.** Typst is under Apache-2.0. Its library as an engine would link it (`typst` and `typst-pdf` =0.15.0) resolves to 298 crates. Every one offers MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC, Zlib or the Unicode licence, but for two that are more permissive still or the same with a permission added: `roman-numerals-rs` (0BSD OR CC0-1.0) and `ar_archive_writer` (Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception). None is under the GPL, the LGPL, the AGPL or the MPL. Two things the licence lines of the crates do not say and that must be read before anything is linked: the fonts and data inside `typst-assets`, which carry licences of their own (the tool can be told to leave its fonts out), and the hyphenation patterns inside `hypher`.

**2. The same bytes from run to run.** With the fonts fixed (`--ignore-system-fonts --font-path` to the three files) and the date fixed (`--creation-timestamp 0`, or `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0`, which gives the same file), two runs give the same bytes. With no date given, two runs two seconds apart differ: Typst writes the day and the hour into the file. It also writes `Creator: Typst 0.15.0`, so the bytes change with its version.

**3. The same bytes across machines.** Not measured: the trial ran on one machine. It is measured the way the engine's own files are, by the identity jobs, once Typst is a dependency under trial at 0.8.0; until then the claim of #73 that the bytes agree when the fonts are fixed rests on Typst's word.

**4. The size.** The program is 44.9 MB on the owner's machine (ARM64 macOS), with its own fonts, its fetcher of packages and its watcher. What the library adds to the engine when linked was not measured, the trial being of the tool alone; it is one of the standard checks of a dependency at 0.8.0.

**5. The speed.** The two pages are set in 0.05 seconds.

**6. How a figure of Zeff is placed.** From the SVG: at 89 by 66 mm, the size it was written for, as lines, sharp at any enlargement; the letters, which the SVG holds as outlines, are drawn as they are, and the words the SVG keeps beside them, unpainted, come through as text, so a search of the PDF finds "Years of schooling"; a page with the figure alone is 65 kB. From Zeff's PDF: at 89 by 66 mm, its text as text in the font Zeff put inside it, whole; 96 kB. From the PNG: at 88.985 by 65.955 mm, which is 1051 by 779 dots at the 300 to the inch the file says; 112 kB, and no words. The SVG with its text as outlines (open decision #126) is the smallest of the three in a Typst page and loses nothing.

**7. How a table of Zeff is placed.** There is no path today: `export` writes a table as `.docx` or `.tex`, and Typst reads neither. The cells of `model.tex` were written by hand as a Typst table with a rule above, under the headings and below, and the three notes under it, which is what a `.typ` writer of `export` would write; it is set as the LaTeX table is, and Typst sets the hyphen before a number as a minus sign.

**8. The fonts.** Given the engine's three font files and told to use no other, Typst sets its own text in IBM Plex, carrying only the letters used, so the text of a document and the text of its figures are one face.

**What this says for #73**, as a reading and not a decision. Nothing found speaks against option A. Open for 0.8.0, in the order they would stop it: the bytes across machines (3), the licences inside the bundled fonts and patterns (1), what the library adds to the size of the engine (4), and the version written into every file (2), which means a PDF set by Typst changes its bytes when Typst is upgraded even if nothing else does.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 22b4; question 1 at the opening of the release ("#73's trial of the typesetting engine ... is run as a tool-only step once the SVG writer exists, with nothing linked into the engine"); open decision #73, whose recommendation asks for "a spike at 0.7.0 beside the plot renderer" with its result reported at 0.7.0.

## 12 November 2026: open decision #106 taken, and step 23 split (release 0.7.0, opening of step 23)

**The decision.** Open decision #106, due before step 23, is taken as option A on the register's recommendation, under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026 ("22b2 onwards don't wait for my permission, continue to next steps. If at any point any decisions to be taken by me, I will go by your recommended decisions."): every mark takes `x:` and `y:`, and each other aesthetic it draws, for its own layer, and an argument given replaces the plot's mapping for that layer. The register's entry holds the rule in full; the owner may overturn it.

**The split.** Step 23 was written as seven catalogued marks on machinery that exists. Two pieces of that machinery do not exist yet: a layer's own mappings (the decision above) and a line with a type in a drawing (decision #118, F9, which this step is to write into section 7.6). The step is split in the checklist into 23a `[engine]`, a layer's own mappings, built on `points`; 23b `[engine]`, lines with a type in the three writers; 23c `[function]`, `lines` and `step`; 23d `[function]`, `area` and `ribbon`; 23e `[function]`, `hline`, `vline` and `rug`. The step as first written stays above them and is ticked when the five are.

## 12 November 2026: a layer's own mappings (release 0.7.0, step 23a; open decision #106)

**Decision.** `points` takes `x:`, `y:`, `color:`, `size:` and `shape:` for its own layer, read as `plot` reads them: the body of `plot` that reads the aesthetics became one function (`grammar::aesthetics`), which `points` calls with its own name on the frame its layer draws, so the two say the same things in the same words. A layer keeps what it names and what it sets (`PlotLayer.mappings`, `PlotLayer.constants`; a size that is a number stays `size`). The scene resolves every aesthetic of a layer in one place (`scene::mapping_of`): the layer's own mapping; nothing, where the layer sets the aesthetic to one value; the plot's mapping otherwise. An axis is trained on the marks of every layer, as before. A scale of colours, sizes or shapes is named by the plot's mapping or, where the plot maps none, by the first layer that names a variable for it, and the categories of a later variable follow those of the first.

**The checker and the interpreter.** An expression given to a mark is over the variables of the frame its layer draws, which only the run knows. The checker therefore opens the scope of a frame for such an argument of a method of a plot, with no list of variables to check it against, and the mark checks the names when it is added (Z0101, with the name of the frame). The interpreter puts the plot's frame in scope for the arguments of its marks, and the layer's own frame in its place when `data:` is given; `data:` is evaluated right after the plot wherever it is written, so that `points(y: hours * 2, data: top)` reads `hours` in `top`. The refusal of an expression where a variable is taken by its name (step 20e) holds for marks too, with help that says to compute it on the frame first.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026, each of which he may overturn. (a) Between them, the plot and the layer must map `x` and `y`; a layer that names one position and lacks the other is told of both places a position may come from. (b) `points` takes the aesthetics it draws: `x`, `y`, `color`, `size`, `shape`. `fill:`, `group:` and `label:` are not options of `points` and are refused as unknown (Z0404), as any argument a function does not have. (c) The options stand in the order `data`, `x`, `y`, `color`, `size`, `shape`, `alpha`, `jitter`; `size:` of `points`, a number until now, is a number or a variable. (d) The layers share one scale of each aesthetic. Of the three only colour can be mapped from two kinds of variable, categories and numbers, and a layer whose colour is of the other kind than the scale's is refused (Z0401) with the two variables named. (e) The title of an axis is that of the plot's mapping even when every layer draws another variable on it, until `labels` (step 26) changes it. (f) A printed plot tells, at the start of each layer's settings, what the layer names of its own (`y fitted, color firebrick`), and says under the aesthetics when no layer takes the colour or the shape the plot gives, as it said of the size.

**The specification.** Section 7.6 already says that a layer may "override a mapping". The usage line of catalogue row 461 gains the five options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`); `points(y: …)`, refused as unknown since step 20, is drawn.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/layers.rs`: the property that a layer naming what the plot maps, on a plot that maps it or on one that maps nothing, gives the scene of the plot alone (200 frames; it found that an empty axis took its range from the plot's variable only, corrected); a layer's own variable on the shared axis, by hand; what a layer sets or names before what the plot says. `tests/printing.rs`: a second variable on the axis of the first, the axis over both, a plot that maps nothing, two variables on one scale of colours, a layer sized by a variable where the plot sets a size, a layer with its own frame, each line checked against counts and ranges from R 4.6.0 (537 rows of 2010 with `educ`, 531 with a wage; limits -4.989 to 205.529 with twice the wage on the axis); ten edge cases; twenty-four messages. The two refusals of `points(shape:)` and `points(size: hours)` left the older snapshot, being drawn now. The help page of `points` is reopened, with the five options and a paragraph on a layer's own variables.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 23a; open decision #106, option A; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("a layer may name its own frame (`.points(data: outliers)`) or override a mapping").

## 12 November 2026: lines with a type in a drawing (release 0.7.0, step 23b; decision #118, F9)

**Decision.** A line of a drawing has a type (`drawing::LineType`, a field of `Stroke`): whole, or ink and gaps by turns. There are six, in the order a scale will give them to the categories of a variable: `solid`, `dashed`, `dotted`, `dash_dot`, `long_dash`, `dash_dot_dot`. The lengths of ink and gap are in widths of the line, so that a thicker line has longer dashes: 4 and 3; 1 and 2; 4, 2, 1 and 2; 8 and 3; 4, 2, 1, 2, 1 and 2. The ink begins where each part of a path begins, and the ends of every piece are cut square, a dot being as long as the line is wide.

**The six, and why these.** Chosen on the recommendation under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026, and his to change: they are the six a draughtsman's set has (whole, dashed, dotted, chain, long dashed, chain with two dots), each told from the others in black on white by the rhythm of its ink alone, which is what F9 asks ("distinguishable in greyscale"). The names are the project's own, in the snake case of its other words. The order puts the whole line first and the three plainest patterns next, so that a plot of two or three groups uses the types easiest to tell apart.

**In each writer.** The SVG says the ink and the gaps of a line that is not whole as `stroke-dasharray`, in points; the PDF as its dash pattern before the line, and a whole line again after it; both leave the ends and the corners to the reader's own rule, which is square ends and pointed corners in both formats. The rasteriser cuts the line into its pieces of ink itself (`raster::pieces`), going round the corners, a piece that passes a corner keeping it so that the corner is drawn, and draws the ink of each piece as it draws any line. A file with no such line is byte for byte what it was: the conformance digests of every figure written before this step did not move.

**What moved to step 23c.** The checklist gave this step the key of a legend for a line, "a piece of line". A legend key is drawn for a mark, and the first mark that is a line is `lines`, of step 23c; the key is built there with it and the checklist says so.

**Tests.** The six in each format on one drawing (`tests/common`, `six_lines`): the SVG read by the independent reader of XML, each line saying the lengths of its type times its width and the whole line nothing; the PDF read by the independent reader, the pattern before each line and a whole line after; the picture at 720 dots to the inch, where a point is ten dots, with the ink of each type counted along the line and equal to what its lengths give over 100 points, and dots that must be ink or page at the ends of a dash and of a dot. `raster::pieces` by hand: a straight line, a piece round a corner, a closed line, the end of a line in ink and in a gap, lengths that are none. A property over 400 lines: the shares of the dots the ink of a cut line covers sum to the length of its ink times its width, to eight decimals. The names, the order and the lengths of the six. The conformance set gains `plot/lines/svg`, `plot/lines/pdf` and `plot/lines/png`, 326 lines.

**Checked by eye.** The picture the engine draws beside Ghostscript's rendering of the PDF of the same drawing: the same six rhythms, the same bent line, the same outlines.

**The specification.** The table of defaults of section 7.6 gains the row "Line types" (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 23b; decision #118, F9 ("Fix the default order of eight shapes and six line types, distinguishable in greyscale"; "F9's line types at step 23").

## 12 November 2026: `lines` (release 0.7.0, step 23c1), and step 23c split

**The split.** Step 23c is split in the checklist into 23c1, `lines` with what a line needs in the scene, on the page and in a legend, and 23c2, `step`, which is `lines` with risers; the first is a step's worth by itself.

**Decision.** `p.lines(data:, x:, y:, color:, group:, linetype:, width:)` adds a layer of lines. In the scene a layer of lines holds its marks in the order they are joined, and for each the line it belongs to (`Layer.line`, from 1), with the type of its lines (`Layer.linetype`, one name or a place on the scale `linetype` for each mark) and their width; the scene's JSON gains `line`, `linetype` and `width` on such a layer and on no other, so every scene written before is as it was and the version stays 1. The layout draws each line as one path of the drawing in the colour and the type of its first mark. The scale `linetype` gives the six types of step 23b to the categories of a variable in their order.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026, each of which he may overturn. (a) The rows are parted into lines by `group:` and, with it, by every variable that `color:` or `linetype:` shows as categories, since a line has one colour and one type; the lines stand in the order their first row comes. (b) Within a line the rows are in the order of `x`, rows of one `x` in the order of the frame, as ggplot2's `geom_line`. (c) A row without `x`, or with an infinite one, is left out. A row without `y`, or with an infinite one, is left out and breaks the line: its neighbours are not joined, so a gap in the data is a gap in the line, as in ggplot2; a note counts the breaks. (d) A row left with no neighbour draws nothing and is counted in a note. (e) A colour by a number without value labels is refused for a layer of lines (Z0401), its own or the plot's, with the two ways out: a line has one colour, and a colour for each piece of it is not drawn at this release. (f) `linetype:` is written as `shape:` is: a bare name is a variable of categories, a string one of the six names; a type written without quotation marks is told so. (g) The options are those the catalogue has with those of open decision #106 and of F9: no `alpha:`, no `size:`, no `shape:`; `width:` is 1 point unless given. (h) The rows without a category have the type of line after the last one given, not a type of their own. (i) The key of a legend of lines is a piece of line 24 points long in the colour, the type and the width of the lines, with a point on it when points read the same scale; one legend serves a variable shown by colour and by type.

**A fault found beside the step, not of it.** The checker's list of the variables of a frame made by `aggregate(..., by: vars(a, b))` lacks `a` and `b` when the result is bound to a name, so a later use of them is refused before the script runs ("no variable `year` in `u`"), though the run itself is right and `by: [a, b]` is taken. It dates from before this release's plots. It is to be corrected in a step of its own, next, and the owner is told.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 462 gains the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/lines.rs`: the order of `x` whatever the order of the frame, ties, a line broken where `y` is missing and a row left alone, the parting by group, colour and type, one legend for two scales, a line as one path with its colour, type and width, the key as a piece of line with and without a point, the scene's JSON, a group of any type; two properties (300 frames: every line has two marks or more in the order of `x`, no row is lost or drawn twice; the lines do not depend on the order of the rows). `tests/printing.rs`: five plots checked against R 4.6.0 and ggplot2 4.0.3 (twelve yearly means with limits 21.9191 to 32.9442; 24 means in two lines with limits 21.131 to 37.1199, where ggplot2 gives 21.13096 and 37.11989; six workers, 30 rows, six lines); thirteen edge cases; twenty-three messages. The help page of `lines`, its examples run. The conformance set gains `plot/lines/stdout`, `stderr` and `scene`, 329 lines.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's steps 23c and 23c1; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": `lines`); open decision #106; decision #118, F9.

## 12 November 2026: the checker and `by: vars(...)` (a correction, after step 23c1 of release 0.7.0)

**The fault.** The schema pass, which tells the checker the variables of a frame before the script runs (release 0.6.0, step 21), read the groups of `aggregate` and the kept variables of `to_long` when they were written as a name or as a list, and took them for none when they were written as `vars(a, b)`. The frame that came out was then believed to lack its groups, and a later use of one, on a result bound to a name, was refused before the run: `let u = w.aggregate(m = mean(wage), by: vars(year, union))` followed by `u.select(year)` gave "no variable `year` in `u`". The run itself was right, and so was every result; nothing wrong was ever computed. Found while the examples of `lines` were written.

**The correction.** The pass reads the names inside `vars(...)` when each is written as a name. Where the groups cannot be read before the run at all, the variables of the result are now unknown to the checker, and not fewer than they are, so nothing is refused that the run would take; the run checks the names itself, as it always did.

**Tests.** `crates/zeff-engine/tests/schemas_verbs.rs`: four chains with `vars(...)`, each compared, name for name, with the frame the run gives.

**Reason.** Section 11 of the Language Reference ("Checking before running"): the checker refuses what the run would refuse, and nothing else.

## 12 November 2026: `step` (release 0.7.0, step 23c2), and step 23c complete

**Decision.** `p.step(...)` is `lines` with risers: the same rows, the same parting into lines, the same breaks and notes, the same options, and one more, `direction: hv | vh | mid = hv`. `lines` and `step` share one body (`marks::joined`). The mark carries the direction (`Mark::Step(Stairs)`), the scene holds the rows as it does for a line and says the direction in its JSON (`"direction": "hv"`, on a layer of steps and no other), and the layout adds the corners: level to the `x` of the next row and then upright (`hv`), upright first (`vh`), or level to halfway between the two rows, upright there and level again (`mid`). A corner that would stand where the line already is is left out, so two rows of one `y` are joined by one level piece.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) The catalogue gave `step` no option but `data:`; it takes those of `lines`, by open decision #106 and for the same reasons. (b) `direction:` is added because R's `geom_step` has the three and Stata's `connect()` two of them, and the owner's rule of open decisions #98 and #99 is that what R or Stata offers for a procedure is an option; the words are R's, `hv`, `vh` and `mid`, which name the order of level and upright as nothing shorter does. (c) Stepping halfway, the line passes through each row in the middle of its level piece and the path of the drawing keeps the row as a place on it; ggplot2 lists the ends of the piece alone, and the two draw the same line.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/lines.rs`: the corners of a rate at four months in each direction against `ggplot2:::stairstep` of ggplot2 4.0.3, place for place; two rows of one value; the direction in the scene's JSON; a property over 200 lines in each direction (every piece is level or upright, the rows are corners of the steps in their order, the steps start at the first row and end at the last). `tests/printing.rs`: four plots, with limits 0.6 to 9.4 and 4.4625 to 5.2875 as `geom_step` gives; nine messages. The help page of `step`, its examples run. The conformance case of lines gains a step plot and the scene and drawing of steps.

**What changes for a user: a script's own function called `step`.** A built-in function captures its bare name, so a script that defines `fn step(...)` is now refused with Z0109, as section 3.6 of the Language Reference says of any name that a built-in and the script both define. The rewrite is a new name for the script's function (the argument `step:` of `iterate` is untouched: `iterate(start: s, step: advance, done: close)`). Two tests of `iterate` named a script function `step`; it is renamed `blanked` there, and the stored message follows, as was done for `now` at release 0.5.0. No sample, help example or text of the specification defines such a function. This is a breaking change for the notes of 0.7.0 (material for step 40c), with the other new names of the release (`plot`, `points`, `lines` and the marks to come). Z0109 is not weakened: the catalogue has reserved `step` for a mark since the freeze.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 463 gains the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's steps 23c and 23c2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": `step`); open decisions #98, #99 and #106.

## 12 November 2026: `area` and `ribbon` (release 0.7.0, step 23d1), and step 23d split

**Decision.** `p.area(...)` fills the space between the line through the rows of each group and zero, and `p.ribbon(low:, high:)` the band between two variables. The two share one body (`marks::filled`) and the machinery of `lines`: the rows are parted, put in the order of `x` and joined by `scene::joined`, which now takes a second variable along `y`, the lower edge, and wants both of a row. The plot value gains the marks `Area` and `Ribbon` and the aesthetics `low` and `high`, which only a layer names. In the scene a filled layer holds, beside what a line holds, `low` (the lower edge at each mark; zero for an area) and `fill` (nothing, a colour, or the place of each mark on the scale `fill`); its JSON says `line`, `low` and `fill`, and neither `linetype` nor `width`. The `y` axis runs over both edges, so the axis of a plot with an area always holds zero. The layout draws each shape as one polygon, along the upper edge in the order of the marks and back along the lower one, as ggplot2's `geom_ribbon` orders its corners, with the opacity of the layer and no outline. The key of a legend of fills is a patch of the fill, 12 points by 8 and as see-through as the marks, as wide as the piece of line where lines share the legend.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) The catalogue gave `area` and `ribbon` no option but `data:`, the two edges and `alpha:`; under open decision #106 each takes `x:` (and `area` `y:`), `fill:` and `group:` for its own layer. Neither takes `color:`: a filled mark has no outline, and `.area().lines()` draws one, so one mark does one thing. (b) An area has one fill from end to end, so a fill by a number without value labels is refused (Z0401), as a colour by a number is on a line; ggplot2 refuses it too. (c) Each area reaches down to zero by itself, and the areas of several groups lie one over another: this is `geom_area(position = "identity")` and Stata's `twoway area`, and it is what the catalogue's `alpha: 0.6` is for. R's own default stacks them. Under the owner's rule of open decisions #98 and #99, that what R or Stata offers for a procedure is an option, `area` gains `position: overlay | stack | fill = overlay` at step 23d2; the default stays the overlay, so that `plot(...).area().lines()` puts an area under each line. (d) The rows are parted by `group:` and by the categories of `fill:`, and also by the categories of a variable the plot maps to `color`, where the layer's frame holds it: ggplot2 parts them so, and without it `plot(color: union).area().lines()` would fill one zigzag under two lines. The areas take no colour from `color`. A layer whose own frame lacks that variable is not refused for it. (e) A band does not read `y`: its two edges are its positions, both required (Z0406 from the function when one is missing, since an option of the usage line cannot be marked as required). Where nothing is mapped to `y`, the axis takes its title from `low:`. (f) A missing or infinite value in `y`, or in either edge, leaves the row out and breaks the shape, as the checklist says; ggplot2 does this for `geom_ribbon` and joins across the gap for `geom_area`. A row left alone fills nothing and is counted. (g) The axis covers the marks that are drawn, as for every layer, where ggplot2 also counts the edge that a dropped row still has. (h) A lower edge above the upper one is drawn as given, without a note. (i) The fill without `fill:` is the colour of the theme's marks.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/fills.rs`: an area and a band against the polygons and the limits of ggplot2 4.0.3, corner for corner; breaks and lone rows; parting by group, fill and the plot's colour; a fill from the layer and from the plot; the polygons and the legend's patches on the page; a band of its own frame; the scene's JSON; a property over 300 frames (two marks or more to a shape, in the order of `x`, each row once, both edges within the axis, a polygon of two corners for each mark). `tests/printing.rs`: five plots of the shipped wages against ggplot2's limits (20.7926 to 34.4123 for the band of two standard errors; -1.62215 to 34.0652 and -1.81966 to 38.2128 for the areas), ten edge cases, nineteen messages. The two help pages, their examples run. The conformance set gains eight cases: what a script of bands and areas prints, and two figures in SVG, PDF and PNG, so that a see-through fill is proved the same bytes on every target.

**The split.** Step 23d is split in the checklist into 23d1, the two marks with each shape by itself, and 23d2, the stacked area.

**The specification.** The usage lines of catalogue rows 465 and 466 gain the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 23d; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": `area`, `ribbon`); open decisions #98, #99 and #106.

## 12 November 2026: stacked areas (release 0.7.0, step 23d2), and step 23d complete

**Decision.** `area` takes `position: overlay | stack | fill = overlay`. The mark carries it (`Mark::Area(Stacking)`, as a step carries its direction), the scene says it in its JSON (`"position": "stack"`, on a layer of areas and no other), and the scene holds the result: `y` and `low` of each mark are the two edges of its area in the stack, so the layout, the writers and Zemp draw a stacked area as they draw any other. `scene::stacked` builds it: the rows are parted as for a line, the groups put in the order of their categories with `NA` last, and at each `x` the areas are put on one another from the last group up, so that the first group is on top and the picture reads downwards as the legend does. A value below zero is stacked downwards from zero, apart from the values above it. With `fill` each edge is divided by the total at its `x`. All three are what ggplot2's `position_stack` and `position_fill` give where every group has one value at every `x`.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) The words: `stack` and `fill` are those of `position:` of `bars` in the catalogue, so one word means one thing on both marks; `overlay` is the project's word for R's `"identity"`, which names nothing a reader can see. (b) The default is `overlay`, where R's is `"stack"` (decided at step 23d1, ruling c). (c) A stack is built only where every area has one value: an `x` at which a group has no row, a row without `y`, or more than one row is left out for every group, the areas are broken there, and a note counts the rows and the values of `x`. Nothing is interpolated. ggplot2 since 3.4.0 interpolates each group at the `x` of the others (`stat_align`), which draws values that were not observed; the engine draws what the frame holds and says what it left out, and a reader who wants the interpolation computes it first. Where every group has every `x` the two agree to the last digit. (d) Shares need amounts: with `fill`, an `x` with a value below zero, or a total that is not above zero, is left out and counted. ggplot2 divides the values below zero by their own total and shows shares from -1 to 0, which are shares of nothing. (e) The areas of a stack keep the layer's `alpha:`; since they do not overlap, nothing shows through but the gridlines.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/fills.rs`: three groups at four values of `x` against `ymin` and `ymax` of ggplot2 4.0.3 for `"stack"` and for `"fill"`, row for row, and the limits -0.4 to 8.4 and -0.05 to 1.05; values below zero against ggplot2; the places a stack leaves out; one group stacked is the area itself; a property over 300 tables with holes (each area stands on the one under it, the top is the total or 1, the thickness of each is its value or its share, a place that cannot be stacked is not drawn). `tests/printing.rs`: six plots of the shipped wages, with ggplot2's limits -3.35374 to 70.4286 for the stacked means; three messages. The help page of `area` gains the option, its details and a stacked example. The conformance case of filled marks gains a stacked plot and one of shares with a place left out.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 465 gains `position:` (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's steps 23d and 23d2; the owner's rule of open decisions #98 and #99; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": `area`).

## 12 November 2026: `hline` and `vline` (release 0.7.0, step 23e1), and step 23e split

**Decision.** `p.hline(at:)` and `p.vline(at:)` add a layer of reference lines, level or upright, from one edge of the panel to the other. The two share one body (`marks::spanning`). The place is stored with the layer as a position of its own: a variable given to `at:` is the layer's mapping of `y` (for `hline`) or `x` (for `vline`), and a number is a constant of that aesthetic, the new `PlotSetting::Place`. The plot value gains the marks `Hline` and `Vline`. In the scene a layer of reference lines has one mark for each line, with a value on the one axis it needs and none on the other (`"x": []` for a level line), `rows` for the lines drawn from a variable and none for the line at a number, and its JSON says `linetype` and `width`. The axis is trained on the places as on any mark. The layout draws each line as a segment across the panel, with the one scale it needs, so a plot with one axis draws them too. A legend of reference lines coloured by a variable has a piece of line for its key.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) A reference line takes nothing from the plot but its axes: not the plot's colour, mapped or set, and a frame given as `data:` needs none of the plot's variables. This departs, for these two marks, from "an argument not given inherits the plot's" of open decision #106: the usual frame of reference lines is a small frame of places, which holds none of the plot's variables, and a line at a number has no row to take a colour from. ggplot2 needs `inherit.aes = FALSE` for the same case. (b) The options added under #106: `color:` (a string, or a variable when `at:` names one; of categories or a number, since each line is one mark) and `width:`. (c) `style:` keeps the catalogue's name and default (`dashed`) and takes all six types of line, not the three first catalogued, since the writers draw six. It is a word, as catalogued, where `linetype:` of `lines` is a string or a variable; the two names stand for now, and may be brought together when the scales are reviewed at step 25. (d) A reference line is 0.5 wide unless `width:` says otherwise, the width of an axis line, where a line of data is 1: a reference should not weigh as much as what is read against it. (e) The axis grows to hold a reference line, as in ggplot2. (f) A line at a number needs the axis to exist already (Z0401 otherwise); a line at a variable's values gives the plot that axis where nothing else is mapped to it. (g) `at:` is required (Z0406 from the function). (h) A bare name given to `at:` is a variable; a number bound to a name is written as an expression. Open decision #127 is raised on this and taken as its option B, built at step 23f.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/rules.rs`: the limits against ggplot2 4.0.3 with a line among the marks, beyond them, and on both axes; a line from edge to edge at its place, in its colour, width and type; lines at the values of a variable of another frame, coloured by it, with `NA` and an infinite value; nothing taken from the plot; a plot with one axis; the scene's JSON; a property over 300 frames (the axis holds every line, each spans the panel). `tests/printing.rs`: seven plots, with ggplot2's limits on the four rows and on the shipped wages; seventeen messages. The two help pages, their examples run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of reference lines prints and its figure in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**The split.** Step 23e is split in the checklist into 23e1, `hline` and `vline`, and 23e2, `rug`; step 23f `[engine]` is added for open decision #127.

**The specification.** The usage lines of catalogue rows 470 and 471 gain the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`); open decision #127 is added to the register.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 23e; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": "`hline` and `vline` take a value or a variable"); open decisions #106 and #127; decision #118, F9.

## 12 November 2026: `rug` (release 0.7.0, step 23e2), and step 23 complete

**Decision.** `p.rug(...)` adds a tick at the margin of the panel for each row. The mark carries its sides (`Mark::Rug(Sides)`, written `x`, `y`, `both`). In the scene a rug along one axis has a value for each mark on that axis and none on the other, as a reference line has, and a rug on both has both; its JSON says `sides`, the length of a tick as `size` (`RUG_LENGTH`, 4.5 points) and its `width` (0.5). The layout draws a tick from the edge of the panel inwards, at the bottom for a place on `x` and at the left for one on `y`, as a path of one piece so that it has the opacity of the layer; with one axis alone the ticks along it are still drawn, so `w.plot(x: wage).rug()` is a plot by itself.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) The catalogue gave `rug` no option but `data:` and `sides:`; under open decision #106 it takes `x:`, `y:` and `color:` for its own layer, and it inherits the plot's as `points` does. (b) `alpha:` is added, with 1 as its default: a rug of thousands of rows is a black bar without it, and R's `geom_rug` has it. (c) A rug along one axis draws every row with a finite value there, whatever the row holds on the other axis; a rug on both sides draws the rows that have both, which are the rows `points` draws, so that the two rugs under a scatter are its two margins. (d) A tick is 4.5 points long, the diameter of a point, and not a share of the panel as ggplot2's 3% is: every mark of the engine is sized in points, and a figure keeps its ticks when it is made larger. It is 0.5 wide. Neither is an option. (e) The sides are the bottom and the left; the top and the right, which ggplot2 also offers, are not: the catalogue's three words stand. (f) The key of a legend of rugs alone is a piece of line; where points share the legend the key stays a point.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/rug.rs`: the rows drawn for each of the three sides, with `NA` and an infinite value, and the same rows as `points` for both; the ticks on the page, from the axes inwards, at their places, with ggplot2's limits; a rug along one axis by itself, coloured, with its legend; a variable of its own and a colour on the continuous scale; a property over 300 frames. `tests/printing.rs`: eight plots, with the counts and limits of the shipped wages against R (18,412 rows, 18,201 with a wage; 7.4 to 20.6 and -3.913 to 159.833); twelve messages. The help page, its examples run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of rugs prints and a figure in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**Step 23.** The seven marks of step 23, `lines`, `step`, `area`, `ribbon`, `hline`, `vline` and `rug`, are built with their pages; the step is ticked. `plot` stands at nine functions.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 469 gains the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's steps 23e and 23e2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": `rug`); open decision #106.

## 12 November 2026: a correction to the colour ramp, found by a property test on CI

**What was found.** The push of step 23e1 failed the `test` job on GitHub, in a test that the step did not touch: the property `every_colour_lies_on_its_scale` of step 20c drew, among its random frames, two rows whose values on the colour scale were 0 and 5e-324, the smallest number above zero. The scale then runs from 0 to 5e-324, and `colour::ramp_entry` gave both values the middle colour where they are the two ends. It halved the limits before taking their width, so that the widest scales do not overflow, and half of the smallest number is zero: the scale had no width left.

**Choice.** The width is taken as it is, `hi - lo`, and the share as `(v - lo) / (hi - lo)`; the halves are used only where one of the two would overflow. Halving is exact for every number but the very smallest, so the two ways give the same share wherever both can be computed, and no published result changes: the conformance report is identical. The failing frame is kept in `packages/tier1/plot/tests/scene.proptest-regressions`, which the property test reads first on every run, and the unit test of `ramp_entry` holds the narrowest scales and a value beyond a limit by more than can be held.

**Why it was not seen before.** A property test draws other frames on every run, and this pair is rare; the local routine and the earlier runs on GitHub never drew it. No figure that anyone has made is affected: the fault needs a colour scale whose whole width is the smallest number a computer holds.

**Reason.** Engine Specification, section 8.3 (a result is the same wherever it is computed, and right at the edges of the numbers); the testing handbook's rule that a failing case found by a property test is kept.

## 12 November 2026: a name that is a variable or a bound value (release 0.7.0, step 23f; open decision #127, option B)

**Choice.** Where a parameter takes a variable or a value, a bare name is resolved when the statement runs, in the order section 3.7 gives for a frame method: the variable of the frame the call draws; where the frame has none of that name, a `let` binding that holds a number or text, as the parameter takes; both at once is the variable, with W0102. The checker cannot settle it, since it does not always know a frame's variables before the run, so it lowers such a name to a new node of the intermediate form, `ExprKind::VarOrBound { name, binding }`, when the name is a `let` binding whose type one of the parameter's value types accepts (`Float`, `Int` or `Str`); the interpreter gives the function `Value::Var(name)` where the receiver's frame has the column, and the value of the binding where it has not. A loop variable or a parameter that holds such a value is lowered to the binding itself, which the interpreter already refuses with Z0106 when the frame has a column of its name. A name that is no such binding stays a variable, as before, and is refused by the function where the frame has none (Z0101).

**What it reaches.** Every parameter typed as a variable or a value: `at:` of `hline` and `vline` (`Float | Var`), `size:` of `plot` and `points` (`Var | Float`), and `color:`, `fill:`, `shape:` and `linetype:` wherever they are `Var | Str`, all in `plot`. The decision was raised for the numbers; the rule is built for text as well, since `let shade = "firebrick"` and `color: shade` is the same question and one rule is easier to hold than two. A parameter that takes a variable or an expression (`x: Var | Expr`) is not touched: there a bare name is a variable.

**An earlier reading, changed.** Steps 20c and 20d read section 7.6 ("a bare name maps a variable and a string sets a constant") as: a bare name never reads a binding, and a constant is a constant only where it is written; `let shade = "red"` and `color: shade` were refused, and tests held that. Open decision #127 changes the reading for a name that is no variable of the frame. The three tests that held the refusal (`color: shade`, `size: s`, `shape: mark` with a bound value of the right type) now hold a bound value of another type, which is still refused, and the sentence of section 7.6 is amended (logged). This is the part of the decision the owner is most likely to want to look at: reverting it is to remove the new node from the checker, when a bound value is again written in place (`at: 0.5`) or as an expression (`at: centre + 0`).

**What changes for a user.** Nothing that ran before means anything else: a name that was no variable was refused. A script in which a `let` binding of a number or of text shares its name with a variable given to such an option draws what it drew and now has the warning W0102, which is material for the notes of 0.7.0 (step 40c).

**Tests.** `crates/zeff-engine/tests/bound_values.rs`: a bound number as the place of a line and as a size, on a mark and on `plot`; bound text as a colour, a fill, a shape and a type of line; the variable first with W0102, by the frame the layer draws; a loop variable and a function's parameter; seven messages (Z0106 for a loop variable that is a variable too, a binding of another type, text for a number and a number for text, a name that is nothing, and a bound value the option refuses). The help pages of `hline`, `vline` and `plot` say the rule; `hline` and `vline` declare W0102.

**The specification.** Section 3.7's table of resolution by parameter type gains the row for a parameter that takes a variable or a value (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** Open decision #127; Language Reference, section 3.7 ("Name lookup", "Resolution by parameter type").

## 12 November 2026: an axis of categories (release 0.7.0, step 24a; open decision #128, option C, its first part)

**Choice.** A Str or a Category variable mapped to `x` or `y` makes an axis of categories; a Bool, an Int and a Float stay on a linear scale, with value labels or without (`scene::placing`). The categories stand at the places 1, 2, 3 in their order, those of a Category by its levels and those of a Str in the order of text, and the scale of the axis says `category`, with the places as its breaks, the categories as its labels and the limits 0.4 and the number of categories plus 0.6, as ggplot2 has them, whatever is drawn. Nothing else of the scene format changes: a mark on such an axis has the place of its category as its `x` or `y`, a number, so the layout, the three writers and Zemp draw it with what they had, and the layout was not touched. The scene computes the places once for the plot (`axis_categories`: the categories of the variable the axis is named by, then those only a layer's own variable has, as a colour scale of categories orders them) and gives every function that reads positions a column of places in the stead of the variable (`placed`).

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) A row with `NA` in a variable of categories on an axis is not drawn and is counted with the rows without a number, as principle 6 has it for every position; ggplot2 gives `NA` a place of its own at the end. (b) An axis shows every category of its variable, a level of a Category with no row among them too, where a colour scale shows the categories of the marks drawn: an empty place on an axis says that the category has no row, and the checklist of `bars` asks for it. (c) The layers share the axis, so a layer that maps a variable of the other kind to it is refused (Z0401, `marks::one_axis`), and so is a layer's own frame that holds the plot's variable as the other kind. (d) What stands at numbers has no place on categories: `area` (down to zero), `ribbon` (two edges), `hline` and `vline` (a number) are refused on such an axis (Z0401, `marks::numbers_along`); `points`, `lines`, `step` and `rug` are placed on it. A reference line at a category is not built; it can be asked for when it is wanted. (e) The edges of a band stay numbers. (f) The order of a Str is that of the language, by code point, where R sorts by the locale: capitals come before small letters here.

**What changes for a user.** `plot(x: industry, y: wage)` was refused and is now a plot. Nothing that drew before draws otherwise. The message for a variable no axis holds (a Date) is reworded.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/categories.rs`: the places, the labels and the limits against ggplot2 4.0.3 on `x` and on `y`; a label under each place on the page; a category that only a layer's own frame has, and a row without a category; a plot that maps nothing; a property over 300 frames. `tests/printing.rs`: ten plots, with the twelve industries of the shipped wages at 0.4 to 12.6 as in ggplot2; twelve messages. Six stored sets of messages follow the reworded refusals, and two cases that are now plots hold a Date. The help pages of `plot` and `points` say the rule. The conformance set gains five cases (what a script on an axis of categories prints and a figure in SVG, PDF and PNG), and the case of points changes where its last plot, by industry, is now drawn.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 24a; open decision #128; section 7.6 of the Language Reference.

## 12 November 2026: `bars` (release 0.7.0, step 24b)

**Decision.** `p.bars(...)` draws a bar from zero at each value of `x`: as high as `y` where the plot or the layer maps something to `y`, and as the count of rows where nothing is. The mark carries how the bars that share an `x` are arranged (`Mark::Bars(Arrangement)`: `stack`, `dodge`, `fill`). `scene::bars` computes them: the rows are parted into groups as for a line, the groups in the order of their categories; a count is one bar for each group at each `x`; stacked, the bars of an `x` are put on one another from the last up, a value below zero downwards from zero, as areas are; as shares each is divided by the total at its `x`; side by side, the groups that are there share the width of one bar equally, the first at the left.
