In the scene a bar is a mark with its `x`, its two ends along `y` (`low` and `y`), how far it reaches along `x` (`span`, new) and its `fill`; the JSON of a layer of bars says `low`, `span`, `fill` and `position`. The layout draws each bar as a rectangle with the opacity of the layer. A legend of bars has a patch for its key (`Mark::patches`).

**The axes.** A plot whose bars count, and that maps nothing to `y`, has a `y` axis titled `count`, which the scene makes for it. The `y` axis holds zero, since a bar starts there. Along `x` the axis is made wide enough for the whole of the first and the last bar: the scale is trained on the edges of the bars, as ggplot2 trains it.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) The options under open decision #106: `x:`, `y:`, `fill:` and `group:`; no `color:`, a bar having no outline. (b) `width:` is a share of the gap between two neighbouring values of `x`, above 0 and at most 1, and 0.9 where it is not given, as in ggplot2; on numbers the gap is the smallest distance between two values of `x` in the layer. A width above 1, which ggplot2 allows with a warning, makes bars that overlap and is refused. (c) `alpha:` is added, 1 unless given. (d) A bar has one fill, so a fill by a number without value labels is refused, as for an area. (e) With `y` mapped every row is a bar; several rows at one `x` in one group are stacked, or with `dodge` drawn in one place, as `geom_col` does, and the help page says to summarise first. (f) Side by side, where a group has no row at an `x` the others there are wider: ggplot2's default (`preserve = "total"`). Bars of one width whatever is missing (`preserve = "single"`) are not offered; they can be asked for. (g) As shares, an `x` with a value below zero or a total that is not above zero is left out and counted, as for the stacked area. (h) `y` must be numbers: a bar is not drawn up to a category. Bars along `y`, from a category on `y`, are `coord(flip)` of step 27. (i) A category of the axis without a row has no bar and keeps its place.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/bars.rs`: the left and right edge and the two ends of every bar against `geom_bar` and `geom_col` of ggplot2 4.0.3, for counts on categories and on numbers and for values stacked, side by side and as shares, with the limits of both axes; values below zero; the rectangle on the page and the patch of the legend; rows without a place or a height, and an empty category; a property over 300 tables (stacked heights sum to the totals, counts to the rows, shares to 1, and side by side the groups share one bar's width). `tests/printing.rs`: eleven plots, with the counts of the twelve industries of the shipped wages against R (200 to 2,871 rows; limits -143.55 to 3014.55); fourteen messages. The help page, its examples run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of bars prints and a stacked figure in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**Known and left for a later step.** Bars by a labelled number, such as `union`, stand at 0 and 1 on a linear axis that reads -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5: the breaks of a labelled variable are the second part of open decision #128, at step 25. An axis of many long categories writes only the labels that fit; step 26 wraps them.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 464 gains the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 24b; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": "`bars` with `y` draws values and without `y` counts, and its baseline is always zero"); open decisions #106 and #128.

## 12 November 2026: a filled mark takes its fill from `color` (release 0.7.0, step 24b2; a correction to steps 23d1 and 24b)

**What was found.** When `bars` was registered, the tests that list the functions the specification's sample script still waits for lost one line, and reading the sample showed how it draws its bars: `plot(means, x: industry, y: mean_lwage, color: female).bars(position: dodge)`, with a legend. Section 6 of the Language Reference says the same of the shared argument `color:`: "Colour points, lines or bars by group within one panel". As built at step 24b a bar was filled by `fill:` alone and parted, but not coloured, by `color`; the sample drew twenty-four grey bars and no legend. Step 23d1 had ruled the same for `area` and `ribbon` ("the areas take no colour from `color`", its ruling d). Where the code and the specification disagree the specification wins.

**Choice.** A filled mark, a bar, an area or a band, on a plot and in a layer that say nothing of `fill`, takes its fill from `color:` of the plot (`scene::borrows_colour`): the colour of each category where `color` maps a variable that shows categories in the frame the layer draws, and the one colour where `color` is set to a string. In the scene this is a mapping of `fill`: the plot has a scale `fill` of that variable beside its scale `color`, the two share one legend, as they do where a script writes both, and the JSON of the layer says `fill` as for any filled mark, so the layout and the writers needed nothing. `fill:` on the plot or on the layer comes first, a variable or one colour. A colour by a number, shown on a ramp, fills nothing, since one shape has one fill; the mark keeps the fill of the theme and the printed plot still says that no layer draws `color`. A layer's own frame that lacks the variable is not refused: its shapes have the fill of the theme. The rule is `ggplot2`'s where a script maps both `colour` and `fill` to one variable; ggplot2 itself fills in grey and draws the outline in the colour.

**What changes.** Step 23d1's ruling (d) is withdrawn in its last sentence: an area and a band now take the colour of their line. `plot(x: year, y: wage, color: union).area().lines()` fills each area in the colour of its line, with one legend whose key is a patch with a piece of line on it. Nothing else of steps 23d1, 23d2 and 24b changes.

**Tests.** `tests/fills.rs`: an area on a plot that maps `color` alone is filled by it, shares one legend with the lines, and a fill of its own, the plot's one colour and a colour by a number each do what is said above. `tests/bars.rs`: the sample's form, bars side by side filled by the colour. `tests/printing.rs`: the sample's bars on the shipped wages (twenty-four bars, a scale of `fill` by `Sex` with its legend), the area and the band of the yearly means, a fill that comes first, and no remark that no layer draws `color`. The help pages of `area`, `ribbon` and `bars` say the rule. The conformance case of bars gains a plot of the kind.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** Language Reference, section 6 (`color:`) and section 7.6; `docs/spec/zeff_samples.zeff`; the rule that the specification wins.

## 12 November 2026: `tile` (release 0.7.0, step 24c)

**Decision.** `p.tile(...)` draws a rectangle at each row's `x` and `y`, as wide and as high as the gap between two neighbouring places: one place on an axis of categories, and on numbers the smallest distance between two values of the rows drawn, taken along each axis by itself (ggplot2's rule for `geom_tile`). In the scene a tile is held as a bar is: its `x`, how far it reaches along `x` (`span`), and its two edges along `y` (`low` and `y`), so the layout draws tiles with the code that draws bars, and the axes are trained on the whole of the outermost tiles. A tile is one row, so its fill may be a number on the continuous scale as well as a category; a row without the number its fill shows is not drawn and is counted, as a point without its colour on a ramp is. The legend of a fill by a number is the bar of the ramp that a colour by a number has (the layout took the bar from the scale of colours alone until now).

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) The catalogue gave `tile` `data:` and `fill: Var`; under open decision #106 it takes `x:`, `y:` and `fill:` for its own layer, `fill:` also as a string for one colour. `alpha:` is added, 1 unless given. (b) Every tile of a layer has one size; a missing cell shows the paper, and several rows in one cell are drawn on one another, the help page saying to summarise first. (c) A tile has no outline. (d) Where nothing says anything of `fill`, a tile takes it from `color:` of the plot, as the other filled marks do since step 24b2, a number included. (e) The continuous scale of fills is that of colours: viridis, from the smallest value drawn to the largest.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/tiles.rs`: the four edges of each tile and the limits of both axes against `geom_tile` of ggplot2 4.0.3, on categories and on numbers; the rectangles on the page in the first and the last colour of viridis, touching, with a bar of the ramp for a legend; a fill by categories with `NA`, and the rows not drawn; a property over 300 frames. `tests/printing.rs`: six plots, with the 144 means by year and industry of the shipped wages against R (19.1973 to 39.4162; limits 2008.9 to 2022.1 and 0.4 to 12.6); seven messages. The help page, its example run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of tiles prints and a heat map in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 468 gains the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 24c; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": `tile`; "`heatmap(vars)` computes the correlations and draws `.tile()`"); open decision #106.

## 12 November 2026: `text` (release 0.7.0, step 24d), and step 24 complete

**Decision.** `p.text(...)` writes the value of `label` of each row at its `x` and `y`. The plot value gains the mark `Text` and a layer gains `nudge`, how far its text is moved from its place, to the right and up, in points. In the scene a layer of text holds the text of each mark (`label`) and its `nudge`, the size of its type as `size`, and the colour of each mark as any mark's; its JSON says `label` and `nudge`. A value is written as it prints, a value with a value label as its label. The layout draws each as a text of one line in the sans-serif face of the theme, centred on its place in both directions and moved by the nudge, in the colour of its mark.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, taken under the owner's standing instruction of 12 November 2026. (a) The options under open decision #106: `x:`, `y:`, `label:` and `color:`. `label:` of the layer takes the place of `label:` of the plot. (b) `nudge:` is in points on the page and not in the units of the data, as R's `nudge_x` and `nudge_y` are: a label is moved to clear a mark, whose size is in points, and the same nudge then serves on every scale and on an axis of categories. It moves nothing on the axes, where R's widens them. (c) `size:` is the size of the type in points, 8 unless given; it is not refused below the 8 points that the theme keeps to for its own text, since the script asks for it. (d) A row without a label writes nothing and is counted, as ggplot2 drops it; an empty text is written and shows nothing. (e) The axes take their limits from the places and not from the extent of the labels, as in ggplot2, so a label near an edge of the panel is cut there. Making room for labels is left to the scales and titles of steps 25 and 26. (f) No `alpha:`: a text of a drawing has no opacity of its own. (g) The key of a legend for text coloured by a variable is the point that marks have, since a letter as a key (ggplot2's "a") says less.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/texts.rs`: the labels, rows and places of a layer, a row without a label, a number written as it prints, and the limits of ggplot2 4.0.3 with `geom_point` and `geom_text` (10.35 to 46.65 and 60.05 to 80.95); each label on the page in its colour and size, three points right of and seven above where it would be centred; a property over 300 frames. `tests/printing.rs`: six plots, on an axis of categories and over bars too; eleven messages. The help page, its example run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of labelled bars and points prints and a figure in SVG, PDF and PNG, where the labels are set in the embedded face.

**Step 24.** The four marks of step 24, on an axis of categories: `bars`, `tile` and `text` are built with their pages, and step 24 is ticked. The eleven marks of section 7.6 are implemented; `plot` stands at twelve functions.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 467 gains the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 24d; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Marks": `text`); open decision #106.

## 12 November 2026: the kinds of scale of an axis (release 0.7.0, step 25a)

**Choice.** A plot holds what the script says of the scale of each axis (`Plot.axes`, a `PlotAxis` with its `AxisKind`: `Linear`, `Log`, `Sqrt`). The scene gives the scale of an axis of numbers that kind (`ScaleKind::Log` is new; `Sqrt` served the sizes already) and takes its limits and breaks accordingly (`scale::log_limits`, `log_breaks`, `sqrt_limits`). The layout places every mark, gridline and tick by `scale::share`, the share of the way a value stands between the limits: in proportion to the value, to its logarithm or to its square root. The logarithm and the power of ten are the engine's own (`zeff_numeric`, the pure-Rust `libm`), so a figure on a log axis is the same bytes on every target; the conformance case `plot/axes/scene` holds one.

**The rules.** (a) The margin of 5% is taken in the logarithm on a log axis and in the square root on a square-root axis, so that it is the same share of the panel at both ends: ggplot2's rule, and the limits agree with it (2.92425753208 and 183.95667758324 for the wages on a log axis; 1.8374864437 and 165.5834864437 on a square-root one). A square-root axis is never below zero. A log axis of one value is a decade around it, and an empty one is 1 to 10. (b) The breaks of a log axis: over three decades or more the powers of ten, one in two or in three where more than seven fall between the limits; from one decade to three, 1, 2 and 5 times a power of ten; under one decade the round numbers of a linear axis. Each is read from its decimal text. This is the engine's own rule, in the spirit of d3, whose defaults the section follows for the linear axis; ggplot2 writes 3, 10, 30, 100 where this writes 5, 10, 20, 50, 100. The breaks of a square-root axis are those of a linear one. (c) A value at or below zero has no place on a log axis, and a value below zero none on a square-root axis: "a log scale on a value at or below zero is an error naming the rows" (section 7.6). `scene::axis_fault` finds the first such thing in a plot, the rows of a variable, a reference line, a bar or an area, which reach down to zero, or an axis of categories, and every mark refuses the plot it would make (`marks::finish`, the ending the twelve marks now share, and `marks::misplaced`, the message). The scene of such a plot, which no script can hold, still stands: the rows without a place are not drawn. (d) A bar and an area are refused on a log axis and drawn from zero on a square-root one.

**Not at this step.** No script can set a scale yet: `scale_x` and `scale_y` are registered at step 25b, where `limits:`, `breaks:` and `labels:` exist, as `lines` followed the line types of step 23b; the checklist entry of step 25a is reworded to say so. The messages of `misplaced` are held by snapshots there.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/axes.rs`: the limits against ggplot2 4.0.3; the breaks over less than one decade, two, six and six hundred; the share of a value on each kind; four decades equally far apart on the page, and 0, 25 and 100 on a square-root axis; what has no place on a scale, with the scene of such a plot; a property over 300 frames on the three kinds (a break is never outside the limits, every mark within them).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25a; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Scales"); Engine Specification, section 8.3, point 3.

## 12 November 2026: `scale_x` and `scale_y` (release 0.7.0, step 25b)

**Decision.** `p.scale_x(...)` and `p.scale_y(...)` say the scale of an axis of numbers: its kind, on the machinery of step 25a, written first and by itself as the sample script writes it (`.scale_y(log)`); `limits:`, `breaks:` and `labels:`. They are in a module of their own (`plot::scales`) and share one body. What they say is held with the plot (`PlotAxis`, which gains the limits, the breaks and the labels), and what is said last of an axis takes the place of all that was said before. The scene derives the scale: an end of the limits that is given is that end exactly, with no margin; the breaks given are those within the limits, with their labels or the numbers.

**The rules.** (a) Decision #118, F5, as the owner adopted it: `limits:` sets the visible range and nothing more. No row is dropped; the marks stay in the scene, the edge of the panel cuts off what lies beyond, so a line runs on to the edge, and a note counts the marks beyond the limits ("N marks beyond the limits of the `y` axis are cut off at the edge of the panel"). ggplot2's `limits` drops the rows, which changes what a layer computes; its `coord_cartesian` is the behaviour here. (b) `limits:` is a list of two numbers with the lower below the upper; `NA` leaves an end to the values drawn. (c) `breaks:` is a list of numbers, put in order, each once; `labels:` is a list of text, one for each break, and needs `breaks:`. A break outside the limits is not shown and nothing is said of it, since no datum is lost. (d) Open decision #128, its second part: on an axis that the script gives no breaks, a variable with value labels has its breaks at the labelled values that the limits hold, written as their labels; `w.plot(x: union, y: wage)` reads `no` and `yes`. Two stored outputs of earlier steps follow. (e) A limit or a break with no place on the scale, zero on a log axis, is refused, and so is the plot whose values have none (step 25a's `axis_fault`), whether the scale or the layer comes last, with the first rows named. (f) An axis of categories is refused: it has its places and no other scale. (g) `date`, and a single string for `labels:`, the pattern an axis of dates is written by, are in the usage line since the catalogue was written and are refused with a message that says they come with the next step; step 25c builds them.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/printing.rs`: eleven plots, with the limits of the wages on a log and on a square-root axis against ggplot2 4.0.3 (2.92426 to 183.957; 1.83749 to 165.583), limits that cut off a mark, breaks and labels of the script's own, a scale said twice, bars on a square-root axis, and the labels of `union` on its axis; twenty-three messages, among them every refusal of step 25a's `misplaced`. The two help pages, their examples run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of scales prints and the wages on a log axis in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**The specification.** The row "Scales" of section 7.6 gains F5 and the two rules of #128 (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`); catalogue rows 476 and 477 are marked `implemented`.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25b; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Scales"); open decisions #118 (F5) and #128.

## 12 November 2026: an axis of dates (release 0.7.0, step 25c1), and step 25c split in three

**The split.** Step 25c was one line of the checklist and three pieces of work: the axis itself (25c1), what `scale_x(date)` and `scale_y(date)` say of it, with a reference line at one date (25c2), and the widening of an expression in a mapping under open decision #107, option B (25c3). Each is a session.

**Decision.** A Date or a DateTime variable mapped to `x` or `y` makes an axis of dates, as a Str makes one of categories: nothing has to be said. In the scene its scale has the kind `date`, and a place on it is a count of microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, the unit of a DateTime; a Date stands at the midnight that starts it, its days times 86,400,000,000, which a double holds exactly for every day of the calendar. One unit for both types, and not days for one and microseconds for the other, so that a layer of times shares an axis of days without a second kind of scale, and the breaks are whole numbers whatever the range. The layout places a date as it places a number on a linear axis.

**The limits.** The extent of the dates drawn with 5% of its width beyond each end, as on a linear axis: on the shipped firms 1947-01-17 to 2012-11-23, which are ggplot2's -8384.25 and 15667.25 days. One date has a day on each side, one instant an hour; no date at all gives the first day of 1970, as a linear axis with no value runs from 0 to 1.

**The breaks** (`packages/tier1/plot/src/dates.rs`). A ladder of steps: under a second 1, 2 and 5 times a power of ten of microseconds; 1, 5, 15 and 30 seconds and minutes; 1, 3, 6 and 12 hours; a day; a week, on Mondays; 1, 3 and 6 months, counted from January; 1, 2 and 5 times a power of ten of years, at the years that are multiples of the step. The step taken is the one nearest in proportion to a fifth of the width (below the geometric mean of itself and the next), a year being taken as 365.2425 days for the choice alone; where fewer than two of its places fall between the limits the next shorter step is tried. An axis named by a Date has no step under a day unless its limits hold no midnight. Every break is found by whole-number arithmetic on the kernel's calendar (`zeff-dates`), so the breaks are the same on every target; the one product of two doubles is in the choice of the step. ggplot2 marks the firms at 1960, 1980 and 2000, Zeff at every decade; on five months both mark the first of each month.

**The labels** (open decision #129, option A, taken on the recommendation). The ISO form of tables, cut to the part the breaks differ in: `2024`, `2024-03`, `2024-03-05`, `14:30`, `14:30:15`, with the day before the time where the breaks fall on more than one day. The layout's thinning writes every second or third label where they would touch, as for any axis. In the printed plot the limits are days, and are written to the second where the axis covers less than two days.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) The layers share the axis: what a layer maps to an axis of dates is a Date or a DateTime, and the two may be mixed; a number there, or a date on an axis of numbers or of categories, is refused with the message of step 24a, which now names three kinds. (b) `area`, `ribbon` and `bars` measure from zero along `y`, and a scale of dates has no zero: dates along `y` are refused for them, and dates along `x` are their usual case. (c) A bar and a tile are as wide as the smallest gap between two dates allows; with one date the gap is a day. (d) `hline` and `vline` stand at each date of a variable (`vline(data: events, at: day)`); a number for `at:` on an axis of dates is refused, and a line at one date written in the call comes at step 25c2. (e) A log or a square-root scale on dates is refused, whichever comes last. (f) Until step 25c2, `scale_x` and `scale_y` refuse an axis of dates with a message that says so. (g) A DateTime is placed by its instant in UTC, as it is stored and printed.

**Two older tests changed on purpose.** `every_message` and `every_message_of_an_axis_of_categories` in `packages/tier1/plot/tests/printing.rs` pinned the refusal "an axis of dates is not in this release yet" for a Date on `x` and on `y`. The step ends that refusal, so the three cases are removed and the new tests draw the same plots. The refusal of a type no axis holds stays in the code for the kinds the engine stores and does not compute on, which no script can make. The help of the message for layers of different kinds now names dates beside categories and numbers, which changes seven stored snapshots by that sentence.

**Tests.** Eleven unit tests of the breaks and labels (one day, a century, the whole calendar, a range across a leap day against the same days of a common year, Mondays, the clock down to a microsecond, limits that hold nothing). `packages/tier1/plot/tests/dates.rs`: eight tests of the scene and the layout (a Date, a DateTime, both axes, one day and no day, the extent before a mark is drawn, a layer of times on an axis of days, the refusal of a log scale, the place of each mark on the page with a snapshot of the drawing) and two properties (a break is never outside the limits, the breaks rise, each has a label of its own, at most sixteen; the limits hold the extent with equal margins). `printing.rs`: twelve plots with the limits of the firms against ggplot2 4.0.3, and eighteen messages. The examples of the pages of `plot` and `vline` are run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of dates prints and the firms against their dates of founding in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**The specification.** The row "Scales" of section 7.6 gains the rule of the axis of dates (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`); open decision #129 is added and decided. No catalogue row changes.

**Dependencies.** None added from outside: the `plot` package now uses the kernel crate `zeff-dates`, which the tier check allows.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25c1; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Scales"); sections 3.7 and 3.8 (dates and how they are printed); open decision #129.

## 12 November 2026: `scale_x(date)` and `scale_y(date)`, and a line at one date (release 0.7.0, step 25c2)

**Decision.** What a script says of a scale of dates is held with the plot as it is for a scale of numbers (`PlotAxis`), with the kind `Date`, the limits and the breaks as instants in the unit of the scene, microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, and the pattern of the labels beside them. The scene uses a setting of the kind `Date` on an axis of dates and a setting of another kind on an axis of numbers, never one on the other; `axis_fault` refuses the plot where they do not meet, whichever came last: a scale of dates on numbers, limits or breaks in numbers on dates, a log or a square-root scale on dates.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) An axis of dates is on the scale of dates whether the word is written or not: `scale_x(limits: [...])` on such an axis is `scale_x(date, limits: [...])`, and `linear` there means the same, since the scale is linear in time. (b) The limits and the breaks are dates, a Date or a DateTime, written with `date` or `datetime` or bound to names; a number among them is refused, as a date is on an axis of numbers, each with a message that names what was given. `NA` leaves an end of the limits to the dates drawn. (c) The limits show and do not select (decision #118, F5), as on an axis of numbers: the marks beyond are cut off and counted. On the firms from 1980 to 2000 the note counts 267 marks, which is R's count. (d) `labels:` as one string is a pattern in the notation of `format` and of the kernel's `format_with`; it is tried on a day when the scale is set, so a pattern with a directive the notation lacks is refused there, with the kernel's own reason. It writes the breaks the scale chooses and those of `breaks:`; a list of labels needs `breaks:`, as on numbers. (e) What is said last of an axis takes the place of all that was said, as at step 25b: a second `scale_x` does not keep the pattern of the first. (f) `hline` and `vline` take one date for `at:` (`at: Float | Date | DateTime | Var`), held as `PlotSetting::Moment`; a date on an axis of numbers and a number on an axis of dates are refused. A bare name bound to a date is that date, by the rule of open decision #127, which the checker's `VarOrBound` now applies to bindings of the types Date and DateTime as well as Float, Int and Str. (g) In the printed plot a line at a date reads `at 2008-09-15`, with the time to the second where it is not a midnight.

**Messages reworded.** The refusal of a scale on an axis of categories now says "of numbers or of dates" and marks the call "the axis is of categories"; `scale_x(date)` and a pattern for `labels:` lose their "not built yet" messages, and the temporary refusal of step 25c1 is gone. Four stored snapshots change by these sentences.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/dates.rs`: four more tests of the scene (limits as the visible range with the count of marks beyond, breaks and labels of the script, a pattern on the scale's own breaks and on the script's, limits that hold no break, the three faults of a scale and an axis that do not meet, a line at one date that counts for the limits). A unit test of the pattern. `printing.rs`: fourteen plots, a bare name bound to a date with the warning where the frame has a variable of the name, and twenty-five messages. The examples of the pages of `scale_x`, `scale_y` and `vline` are run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of date scales prints and the firms from 1970, with a pattern and two lines at dates, in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**The specification.** Catalogue rows 470 and 471 and the row "A variable or a value" of section 3.7 (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25c2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Scales"); open decisions #118 (F5), #127 and #129.

## 12 November 2026: the functions of `time` and `text` in a mapping (release 0.7.0, step 25c3a), and step 25c3 split in three

**The split.** The widening of open decision #107, option B, is three pieces of work of different kinds: the functions of `time` and `text`, with what an expression may give (25c3a, here); the four functions of `core` written in Zeff, whose bodies only the interpreter runs (25c3b); and `case`, whose row-by-row code lives in the interpreter and must be shared (25c3c).

**Decision.** The checker admits in a mapping the calls of `core`, `time` and `text` (`not_kept` in `crates/zeff-ir/src/check.rs`); a function of any other package, the reducers of `data` among them, is refused as before, with a help that names the three. The `plot` package finds the bodies in `zeff_time::functions()` and `zeff_text::functions()` beside those of `core`: it now depends on the two packages, which come before it in tier 1, so the tier check allows it. The expression is computed by the row-by-row kernel of `core` that `add` uses, so `x: year(founded)` has the values of `add(y = year(founded))`, which a test compares.

**What an expression may give.** For `x` and `y`: numbers, as before; text or a category, which make an axis of categories; dates, which make a scale of dates; each as a variable of that type does. So `x: category(educ)`, which the advice of several messages already named, now draws, as do `x: upper(industry)` and `x: add_months(hired, 6)`. One value alone is that value in every row: `x: "all"` is one place for every row. The edges of a band, `low:` and `high:`, stay numbers. An axis is placed by what the expression gives (`placing_of` in the scene reads the computed column), so every rule of steps 24a and 25c1 holds for an expression: the layers share the axis, `area`, `ribbon` and `bars` keep numbers along `y`, a scale of dates is refused on numbers.

**A layer with its own frame.** The plot's expression is computed again on the frame of the layer, and must come to the same kind of value there, numbers, text or dates: Z0401 otherwise, naming the two types. Before, the kind could only be numbers.

**What changed on purpose in stored results.** Three cases of `every_message_of_an_expression` drew a refusal that the step ends (`upper(industry)`, one text for `y`, `category(educ)`): two are removed and one is replaced by the edge of a band that is text. One case of the conformance set changes: the script of `plot/expression` ends with `w.plot(x: category(educ), y: log(wage))`, which was a refusal and is now a plot on an axis of categories. The help of the refusal of a function of another package names `time` and `text`, which changes four stored snapshots by that sentence.

**Found and not changed: an internal error in `add`.** A function of `time` or `text` given a column of a type it does not take stops with Z9001, "this is a bug in Zeff", in `add` since release 0.6.0 (`f.add(y = year(industry))`), and so now in a mapping. It is the question of open decision #108, where it is recorded with its examples; the step for it is planned for 0.8.0 and the rule is the owner's.

**Tests.** `printing.rs`: twelve plots (the year of a date against the variable `add` makes, text of a category, a date moved by a year, bars by quarter, a logical result on 0 and 1, `category` of a number, one text, one date, a layer of its own frame with a category the plot lacks) and ten messages. The example of the page of `plot` is run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of such mappings prints and the firms against the year each was founded in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**Dependencies.** None from outside; `zeff-time` and `zeff-text` join the `plot` package's own.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25c3a; open decision #107, option B; section 3.7 of the Language Reference ("Columns and scalars").

## 12 November 2026: the four functions of `core` written in Zeff, in a mapping (release 0.7.0, step 25c3b)

**Decision.** `logit`, `inv_logit`, `clamp` and `fill_missing` are computed inside a mapping. Their bodies run in the interpreter alone, and the `plot` package, which keeps a mapped expression to compute it on the frame of each layer, cannot call them. So the interpreter takes the body into the expression it hands over (`kept_body` in `crates/zeff-engine/src/interpreter.rs`): where a kept expression calls a built-in written in Zeff whose body is one expression of its parameters, the call is replaced by that expression with each parameter replaced by its argument. `logit(share)` is kept as `log(share / (1 - share))`, which the `plot` package computes with the kernels of `core` as it computes any other expression. The scalar form of the body is taken, and each call in it applies row by row where an argument is a column, by the rule the interpreter already has for a column that shadows a binding (`kept_call`, now shared).

**Why not a second evaluator.** The other way was to let the `plot` package run Zeff bodies, which would bring the interpreter under a package (against section 8.1) or a second copy of it. Taking the body in keeps one evaluator of expressions and one of statements.

**What is taken in, and what is not.** A body of one expression, with no statement before it, whose parameters are all given: the four of `core`. A body with statements (`assert`), a parameter left to its default, a body that reads the enclosing frame: refused with Z0401, "cannot be computed inside a mapping", and the advice to use `add`. None of the three can be reached by a script today: `assert` gives no value, which the checker refuses first, and the built-ins of `data` and `regress` written in Zeff are functions of packages a mapping does not call.

**The values and the warnings are those of `add`.** A test draws each of the four in a mapping and beside it the same value made a variable with `add`, and compares the limits, the breaks, the warnings (W0204 for the log odds of a share of 0) and the notes. A message of the body names the function the body calls: a fill of another type is refused by `coalesce` (Z0214), as in `add`.

**A formula still refuses the four** (`design.rs` of the `results` package), as open decision #107 recorded: that is not a mapping, and the decision widened mappings alone.

**Tests.** `printing.rs`: the five comparisons with `add`, seven plots (a text variable filled, which gives an axis of categories with a place for the filled rows; one number for every row; a layer of its own frame that maps `logit` itself) and four messages; the case of `every_message_of_an_expression` that pinned the refusal of `logit` is removed. The conformance set gains two cases: what a script of the four prints, and its messages.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25c3b; open decision #107, option B.

## 12 November 2026: `case` in a mapping (release 0.7.0, step 25c3c), and step 25c complete

**Decision.** `case` is computed inside a mapping, row by row, by the code that computes it in a script. That code was in the interpreter (`eval_case` and `eval_case_rows`); it is now a kernel of `core`, `zeff_core::cases`, which the interpreter and the `plot` package both call. The kernel decides which arm gives the value, for one value and for every row of a column, and asks its caller for the parts of the arms it needs, a condition or a value, so that the arms are evaluated by whoever holds them: the interpreter evaluates expressions of the script, the `plot` package the kept expression of a mapping. A value is still asked for only when its arm supplies a row. The warning of the rows no arm matches (W0208) and the five refusals (a condition that is not a Bool, a column of another length, a Category arm, an opaque arm, arms of more than one type across the rows) are built in the kernel, in the words they had.

**Why a kernel and not a second copy.** Two copies of the rule would drift: the order of the arms, the row that `NA` leaves to the next arm, the join of Int and Float. One piece of code gives a mapping the values of `add` by construction, and a test compares them.

**Nothing published changed.** The interpreter's tests of `case` pass with their stored messages untouched, and the conformance set shows no difference in any earlier case.

**The kept expression.** `ColumnExpr` gains `Case`, a list of arms, each with its condition, the condition as the script wrote it (for the message of a condition that is not a Bool) and its value. The checker admits `case` in a mapping (`not_kept`) and looks into its arms, so a reducer of `data` in an arm is refused as anywhere else in a mapping; `if` stays refused, since it decides what a script does and takes one value. A formula keeps no `case`: the three places of the `results` package that read a kept expression give it a plain refusal or pass over it.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) A refusal of a `case` in a mapping is underlined at the whole mapping, as every refusal inside a mapping is, and not at the arm. (b) The title of an axis mapped from a `case` is `case { … }`, the short form the engine already writes for a `case` wherever an expression is named; two such axes read alike, and so does a note that names them. A title of the script's own comes with `labels` at step 26.

**Step 25c is complete**: an axis of dates (25c1), the scale of dates and a line at a date (25c2), and the widening of open decision #107, option B, in three parts (25c3a to 25c3c).

**Tests.** Five unit tests of the kernel (the first true arm and the parts asked for, no arm matched, a column that turns the rest row-wise with Int joining Float, a catch-all and an arm that supplies no row, every refusal, a failure of the caller passed on). `printing.rs`: four comparisons of a `case` in a mapping with the same value made by `add` (limits, breaks, the warning and the notes), five plots (a wage held at 100, three groups of schooling as text on an axis of categories, a `case` with no catch-all, a layer of its own frame, a bound number in an arm) and seven messages; the case of `every_message_of_an_expression` that pinned the refusal of `case` is removed. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of such mappings prints and one figure in SVG, PDF and PNG. The advice of the refusal of what a mapping cannot hold now names `case`, which changes six stored snapshots by that sentence.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25c3c; open decision #107, option B; sections 3.7 and 5.1 of the Language Reference.

## 12 November 2026: `scale` (release 0.7.0, step 25d)

**Decision.** `p.scale(color:, fill:, size:, shape:)` says what the scales that are not positions show their values as. What it says is held with the plot (`Plot.scales`, a `Palette` for each of the four aesthetics, the last said of each), and the scene derives the scales from it, as it does for the axes. A scale's colours in the scene are now owned text (`Range::Colours(Vec<String>)`), since a script's colours are not among the engine's constants; the writers read them as before.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) Colours for categories: the list is given to the categories in their order, `NA` keeps its grey, a longer list is used as far as needed, and a shorter one repeats from the first with a note (open decision #109, question 1, option A, taken at this step: a plot is drawn and says what is wrong, where ggplot2's manual scale stops). (b) `viridis` for categories gives them its colours at equal steps from the first to the last, which has a colour for every category however many and suits categories with an order; `okabe_ito` says the default outright. (c) Colours for a number: a list of two colours or more is a ramp of 256 colours, the given ones at equal distances and each colour between two of them a mixture of the two in proportion to its place, of their red, green and blue, by whole-number arithmetic, so the ramp is the same on every target. ggplot2's `scale_colour_gradientn` mixes in another colour space (CIELAB), so a ramp between two colours is a little different in its middle and the same at its ends; mixing there needs cube roots on a result-bearing path, which is not taken for a matter of appearance. `okabe_ito`, and a list of one colour, are refused for a number, whichever of the scale and the layer comes last (`palette_fault`). (d) A fill that a plot borrows from its colour (step 24b2) takes the palette of the colour where nothing is said of `fill`, so `plot(..., color: female).bars(position: dodge).scale(color: [...])` colours the bars. (e) Sizes (open decision #110, question 1, option C): one number is the largest mark with a size shown by area from zero, as without `scale`; two numbers are the marks of the smallest and of the largest value drawn, the areas between in proportion, as ggplot2's `scale_size(range = ...)`. Under the second reading a value of 0 or below has its size like any other and no row is dropped for it. The form, a list of one or of two, is the reading of `size: List` in the catalogue. (f) Shapes: a list of the names a string for `shape:` takes, one for each category; a shorter list repeats with a note; `NA` keeps the asterisk. (g) What a later `scale` says of one aesthetic takes the place of what was said of it and leaves the others. (h) In the printed plot a colour of the script is named as the script wrote it, a ramp reads "a ramp through white, steelblue", viridis for categories "viridis at equal steps", and two sizes "from 2 to 12 across".

**The notes of a chain** (open decision #130, option A for 0.7.0). A note that a layer raised before `scale` in the same chain is printed though `scale` may undo its cause. Withdrawing it was tried and taken back: the interpreter keeps positions in the list of a statement's messages, and a call that removes one stops the run. The page of `scale` says to write it before the layers.

**Open decision #109** is decided at this step as recommended (A, A, A). The option to keep every level of a Category in the legend, which its second recommendation named, is not built: it needs a new argument of `scale`, which is put to the owner with a deadline of 0.8.0.

**Tests.** Two unit tests of the ramp and of viridis at equal steps. `packages/tier1/plot/tests/palettes.rs`: nine tests of the scene and the layout (colours for categories in their order, fewer colours than categories, viridis for categories, a ramp through the script's colours with the scale unchanged, a borrowed fill, the two readings of a size with the row below zero, shapes, the faults of a continuous scale, the legend drawn in the script's colours and sizes with two snapshots of the drawing) and a property (a ramp of 256, its ends as given, every colour within the given ones channel by channel, each channel moving one way between two colours). `printing.rs`: fifteen plots and twenty messages. The three examples of the page of `scale` are run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script of scales prints and a ramp through three colours in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 478 is marked `implemented`; its usage line is as it was. Open decision #109 decided; open decision #130 added and decided.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25d; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Scales", "Colour"); open decisions #109, #110 (question 1) and #130.

## 12 November 2026: `legend(right | top | bottom | none)` (release 0.7.0, step 25e1), and step 25e split in two

**The split.** Four of the five places move the legends that exist; `direct` draws something else, the name of each line at its end, with its own questions of room and of names that would touch. It is step 25e2.

**Decision.** The place the script says is held with the plot (`Plot.legend`) and carried by the scene (`Scene.legend`), whose legends are, as before, their content alone. In the scene's JSON the place is the key `legend`, written when it is not `right`, so a scene made before the function existed reads the same and no earlier published scene changes. The layout gives the legends their room by the place.

**Above and under the panel** (rulings where the text is silent, each the owner's to overturn). (a) The legends stand side by side from the left edge of the panel, each with its title above its keys, as at the right; a legend that does not fit beside the one before it starts a new band under it. ggplot2 centres them over the plot and sets the title beside the keys. (b) The keys are laid in as few rows as the width holds, by the code that lays them in columns at the right: the width allowed is the page less its margins and a sixth of the page for the labels of the `y` axis, whose room is not known when the legends are measured. (c) The bar of a continuous scale lies down, 256 colours to a row, the smallest value at the left, a tick and a label under each break. (d) `bottom` is under the title of the `x` axis and above the notes of a figure written with its notes. (e) The room is taken from the height of the panel; a legend that leaves the panel less than its smallest size is refused by the existing refusal of a page too small, at `export`, which names the room left.

**`none`** draws no legend and gives the panel the room, to the last point: the panel is that of the same plot without the variable. The scales, and so the colours of the marks and the printed plot, are unchanged.

**The printed plot** says the place on its last line, `legend: above the panel`, when it is not at the right.

**`direct`** is refused with a message that says it comes with the next step.

**The sample script.** The specification's sample writes `.legend(top)`. The two stored checks of that script (`formulas__sample_script_check` and `script_tests__sample_script_with_module`) lose the line "no function is called `legend`" and nothing else, as they lost `bars` at step 24b and `scale_y` at step 25b.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/legends.rs`: six tests (the place in the scene and its JSON; the items of a legend at the right, above and under the panel, with the panel wider and lower; no legend and the panel of the plain plot; a ramp lying above the panel and standing at the right; forty categories under a panel of two columns in more than one row, and refused on one column; two legends side by side with a long title broken) and four snapshots of drawings. `printing.rs`: nine plots and six messages. The two examples of the page of `legend` are run. The conformance set gains six cases: what a script of the places prints, the keys above the panel in SVG, PDF and PNG, and the lying bar in SVG. No snapshot of an earlier step changes: a legend at the right is laid out as it was.

**The specification.** No change; catalogue row 482 stays `planned` until `direct` is built at step 25e2.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25e1; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Guides and theme"); the specification's sample script, which writes `.legend(top)`.

## 12 November 2026: `legend(direct)` (release 0.7.0, step 25e2), and step 25 complete

**Decision.** `p.legend(direct)` writes the name of each line at its end, in the place of a legend. The scene carries the place, as for the other four; the layout does the work from the layers of the scene (`end_labels` in `packages/tier1/plot/src/layout.rs`). A legend is replaced when a layer of lines, `lines` or `step`, reads one of its scales of categories by its colour or its type of line (`Scene::named_at_ends`, which the printed plot uses too). For each category the name is written beside the right edge of the panel, at the height its line ends at, in the colour of the line, in the type of the labels of an axis; the legend is not drawn, and the panel gives up the width of the longest name and no more.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) The names stand in one column beside the right edge of the panel and not at the last point of each line, so that they have their room whatever the lines do and read as a list; a line that ends before the edge is named at the edge, at its own height. (b) Names that would touch are moved apart (`spread`): they keep their order down the page, a name is moved down to clear the one above it, and where the foot of the panel is passed they are moved back up; with more names than the panel is high they run past its top. No leader is drawn from a moved name to its line: the colour ties them. (c) A category drawn as several lines, parted by `group:`, is named once, at the line that reaches furthest along `x`. (d) A legend that no line reads, the bar of a continuous scale, the keys of points, of sizes, of filled marks, stands at the right as usual, beyond the names; a plot in which no legend is replaced is drawn exactly as with `right`. Nothing is refused and no note is raised, since the layer of lines may come later in the chain (open decision #130); the last line of the printed plot says which of the three it is. (e) Where a legend is of colour and of type of line together, the names take the colour.

**Step 25 is complete**: the kinds of scale (25a), `scale_x` and `scale_y` (25b), the axis of dates, its scale and wider expressions in a mapping (25c), `scale` (25d) and `legend` (25e). Four functions joined the catalogue as implemented: `scale_x`, `scale_y`, `scale` and `legend`; `plot` stands at sixteen functions built.

**Tests.** A unit test of `spread` (names far apart, two that would touch in either order, the foot of the panel, heights beyond the panel, more names than the panel holds). `packages/tier1/plot/tests/legends.rs`: five more tests (three names at the ends in the colours of their lines, at the heights the lines end at, with the panel wider than beside a legend, and a snapshot of the drawing; four lines that end together, a line of text apart and in order; a legend no line reads, drawn as with `right`; a category of several lines named once; names beside the keys of a legend they do not replace). `printing.rs`: four more plots, with the three last lines the printed plot can end with. The example of the page of `legend` is run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script prints and twelve lines named at their ends in SVG, PDF and PNG.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 482 is marked `implemented`; its usage line is as it was.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 25e2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Guides and theme": "direct labels the series at their ends" in the catalogue).

## 12 November 2026: `labels` (release 0.7.0, step 26a), and step 26 split in three

**The split.** Step 26 named three functions and the labels of a crowded axis: `labels` (26a), `theme` (26b), and `annotate` with the crowded axis (26c).

**Decision.** `p.labels(title:, subtitle:, x:, y:, color:, caption:)` gives a plot its words. They are held with the plot (`Plot.labels`), and the scene derives from them: the titles of the scales `x`, `y` and of the legend of colour, in the place of the label of the variable, and three new parts of a scene, its title, subtitle and caption. In the scene's JSON the three are the key `titles`, written when one of them is set, so a scene with none reads as it did; each scale already has a key `labels`, the labels of its breaks, which is why the new key has another name.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) The title, the subtitle and the caption start at the left margin of the page and are broken between words to the width of the page, not to that of the panel, so that their room does not depend on the labels of the `y` axis; ggplot2 starts them at the left edge of the panel by default and sets the caption at the right. (b) The type: the title at 10 points in IBM Plex Sans SemiBold, the face the theme of step 21a ships "for the titles"; the subtitle at 9 points and the caption at 8, in the regular face. The theme gains one value for it, `heading_size`; the values frozen at step 22 are as they were, and the test that pins them names the addition. (c) Order down the page: title, subtitle, a legend placed above, the panel, the title of the `x` axis, a legend placed under, the caption, the notes of a figure written with its notes. (d) An empty text, or one of spaces alone, takes a title away: `x: ""` leaves an axis untitled and gives the panel the room; `title: ""` takes back an earlier title. (e) What a later `labels` says of one of the six replaces what was said of it and leaves the other five, as `scale` does. (f) `color:` titles the legend of the variable mapped to `color`, and the legend of fills where nothing is mapped to `color` or the fill is borrowed from it; the legends of sizes and shapes by other variables keep the labels of their variables (open decision #131: the arguments for them at 0.8.0). (g) A title that leaves the panel less than its smallest size is refused at `export` by the existing refusal of a page too small. (h) The printed plot shows the titles of axes and legend in their rows and the title, subtitle and caption on its last lines.

**The sample script.** The specification's sample writes `.labels(title: ..., y: "log wage")`. The two stored checks of that script lose the line "no function is called `labels`" and nothing else.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/titles.rs`: five tests (the label of a variable until the script says otherwise, with the marks and breaks unchanged; a title, subtitle and caption with their faces, sizes and places, and a snapshot of the drawing; an empty text; a long title broken between words, a word longer than its line, and a title that leaves no room; the legend of fills titled by `color:` and the count axis by `y:`). `printing.rs`: ten plots and six messages. The two examples of the page of `labels` are run. The conformance set gains five cases: what a script prints and a titled figure in SVG, PDF and PNG. No snapshot of an earlier step changes.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 481 is marked `implemented`; open decision #131 added and decided.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 26a; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Guides and theme"; "A variable's label becomes its axis title").

## 13 November 2026: `theme` (release 0.7.0, step 26b)

**Decision.** `p.theme(name: journal | minimal | slide, base_size:)` sets the theme a figure is drawn by. It is held with the plot (`Plot.theme`) and carried by the scene (`Scene.theme`; the key `theme` of its JSON, written when it is not `journal` at its own size, so an earlier scene reads as it did). The writer of a figure builds the theme from it (`Theme::of` in `packages/tier1/plot/src/layout.rs`) where it used the constant `JOURNAL`; `journal` with no base size is that constant, value for value, which a test asserts, and no figure of an earlier step changes by a byte.

**The three themes** (rulings where the text is silent, each the owner's to overturn; the catalogue says of a theme "white background, major gridlines only, text in points" and no more). (a) `journal` is the theme frozen at step 22. (b) `minimal` is `journal` without the lines of the two axes and without their ticks: an axis is its labels and its title, the labels a tick nearer the panel, and the gridlines carry the eye. The theme has a new value for it, `axis_lines`. (c) `slide` is `journal` at a base size of 18 points, twice that of an article, for the size `slide` of `export` (254 by 143 mm). (d) The three share one page, one ink and one grey of gridlines: a theme of another colour is not among the three.

**The base size.** It is the size of the titles of the axes and legends, 9 points in `journal`, as the catalogue's `base_size: Float = 9` has it; every other size of the theme is a fixed share of it: the labels eight ninths, the title of the figure ten ninths, and the widths of lines, the lengths of ticks, the margins, the gaps and the bar of a continuous scale in the same proportion. The default of `slide` is 18 and not 9: the usage line's `= 9` holds for the two other themes, and the help page says so. A base size below 9 is refused, since the labels would be set below 8 points, which no text of a figure is (the rule of step 21b).

**What a theme does not size: the marks.** The diameter of a point and the width of a line are given in points by the marks (`size:`, `width:`), and a scene holds them as it holds the data. A larger base size leaves them as they are, as ggplot2's `base_size` does, so on a slide the type is twice as large and a point of the default size is not. The help page says to give the marks a size to match. Scaling them with the theme would make `size: 6` mean two things; scaling only the sizes the script did not write would need the scene to tell a default from a number that was written, which it does not. The question is the owner's if he wants the marks of a slide larger by default.

**What is said last replaces all that was said**: `theme(base_size: 12)` after `theme(slide)` is `journal` at 12 points.

**The printed plot** says the theme on its last line when it is not `journal` at its own size.

**The sample script.** The specification's sample writes `.theme(journal)`. The two stored checks of that script lose the line "no function is called `theme`" and nothing else.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/themes.rs`: five tests (`journal` is the frozen theme; every size in proportion to the base size, eleven of them, with the colours and the leading unchanged, and `slide` at 18; the theme in the scene and its JSON, with the scales and marks unchanged; `minimal` with no line and no tick, every label still written, the gridlines kept and the panel larger by a tick each way, with a snapshot of the drawing; a slide with labels at 16 and titles at 18 points and the points at their own 4.5, with a snapshot, and a base size of 12 on one column). `printing.rs`: nine plots and seven messages. The two examples of the page of `theme` are run. The conformance set gains six cases: what a script prints, the minimal figure in SVG, PDF and PNG, and a slide in SVG.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 483 is marked `implemented`; its usage line is as it was.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 26b; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Guides and theme": "One default theme: white background, major gridlines only, no chart junk").

## 13 November 2026: `annotate`, and the labels of a crowded axis (release 0.7.0, step 26c); step 26 complete

**`annotate`.** `p.annotate(text:, x:, y:, size:)` writes one text at a place of the data. It is a layer of the mark `text` of one row, in a frame of its own called `annotation` with the variables `x`, `y` and `text`, which the function makes and the scene and the writers treat as any layer of text: nothing new is drawn, and an annotation is placed by the scales of the plot whatever they are. The printed plot reads such a layer as what it is, `"steepest here" at 2.5, 1.2, size 8`.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) A place is of the kind its axis holds: a number on an axis of numbers, the name of a category the axis has on an axis of categories, a date on an axis of dates; another kind, and a category the axis lacks, are refused with the nearest name offered. The catalogue's usage line is widened for it (logged). (b) An annotation counts for the limits of the axes, as a mark does and as ggplot2's `annotate` does: a text placed beyond the data widens the axis. (c) The text is centred on its place and cut off at the edge of the panel, as the marks are; the help page says to place it further in or to widen the limits. (d) `size:` is the size of the type in points, 8 where it is left out, and the base size of a theme does not change it, as it changes no mark. (e) The plot must map something to `x` and to `y` first: a place needs its axis. (f) The words must not be empty.

**The labels of a crowded axis.** The checklist asks for labels "wrapped or thinned, never overlapping". Thinning was built at step 21b for both axes: labels that would touch are passed over, every second or third being written, with a tick at every break. This step adds the wrapping, along `x`, for an axis of categories: each label wider than its place is broken between words, a word longer than the place standing alone on its line; where the broken labels can then all be written without touching, in three lines at most, they are written so and the panel gives up the room of the lines; where even so some would have to be passed over, the labels stay whole on one line and are thinned as before. All or none: an axis on which some labels are broken and others left out reserved room for lines that were not written, which the first form of the rule did. An axis of numbers or of dates is not wrapped. No drawing of an earlier step changes: where labels were thinned before, breaking them would not have let all be written.

**What is not done.** A figure whose axis of categories has labels passed over says nothing of it: the layout knows which labels it left out, and the writer of a figure returns bytes and no notes. Turning the labels on their side is not among the three themes; the categories along `y`, where each has a line of its own, is the remedy today, and `coord(flip)` of step 27 will make it one word.

**Step 26 is complete**: `labels` (26a), `theme` (26b), `annotate` and the crowded axis (26c). `plot` stands at nineteen functions built.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/crowded.rs`: four tests of the layout (five regions written on two or three lines, word for word, a line apart, none touching, with a snapshot of the drawing; a word too long for its place, where the labels stay whole and some are passed over, and all four written on a page of two columns; two hundred categories on three sizes of page and along `y`, evenly passed over, none touching, a tick at each; an axis of numbers as it was). `printing.rs`: nine plots with annotations at a number, a category and a date, beyond the data, twice on one plot and on a log scale, and fifteen messages. The two examples of the page of `annotate` are run. The conformance set gains six cases: what a script prints, an annotated series in SVG, PDF and PNG, and the broken labels in SVG.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 484 (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`) is marked `implemented`.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 26c; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Guides and theme"; "Defaults": labels never overlapping).

## 13 November 2026: `coord(cartesian | flip)` (release 0.7.0, step 27a), and step 27 split in five

**The split.** Step 27 of the checklist held two functions with seven behaviours between them, three coordinate systems and four arrangements of panels, each of which changes the layout. It is split by the rule that a step too large is split and not pushed through: 27a `coord(cartesian | flip)`, 27b `coord(fixed, ratio:)`, 27c `coord(polar)`, 27d `facet(by:)`, 27e `facet(rows:, cols:)` with the four `scales:`. Step 27 is done when the five are.

**What a flip is.** The coordinates are held by the plot (`Plot.coord`) and carried by the scene. A flipped scene is the upright scene with one word more: its scales, their limits and breaks, and the positions of every mark are those of the data, untouched. The scene says `"coord": "flip"`, a key written only when the coordinates are not cartesian, as the other optional keys of version 1 are, and gives the axis of `x` the left side and the axis of `y` the foot. The layout does the rest: it lays the marks in the frame of the data, as wide as the panel is high, and turns each drawing primitive onto the page by one function (`turned`: a place `u` across and `v` down in the frame is at the left of the panel plus the frame's height less `v`, and at its top plus the frame's width less `u`). Points, segments, polygons and paths with their curves and arcs are turned; text is placed on the page directly and stays upright. Nothing of a writer changed: SVG, PDF and PNG draw the primitives they are given.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) `coord` sets the coordinates and does not toggle them: `flip` written twice is still flipped, and a later `coord(cartesian)` stands the plot up again, as a later coordinate system replaces an earlier one in ggplot2. (b) The first category of `x`, and its smallest number, is at the foot of the side, as the smallest number of `y` is in an upright plot and as `coord_flip()` has it. (c) A mark reads its positions as in the upright plot: bars start from zero along `y`, `hline` is a line at a value of `y` and so runs down the flipped panel, a `step` holds `y` while `x` moves; the sizes of points and the widths of lines are unchanged. (d) `legend(direct)` writes names at the right-hand ends of lines; in a flipped plot the lines end at the top, so the legend is drawn at the right in its place and nothing is refused. (e) Labels at the left, those of `x` in a flipped plot, are written whole on one line each and never broken; where they leave no room for a panel the figure is refused by the message the layout already had, which says the room there was. Labels along the foot of a flipped plot, those of `y`, are broken or thinned exactly as those of `x` are upright. (f) The printed plot keeps its table of axes in the names of the script, `x` and `y`, and says "coordinates: flipped, `x` up the side and `y` along the foot" on a line of its own.

**What is not built yet.** `coord(polar)`, `coord(fixed)` and `ratio:` are refused with "is not built yet: it comes with a later step of this release" (steps 27b and 27c). The help page says so. Catalogue row 479 stays `planned` until step 27c completes the function and its page.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/coords.rs`: eight tests and one property (the scene carries the coordinates, puts each axis on its side and is otherwise the upright scene; twelve bars with long names lie along the page from the zero of `y`, the first at the foot, every name written at the left, with a snapshot of the drawing; a line across becomes a line down and each text stays upright at its point; a log scale runs up the side with equal ratios at equal distances, and `legend(direct)` falls back to the right; every mark drawn in the units of the data, twelve cases over points, lines, the three steps, area, ribbon, the two reference lines, bars stacked and side by side, and tiles, has its corners where the upright plot has them with the two shares exchanged; a flipped plot with its two positions exchanged is the upright picture, line for line; the rug of `x` stands at the left; and, whatever the rows, a flipped point stands at the shares of its two values). One unit test of `turned` in the layout. `tests/printing.rs`: the printed plot in seven forms, an export, and every message of `coord` (eight). Two verified examples in the help page. One conformance case (`plot/coord`: what the script prints and four figures), which brings `zeff selftest` to 390 of 390.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27a; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Coordinates": `coord(flip | polar | fixed)`); catalogue row 479.

## 13 November 2026: `coord(fixed, ratio:)` (release 0.7.0, step 27b)

**What fixed coordinates are.** `Coord::Fixed(ratio)` in the plot and the scene: cartesian, with one unit of `y` as long on the page as `ratio` units of `x`, the meaning ggplot2 gives `coord_fixed(ratio = )`. The scene is the cartesian scene with `"coord": "fixed"` and `"ratio"`, two keys written only then; its scales, limits, breaks and marks are untouched. The layout gives the panel its shape: its height is to its width as the units `y` runs over between its limits, times the ratio, are to the units `x` runs over (`scale::units`). The panel is the largest of that shape that the room holds, the room being the panel the same plot would have without fixed coordinates; the titles of the axes are broken to the sides of the shaped panel, in the two rounds the layout already had.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) A unit: one on an axis of numbers; the place of one category; a power of ten on a log axis, as ggplot2 has it for a transformed scale, so that a slope of one on the page is an elasticity of one; one of the square root on a square-root axis; a day on an axis of dates, whether it holds dates or times. (b) `ratio:` belongs to `fixed`: with `cartesian`, `flip` or no word it is refused and the message gives the call to write; left out with `fixed` it is 1; zero, a number below zero and what is not finite are refused. (c) The panel stands in the middle of its room, across and down, and what belongs to it goes with it: the labels and titles of the two axes, a legend at the right, the legends above or under the panel, the names at the ends of lines. The title, the subtitle and the caption of the figure and its notes stay at the edges of the page, where step 26a put them. (d) A panel less than 12.7 mm wide or high, the smallest the layout draws, is refused when the figure is written, by a message of its own (`LayoutError::TooThin`): it says how many times as high as wide the panel is, its size on the page, and the ratio, to two figures, at which the panel fills the page; a page too small for any panel is still said to be too small. The printed plot refuses nothing: the shape depends on the page. (e) Fixed and flipped together are not offered: the catalogue has one word for the coordinates, as a plot of ggplot2 has one coordinate system.

**Nothing drawn before has moved.** The panel is moved by half the room it leaves, which is nothing without fixed coordinates: the 390 earlier conformance cases and every stored drawing are byte for byte as they were.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/coords.rs`: five tests and one property more (the scene carries the ratio and is otherwise the cartesian scene; a square of the data is a square on the page, and at four ratios a unit of `y` is that many times a unit of `x`, with a snapshot of the drawing; the panel keeps one side of its room and stands in the middle of the other, with the labels and title of `y` and the legend as far from it as they were; a unit on an axis of categories, a log axis, a square-root axis and an axis of dates; a panel a thousand times as wide as it is high refused, drawn at the ratio the refusal names as the room itself, the other way refused too, and a page too small still said to be too small; and, whatever the rows and the ratio, a unit of `y` is as long as the ratio says, the panel no larger than its room and as large as it one way, or the panel was too thin). `tests/printing.rs`: the printed plot in eight forms, an export in the three formats, and the messages of `coord` now eleven (a ratio without `fixed`, with `flip`, of zero, below zero, a panel too thin and one too flat are new; "`fixed` is not built yet" is gone, as the step ends that refusal). Two more verified examples in the help page. One conformance case (`plot/fixed`), which brings `zeff selftest` to 396 of 396.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 479 stays `planned` until step 27c completes the function.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27b; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Coordinates"); catalogue row 479.

## 13 November 2026: the polar frame (release 0.7.0, step 27c1), and step 27c split in two

**The split.** Polar coordinates change the scales, the layout of the panel, every mark and both axes. The step is split by the rule that a step too large is split: 27c1, the frame (the scene, the circle, the marks wound, the gridlines), reached by the tests and by no script; 27c2, the guides (the labels round the rim, the axis of `y`, the titles), what polar coordinates refuse, and the function opened with its messages, its help page and a conformance case. Until 27c2 `coord(polar)` answers "is not built yet", so no script sees a circle without labels.

**What polar coordinates are.** `Coord::Polar`: `x` is the angle, which starts at the top of the circle and turns clockwise, once round over the limits of `x`; `y` is the distance from the centre, its lower limit at the centre and its upper on the rim. The catalogue gives `coord` no argument to say otherwise; open decision #132 asks whether it should.

**The scales of a polar scene have no margin** (rulings, the owner's to overturn; they are ggplot2's, except the second half of (b)). (a) An axis of numbers or dates runs from the lowest value to the highest exactly, where a cartesian axis adds a twentieth at each end: the angle then goes once round over the data, with the lowest and the highest value of `x` together at the top, so that the hours 0 to 24 or the days of a year close the circle; and bars, which start at zero, start at the centre. A script that wants the circle to end elsewhere sets `limits:` with `scale_x`, which are kept as given. (b) An axis of categories runs half a place beyond its first and last category, where a cartesian one runs 0.6: round the circle each category has the same share, and along the radius the first category is a disc round the centre and each of the others a ring of the same width (ggplot2 puts the first category at the centre itself, where a tile has no room). (c) One value alone, and values that a log or square-root axis cannot place, keep the limits they have elsewhere. This is the one place where the scales of a scene depend on its coordinates.

**The layout.** The panel is a square, the largest the room holds, in the middle of that room, by the machinery of fixed coordinates; the circle is in the middle of the square, with room between its rim and the square for the labels of step 27c2. The marks are drawn in a frame that is the circle unrolled, as wide as the rim is long and as high as the radius, by the code that draws them in cartesian coordinates, and each drawing primitive is wound onto the page by one function (`wound`): a place `u` along the frame and `v` down it stands at the angle `u` over the radius and at the radius less `v` from the centre. A straight line of the frame becomes an arc where it runs level, a piece of a radius where it runs upright and a spiral between, and is drawn as straight pieces of two degrees at most, at which a chord of a circle a hundred points across is a hundredth of a point from its arc; polygons, rectangles and paths are wound edge by edge, a curve as sixteen lines. The sine and cosine are the engine's own (`zeff_numeric::maths`), so the bytes of a figure are the same on every machine. A point keeps its shape and its size, and a text is placed at its wound place and stays upright.

**What is beyond the limits** a script sets. A panel cuts off what is beyond its edge, and a drawing has no clip in the shape of a circle. So a mark with an extent, a bar, a line, a band, is brought to the edge of the frame, which is the rim, the centre, or the two ends of the turn: a bar higher than the upper limit ends at the rim. A point or a text beyond the limits is not drawn. The scene's note counts them as it does in cartesian coordinates.

**The gridlines.** A spoke from the centre to the rim at each break of `x`, the two ends of an axis of numbers being one spoke drawn once; a circle at each break of `y` that is not the centre itself, as two half turns of an arc.

**`legend(direct)`** in polar coordinates is drawn at the right, as in flipped ones: a line has no right-hand end beside the panel.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/coords.rs`: eight tests and one property more (the limits of a polar scene: numbers, categories on either axis, bars from zero, a log axis, one value alone, limits the script sets, and the line of the printed plot; the grid as spokes and circles in a square panel in the middle of its room; four bars as wedges of one circle, each a quarter less a tenth, from the centre to the share of its value, with a snapshot; one category as a wedge of nine tenths of the circle; a line of the hours of a day wound round the centre, on the rim from the first hour and ending where it began; a line across as a circle of 180 pieces and a line down as a spoke; tiles as pieces of rings with their texts upright in their middles; what is beyond the limits staying in the circle; and, whatever the rows, a point at the angle and the distance its two values give). One unit test of `wound` in the layout. The message "`coord(polar)` is not built yet" is still pinned.

**The specification.** Open decision #132 is recorded, with its recommendation taken. Catalogue row 479 stays `planned` until step 27c2.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27c1; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Coordinates": `coord(flip | polar | fixed)`).

## 13 November 2026: the guides of a polar plot, and `coord(polar)` opened (release 0.7.0, step 27c2); step 27c complete

**The function.** `p.coord(polar)` sets `Coord::Polar`; the refusal "is not built yet" is gone, and with it the last of its kind in `coord`. `ratio:` with `polar` is refused as with any coordinates but `fixed`.

**The panel of a polar plot** (this replaces the square of step 27c1, which left no circle beside long names). The room is what the page leaves after its margins, the labels and title of `y` at the left, the title of `x` under the panel, and the legends; no row is kept under the panel for labels of `x`, which are round the rim. In that room the circle is the largest for which every label of `x` stays in the room: a label stands a tick and a gap out from the rim at the angle of its break, reaching sideways by its width (half of it where it is centred) and half a letter more, and upwards or downwards by the height of its lines.
