The panel is then as wide as the circle and its labels need at the two sides and as high as they need at the top and the foot, with the circle in its middle, and it stands in the middle of the room by the machinery of fixed coordinates, so that the axis of `y`, the titles and the legends go with it. A circle of less than 12.7 mm across is refused as a page too small.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) The labels of `x` are upright, never turned to follow the rim: at the right of the circle a label starts at its tick, at the left it ends there, and within about eleven degrees of the top or the foot it is centred on it; it stands over the rim at the top, under it at the foot, and level with its tick at the sides. (b) A label wider than a quarter of the room is broken between words, into three lines at most, as the labels of a crowded axis have been since step 26c; with it the twelve industries of the shipped wages have a circle 23 mm across on a figure of one column, which names left whole would make smaller still. (c) Where two labels would touch, every second, or third, is written, the first step at which none of those written touches another, the last and the first of the round among them; every break keeps its tick. (d) The two ends of an axis of numbers are one place, the top: a break at each is one tick and one label that names both with a stroke between, `0/24`, as ggplot2 writes it. (e) The axis of `y` stands at the left edge of the panel, beside the radius that goes up from the centre, as ggplot2 draws it: its line from the height of the top of the rim down to that of the centre, a tick at the height of each circle of the grid, its labels ending at the ticks, its title turned and centred on the panel. Labels along a spoke, inside the circle, were weighed and set aside: they lie on the marks. (f) The rim is the line of the axis of `x`, drawn in `journal` and `slide` with a tick outwards at each break, and not drawn in `minimal`, which has no line of an axis. (g) The title of `x` is under the panel, centred on the circle. (h) A rug in polar coordinates is refused, whichever of `rug` and `coord(polar)` is written last, at the call that brings the two together: its ticks stand along the straight edges of a panel. ggplot2 refuses it too.

**The first and last of a round that do not close.** The years 2010 to 2021 round a circle put 2010 and 2021 at one angle, as ggplot2 does; the help page says to give the axis room with `scale_x(limits:)`. An axis that knew its values were a cycle could do better, and nothing in the catalogue says so today; it belongs with open decision #132.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/coords.rs`: six tests more (six names round the rim, each beside its tick, upright, outside the rim and in the panel, by the right anchor, with the rim and its six ticks and a snapshot of the drawing; the two ends of an axis sharing the top, written once as `0/24` with one tick; a long name broken, and two hundred categories with a tick each and every so many labels written, none touching; the axis of `y` beside the upward radius with its ticks at the heights of the circles, and the two titles; `minimal` with no rim and no tick, and `legend(direct)` at the right; a page too small for a circle and its labels refused, and drawn on a larger page). The test of the grid at step 27c1 no longer asks for a square panel, which this step ends on purpose. `tests/printing.rs`: the printed plot in six forms with the limits of each, an export in the three formats and on a slide, and the messages of `coord` now fourteen (a ratio with `polar`, a rug before and after `polar`, and a page too small are new; "`coord(polar)` is not built yet" is gone). Two more verified examples in the help page, which is complete. One conformance case (`plot/polar`: what the script prints and five figures), which brings `zeff selftest` to 403 of 403.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 479 is marked `implemented`; its usage line is as it was.

**Step 27c is complete**: the polar frame (27c1) and its guides (27c2). `coord` has its four forms, `cartesian`, `flip`, `fixed` and `polar`; `plot` stands at twenty functions built.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27c2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Coordinates"); catalogue row 479.

## 13 November 2026: a scene of more than one panel (release 0.7.0, step 27d1), and step 27d split in three

**The split.** `facet(by:)` needs a scene of several panels, a layout that draws them, and the function. Each is a step: 27d1 the scene, reached by the tests alone; 27d2 the layout; 27d3 the function with its messages, its help page and a conformance case. Until 27d3 no function is called `facet`.

**The facets of a plot.** `Plot.facet`, the variables its rows are parted by (`PlotFacet { by }`). The scene format had its panels, each with a row and a column, since step 20; a panel now also has what is written over it (`strip`), and the scene says the strips of its panels in one key, `"strips"`, written only for a plot with facets, so that the scene of every other plot is byte for byte as it was.

**How the marks are parted.** The marks of a layer are built once, over all its rows, by the code that builds them for one panel, and then dealt to the panels by the row each is drawn from. Three kinds of mark depend on their neighbours, and each is kept within its panel where it is built: a line, an area and a band are parted into groups by the panel as they are by a colour, so no line joins two panels; bars that share a place are stacked, or set side by side, among the bars of their own panel (the panel goes before the place in the order `bars` arranges them by); stacked areas are stacked panel by panel. Everything else is as in a plot without facets, which gives three things for nothing: the scales are trained over all the panels, so that the panels share them; the width of a bar and of a tile, a share of the smallest gap between two places, is that of the whole layer, as in ggplot2; and each note counts over all the panels, once.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) A panel for each value of the variable that the plot's frame holds, in the order of its categories, the order an axis or a legend has them in; a value that only the frame of a layer holds is a panel more, after those. (b) A row without a value of the variable has a panel of its own, the last of its frame, with `NA` written over it, as a row without a colour is drawn in the colour of `NA` and not dropped. (c) What is written over a panel is the value label where the variable has one and the value as it prints where it has none (decision #118, F8); with several variables there is a panel for each combination that is there, the values written with a comma between. (d) A layer whose frame lacks a variable of the facets, a line across at a number, an annotation, a layer with `data:` of its own, is drawn whole in every panel, as in ggplot2. (e) The panels are laid in rows from the top left: one row up to three panels, two up to six, three up to twelve, and beyond that as many columns as the square root of their number rounded up, which is how ggplot2's `facet_wrap` lays them; forty panels are six rows of seven. (f) A variable the plot's frame does not hold parts nothing; the function will refuse it at step 27d3. (g) The printed plot counts the marks of each layer over all its panels and says "panels: 3 by site" on a line of its own.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/facets.rs`: eight tests and one property (three sites as three panels with their rows, places and strips, on the scales of the plot without facets, with a snapshot of the scene; the rows and columns for 1 to 40 panels; bars stacked, side by side and counted within their panel; a line in each panel and none between, and stacked areas equal to each site drawn alone; a line across, and a layer with a frame of its own, in every panel, and a layer parted by its own frame with a panel more; an empty panel, a row without a value, value labels and two variables; one panel, forty panels, and a variable the frame lacks; the printed plot; and, whatever the rows, every row that is drawn in exactly one panel, that of its category, at the same place, with the same scales and notes).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27d1; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Facets"); decision #118, F8.

## 13 November 2026: the layout of several panels (release 0.7.0, step 27d2)

**One grid.** The layout draws the page as before, its margins, titles, notes and legends, and in the room that is left a grid of cells, one for each panel of the scene. The part of the layout that drew the one panel, its gridlines, its marks behind their clip and its two axes, is now run once for each cell; nothing of it was written a second time. A plot of one panel is a grid of one, and every figure drawn before is byte for byte as it was: the 403 conformance cases and every stored drawing are unchanged.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) The panels are of one size, a gap apart: a line and a half of the labels down the page, and across it as much as the last label of one panel and the first of the next need to stand clear of each other. (b) What is written over a panel is plain text of the size of the labels, centred over it, with no band behind it: the theme has nothing drawn for ornament. (c) The labels of `y` are written beside the first panel of each row and those of `x` under the lowest panel of each column, which in a last row that is not full is the panel above the gap; every panel keeps the line and the ticks of its axes. In polar panels the labels round the rim are written in every panel, for they are inside it. (d) Each axis has its title once, centred on the grid and broken to its width or height. (e) The grid of panels stands in the middle of the room, as one fixed panel has done since step 27b: fixed and polar panels stand together and not each in the middle of a cell of its own, and the axes, their titles and the legends go with the grid. (f) `legend(direct)` in a plot of several panels is drawn at the right, as in flipped and polar plots. (g) The scene says how the panels follow one another (`wrapped`, written only then): where its grid, which is ggplot2's, would leave each panel less than the 12.7 mm a panel needs, the layout lays them in the nearest number of columns that does not, more columns before fewer. Forty panels on a page of two columns are four rows of ten and not six of seven. A grid whose rows and columns each mean a value, which step 27e builds, is never laid otherwise. (h) Where no number of columns gives the panels their room, the figure is refused when it is written, by a message of its own (`LayoutError::TooMany`) that says how many panels there are and what each is left.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/facets.rs`: four tests and one property more (twelve panels in three rows of four, in line, with their strips, the labels of `y` beside the first of each row, those of `x` under the last row, each title once, the points of each panel in it, with a snapshot of the drawing; five panels with a last row that is not full, and one panel with its strip; forty panels on two columns, none overlapping, all on the page, and refused on one; flipped, fixed and polar panels, the legend at the right of the grid, fixed panels together in the middle of the room and each polar panel with its rim labels; and, whatever the rows, as many panels as the scene has, of one size, none overlapping, on the page, each with its points, or a page too small). A faceted plot of a frame with no row has one panel: found by the property, and fixed in the scene.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27d2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Facets"; "Guides and theme").

## 13 November 2026: `facet(by:)` opened (release 0.7.0, step 27d3); step 27d complete

**The function.** `p.facet(by: Var | Vars, rows: Var, cols: Var, scales: fixed | free | free_x | free_y = fixed)`, registered with the catalogue's usage line. It sets the facets of the plot (`Plot.facet`) and gives the plot back; the scene and the layout of steps 27d1 and 27d2 do the rest. At this step `by:` is the whole of it: `rows:`, `cols:` and the three free `scales:` are refused with "is not built yet: it comes with a later step of this release", which step 27e ends.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) `facet` without `by:` is refused (Z0406), with the two forms of the call in the help. (b) Every variable of `by:` must be one of the plot's frame, and is refused by the message every function has for a variable the frame lacks. (c) A variable named twice in `by:` is refused: it would write each value twice over every panel. (d) What a later `facet` says takes the place of what an earlier one said, as with `coord`, `theme` and `legend`. (e) Any variable parts a plot, whatever its type: a number has a panel for each of its values, as it has a category for each on an axis of categories; the page then says whether they fit. (f) The printed plot says "panels: 2 by site: north, south": how many, the variables with "and" between, and what is written over the panels, the first five and a count where there are more than six; a plot parted by a variable of one value says so too.

**A correction in passing.** The declared diagnostics of `coord` still said "polar, fixed and ratio:, which are not built yet", which steps 27b and 27c2 had made untrue; they now say what `coord` refuses: a ratio that is not above 0 or goes without `fixed`, and a rug in polar coordinates.

**Against R.** For the help page's example, ggplot2 4.0.3 (`facet_wrap(~ site)`) has the same two panels in the same order, the same shared limits (0.95 to 2.05 and 3.75 to 9.25; with bars 0.455 to 2.545 and -0.45 to 9.45), the line across in both panels, and for 3, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 40 panels the rows and columns of the scene.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/printing.rs`: the printed plot in seven forms (one variable, two, `scales: fixed`, a later `facet`, with bars flipped and a legend above, a line and a reference line with a title, one value), an export in the three formats and of six polar panels, and every message of `facet` (thirteen). Two verified examples in the help page. One conformance case (`plot/facet`: what the script prints and five figures), which brings `zeff selftest` to 410 of 410. The two stored checks of the specification's sample script lose "no function is called `facet`".

**The specification.** Catalogue row 480 stays `planned` until step 27e completes the function.

**Step 27d is complete**: the scene of several panels (27d1), their layout (27d2) and `facet(by:)` (27d3).

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27d3; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Facets"); catalogue row 480.

## 13 November 2026: `facet(rows:, cols:)` (release 0.7.0, step 27e1), and step 27e split in two

**The split.** A grid of panels and free scales are two things, each with its scene, its layout and its part of the function: 27e1 the grid, 27e2 `scales: free | free_x | free_y`. Step 27 is done when 27e2 is.

**The grid.** `PlotFacet` holds the variable of the rows and that of the columns beside the variables of `by:`. The parting of step 27d1 now gives each panel its row, its column, what is written over it and what is written beside it; a grid has a panel for every pair of a row and a column, numbered row by row, and the rest of the scene builder deals the marks to the panels as before. A panel of the scene has `side` beside `strip`, and the scene says the sides of its panels in one key, `"sides"`, written only for a grid with rows. A grid is not `wrapped`: the layout lays it as the scene has it.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) Every cell of the grid is a panel, whether a row of the data falls in it or not, as in ggplot2's `facet_grid`: an empty cell is drawn with its gridlines and axes, so that the rows and the columns of the page each mean one value. (b) The values of a variable are those some row holds, in the order of their categories, a row without one last as `NA`; a level of a Category that no row has gives no row or column. (c) The values of the columns are written over the panels of the first row, and those of the rows beside the panels of the last column, read downwards, where ggplot2 writes them; the room for them is taken once, at the top and at the right, and not in every row as for panels that follow one another. (d) `rows:` alone is one column of panels, `cols:` alone one row. (e) A layer is parted where its frame holds both variables of the grid; a layer that lacks either is drawn whole in every panel (ggplot2 repeats such a layer along the variable it lacks, which the catalogue's two arguments do not ask for). (f) `by:` with `rows:` or `cols:` is refused, with the two calls it could have meant; one variable for both `rows:` and `cols:` is refused; `facet` with none of the three says it needs one. (g) The printed plot says "panels: 6, 3 rows by site (east, north, south) and 2 columns by arm (a, b)".

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/facets.rs`: three tests more (three sites by two arms as six panels in their places, with what is written over and beside them, their rows and the scales of the plot without facets, with a snapshot of the scene; a cell with no row, a row without a value, rows alone, columns alone, a layer that lacks the variables, and a variable the frame lacks; the grid on the page, with the columns named above and the rows at the right, read downwards, each at the middle of its row, the rows a gap apart, never laid otherwise and refused on a page too small, with a snapshot of the drawing). `tests/printing.rs`: the printed plot in six forms, an export in the three formats, and the messages of `facet` now eighteen (a grid with `by:`, one variable down and across, a row the frame lacks, a column in quotation marks, two variables down and a grid too large for the page are new; "`rows:` is not built yet" and "`cols:` is not built yet" are gone). One more verified example in the help page. One conformance case (`plot/grid`), which brings `zeff selftest` to 416 of 416.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27e1; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Facets": `facet(by:, rows:, cols:, scales:)`); catalogue row 480.

## 13 November 2026: `scales: free | free_x | free_y` (release 0.7.0, step 27e2); steps 27e and 27 complete

**Axes of their own.** `PlotFacet.scales` holds the word of the script (`FacetScales`). A panel of the scene may carry a scale of `x` and a scale of `y` of its own (`own_x`, `own_y`): the scale of the plot, with its kind and its title, and with the limits, breaks and labels of the marks of that panel alone. The code that builds an axis of numbers or dates from the extent of the marks was made a piece of its own in the scene builder (`numbered`), run once for the plot as before and once more for each panel, row or column with an axis of its own; nothing it gives for the plot has changed. The scales of the plot stay in the scene as they were, and the scene says the panels' own in one key, `"own_scales"`, written only then. The layout draws each panel by its own scales where it has them.

**Rulings where the text is silent**, each of which the owner may overturn. (a) With `by:`, each panel has its own axis; in a grid of `rows:` and `cols:` each row of panels has its own `y` and each column its own `x`, as in ggplot2's `facet_grid`, so that an axis still runs along a whole row or column. (b) An axis of categories is never free: every panel keeps a place for every category, where ggplot2 drops the categories a panel lacks. The places of the categories are the plot's, and a mark keeps its place; dropping them belongs with an argument of its own, if it is wanted. (c) A panel with no mark has the axis of the whole variable. (d) Limits and breaks that `scale_x` or `scale_y` set hold in every panel. (e) Bars and areas start at zero in every panel, as in a plot of their own. (f) The labels of an axis are written at the edge of the grid, as before, and wherever the axis of a panel is not that of its neighbour: beside a panel whose scale up the side differs from that of the panel at its left, and under one whose scale along the foot differs from that of the panel below. Panels that follow one another with free scales stand further apart, by the room of those labels; a grid keeps its gaps, for its labels stay at the edges. (g) Free scales are refused in `fixed` and `polar` coordinates, whichever of `facet` and `coord` is written last: there the scales give a panel its shape or its circle, and ggplot2 refuses them too. Flipped coordinates take them. (h) The printed plot says which axes the panels have of their own, and its table of axes stays that of the whole plot.

**Against R.** For the help page's example, ggplot2 4.0.3 (`facet_wrap(~ site, scales = "free_y")`) gives the north the limits 3.95 to 5.05 and the south 69 to 91, which are those of each site drawn alone in Zeff; `x` is shared at 0.95 to 2.05 in both.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/tests/facets.rs`: four tests and one property more (three sites with `y` free, each with the scale of its rows drawn alone, the scales and marks of the plot unchanged, then `free_x` and `free`, with a snapshot of the scene; an axis of categories shared, bars from zero in every panel, and a panel with no mark; a grid whose rows share a `y` and whose columns share an `x`; the labels of a free axis in every panel, the panels further apart for them, the shared axis labelled once, and flipped, with a snapshot of the drawing; and, whatever the rows, every point within the limits of the scales of its own panel and drawn inside it). `tests/printing.rs`: the printed plot in eight forms, an export in the three formats, and the messages of `facet` now twenty-one (free scales in fixed coordinates, fixed coordinates after free scales, free scales in polar coordinates and scales in quotation marks are new; "`scales: free_y` is not built yet" is gone). One more verified example in the help page, which is complete. One conformance case (`plot/free`, with the specification's sample), which brings `zeff selftest` to 422 of 422.

**The specification.** Catalogue row 480 is marked `implemented`; its usage line is as it was.

**Step 27 is complete**: `coord` (27a flipped, 27b fixed, 27c polar) and `facet` (27d panels by a variable, 27e a grid and free scales). `plot` stands at twenty-one functions built.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 27e2; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Facets": "panels share scales unless told otherwise"); catalogue row 480.

## 13 November 2026: `histogram` (release 0.7.0, step 28a), and step 28 split in four

**The split.** Step 28 is four functions, each with its numbers checked against R: 28a `histogram`, 28b `density`, 28c `boxplot`, 28d `errorbars`. The grammar stands at 25 of 25 when the four are done.

**A layer that computes.** A layer may now hold what it computes from its rows before it draws them (`PlotLayer.stat`); a histogram holds its rule, its width, its start and its scale (`Stat::Bins`). It is drawn as bars, by the mark `bars` and everything that draws it, so that nothing of the layout or of a writer changed; the scene builder counts the rows in bins where a layer of bars holds a `stat`. The bins themselves are a module of their own (`bins`).

**The bins** (rulings where the text is silent, each the owner's to overturn). (a) They are of one width and begin at `start:`, which is the smallest value where the script says nothing, as Stata's `histogram` has them. R's `hist` moves the edges to round numbers (`pretty`), so that its bins are other bins even where their number is the same; the checklist's reference test, "`hist` on the same breaks", is met by giving `hist` these breaks. (b) With a number of bins, or a rule, the bins reach from the start to the largest value exactly; with `binwidth:` there are as many as reach it, and `bins:` is not read, as in ggplot2. (c) A bin holds its left edge and not its right, and the last holds both, as Stata's and as `hist(right = FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE)`. The end of the last bin is kept and not worked out again from the start and the width, so that the largest value is counted whatever the rounding: a property test found two values and one bin that lost the larger. (d) The three rules give the numbers of bins of `nclass.Sturges`, `nclass.scott` and `nclass.FD`, the last with R's rounding to five figures and its wider quantiles where the interquartile range is zero. The cube root is the engine's own power function. (e) Values that are all one value have one bin, one unit wide, round the value. (f) `start:` above the smallest value is refused, with the value: the rows below it would be in no bin. (g) A histogram has a thousand bins at most (`MOST_BINS`): a number or a width that asks for more is refused, and a rule that asks for more, as Freedman and Diaconis's does where one value lies far from all the others, is given a thousand with a note. Without a limit such a series asks for millions of bins, which the first run of the property test did.

**The scale.** `count`, `density` (the count over the number of rows and the width), `fraction` and `percent`. The number of rows is that of the panel, over all its groups: where the plot fills by categories each bin has a bar for each, stacked, the first on top, and the stack is the histogram of all the rows, of area one under `density`. ggplot2 scales each group by itself, which makes a stack of area as many as there are groups. The axis of `y` is named by the scale.

**What a histogram takes.** The variable the plot maps to `x`, which must be numbers; a plot that maps `y` is refused, for a histogram has its own. An axis of dates has no histogram yet: `binwidth:` would need a unit of time, which the usage line does not have. In a plot parted into panels the bins are those of all the rows of the layer, the same in every panel.

**The printed plot** names the layer `histogram` and says its bins: "5 bins of 1.6 from 1".

**Against R** (4.6.0). On five series (200 values, 57 with ties, forty equal values with two apart, a thousand spread evenly, ten equal) the three rules give `nclass.Sturges`, `nclass.scott` and `nclass.FD`; on the first, the counts and the densities are those of `hist` on the same breaks to thirteen places. For the help page's ten scores R gives five bins by Freedman and Diaconis, 1.6 wide from 1, as here.

**Tests.** `packages/tier1/plot/src/bins.rs`: three unit tests (the three rules on the five series; the counts and densities of `hist`; a width, a start, an edge, values that are one value, no value, the limit, and the largest value in the last bin). `tests/histograms.rs`: four tests and one property (the layer against `hist`, with the axis named by the scale and a snapshot of the scene; a width, a start and rows that are not counted, with their notes; one value and no value; groups stacked and panels sharing their bins; and, whatever the rows and the bins, counts that sum to the rows, an area of one under `density`, fractions that sum to one and percentages to a hundred). `tests/printing.rs`: the printed plot in ten forms, an export in the three formats, and every message of `histogram` (sixteen). Three verified examples in the help page, which is complete and says what R, ggplot2 and Stata do by default. One conformance case (`plot/histogram`), which brings `zeff selftest` to 429 of 429.

**The sample script.** The specification's sample writes `wages.histogram(lwage, bins: 40, by: female)`, the shorthand on a frame, which step 29 builds. Until then the two stored checks of that script say "`histogram` cannot be called on a Frame" where they said "no function is called `histogram`": the name is now a function, of a plot.

**The specification.** The usage line of catalogue row 472 gains the options (logged in `docs/spec_changes.md`); the row stays `planned` until step 28 is complete.

**Dependencies.** None added.

**Reason.** The checklist's step 28a; section 7.6 of the Language Reference ("Statistical layers"); open decision #99, question 2; catalogue row 472.
